News.title: Drayton Manor theme park forced to close due to flooding - all tickets cancelled
News.content:
Drayton Manor theme park forced to close due to flooding - all tickets cancelled

Drayton Manor Resort in Tamworth, Staffordshire, was forced to close on Thursday 'due to adverse weather and flooding'

View 2 Images Drayton Manor Resort was shut on Thursday (Image: Drayton Manor Resort)

A popular theme park in Staffordshire has been forced to close for the day "due to adverse weather and flooding".

‌



Drayton Manor Resort, located in Tamworth, announced on social media on Thursday morning that it had made the "difficult decision" to close the resort to keep its guests and team safe amid the thunderstorms and heavy rain.

‌



Staffordshire is among parts of England and Wales under a yellow thunderstorm warning, in place from 5am on Thursday until 10pm. The Met Office warning covers parts of the East Midlands, east England, London and south-east England, north-west England, south-west England, the West Midlands, Yorkshire and the Humber, and Wales.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

A statement posted on Drayton Manor Resort's social media accounts on Thursday morning read: "Due to adverse weather and flooding, Drayton Manor Resort will be closed today. We know many of you were looking forward to visiting, and we’re very sorry for the disappointment and inconvenience this causes.

"There’s no need to contact us at this stage. We’ll be in touch with affected guests shortly with information on how to rearrange your visit for another date."

‌



The theme park managers thanked visitors for their patience and understanding.

The Met Office warned that a broad band of thunderstorms and heavy rain would move north across England and Wales, with 20-30mm of rain possible in an hour in some areas and 30-40mm falling fairly widely. It said up to 50mm was possible over a 12-hour period in places.

View 2 Images Two yellow warnings for thunderstorm are in force on Thursday (Image: Met Office)

‌



It added that there was a small chance of more than 50mm falling in three hours and more than 75mm over 12 hours, particularly over east-facing high ground.

Another yellow thunderstorm warning has been issued for parts of east and south-east England, the East Midlands and Yorkshire and the Humber from 5pm on Thursday until 7am on Friday.

The Met Office said heavy, thundery rain is expected to develop across France this afternoon before moving north across, or close to, parts of east and south-east England overnight.

Article continues below

While there is a chance the rain could remain offshore in the North Sea, it is more likely than not to affect at least some areas covered by the fresh warning. Those affected "could see frequent lightning, hail and strong, gusty winds, in addition to heavy rain", the weather service warned.

Some areas could receive up to 50mm of rain, with much of this falling in less than three hours. There is also a small chance that some places could see up to 75mm.

News.title: Nepal-Tibet floods live: King Charles 'heartbroken' with 100s missing including Brit kids
News.content:
A 13-year-old girl and a 14-year-old boy are among 33 British tourists missing in Nepal and Tibet after an avalanche led to major flooding along the Bhotekoshi River

King Charles said he and the Queen are "heartbroken" by the "devastating" flash floods in a Nepal border area, where dozens of British nationals are among the hundreds missing and feared dead.

At least 389 people have died in Nepal and more than 900 are missing, while 558 people are missing in Tibet, where three people have been confirmed dead.

On both sides of the border, hundreds of foreign nationals are among those missing, including 33 British citizens. A 13-year-old girl and a 14-year-old boy are believed to be the youngest UK citizens unaccounted for.

The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said river levels rose by up to nine metres in just 30 minutes at the height of the flash floods on Wednesday.

According to the Red Cross, "entire villages and market areas" have been wiped out by the torrent of water and mud, which has flattened all in its path along the Bhotekoshi River.

News.title: Andy Burnham faces pressure on council tax as two thirds of Brits brand system unfair
News.content:
Andy Burnham faces pressure on council tax as two thirds of Brits brand system unfair

EXCLUSIVE: Reducing or replacing council tax was the second most popular measure (34%) to ease pressure on household - just behind cutting energy bills (49%), according to a poll

View 2 Images A majority of voters think council tax is unfair and worry about paying their bills (Image: Getty Images/EyeEm)

Nearly two thirds (63%) of Brits think council tax is unfair, polling shows, with half (52%) worried about paying their bills next year.

‌



Reducing or replacing council tax was the second most popular measure (34%) to ease pressure on household budgets when voters were asked to rank a range of options - behind cutting energy bills (49%). The idea was more popular than cutting income tax bills by raising the personal allowance (29%).

‌



The poll of more than 2,000 people for Fairer Share found more than twice as many people said council tax was unfair (63%) compared to those who said it was fair (25%).

‌



Andy Burnham has previously argued that land is undertaxed and criticised the unfairness of the current system in England, which bases valuations on property values from 1991. The out-of-date measure can mean people in the North and the Midlands pay higher rates than people in the South where property prices have risen more quickly.

Angela Rayner urged to U-turn on rent controls decision after study shows benefits READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham is facing pressure to look at property taxes after previously branding council tax unfair (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Burnham ruled out immediate changes to council tax and stamp duty after becoming Prime Minister. Asked in July if he could scrap both taxes and replace them with a new alternative property tax, he said: "That won't be happening... It’s just not the case that we are bringing forward plans on that scale at this moment in time.”

‌



But the PM is facing calls to consider a property tax overhaul amid significant pressure on the public finances as Donald Trump's war with Iran threatens to erode the headroom left by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

Fairer Share has proposed replacing council tax and stamp duty with an annual proportional property tax (PPT), based on current property values and levied on owners, rather than tenants. The idea was backed by nearly half of respondents (47%) while one in seven (13%) opposed, and around a quarter (27%) neither supported or opposed it.

Andrew Dixon, founder of Fairer Share, said: “The Prime Minister was right not to rush into a major reform of property taxation without properly considering the consequences. But caution should not become an excuse for putting council tax back in the ‘too difficult’ box for another generation.

‌



“This polling shows that the public knows the current system is unfair, wants government to address it and is open to serious reform. It also provides little evidence of the political backlash that is so often assumed when property taxation is discussed."

He called for an independent review into council tax and stamp duty, to consider the impact of alternatives on households and the housing market - and how a transition could be fairly managed.

Jonathan Brash, Labour MP for Hartlepool and member of Labour MPs for Fairer Council Tax, said: “Council tax is one of the most regressive taxes in Britain. It hits hardest constituencies like mine, where people pay more despite often having less. That takes money out of working people’s pockets, away from our high streets and out of local economies that have been neglected for far too long.

‌



“As this polling shows, if we want to rebuild our coalition and put more money into people’s pockets, breathe life back into our town centres and prove that Westminster can work for ordinary people again, replacing council tax with a fair proportional property tax is the place to start.”

Afzal Khan, Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme, said replacing council tax with a more progressive levy on property would make a huge difference to families on his patch.

“In my constituency over 90% of households would save an average of £500 every year, with only the broadest shoulders expected to pay that bit more," he said. "It’s no wonder people see it as a brilliant idea, and it is exactly what a government focused on the cost of living should consider.”

Article continues below

:: JL Partners conducted a representative online poll of 2,048 adults in Britain between August 1 and 4 ::

News.title: School WhatsApp groups 'essential tool' for parents
News.content:
School WhatsApp groups 'essential tool' for parents

Eight in ten parents said they would be lost without school WhatsApp groups.

Lou Beckett's top tips for managing the back-to-school period

Parents have described school WhatsApp groups as an 'essential tool', according to research. More than eight in 10 (82%) of those who use them believe they would be lost without them.

‌



According to the survey, 65% admit they would forget important school events, if it wasn't for the group. These include non-uniform days, sports days and even school inset days. One in five parents (20%) said it makes the September return to school easier to manage.

‌



The poll of 1,000 parents of six to 11-year-olds, by home appliance brand Beko revealed 74% consider the back-to-school period the most challenging time of the year.

‌



View 3 Images WhatsApp groups help parents remember key events (Image: Getty Images)

Former teacher and mum of two Lou Beckett, who has partnered with Beko to launch the Beko Back to School Helpline, hosted on WhatsApp p, said: "As a parent, I know just how hectic the back-to-school period can be.

"It rarely looks like the picture-perfect planner stuck on the fridge. In reality, it's a missing PE kit or a stained shirt and by 8am the only thing still running smoothly is the washing machine.

‌



"That's why Beko has created a Back to School Helpline on WhatsApp - so parents have somewhere to turn when those last-minute worries feel huge.

"If you're not stressing about uniforms drying in time or how to keep packed lunches fresh for the week ahead, it's much easier to focus on what really matters – helping your kids feel confident and ready to walk through the school gates."

View 3 Images Getting back into a routine after school holidays can be difficult for families (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Re-establishing bedtime and morning routines tops the list of back-to-school challenges for 41% of parents, followed by getting children out of bed and ready in time for the school bell (38%).

Other common pressures include prepping packed lunches (25%), coaxing children into the car and convincing them to pose for the classic back-to-school snapshot (both 10%).

For 34% of parents, their alarm clock is the most useful tool for getting their children ready for school. Meanwhile, one in 10 opted for the washing machine, and 9% even credited the family itself.

‌



But one in five parents leave back-to-school preparations until the last minute, with haircuts, buying school shoes and washing uniforms among the tasks most commonly left to the eleventh hour.

View 3 Images WhatsApp groups can make preparing for going back to school easier (Image: Getty Images)

The research, conducted via OnePoll, also revealed that on average, it takes families two weeks to fully settle back into the routine of term time.

‌



Salah Sun, head of product management at Beko, said: "September has a way of arriving faster than anyone's ready for. One minute it's sandcastles, the next it's a scramble to get school uniforms and PE kits washed.

"When family life is demanding, having appliances you can rely on means one less thing to worry about. We stress-test our appliances for proven durability, so they can keep up with the demands of busy family life – from last-minute uniform washes and keeping lunchbox favourites fresh to the daily after dinner clean-up.

"For parents, that means dependable performance when they need it most, fewer everyday disruptions and greater confidence that their appliance will continue to make life easier for years to come."

‌



From 6pm-9pm on Tuesday 1st September, parents can receive practical advice from Lou and the experts at Beko on the Back to School Helpline for when those last-minute worries begin to feel overwhelming.

LOU BECKETT’S TIPS FOR MAKING THE BACK-TO-SCHOOL TRANSITION LESS CHAOTIC:

Run a stealth routine reboot

A week before term starts, bring bedtime and wake-up alarms forward by 15 minutes each day. Getting children back into the ‘out of bed, teeth-brushed, actual clothes on’ rhythm early will save you from wrestling a reluctant child out of their duvet on day one.

Put the logistics on one shared calendar

Whose turn is it for pick-up? Is football today or tomorrow? This is where entire weeks quietly fall apart. Get every drop-off, pick-up and after-school club onto one shared calendar at the start of term, on the fridge, on your phone, wherever it'll actually get looked at, so nobody's relying on memory alone by week three.

‌



Retire as the morning short-order cook

If you spend school mornings pouring cereal bowls and making toast while trying to get yourself caffeinated and ready, you're doing too much. Put cereal, snacks and breakfast basics into child-friendly containers on reachable shelves so the kids can sort themselves out. Tell them the kitchen is now self-serve, they'll enjoy the independence, and you'll buy a few precious minutes for a hot cup of coffee before the madness starts.

Enforce a ‘soft landing’ for week one

Teachers know kids’ brains will be fried by the time the bell rings during the first week of term. This is not the moment to introduce evening chore charts or strict homework routines. Treat week one like recovery from severe jetlag – feed everyone, let your home appliances handle the domestics, and put the kids to bed nice and early, before you lose your mind!

Ditch uniform perfectionism

Unless your child spends their lunch breaks mud wrestling, they don’t need a new set of immaculate uniforms every day. Teachers just want children to be comfortable, clean and ready to learn.

Article continues below

But when the last-minute realisation hits that a dirty PE kit is languishing at the bottom of the laundry basket, don't panic. A trusty washing machine with a quick-wash setting can handle the rescue mission, so you can still get to bed on time.

News.title: 'I've covered Prince Harry's UK visits and noticed a surprising change in his behaviour'
News.content:
'I've covered Prince Harry's UK visits and noticed a surprising change in his behaviour'

A royal expert has spotted a noticeable change in Prince Harry whenever he returns to the UK, despite the difficult circumstances surrounding some of his recent visits.

View 3 Images Prince Harry (Image: Getty)

Prince Harry has been described as appearing happier whenever he returns to Britain by a royal expert who has covered several of his UK visits.

‌



The Duke of Sussex is back in the UK with Meghan Markle and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, following six years living in the US.

‌



Roya Nikkhah, chief royal correspondent of The Sunday Times, has closely followed Harry's appearances on home soil and believes there is a noticeable difference in his demeanour when he is here.

‌



Discussing the Sussexes' return on The Royals with Roya and Kate podcast, Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent at The Sunday Times, suggested Harry may have grown bored with life in America after almost seven years away.

Roya agreed with her guest, saying: "He was. Yeah. He has looked much happier, as you touched on earlier, every time he comes back."

She reflected on Harry's latest UK visit, which coincided with a turbulent period for the Duke.

‌



Harry had travelled to Chatham House to speak about the Invictus Games when the judgment in his legal action against Associated Newspapers Limited was delivered, with the Duke losing his claims against the publisher.

View 3 Images Prince Harry (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

His visit was also overshadowed by tensions with Buckingham Palace over whether he would stay at a royal residence.

‌



But, according to Roya, Harry appeared to regain his spirits as the week went on.

"But then, at the end of the week, he sort of pulled it back up and was on great form, doing his stuff," she said.

The royal correspondent pointed to his appearances in Birmingham, where he carried out Invictus-related engagements before taking part in an event for Scotty's Little Soldiers.

‌



Harry was also photographed doing yoga with children, something Roya said showed him "basically in his element".

His visit ended with the reunion he had been hoping for, when he met King Charles and spent time with his children.

Reflecting on Harry's behaviour during his trips back to Britain, Roya concluded: "So, however difficult things get for him, when he is back on home soil these days, he just does look a lot happier."

‌



The comments come as Harry and Meghan have returned to the UK with Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, for what is expected to be an extended stay.

View 3 Images Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex (Image: Ronald Martinez, Getty Images)

The family arrived at Birmingham Airport on Wednesday after flying from California on a private jet. A spokesperson declined to discuss the journey, citing privacy and security.

‌



"This is not something we would comment on," they said.

Their chickens have reportedly remained at their Montecito home, while dogs Mia and Pula travelled with the family.

Archie and Lilibet have also been enrolled at British schools ahead of September, with the Cotswolds reportedly among the locations being considered for the family's new base.

Article continues below

Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020 before relocating to the US, where they have since spoken publicly about their experiences with the Royal Family.

They remain non-working royals and are not expected to resume official duties despite their return to Britain.

News.title: HMRC sending letters to one million people who missed out on free pension top-up
News.content:
HMRC sending letters to one million people who missed out on free pension top-up

A consultation in 2021 estimated that the average payment would be around £53, though the exact figure will depend on how much was paid into the pension by each individual

View 2 Images HMRC is writing to around one million people who may have missed out a Government top-up to their pension. (Image: GETTY)

HMRC is writing to around one million people who may have missed out a Government top-up to their pension.

‌



Pension tax relief is where the tax you would normally pay on your income, is added to your pension pot instead. There are normally two different ways this is applied. If you pay into a pension from your take-home pay, so after income tax has been applied, then your pension provider will claim the tax relief from HMRC and add it to your pot.

‌



If you are a basic rate taxpayer, it means for every £80 you pay into your pension, the Government adds £20 in tax relief, giving you a total saving into your pension of £100.

‌



But if your pension contribution is deducted from your gross pay, so before income tax has been taken off, you effectively get the tax relief straight away as less of your income is subject to tax.

Under pension auto-enrolment rules, people can be enrolled into their workplace pension scheme despite being under the threshold to pay income tax. You can be auto-enrolled into a pension scheme if you earn more than £10,000 a year, while the threshold for when you start to pay income tax is £12,570 a year.

View 2 Images Nearly a million eligible pensioners are believed to be missing out on Pension Credit (Image: GETTY)

‌



People who are non-taxpayers still qualify for pension tax relief. However, if the pension contribution is deducted from gross pay, the individual misses out on tax relief because they are not a taxpayer – because reducing their taxable income has no effect on their tax bill.

HMRC will initially write to people and encourage them to claim any missed top-ups for contributions made in 2024 and 2025. Once they have registered, a more automated system will be put in place for later years.

A consultation in 2021 estimated that the average payment would be around £53, though the exact figure will depend on how much was paid into the pension by each individual.

‌



However, former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb has warned that there is a risk people may not realise the letters from HMRC are genuine.

Sir Steve, partner at pension consultants LCP said: “It is clearly unfair that around one million low earners have missed out on pension tax relief, simply because of the way in which their workplace pension is administered.

‌



“But the process of getting these payments to the right people is going to be incredibly painful and there is a real risk of huge non take-up. Most people will not have a clue about this issue and may be suspicious of a letter out of the blue from HMRC offering them free money.

“Some may suspect it is a scam. It is vital that communications are effective to make sure that people get the money to which they are entitled.”

An HMRC spokesperson said: “Customers don’t need to apply or contact us – we’ll send them information about how to receive their payment via post or their online tax account. We know some people may be cautious about unexpected contact, which is why we provide clear information about what to expect and how to verify the contact is genuine.

“Customers can check a letter is genuine on GOV.UK and should only respond via official HMRC channels. We’ll never ask for passwords, PINs or money to be transferred to claim a payment.”

News.title: HMRC could raid your bank account for tax debt under new powers with deadline this week
News.content:
HMRC could raid your bank account for tax debt under new powers with deadline this week

Under current rules, the tax office can apply to take money directly out of the bank accounts of people who owe more than £1,000 - but it could be set to lower this threshold

View 2 Images HMRC wants to tackle smaller tax debts (Image: coldsnowstorm via Getty Images)

HMRC could soon be granted greater powers to take debt repayments directly from bank accounts.

‌



HMRC wants to introduce new ways for it to recoup smaller tax debts. Under current rules, the tax office can apply to take money directly out of the bank accounts of people who owe more than £1,000.

‌



The person must be left with at least £5,000 across their accounts once the debt has been settled. But new proposals would give HMRC powers to reclaim tax debt on smaller amounts owed through direct monthly payments.

‌



The measures could apply to debts of up to £5,000 for individuals and £10,000 for businesses, and would only be used as a last resort, if the individual has repeatedly ignored communications from HMRC.

Thousands of people claiming benefits including Universal Credit will get paid early this week READ MORE :

HMRC sending out inspectors to value homes - and you may be hit with tax bill READ MORE :

View 2 Images HMRC wants to expand its powers to reclaim tax debt directly from bank accounts (Image: Getty)

It is estimated that up to 4.8 million individuals and businesses owe around £4billion in low debts and could potentially fall within the scope of these new rules. However, HMRC suggests it expects less than 250,000 companies and individuals would be eligible per year.

‌



Ahead of the consultation closing this Friday, August 28, tax advisory firm BDO has called for more details to be published about the taxpayers who could potentially be affected.

Dawn Register, a tax dispute resolution partner at BDO, said: "These proposals would give HMRC the ability to recover lower value tax debts by taking money directly from individuals' and businesses' bank accounts. For millions of taxpayers, that represents a significant new intervention by the tax authority and it is essential that the safeguards are robust.

“While we support HMRC taking action against those who deliberately refuse to pay tax or engage with the tax authority, the proposals raise important questions around affordability, taxpayer rights and whether HMRC has sufficient resources to operate the system fairly."

‌

As part of its current safeguards, HMRC must make a face-to-face visits to assess for vulnerabilities, and discuss other payment options, before they can apply to recover tax debts from bank accounts.

A formal 30-day notice must also be issued before any money is taken so people have time to appeal or set up a payment plan.

Article continues below

An HMRC spokesperson said: “The portrayal of these figures is highly misleading. In 95% of debt cases, the support we provide means customers pay the tax they owe without the need for further action.

"Only a small minority of taxpayers who can afford to pay but repeatedly refuse to do so could be affected by these new measures, which will ensure fairness for all taxpayers and be subject to robust safeguards.”

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle issue statement on landmark Meta trial after touching down in the UK
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle issue statement on landmark Meta trial after touching down in the UK

Just hours after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed in Birmingham to start the next chapter of their lives in Britain, they issued a joint statement after it was announced Meta will pay billion in a child safety case

View 5 Images Harry and Meghan have long been passionate and outspoken about their wishes for more regulation around social media use for children (Image: PA)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have issued a statement just hours after they touched down in the UK to start the next chapter of their lives in Britain.

‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, along with their children Archie, seven, and five-year-old Lilibet, arrived at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday, just one week after their move back to Harry’s home country was announced.

‌



Now, Harry and Meghan have issued a joint statement following news that the social media company Meta will pay billions in a child-endangerment settlement. The company agreed to pay up to $18 billion (£13.3 billion) to settle claims that its platforms pose a danger to children.

‌



View 5 Images Harry and Meghan have issued a statement on the Meta lawsuit (Image: Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

The Duke and Duchess have long been outspoken on the issue of child safety online, and shared a lengthy statement to their website, in which they expressed their disappointment that Meta will avoid a 'accountability' with trial by agreeing on a settlement sum.

The statement, which is their first public notice since landing in the UK, read: "The historic trial against Meta over claims that its products endanger children has resulted in a settlement in which they will pay up to $17.1billion (£12.5bn). The settlement requires Meta to pay financial penalties for violating federal child privacy and states’ consumer protection laws.

‌



"By choosing to settle, the company paid to avoid yet another trial outcome that would force it into accountability. Because of the data-extraction business model Meta has used on our children and all users for years, it has more than the means to pay this settlement. Reports estimate Meta will make the equivalent of the $17bn pay out back in profit in the next 30 days."

View 5 Images The Sussexes arrived in the UK on Wednesday (Image: JOEL CARRETT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Harry and Meghan went on to outline some of the changes Meta agreed to as part of the settlement, such as restricting usage for children between the hours of 12am and 6am "quickly sparks change from other tech leaders across the industry".

‌



Other changes include not allowing notifications during school hours, the removal of beauty filters deemed harmful to mental health, and the introduction of an optional chronological feed to replace algorithm-driven content recommendations.

The Duke and Duchess continued in their statement: "This result clearly signals that Meta and social media companies understand they are up against an immovable force of parents, survivors, and advocates who will not back down until we see change in how our young people interact with online spaces. It is a positive step for everyone advocating for safer online spaces and at the same time – far from the end of the journey to a better online world."

View 5 Images Meghan delivered a speech on online safety in Geneva in May (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Harry and Meghan are fierce campaigners for tougher regulations when it comes to children using social media. In June, they weighed in on the UK government’s decision to ban certain social media for children under the age of 16, as they said the decision is “a welcome step forward” but added more needed to be done to keep children away from harmful material.

The Sussex’s welcomed the incoming social media ban, but warned “while measures such as these help reduce harm, they do not fix the problem at its source”.

In May, Meghan urged global health leaders to act to keep children safe online at the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial in Geneva, Switzerland. Speaking at the memorial for people who have died after suffering digital harm, the duchess described children’s online safety as a “public health issue”.

‌



View 5 Images The Duke and Duchess spoke about their own children at a mental health gala in New York last year (Image: John Angelillo/UPI/Shutterstock)

The couple also spoke about their own children during a campaign for a crackdown on social media regulations for children, addressing a crowd in New York for the World Mental Health Day Festival in October as Meghan said she and her husband often discussed how they would protect their own children from online dangers as they grow older.

Article continues below

On Wednesday afternoon, Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet arrived in the UK on a private jet. They were not met by any taxpayer-funded close police protection or had a police convoy - something they previously had when working royals - and were supported by their own private security team.

They are to settle themselves in the UK for an “extended period”, with the children enrolled in British schools ready to start in September.

News.title: Uefa preparing criminal legal action against Infantino
News.content:
Uefa also claims that the valuation of the stakes to be sold were not independently verified and would have been offered too cheaply, calling the proposed sale "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit".

The application adds: "Under the terms Infantino announced, those investors stood to acquire a permanent financial interest in Fifa's commercial arm for $4.2bn, implying an absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn, a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer."

In the application, Uefa is applying to a court in Florida to attempt to access files held by two Fifa businesses - Fifa Americas and FWC2026 - to be used to pursue the criminal charges in Switzerland at a later stage.

The two businesses are based in Florida.

Uefa claims that its 55 member nations would have potentially been harmed by the sell-off plan, and that it may pursue criminal proceedings against other Fifa officials as well as Infantino.

"Uefa and other interested parties are preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other Fifa officials and advisors for criminal mismanagement," the application states.

"The secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing inflicted direct and concrete injury on Fifa's reputation, governance authority, and commercial relationships to the detriment of Fifa as well as its 211 members, including Uefa's 55 member associations."

Uefa insists that the plan was concocted without the knowledge of them or other key stakeholders in football, and that it had been long in development.

The applications says: "On July 28, 2026, without consulting the Fifa Council, Uefa, or any of the other confederations, or any of the 211 Fifa member associations, Infantino, purportedly acting on behalf of Fifa, publicly announced a plan to place the commercial rights to the men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup into a new subsidiary: Fifa Forward Enterprise.

"That announcement by Infantino was the public unveiling of a plan that he and a small circle of co-conspirators had conceived and reportedly been developing in secret for more than a year."

Uefa states in the document that there has been "an enduring history of corruption among Fifa officials" and claims that world football's governing body only relents on its plans when pressure comes from outside the sport.

"Fifa's extraordinary power over world football has operated largely without meaningful internal constraint, with accountability coming principally through external forces, including political pressure, public scrutiny, and intervention through international criminal law enforcement," the application adds.

Fifa's headquarters are in the Swiss city of Zurich, and Uefa says that its plan to eventually pursue criminal charges against Infantino is backed up by Swiss law.

"Swiss counsel has confirmed [...] that the proceeding is within reasonable contemplation for purposes of Swiss law and that Uefa has standing, as a complainant, to file a criminal complaint for criminal mismanagement against Infantino and potentially other Fifa officials as may be warranted."

BBC Sport has been told that a separate filing has been lodged to a court in New York, where Uefa are seeking documentation from Thrive Capital, the business proposed to take up an interest in FFE, and its founder Josh Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump's son-in-law.

The American investment bank JP Morgan is also named in the application.

A third application has also been made in Colorado, relating to former Formula 1 chief Greg Maffei, who is referred to in the court filings as "the key commercial adviser" on the proposed FFE transaction, and his Bann Ventures firm.

BBC Sport has also approached Uefa for comment.

News.title: Dame Jenni Murray died days after car crash, inquest hears
News.content:
BBC broadcaster Dame Jenni Murray died days after being involved in a car crash in which she was dazzled by headlights, an inquest was told.

Dame Jenni, who was the longest-serving presenter of BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour, died aged 75 on 12 March, eight days after a collision in north London.

North London area coroner Tony Murphy ruled her cause of death was bronchopneumonia caused by fractures to her rib and sternum fractures sustained in the crash.

A statement from Dr Clare Morkane, a consultant at the Royal Free Hospital where Dame Jenni died after being admitted on 4 March, stated: "Jennifer had been driving when she became dazzled by vehicle lights and collided with two stationary vehicles."

Dr Morkane added: "Following the collision, Jennifer was unable to recall events, exited the vehicle independently and she was conveyed to hospital."

The crash took place near Hampstead Heath, at around 19:45 GMT, the inquest heard.

It resulted in "multiple rib fractures", a fracture to the upper sternum and a collapsed lung.

The broadcaster was initially placed on non-invasive ventilation before being moved to intensive care, but she developed bronchopneumonia.

The Metropolitan Police investigated the crash but closed its investigation with no further action.

News.title: UK salmonella cases nearing 500 as egg investigations continue
News.content:
Close to 500 people have become ill with salmonella linked to imported eggs, say UK authorities, who say they have identified two new clusters of the infection.

The UK Health Security Agency, external reported 207 cases last week. That has been increased to 259, with the two new clusters bringing the total to 474. There have been two deaths recorded.

Some of the cases date back a year, but all involve bacteria that are almost genetically identical, suggesting a common food source.

Investigations are ongoing, but based on what is known so far, experts say people have fallen sick after eating out rather than cooking eggs at home.

Cases of salmonella are being seen in other European countries, external too - Austria (2), Belgium (15), Denmark (1), France (4), Germany (6), the Netherlands (106).

Investigations in the Netherlands suggests a link with chicken meat, rather than eggs.

Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.

More than a third of those ill in the UK - some babies and others as old as 92 - have needed hospital care.

Most people get better without treatment, however.

While salmonella cases can happen any time, the UK outbreak involves a few specific, near-identical genetic clusters called t5.9411, t0.24068 and t5.9765.

There have been:

259 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.9411

38 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.9765

177 confirmed cases linked to the t0.24068

Most have been recorded in recent weeks and months, but the investigations go back to cases as far as August 2025.

The majority have been in England, with many in London and Yorkshire and Humber.

There have been a small number of cases in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.

News.title: Top Gear to return to TV four years after Flintoff crash, BBC confirms
News.content:
Top Gear is to return to TV, the BBC has confirmed, four years after the show was "rested" when co-host Andrew Flintoff was injured in a crash during filming.

The long-running motoring programme has been off air since 2022, when the former cricketer suffered serious facial and rib injuries when his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test track.

He was one of three presenters at the time along with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.

The hosting line-up for the comeback has not yet been announced, although the Sun newspaper last week reported that comedian Jimmy Carr was in talks to join.

News.title: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies
News.content:
Actor Peter Cullen, who voiced popular characters including Optimus Prime in Transformers and Eeyore in Disney's Winnie the Pooh franchise, has died at the age of 85.

The Canadian actor began his most famous role - as the heroic deep-voiced Optimus Prime - for the Transformers TV series in 1984, then returned for seven Hollywood films from 2007 to 2023 and other spin-offs.

He voiced depressive donkey Eeyore in TV animation The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games.

His other memorable voice parts included KARR, the evil counterpart to KITT in TV show Knight Rider; the clicking vocalisations of The Predator in Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1987 film; and the roars of King Kong in 1976.

News.title: Blake Lively awarded $400,000 of $8m she claimed for legal fees in Baldoni battle
News.content:
Actress Blake Lively has been awarded $400,000 (Â£340,000) of the $8m (Â£6.9m) she tried to claim from her former co-star Justin Baldoni to cover her legal fees and costs to fight a defamation case he brought.

Lively initially sued Baldoni, her co-star and director of the 2024 film It Ends With Us for sexual harassment and retaliation, before he countersued for defamation.

A judge dismissed his defamation complaint in 2025, and she argued she was entitled to $7.5m (Â£6.4m) to cover her lawyers' fees and $540,000 (Â£460,000) for other costs.

But the judge said she should receive considerably less - a total of $407,451 - because she requested money for more people and time than were necessary to defend the defamation claim.

She should not have claimed money for other "intertwined" costs to do with the wider legal battle, and took a "blunderbuss approach" to calculating how many hours of lawyers' time she could claim for, the judge said.

News.title: King 'heartbroken' by floods as search for missing, including 33 from UK, continues
News.content:
The King says he and Queen Camilla are "heartbroken" by the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border, as 33 people from the UK are missing including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.

The Prince and Princess of Wales also expressed their shock, saying they were "thinking of everyone caught up in this terrible disaster".

The death toll from the floods has risen to at least 359, with more than 1,300 people missing, 644 of whom are tourists according to Nepali authorities.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered Â£5m to help the Nepalese government following the floods, adding it was a "very distressing and devastating situation".

King Charles said that he and the Queen were sending their "most profound sympathy to all those who have so tragically lost their loved ones".

"Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world," the King's statement continued.

"We feel deeply for the many families awaiting anxiously the news of friends and relations.

"Our hearts go out also to the families of all the police and armed forces personnel who lost their lives while carrying out their courageous duty in the service of others."

News.title: Two teenagers, 13 and 14, among 33 UK nationals missing in Nepal floods
News.content:
It also reported four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The company's manager Kumar Adhikari said he was in contact with the guides until 08:40 when they were expected to be at Tibet's immigration office, but their phones were disconnected.

"We were hoping that inside it was safe," he told PA, "but later the video came from China's government which [showed] even Tibet's side was hit by the flood."

Adhikari said he was "slowly responding to" the families of the Britons but has been unable to give them any updates, adding he has been in contact with the British consulate and forwarded them copies of the clients' passports.

"I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next...We are in pain at the moment, deep pain."

Other tour companies have also been impacted by the flash floods, with British citizens among other tours being affected.

The Trekkers' Society, which organises tours in Nepal, Tibet, and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash are missing after they crossed the Nepal-Tibet border.

It said four males, aged between 14 and 50, and five females aged 40 - 53 remained unaccounted for.

The society's general manager said the group were at Chinese immigration at the border when the flood happened, but it has no contact with the tour guide since.

Himalayan Glacier US told the BBC they have lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff who where making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which is considered the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.

It said the group included two British citizens.

Kailash Journeys also reported a group of 27 guests and staff missing, with a spokesperson saying they were last in contact with them early Wednesday morning local time.

A list of names provided to the BBC included two men who are British citizens.

Fishtail Tours, a Nepali travel agency offering several climbing expeditions and tours of Nepal and Bhutan, said one British person was missing.

News.title: Number of asylum seekers in hotels halves in a year
News.content:
There was also a fall in the number of family members coming to the UK to join someone already legally in the country, while asylum claims were also down by a fifth.

Some 38,000 illegal arrivals were detected in the year to June - 33,000 of them on small boats across the sea from France.

More up to date figures show the trend in small boat arrivals has continued to be lower than last year. Correspondingly, claims for asylum have also fallen.

Some 86,000 people sought asylum - down a fifth on the previous year. About half of those applications for help came from people who were already legally in the UK, rather than having arrived on a small boat.

The rise in the use of hotels coincided with an increase in arrivals across the English Channel from 2019 and a slowing down of Home Office decisions as to how many of these claimants had a genuine right to stay in the UK or should be told to leave.

One of the first decisions of the new Starmer government in July 2024 was to order officials to work faster in deciding these claims, with a target of ending the use of hotels within five years.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "A little over two years into office and the asylum backlog is down, the number of asylum seekers in hotels is falling, illegal working arrests are at record levels, and deportations and returns are up markedly.

"Small boats numbers are also now falling, but we are not complacent and there is more we must do."

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Labour was "moving illegal immigrants out of hotels and into flats in your building."

He said a Conservative government would deport every illegal immigrant and leave the European Court of Human Rights.

"The surest way to empty the accommodation is to make plain that nobody who crosses the Channel gets to stay," he added.

In response to the new figures, Reform UK said Britain was at "breaking point".

Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesman, said "Under Reform, illegal boats in the Channel will be stopped by our Navy, and all those here illegally will be detained and deported."

The number of people in houses around the country paid for by the Home Office has gone up from 65,000 at the end of 2024 to 69,000 in June this year - arrangements that are part of a decade-long standing contract with private providers.

The number of asylum claimants waiting for an initial ruling on their case - meaning they are told whether they have a genuine case for protection or should leave the UK - was 40,000. That is down from the peak of 175,000 in June 2023.

Meanwhile some 40,000 found not to have a reason to be in the UK - either foreign offenders, visa overstayers or failed asylum applicants - were removed from the country in the year to June 2026, an 8% increase on the year before.

Officials say about a third were failed asylum seekers - the highest number for 16 years and double the rate of removals that occurred in 2021.

News.title: One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review
News.content:
Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - according to data published ahead of a major report about a "lost generation".

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were Neet between April and June. That is about one in eight people in that age group.

The final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC ministers would "take those [recommendations] forward".

News.title: Residents need to feel safe after deadly crash and fire near Middlesbrough, council leader says
News.content:
People living in a town where a car crash and a house fire have left nine people dead deserve to "feel safe in their own homes", the local council leader has said.

Alec Brown's comments came in response to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, in the crash at South Bank near Middlesbrough on Saturday, followed by a house fire in Grangetown on Wednesday that claimed the lives of a woman aged 34 and a seven-year-old girl.

Brown told Radio 4's Today programme he would be meeting with councillors, police and social housing providers on Friday.

Meanwhile Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "all of the support will be provided to get to the heart of what has happened".

Brown, the Labour leader of Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council, said he understood people from the area might feel "left behind".

"I'm from an estate, from the same ilk," he said.

"You live around people that may be suffering poverty or other social issues, it can be that uniform sort of consciousness that 'we're left behind'.

"But I can assure the people of Grangetown and South Bank they're as important to me as people from any other estate in the borough."

News.title: Teacher guilty of indecent assaults against two pupils
News.content:
A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.

Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ's College in Finchley, north London, assaulted the boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.

On Thursday, a jury at Harrow Crown Court found the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after deliberating for six hours and 29 minutes.

One complainant told the court he had sex with the teacher "about 20 or 30 times" over several months. He said he visited her at home, considered her his girlfriend and had fallen in love with her.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court she had "drummed it" into him that he must not tell anyone about them and to keep it a secret.

A second complainant told jurors he had kissed Bowen in a cafÃ© after being "goaded" into it by other boys.

A former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that she acted like she was in "a Sabrina Carpenter video" while in the classroom and "dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers".

"The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual," said Oliver, who did not know the complainants.

He recalled incidents where Bowen flashed her underwear to a class while sitting on a table and went through and discussed a "sex manual" a student had brought in, which Oliver believed to be the Kama Sutra, with the class.

Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered receiving a complaint from the first alleged victim's mother after she was worried that her son was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.

During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were a "total fabrication" and that she had a medical condition which had not been diagnosed in the late 1980s and made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was granted bail.

She will be sentenced on 20 November.

News.title: PM says he is 'open' to devolving policing in Wales
News.content:
Calls for the devolution of policing and criminal justice had been shared by Plaid Cymru and the Senedd's Welsh Labour politicians, but not the previous UK Labour government led by Sir Keir Starmer.

In January, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said plans to overhaul policing services would not see the Welsh government given new powers.

Burnham, who succeeded Sir Keir in July, made the comments at the Port Talbot steelworks, on his first official visit to Wales since he entered No 10.

Labour had been unseated from the Welsh government for the first time in its history by Plaid Cymru in the Senedd election in May.

Burnham met Welsh government Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams in Port Talbot on Thursday, with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth currently on leave.

Ap Iorwerth made negotiations with Westminster for more powers a key part of his election campaign.

Burnham said he had promised the Welsh government "to look at any asks for further devolution and policing has been specifically mentioned within that".

"That's an issue I'm certainly prepared to look at, and I hear what you're saying," he said.

"As a former mayor that had those responsibilities, I understand how much you can do when you can really make policing right for the places and the people where you are.

"So I hear that call, I'm open to the discussion with the Welsh government

"As part of the wider policing reform that's going on, it seems a good time to have a look at those issues.

"So I can't promise today, but what I can say is I'm open to the conversation."

The Press Association reported that Wales' appeals to get control over the Crown Estate - revenue raised from land owned by the monarch - would be given a "fair hearing" by Burnham at the October summit.

"Maybe there's an argument for deeper devolution, so more power into the cities and the regions of Wales, to north Wales working more with the North West, or mid Wales more with the West Midlands, of the kind of devolution that is developing now quite quickly across England," Burnham said.

In a book two years ago Burnham said it had been time to "tear up" the Barnett Formula funding arrangements.

BBC Wales reported in June that Burnham had no intention of reforming the system that allocated cash to Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland based largely on their share of population.

Critics have argued that it did not fully take Wales' needs into account.

In Port Talbot, Burnham indicated that reform of Barnett was still not on the table.

He said: "I have a very clear view about creating a Britain that's fair, that treats all people and all places equally.

"I'm well aware of the concerns about the Barnett formula here in Wales.

"I have to be honest and say - there's only so many things I can do in the time that I've got.

"At the moment I can't promise there will be moves to review that."

Burnham's comments on policing prompted concern from one Labour MP, who told BBC Wales: "It will be a travesty and not in Wales's interest."

They said it would not be "welcomed by a majority" of Welsh Labour parliamentarians in Westminster.

Another Labour MP said it was "good" that the prime minister was open to the devolution of policing, and there was "no harm" in discussing it.

But they added: "My feeling is they shouldn't devolve anything until we've got a grip of the NHS and education and Plaid have earned their stripes."

Welsh Deputy First Minister, Sioned Williams, said: "I was pleased to have a constructive meeting with the prime minister today and discuss areas of shared interest between our two governments.

"We have been clear that the case for devolving policing is open and shut, so the prime minister's willingness to engage on the issue is a welcome change in tone."

Reform Wales Leader Dan Thomas objected to the devolution of policing, adding: "Plaid's record on devolution, in cahoots with Labour over the past 27 years is one of failure and chaos.

"Wales has a failing health service, falling education standards and a struggling economy. Can you imagine what Plaid will do to policing here in Wales?"

Additional reporting by Bethan James.

News.title: Burnham says united Ireland poll is 'off the table' during first NI visit
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a referendum on Irish unification, describing a border poll as "off the table".

The Labour leader said votes on Brexit and Scottish independence showed the "risks that come from those situations take a long time to heal".

Speaking during his first official visit to Northern Ireland, he said the focus should instead be on public services and tackling cost-of-living pressures.

"We need to fix the things right in front of us in the here and now," he told BBC News NI.

Burnham is meeting Stormont's first and deputy first ministers and the leaders of the Northern Ireland Assembly's main parties.

His visit comes amid calls from the power-sharing executive for increased funding from the government to ease budget pressures.

The four-party coalition has yet to set a budget nearly five months into the financial year.

Stormont departments are facing a shortfall of up to Â£1.6bn, external, according to a spending watchdog.

With no agreed plan, public services have been operating under contingency arrangements.

News.title: Bobby Vylan faces no further action over IDF chant
News.content:
Punk rapper Bobby Vylan will face no further action from the Met Police for chanting "death, death to the IDF (Israel Defense Forces)" at an Al Quds Day demonstration in central London.

The force said it had investigated chants made by the performer on 15 March at a static rally held on the Albert Embankment.

A Met Police spokesperson said they looked into the language used, adding they "recognised the concerns caused, particularly among London's Jewish communities".

The artist, whose real name is Pascal Robinson-Foster, performs as one half of the duo Bob Vylan.

News.title: What triggered Nepal flash floods? Glacier collapse so powerful it registered as an earthquake
News.content:

The Himalayan flash floods that have killed at least 380 people and left some 1,500 missing across Nepal and Tibet were not triggered by an earthquake, contrary to initial reports, but by a glacier collapse so violent it produced its own seismic signal, the United States Geological Survey said.

The agency initially recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake along the Nepal-China border, north of Kathmandu, at about 8.37am local time on Wednesday, before revising its assessment in a statement issued that evening.

It said the seismic signal had come from “a glacial collapse and debris flow” rather than a tectonic quake, and that the collapse alone had caused the catastrophic flooding downstream. Once reclassified, the event registered at magnitude 5.2, a measure of the force of the ice and rock striking the valley floor rather than of any movement underground.

open image in gallery Army personnel rescue flood-affected residents using a helicopter following flash floods, as they arrive at an army camp in Battar Bazar town in Nepal’s Nuwakot district ( AFP/Getty )

An initial study of satellite imagery from Planet Labs showed a large section of the lower end of a glacier breaking away at an altitude of about 5,200m (17,000ft) and falling roughly 1,200m (3,900ft) onto the valley floor, gathering rock and debris as it went.

The resulting avalanche struck the Lhende River in Tibet, about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing with Nepal, temporarily damming the water before the barrier gave way and released a powerful flood downstream.

The surge fed into the Bhote Koshi River and crossed into Nepal at around 9am local time, then continued into the Trishuli River, where water levels rose by as much as nine metres in just half an hour.

open image in gallery Houses deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality, along the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on 27 August 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Officials were caught off guard because there had been no rain, according to local news reports, and some residents ignored early warnings from neighbours precisely because the danger did not resemble the monsoon flooding they were used to.

Nepal’s Rasuwa district, immediately south of the border, bore the worst of the damage, with the flood also reaching Nuwakot and Dhading further downstream. At least 19 bridges and around 40km (25 miles) of roads have been destroyed, and damaged hydropower infrastructure has left some areas without electricity.

open image in gallery Family members gather in a hospital to check the list of injured people following deadly floods, in Kathmandu, Nepal, 27 August 2026 ( Reuters )

Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist and polar engineer at the University of the Sunshine Coast, said the disaster had the hallmarks of a glacial lake outburst flood, in which meltwater builds up behind a natural dam of rock and ice before breaking through.

“As glaciers melt and recede, ice turns to water, the water is stored behind natural moraine dams, but when those dams breach, tremendous amounts of water can be released down a valley, taking out everything in its path,” he said.

Ruth Gamble, an environmental historian and director of La Trobe Asia at La Trobe University, said the flood behaved “like an inland tsunami”, travelling nearly 170km (105 miles) down the Bhote Koshi valley into central Nepal, along a route also used by tourists travelling between Kathmandu and Lhasa.

Why are experts worried a second flood is coming?

Nepal and China have both warned of fresh risks of flooding in the Himalayas as two lakes that have developed on either side of their border threaten to burst.

Experts are assessing whether debris from the flood temporarily blocked Nepal's Trishuli River at a narrow section, forming a landslide dam, the Nepal-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said.

Such a blockage can create a secondary hazard if impounded water is suddenly released.

“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border, authorities warn a second flood is imminent,” Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks, at ICIMOD, said.

He added that evacuation orders were in place for Jilong Port along the Nepal-Tibet border based on the risk of a second wave of flooding.

China warned that 3 million cubic meters of water — the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — are expected to flow into an already dammed lake on ⁠its side of the border over the next three days, creating a high risk of a breach, with peak flow expected around September 1.

Rainfall forecast over the coming week will exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the Chinese water resources ministry.

"The volume of water is continuing to increase, and so is the risk," Zhu Jinfeng, a researcher at the ‌water resources ministry's hydrology department, told state broadcaster CCTV.

open image in gallery A resident sits near a collapsed house lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district ( AFP/Getty )

Scientists cautioned it was too early to say how much climate change contributed to the collapse itself. Glaciers across the wider Hindu Kush Himalaya region, which spans Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Bangladesh, lost ice 65 per cent faster between 2011 and 2020 than in the previous decade, and Nepal’s own glaciers have lost close to a third of their ice volume over roughly three decades.

Satellite observations showed unusually warm conditions and reduced snow cover around the glacier before it collapsed, exposing more bare ice, though researchers have not yet established a direct link to this week’s disaster.

Nader Naderpajouh, head of the school of project management at the University of Sydney, said the disaster could prompt the introduction of early-warning systems similar to those developed after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, since a build-up of water behind a glacial dam can sometimes be detected before it bursts.

“Such communications and preparations can save lives and reduce the impact at scale,” he said.

News.title: Anti-migrant activist charged after ‘breaking into Port of Dover to shout at boat arrivals’
News.content:

A man is facing charges of trespass and harassment after allegedly breaking into the Port of Dover to film and shout at boats arriving on the British coast.

Daniel Thomas, who describes himself as an anti-migrant activist, is facing six charges brought by the private police force for the Port of Dover over activities in March and April this year.

At Margate magistrates court on Thursday, Mr Thomas, who is also known as Danny Tommo, pleaded guilty to going into a restricted harbour area at Western Jet Foil, a short-term holding facility for small boat migrants, without lawful authority or reasonable excuse on 31 March.

Mr Thomas, 37, pleaded not guilty to the other five charges, which included using threatening or abusive words or behaviour to cause distress on 1 April, and trespassing on Dover Western Docks and the Dunkirk Jetty “to film and shout at vessels arriving” on 6 April, as well as using racially-abusive words or behaviour to cause harassment or distress.

open image in gallery Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, appeared in Margate magistrates court on Thursday ( PA )

The Port of Dover has a non-Home Office police force funded by the port authority not the government. Officers in the force have the same powers as other constables in forces throughout the UK.

The court heard that Mr Thomas is currently living in a caravan.

Speaking ahead of his court appearance on Thursday, Mr Thomas said: “The reason I am hear is because of my activism and my exposés in Dover. I did what I did to bring you, the public, some of the truth of what is happening on the south coast.”

News.title: Chelsea v Luton LIVE: Xabi Alonso considers Carabao Cup changes as Leeds await winners in third round
News.content:
Why Chelsea Are SERIOUS Title Contenders

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso takes charge of his first competitive game at Stamford Bridge as Luton Town arrive for a Carabao Cup second-round tie, with Leeds United awaiting the winners in the third round.

The Blues, with such squad depth available to Alonso, are set to ring the changes but it will be curious to see if Enzo Fernandez, still subject to transfer interest from Manchester City, features in the squad - and more curious still to see how home fans greet his presence.

Alonso watched Chelsea’s attack dazzle in a thrilling 3-2 win at Fulham on Monday for his first Premier League win, with Cole Palmer starring. League One side Luton won 3-0 away to Gillingham in the opening round to set up a glamour tie and have claimed four points from their opening two games.

News.title: Champions League draw LIVE: Arsenal, Man Utd, Liverpool, Aston Villa and Man City all learn opponents
News.content:
Copa Independent | Transfer window special: £100m dominoes, Villa’s woes and the incoming deadline day frenzy

Arsenal host Real Madrid, Aston Villa play holders Paris Saint-Germain, while Manchester United will mark their Champions League return against Bayern Munich as the league phase draw was revealed.

Premier League champions Arsenal, runners-up to PSG last season, will also visit Bayern Munich, host Borussia Dortmund and travel to Napoli in their campaign. The Gunners also play Real Betis, Lille, Azerbaijani debutants Sabah and Slavia Prague.

Michael Carrick’s United, in their first Champions League campaign in three years, have Bayern Munich at home and Atletico Madrid away among their eight league phase fixtures. There are also ties against Roma, Sporting, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Sabah and Como.

Liverpool will once again go to Inter Milan and host Atletico Madrid, two repeat fixtures from last season, as well as games against Porto, Villarreal and a tough trip to Turkey to play Fenerbahce. Andoni Iraola’s men also play Club Brugge, Lens and Austrian champions LASK.

Manchester City will play both holders PSG and Barcelona in a tough first campaign for Enzo Maresca and also face a reunion with Kevin De Bruyne as they drew Napoli at home. Sporting, Porto, Leipzig, AEK Athens and Lens complete their fixture schedule.

Europa League winners Aston Villa will go to Barcelona and the Camp Nou, as well as hosting holders PSG in a rematch of their epic quarter-final clash from two years ago. Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is in the hands of a jury after a month of searing testimony about the deaths of her three children in 2023 and the psychiatric problems she experienced before she killed them. Closing arguments concluded Thursday in the case, which has sparked debate online and demonstrations outside the courthouse over maternal well-being and the mental health system. The jury was sent off to deliberate at around 12:30 p.m. Here are some basics about the case.

Who is Lindsay Clancy?

Clancy, 36, is a Massachusetts woman who is charged with murder in the deaths of her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. She hasn't disputed killing them but has pleaded not guilty to murder by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

Clancy was on maternity leave from her job as a labor and delivery nurse when the children were strangled on Jan. 24, 2023. She has been in custody since.

What happened to her family?

The children were strangled with exercise bands in their home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts. Their father, Patrick Clancy, discovered them in the basement when he returned from errands Lindsay Clancy had asked him to run. He found her badly injured in the yard, where she landed after jumping from a second-story window. She remains paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair.

___

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

___

What is the trial about?

The trial hinges on Lindsay Clancy's mental health and whether she understood that killing the children was wrong.

Prosecutors contend that she did and that she acted intentionally. They noted she was involved in everyday activities the day of the killings, such as taking her children to the doctor and playing with them in the snow. The prosecution claims she deliberately sent her then-husband on errands to get him out of the house, and prosecutors have questioned the seriousness of her suicide attempt.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, maintains that she was so mentally ill that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for the killings. According to her defense, she had bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis and, ultimately, it led her to believe she heard a voice telling her to kill the children so she could end her own life.

In diary entries Clancy wrote in the months before the killings, she described feeling anxious, overwhelmed, preoccupied with the details of her infant's care, beset by “brain fog,” and “desperate to get a mental break from taking care of everyone.”

Both the prosecution and the defense have drawn on expert testimony to support their contrasting views of Clancy’s mental state at the time of the killings.

One forensic psychiatrist, testifying for the defense, said Clancy was “clearly psychotic” and held a delusional belief that her children would be better off dying with her than being left behind. The prosecution's experts agreed that she had serious psychological problems, but said she wasn't psychotic. They also questioned Clancy's account of being commanded by a voice and asserted that she knew right from wrong and had control of her behavior.

What is postpartum psychosis?

It's a rare and serious condition that can cause disorganized thinking, delusions, hallucinations and other symptoms. It affects an estimated 1 to 2 out of 1,000 women after childbirth, but the risk is somewhat higher for people with certain mental health conditions such as bipolar disorder.

Postpartum psychosis is different from postpartum depression, a more common mood disorder.

Did Clancy try to get help?

According to court testimony and exhibits, Clancy's psychiatric decline began about three months after Callan was born, as she looked ahead to returning to work. Starting in September 2022, she sought help from multiple providers and programs, even checking herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days in early January 2023.

Her defense maintains that her care was disjointed and that her medications were poorly managed or even improper. Clancy and her husband have separately sued several people who treated her. Those claims haven't yet played out in civil court.

Prosecutors sought to underscore that Clancy had ample access to care but sometimes disregarded providers' advice, switched among providers and stopped taking certain medications. The clinicians testified that although she reported feeling suicidal, she denied having a plan to harm herself or anyone else and didn’t exhibit signs of mania or psychosis.

According to Clancy's mother, however, Clancy told her mom and then-husband in December 2022 that she thought about harming the children.

Did Clancy testify?

She chose not to take the witness stand. She watched the proceedings from the defense table, occasionally weeping, as when prosecutors showed autopsy photos of the children to the jury.

What are the possible outcomes?

If Clancy is convicted, her sentence could be as severe as life in prison without the possibility of parole. If she's found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, the court will decide whether she can be released from custody or should remain confined in a state mental health facility.

If the jury can't reach a verdict, prosecutors would have to decide whether to retry the case. If a mistrial were declared for some other reason, the next steps could depend on the circumstances.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez officially rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York chapter this week after previously letting her membership lapse, and the organization said the potential 2028 contender remains in “good standing” with the group.

The move to officially associate herself with the organization comes as the association is under the spotlight of political elites in D.C. as it has proven a major force in Democratic Party primaries this cycle. Candidates aligned with the socialist platform won not only in New York but also notched a victory in Florida with the victory of Angie Nixon. Left-leaning progressives in general have been on an upswing this cycle, winning key races in Minnesota and Michigan earlier in August and ousting several House Democratic incumbents.

New York’s Ocasio-Cortez is one of the few progressives who has explicitly embraced the organization, which is home to a wide variety of leftists and has both in the past and recently included local chapters that staked out far-left positions that threatened to alienate voters. In Wisconsin, concerns about Francesca Hong’s past criticism of the Thanksgiving holiday contributed to the downfall of her gubernatorial campaign. Hong was endorsed by her local Democratic Socialists chapter, and was a member of the organization.

In a statement, a Democratic Socialists of America spokesperson said that Ocasio-Cortez’s membership (which is dues-based) lapsed without the congresswoman’s knowledge, and stated that she was simply rectifying the mistake.

“Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” read an email to DSA members shared with the New York-based news outlet City & State.

open image in gallery Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is regularly eyed as a serious 2028 presidential contender and has now rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York chapter ( Getty )

“Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.”

Other progressives, such as House candidate Will Lawrence in Michigan, chose to allow their memberships to lapse or left the organization entirely to avoid negative baggage associated with the movement.

Many Americans, particularly older generations, still view the “socialist” label with suspicion. Those views are evolving, however, and recent Gallup polling has shown that among Democratic voters, views of capitalism and socialism are reversing as less than half of the party’s voters now have a positive view of capitalism while a much higher percentage (66 percent) view socialism favorably.

The Democratic Socialists of America got its first major boost with the victory of Zohran Mamdani in the New York mayoral election. Volunteers organized en masse for the younger progressive as he faced Andrew Cuomo and a torrent of attacks from both the right and the center-left. Democratic Party leadership reluctantly endorsed him after his victory, and spent months over the course of 2026 trying to oppose similar candidates in races around the country.

The New York congresswoman’s choice is highly notable as it is strongly expected by many Democrats and political watchers alike that she will run for higher office in 2028. Ocasio-Cortez is already talked about as a presidential contender and her name regularly appears in polling of the potential Democratic primary field, often showing competitive numbers but trailing behind other Democrats such as Kamala Harris.

open image in gallery Clashes over the Democratic Socialists of America and the future direction of the Democratic Party took center stage in the Michigan primary, won by Abdul El-Sayed ( Getty )

Ocasio-Cortez hasn’t made her 2028 plans clear, and as with most politicians of all political stripes eyeing potential presidential bids, she isn’t likely to announce those plans before the November midterm elections. The performance of the party’s left flank in those midterms is likely to factor into her decision, though the congresswoman herself is expected to easily coast to victory in her House race.

Should she decline to run for president in two years, many progressives also are hopeful the 36-year-old Bronx and Queens-area representative will take a swing at unseating Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader and head of the Democratic caucus, who represents New York as its senior senator. He’ll be up for re-election in 2028, giving Ocasio-Cortez a clear second choice for the upcoming primary cycle.

Schumer polled behind Ocasio-Cortez in a Data for Progress poll of that hypothetical matchup, though the 75-year-old senator could opt for retirement rather than face a tough primary fight. Regardless of Ocasio-Cortez’s plans, progressives in New York are incensed at Schumer’s leadership through 2025 and 2026, and are eagerly awaiting the chance to support a challenge against him.

Numerous Senate candidates this cycle have already refused to support Schumer as a potential future Senate majority leader, though no Democrat in the Senate has signaled plans to challenge him for the role.
