The U.S. military is reportedly experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe, largely driven by President Donald Trump’s war with Iran.

Citing a U.S. defense official in Europe and a NATO official, The Associated Press reported Thursday that the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in NATO countries to a potential Russian attack.

The NATO official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles, among American and NATO forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.

In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the U.S. defense official said.

open image in gallery Patriot missiles are seen at the Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport, March 25, 2022, in Jasionka, Poland ( AP Photo/Evan Vucci )

In Europe, the American military “definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have “very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the U.S. official said.

It illustrates the cascading fallout from Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran, a conflict that reaches the six-month mark on Friday. U.S. missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where U.S. and Gulf allies have fired off significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriots, to thwart Iran’s drones and missiles. Some of those attacks have killed and wounded American troops.

Though a Russian ballistic missile attack against NATO countries is not imminently expected, CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump played down the significance of the rare and secretive trip, saying it was “sort of semi-routine.”

European and NATO officials say Russia could be in a position to attack countries in the alliance by 2030. Patriot stockpiles are projected to rebound by then. In the meantime, Russia’s war in Ukraine could hinder its ability to carry out any missile attack on Europe as it would be a challenge for Moscow to fight an air war on two fronts.

US Patriot transfers to Ukraine played a role in drawdown

The Patriot missile shortage is most acutely felt in Ukraine, where officials are begging for more air defense support and where previous U.S. transfers also have drawn down some supply. Kyiv says only U.S.-made Patriots can stop Russia’s advanced ballistic missiles, which increasingly are getting through Ukrainian defenses, including as part of a barrage overnight into Thursday.

The U.S. supplied hundreds of Patriot missiles to Ukraine over the course of the 4 1/2-year-long conflict, but the Iran war was the tipping point for shrinking inventories, said Ed Arnold, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a military think tank in London.

The supply to Ukraine was planned for and reasonably measured, he said, whereas stocks in the Middle East have been unexpectedly and quickly drained, exposing supply chain constraints.

open image in gallery The Patriot missile shortage is most acutely felt in Ukraine, where officials are begging for more air defense support ( Ukrainian Presidential Press Service )

The U.S. military in Europe also is grappling with critical shortages of the Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACMS, a medium-range ballistic missile designed to strike behind enemy lines, the two officials said. But the overall munitions picture in Europe is less dire than on air defenses alone because some European militaries have their own offensive missiles, such as the Taurus and Storm Shadow, which are both long-range air-launched bunker-busting missiles.

The Pentagon said it would not discuss weapons stockpile levels for security reasons. U.S. Army Col. Martin O’Donnell, a senior NATO military spokesperson, said it is “simply not the case” that the number of Patriot missiles in Europe is beyond critical.

NATO, he said, is able to “block punches” and has enough air defense munitions available to defend itself as well as to donate to Ukraine.

Europe has few alternatives while stocks are low

The dearth of Patriot interceptors in Europe would leave few alternatives for shooting down Russia’s more advanced ballistic missiles, which can be combined with swarms of inexpensive drones to overwhelm defenses, experts say.

Ukraine and some allies already use systems that can destroy slower-moving drones without expensive missiles. But ballistic missiles are a challenge because they dive steeply toward targets at more than five times the speed of sound, leaving little time to stop them.

The Patriot system tracks the missile, predicts its path and launches within minutes, all while carrying out complex calculations to ensure the interceptor finds its target. One Patriot battery can only cover a limited area: for example, a small military base but not a whole city.

One alternative could be France and Italy’s SAMP/T NG air defense system. France has promised to speed up the delivery of the system — the upgraded version of the current SAMP/T — to Ukraine, which the manufacturer says is better able to counter ballistics.

The new iteration, however, has not yet been battle tested and the current version of the SAMP/T has a smaller range than the Patriot.

While U.S. and European militaries have warships that can serve as mobile air defense, they may be too far from a target to protect it and could risk getting sunk.

Patriot stocks have plunged during the Iran war

Ukraine has received Patriots from American and European stockpiles since Russia's 2022 invasion, with the U.S. providing about 600 of the interceptors during the Biden administration, said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank.

But the greatest expenditure has been during the Iran conflict, which has used up 65% of U.S. Patriots, amounting to roughly 1,500 of the nation's 2,330 interceptors, CSIS says. About 600 missiles, including those destined for Europe, should be made this year, with a production goal of 2,000 Patriot missiles a year set for 2030, Cancian said.

open image in gallery A Patriot missile battery seen near Prince Sultan air base at al-Kharj on February 20, 2020 ( AFP/Getty )

NATO says Europe’s first Patriot missile production facility is expected to open in Germany in September, with deliveries possibly beginning early next year. The first deliveries should go to countries that have already placed orders, including Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, the U.S. defense official said.

But for now, that means some countries, such as Germany, have bought expensive Patriot systems but are in the “ridiculous” position of not having any ammunition to fire from them, said Arnold of the London think tank.

Germany's defense ministry said it does not comment on stockpiles.

Russia also has limitations

Moscow likely cannot carry out a sustained air assault on a NATO target while it launches almost nightly attacks on Ukraine, Arnold said.

Ukraine's recent strikes into Russia also have exposed weaknesses in Russia's air defenses, which could prompt Putin to think twice about provoking a retaliatory attack.

“The uncomfortable truth is possibly the best air defense that we have is Russian constraints,” Arnold said.

Manchester United are back in the Champions League after two seasons away with Michael Carrick eager to extend their good form since confirming his elevation from caretaker boss to permanent manager.

After an early setback at Hull City, United will be tasked with juggling commitments at home and in Europe and Carrick faces an early headache with Premier League games at home to Ipswich and Everton away before beginning their European campaign.

In their last Champions League appearance, in the 2023/24 campaign, before the league phase was introduced, United exited in the group stage, finishing bottom after two defeats to Bayern Munich and a loss against each of Galatasaray and Copenhagen.

It means United have spent more than two and a half years outside of Europe’s top competition, and their coefficient saw them enter the draw in pot two, alongside Borussia Dortmund, Porto, Brugge, Real Betis, PSV, Aston Villa, Roma and Sporting Lisbon.

See below for all of Man United’s opponents in the league phase of the Champions League.

Man United’s Champions League draw

Bayern Munich (H)

Atletico Madrid (A)

Roma (H)

Sporting Lisbon (A)

Leipzig (H)

Villarreal (A)

Sabah (H)

Como (A)

The dates and times for the fixtures are expected to be released in the next 48 hours. Uefa confirms at the latest on Saturday.

How does the league phase work?

The league phase has 36 teams with every team handed eight games. The 36 teams are split into four pots of eight teams based on their Uefa coefficient, with the opponents generated by automated software.

The opponents then come from each pot, with two teams selected from each, one home and one away.

Teams cannot play another team from the same country and are not permitted to face more than two teams from one country.

Those finishing inside the top eight go straight into the last 16, then the next 16 teams advance to the play-off stage, with eight of those 16 teams progressing to the last 16.

News.title: Ebola response shifts to Congo’s river network
News.content:
Stacked with logs and crammed with hundreds of passengers, the giant barges are nudged day after day along one of Africa’s greatest waterways.

The weeks-long voyage looks sedate, but the tugs are pushing their heavily-laden charges along an unstoppable aquatic superhighway.

Sharing the Congo river with these trade behemoths are canoes, fishing boats and smaller wooden cargo ships.

The river connects the wild east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to the capital Kinshasa, in a vital economic artery and transport corridor nearly 1,100 miles long.

The waterway is a lifeline for passengers, timber, produce and goods. Roads are rare and unreliable, and airfares are far too expensive for most.

Now there are concerns the river risks becoming a conduit for something else heading to the capital of nearly 18 million people: the deadly Ebola virus.

News.title: Great British fry-up implicated in Salmonella outbreak
News.content:
The outbreak, which involved packets of chicken-flavoured instant dried noodles, was traced back to a manufacturing plant near Kyiv by the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC) in June.

“Epidemiological investigations have found that cases in Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Latvia and Lithuania had consumed flavoured noodle products from the same brand. Investigations have linked the products, which were distributed in several countries, to the same producer in Ukraine,” the ECDC said in a statement at the time.

Another outbreak, which lasted from 2021 to 2024, sickened 174 people in the UK and killed one. It was linked to frozen, steam-cooked chicken breast fillets produced in Ukraine.

Although it is not known if the latest outbreak is linked to Ukraine (the UK also imports eggs from countries including Poland, Spain, and Belgium ), Ukraine sits outside of the EU and Salmonella contamination is common in many of the country’s poultry farms.

A senior figure investigating a connected outbreak of Salmonella in the Netherlands told The Telegraph that the “working hypothesis” among British health officials is that the contaminated products have come from Ukraine.

“In Ukraine, thousands of salmonellosis cases are reported each year. The highest incidence is observed among children,” said a study published in the academic journal Advances in Animal and Veterinary Sciences earlier this year.

“The main sources of the pathogen are eggs, chicken meat, and meat and dairy products. Analysis shows that frequent outbreaks are associated with poor food storage conditions [...] predominantly in the southeastern regions of Ukraine,” added the authors from the Institute of Laboratory Diagnostics and Veterinary-Sanitary Expertise in Kyiv.

Britain’s egg consumption has boomed over the last two decades, with 209 eaten per person on average every year compared to roughly 163 per person in 2000.

The rise is thought to have been driven by a spike in baking during the pandemic, the rise of brunch culture and the rise of a focus on diets rich in protein among the young, according to experts.

News.title: Heading to a festival this weekend? Here’s how to fold down a pop-up tent in 60 seconds
News.content:
A pop-up tent can be pitched in seconds and, theoretically, taken down in less, making them perfect for music festivals, casual camping or even waiting in the queue at Wimbledon overnight.

Their problem is that they’re not actually as easy to put away as they should be. Angle it right, and the tent folds away as easily as it popped up. Approach without a plan, and you’ll find yourself wrangling with a seemingly live tent that refuses to fold back into its circular bag.

Here’s my step-by-step guide on how to put away a pop-up tent in less than 60 seconds, to help you avoid that problem. Watch the video to see exactly how I do it.

1. Unzip the doors

This is to let any air escape. Otherwise, you’ll find it balloons out as you try to fold it.

2. Gather the poles

Find the highest arch on both sides, then pull them together into the middle.

News.title: Savio scores on debut as Spurs cruise past Charlton in Carabao Cup
News.content:
It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

“A perfect day for him,” said De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

“We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”

News.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after mosquito imported on plane
News.content:
Five airport workers in Frankfurt have been infected with malaria and one has died after being bitten by a stowaway mosquito, health officials have said.

The employees are thought to have been infected in early July, but their diagnosis was delayed due to a lack of travel history to malaria-endemic regions, according to the Robert Koch Institute, Germany’s federal agency responsible for disease control.

It is believed that they were bitten by mosquitoes which arrived at the airport on a plane, most likely from Africa, where 95 per cent of global malaria cases are found.

The five surviving airport workers – who are all male and are said to work in different parts of the facility and in different jobs – are undergoing medical care.

Traps have now been installed across the airport in an attempt to catch any remaining mosquitoes and analyse their origin, according to an airport spokesperson.

It is not the first time that Frankfurt Airport, Germany’s busiest travel hub, has recorded a case of malaria, according to the Robert Koch Institute, which added that there was another incidence in 2023.

More than 610,000 people die of malaria every year, the overwhelming majority children under five in Africa who are unable to quickly access treatment.

The disease, which is caused by a parasite carried by infected mosquitoes, is largely curable if treated early with antimalarials.

In Britain and Europe, there are thousands of imported cases of malaria every year reported in returning travellers from Africa and Asia – but local transmission is exceedingly rare.

Of the 5,000 or so cases recorded in Europe every year, typically just five are caught locally – either from an airport or from a non-infected European mosquito picking up the disease from a sickened person and spreading it to others.

Early symptoms include fever, headaches, and chills, which can quickly develop into multi-organ failure.

Vaccines were made available for the first time in 2024 and are licenced for use in young children in Africa, although they are thought to be only between 30 and 50 per cent effective at preventing the disease.

News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”

News.title: The five best coastal places to retire in the UK
News.content:
How equity release can help you purchase a seaside property

UK homeowners aged 55 or over may be able to use equity release in two main ways: either to help fund the purchase of a second home, or to buy a new home and release equity from that property as part of the same legal transaction. Seeking professional advice is key to understanding which option may be right for you.



The most popular equity release product is a lifetime mortgage. A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home. It will reduce the value of your estate and could affect your entitlement to means-tested benefits. There is no obligation to make monthly repayments with a lifetime mortgage, although you can choose to make some if you wish. Instead, the full amount plus interest is only repaid when the last homeowner dies or enters permanent long-term care, and this is usually done with the sale of the home.



You must always seek professional help when considering equity release. Make sure your adviser is looking at products from lenders that are members of the Equity Release Council. The Equity Release Council, the industry trade body, requires its members to offer plans that comply with its product standards.

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

Sports.title: Ex-Chelsea star’s footballer son, 34, died with his pal in 40C heat while hiking in Dubai’s ‘desert valley’
Sports.content:
Add us as a preferred source

HIKE TRAGEDY Ex-Chelsea star’s footballer son, 34, died with his pal in 40C heat while hiking in Dubai’s ‘desert valley’

A FORMER Chelsea star’s son died with his friend in Dubai’s desert valley as temperatures reached 40C, an inquest heard.

Cassius Newton, 34, of Poole in Dorset, and 33-year-old Aran Martinson, of Essex, were discovered dead by rescuers on July 18.



The men both worked in the United Arab Emirates and had set off for a hike earlier that morning.

Cassius – a non-league footballer – was the son of former Chelsea star and assistant manager Eddie Newton.



An inquest heard how the friends’ provisional causes of death included cardiac and respiratory arrest.

Area coroner Michelle Brown said severe rising body temperature and organ failure, and heat stress due to exposure to high temperature were also factors.



The court in Chelmsford was told the pals lived in the luxury resort of Ras Al Khaimah – around 75 miles north of Dubai.

Cassius’ wife, who was in the UK, reported her husband missing when he failed to contact her after the hike.



His body was later discovered alongside dad-of-three Aran between 3km and 4k from their vehicle.

The coroner said Cassius and Aran were both lying on their backs surrounded by large rocks.

She adjourned both inquests until a date to be fixed.

Tributes flooded in for the pair following the tragedy earlier this year.

Aran’s wife said he was “incredibly driven, hardworking and ambitious” on a public LinkedIn post.



She added: “He had only recently started a new chapter in his career, and I know how excited he was about it.”

National League side Eastleigh – where Cassius used to play – said the club was “deeply saddened” by his death.

His dad Eddie played for Chelsea between 1990 until 2001 where he famously scored in the 1997 FA Cup final.

The defensive midfielder also played for Cardiff City, Birmingham City, Oxford United and Barnet.

After hanging up his boots, Eddie was assistant manager at MK Dons and West Brom before returning to Chelsea.



He served as assistant manager to Roberto Di Matteo and Rafael Benítez.

Sports.title: Reiss Nelson agrees to rip up Arsenal contract a year early with English clubs considering transfer for free agent
Sports.content:
REISS NELSON has left Arsenal after his contract was terminated.

The winger, 26, is free to find a new club after agreeing with Gunners chiefs to end his deal a year early.



Nelson featured for Mikel Arteta‘s men early in pre-season but was not in first team contention in recent weeks.

He will now mull over potential suitors in England and abroad.



The winger was recently linked with West Ham, and could yet decide to move to the Hammers on a free transfer.

Confirming Nelson’s exit, an Arsenal statement read: “Together with Reiss, we agreed to terminate his contract with immediate effect for him to become a free agent.

“Reiss, 26, spent 18 years with us, developing through our academy into senior level, making 90 first-team appearances, scoring eight goals and assisting nine times. He won the FA Cup in 2020 and played his part in our FA Community Shield victories in 2017 and 2020.

“Reiss made 68 appearances across our youth teams before signing his first professional contract with the club in December 2016.

“He had four loan spells during his time with us, firstly with Bundesliga team Hoffenheim in the 2018/19 season, then with Dutch club Feyenoord in 2021/22. He spent the 2024/25 campaign at Fulham, before remaining in west London with Brentford last season.

“Everyone at the club thanks Reiss for his contribution to Arsenal. We wish him and his family well for the future.”



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Nelson had a year remaining on his Arsenal contract, with the Gunners possessing an option to extend by a further 12 months.

But the Londoner will now begin a new chapter.

Nelson came through Arsenal’s academy and made his senior debut under Arsene Wenger.

He went on to play 90 times for the Gunners’ first team, with the last of those competitive appearances coming in August 2024.

The former England youth international went on four loan spells during his Arsenal stint.



Nelson spent the 2018-19 season at Hoffenheim and 2021-22 campaign at Feyenoord.

During the last two years he has had underwhelming loans at Fulham and Brentford, managing 12 outings with the former and 10 Prem runouts with the latter during an injury-hit spell.

Sports.title: Chelsea star Cole Palmer takes swipe at Maresca and Rosenior’s ‘safe zones’ as he reveals secret behind resurgence
Sports.content:
COLE PALMER is loving life under Xabi Alonso already.

Seemingly for one key reason – compared to playing under Enzo Maresca and Liam Rosenior last season – freedom.



Palmer, 24, bagged a goal and an assist in Chelsea‘s opening game of the season, a 3-2 win over Fulham at Craven Cottage, with fans raving over the Blues’ new front line.

The forward is starting in a right-sided number 10 position, with best pal Morgan Rogers on the opposite side, with both of them being given the chance to move about the pitch to maximise their threats.



At times last season, the Chelsea number ten was subject to claims he was being held back by the rigid tactical setups of Maresca and Rosenior.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Palmer appeared to take a cheeky dig at his former bosses over ‘safe zones’ when explaining exactly what he liked about Alonso’s new system.



Palmer said: “He [Alonso] just said I’d have more freedom to drift about the pitch. Just like you saw [against Fulham] with the goal I scored.

“Last season, I wouldn’t have even made that run because it’s not a ‘safe zone’. But he’s saying move across that zone, drop into play, come get on the ball, create and just do what you do.”

This season, if Palmer is back to his frightening, ice-cold best, he will be a serious problem for the rest of the Premier League.

Since Mauricio Pochettino left Chelsea, Palmer hasn’t been the same player due to a mix of fitness problems, managerial switches, and seeming confidence issues in front of goal at times.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

A serious groin issue was a big part of his disappointing campaign last season, but Palmer insisted that he is over that now after having the summer off and missing the World Cup.

He added: “Physically I feel good, probably the best I’ve felt in ages, but I think I can [get fitter] with games and more minutes,” Palmer told Sky Sports.

“Before my groin injury, I’d never really been injured. Well, rarely [injured]. So then I would just come back and play when I shouldn’t have played.

“Obviously the World Cup was coming up, so I was in a bit of a dilemma thinking: ‘if I don’t play I’m not going to go. But if I play then, I can’t play [properly]’.



“It was just a bit of a sticky situation. I didn’t really know how to deal with it, but it’s one of those things. I was just seeing different people, getting different ideas of why I was injured and what it was.

“Since I’ve come back I’ve been working every day to obviously stop it happening again. I just want to stay injury free, and if I’m on the pitch then I know what I can do.”

Sports.title: Gary Neville net worth 2026 – what businesses does the footballer have, and why is he on Dragons’ Den?
Sports.content:
GARY Neville transitioned from legendary Manchester United defender into one of the UK’s most prolific businesspeople.

The entrepreneur is appearing on Dragons’ Den – which is back for the second part of its 23rd series – and has a diverse portfolio of business interests deeply rooted in his passion for Northwest England.



What businesses does Gary Neville have?

Companies House has listed Gary Neville as a director of 56 businesses, spanning sport, media, hotels, pubs, restaurants, education and property development.

The footballer first got into property development in his early 20s and owns a chain of hotels and townhouses, as well as development projects.



Among these is Hotel Football, complete with a rooftop five-a-side pitch overlooking Old Trafford.

Alongside former teammate Ryan Giggs, Neville owns a 40 per cent stake in the Stock Exchange development, which is close to Piccadilly Gardens, Manchester.

He owns real estate development company St Michaels UK PropCo2 with Betfred CEO Fred Done, as well as image rights and media company Tiger Sports Management.

Then there’s Buzz 16 Productions, the parent company of his Overlap podcasts.

In January 2026, Neville sold a majority stake in The Overlap to radio firm Global.

The England legend said: “The Overlap started as an idea that we thought people might like and we went for it.



“What has happened since then has been a great journey and it’s a team that I love working with and I’m incredibly proud to be a part of.

“We never thought of it as a business, we just wanted to create something that people loved and would come back to watch every week.”

Alongside David Beckham, Gary also in charge of Salford City FC, which was initially bought by five members of the ‘Class of 92‘, though the rest have since relinquished their shares.

What is his net worth?

On top of his vast business empire, Neville has earned many millions from his other endeavours.

He built his vast wealth during his 19-year playing career, which he spent entirely at Manchester United.



I hope my personal journey shows that you can take the experiences you’ve had in one part of your career and use them to do something entirely different and make it a success Gary Neville ,

When he stopped playing, he became the UK’s best-paid pundit – he earns an estimated £1.1million a year from Sky Sports.

Neville’s businesses are now worth about £200million, latest accounts show.

When did Gary Neville join Dragons’ Den?

Neville joined Dragons’ Den as guest Dragon for series 21, and has been a recurring Dragon ever since.

His addition to the panel was announced in October 2023, with episodes featuring the former defender airing from January 2024.

At the time he said: “I am excited to join the Dragons, and to meet the entrepreneurs brave enough to face us in the Den.



“I hope my personal journey shows that you can take the experiences you’ve had in one part of your career and use them to do something entirely different and make it a success.

“Business is all about managing people and managing yourself and I’m looking forward to sharing my experience to help the entrepreneurs we’ll meet in the Den reach their potential.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Show regular Deborah Meaden was quickly impressed, saying Neville has “a really good business brain”.

She explained: “You’d think he had been a Dragon his entire life… He was fantastic, I’m not kidding you, and he’s prepared to invest.”

Sports.title: Former Man Utd star explains why he is now playing for FREE at new club
Sports.content:
Former Man Utd star explains why he is now playing for FREE at new club

Ander Herrera has rejoined boyhood club Real Zaragoza on a free transfer, but the former Manchester United midfielder won't take home a salary in the Spanish third division

View 3 Images Ander Herrera has made a kind gesture (Image: Real Zaragoza)

Ex-Manchester United star Ander Herrera has explained why he's chosen to play for Real Zaragoza for FREE. Herrera, 37, returned to his boyhood team in July after spending the last 18 months with Argentine giants Boca Juniors.

‌



The midfielder wants to help Zaragoza climb out of the Spanish third division and aid them off the pitch, too. Instead of taking home a wage, Herrera will donate his salary to the club's foundation which helps with funding grassroots sports, running educational programmes and other charitable projects.

‌



"I don't need a contract. I have a very successful career. I have taken care of my money," Herrera told BBC Sport. "I can give this present to myself.

‌



"To put that shirt on... for free because I wanted to help my club, my team, my city. It's something that I wanted to do. It's something that I am able to do and it's something that makes me feel so proud to be able to be here just to help.

‌



"I am not thinking about money or contracts. I feel a privilege to be able to do that."

Herrera left Zaragoza in February 2011 when the club were in financial trouble. The Spaniard made 86 senior appearances, predominately in La Liga, during his first spell at La Romareda before signing for Athletic Club in a €7.5million (£6.4m) deal.

After thee-and-a-half years in Bilbao, Herrera made the move to United for £28m and became Louis van Gaal's first signing. He made 189 appearances during his time at Old Trafford, winning the FA Cup, EFL Cup and Europa League.

‌



Should Manchester United have kept Ander Herrera? Have your say in the comments section.

View 3 Images Ander Herrera's exit still divides Manchester United fans (Image: Clive Rose/Getty Images)

Herrera left United in 2019 upon the expiry of his contract, having wanted a longer extension than the terms United were offering him. "It was not about money," he insisted to The Athletic.

‌



"It was not about the duration of the contract offer. In my opinion, I waited too long (for an offer) and deserved more attention from the club.

"I was a player that gave everything. I never complained. I never went to the media to complain about anything. I never put a bad face to any manager, to any member of the board, and they waited until I had five or six months left on my contract. That's why I had some disagreements with them."

Herrera subsequently joined Paris Saint-Germain on a free transfer, helping Thomas Tuchel's side reach the Champions League final during his first season. But he slowly fell out of favour in the French capital before returning to Bilbao in 2022 for a two-and-a-half year stint.

‌



It was then when he signed for Boca and now he's come full circle in a bid to turn Zaragoza's fortunes around. "It has been so sad, of course, for all us Zaragozistas," the 37-year-old admitted.

View 3 Images Ander Herrera came through Real Zaragoza's academy (Image: David Ramos/Getty Images)

"Real Zaragoza belong to Europe, they belong to compete for trophies, to be fighting with the biggest clubs in Spain and in Europe. I want to put my quality, my experience and my passion to try to help my team to come back where I think we belong.

‌



"But since the first day I came, I don't want to talk too much about the past. We have been talking too much about what we have done wrong. It's always killing our minds why that happened, always thinking about negative things.

"Let's stop crying about what happened in the past. Let's build on the future. Let's come every day to training with a smile."

UEFA is considering launching criminal proceedings against FIFA president Gianni Infantino in an audacious attempt to oust him from power.

‌



The scandal in the wake of Infantino's failed attempt to sell shares in FIFA tournaments to external investors has faded in recent weeks. But legal documents filed in the United States shows that UEFA has now stepped up their efforts to topple Infantino.

‌



UEFA is subpoenaing FIFA and the financial institutions involved in the failed plot in an attempt to obtain documents. European football's governing body then plans to launch legal action in Switzerland - the home of FIFA.

‌



As reported by Sky News, the document states: "UEFA and other interested parties are preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials and advisors for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code and such further or alternative charges as the developed factual record may support, arising out of the secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing of a transaction that inflicted direct and concrete injury on FIFA's reputation, governance authority, and commercial relationships to the detriment of FIFA as well as its 211 members, including UEFA's 55 member associations."

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

As well as Infantino, the application in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York is against JP Morgan Bank, planned lead investor Thrive Capital and its CEO, Joshua Kushner.

‌



The legal document alleges: "It was a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from FIFA's most valuable assets to the detriment of FIFA, its members, and other parties within the football family."

The news comes just a day after UEFA dropped its threat to boycott FIFA tournaments. European football's governing body feels its two conditions have been met, namely that FIFA drops the idea of selling off stakes in its tournaments and that they receive assurances it doesn't happen again.

UEFA and its president Aleksander Ceferin have been leading the campaign against Infantino this summer. The body's 55 member associations are due to meet on Thursday ahead of the Champions League draw in Monaco, where the situation will be discussed further.

‌



View 2 Images Aleksandr Ceferin is leading the campaign against Gianni Infantino (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

UEFA have received support from Confederation for North America and the Caribbean (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). However, Infantino has managed to claw back support from elsewhere.

African Football Confederation (CAF) and Confederation for South America (Conmebol) have thrown their support behind the Swiss bureaucrat, who will go for re-election next year.

‌



If UEFA fail to oust Infantino, then they will have to support a rival candidate in the FIFA elections next year. "Things are changing every day. Every day, there are different discussions. I didn't speak with him. But there are two options," Ceferin said on The Rest is Politics.

"One option is that he realises that he doesn't have the support, and that's not only a political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches.

"And the second option that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against him. I don't know yet who."

Sports.title: Bradley Barcola has already told Liverpool one thing he wants as transfer agreement emerges
Sports.content:
Bradley Barcola has already told Liverpool one thing he wants as transfer agreement emerges

Bradley Barcola could enjoy a dream start to life at Liverpool this month

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola is nearing his long-awaited move to Anfield (Image: Aurelien Meunier - PSG/PSG via Getty Images)

Bradley Barcola will be able to keep his promise of retaining his favourite shirt number after Liverpool secured an agreement with PSG to sign the winger. The Frenchman's long-awaited move to Anfield nears closer after a compromise was found between the two clubs.

‌



The September 1 deadline threatened the viability of the transfer, but Barcola now looks set to become the second-most expensive player in Liverpool history. According to The Athletic, the two clubs have agreed on a package valued at £120million, with £100m of the sum to be guaranteed.

‌



While the deal has yet to be finalised, it presents the 23-year-old with the biggest challenge of his career and his first club venture outside of France. A move to Anfield will be new territory for Barcola, who'll have his international team-mates Hugo Ekitike and Jeremy Jacquet helping him settle.

‌



Should Barcola complete his move to Anfield before the summer transfer window closes, he'll have the opportunity to wear his cheshired No. 29 shirt. The 23-year-old presently sports the number for PSG and would be the first Liverpool player to don it since Arthur Melo during the 2022/23 campaign.

It carries particular importance to Barcola, who has previously outlined the story behind his affection for the number. Speaking to Club Legacyz, he said: "It's actually a funny story. When I was younger, I used to play FIFA. In the story mode with Alex Hunter, this number became symbolic for me.

"I thought to myself, 'The day I go pro, it'll be number 29.' And here I am, I adopted it, and now I'll never let it go." Yet Barcola could choose to take a fresh direction in keeping with a new chapter in his footballing journey.

Having been identified as Liverpool's number one choice to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah, he could further cement that role by inheriting the iconic No. 11 shirt - left empty by Salah following his departure earlier this summer.

Sports.title: Tottenham sign Marmoush on loan with obligation to buy
Sports.content:
Tottenham have confirmed the signing of Manchester City forward Omar Marmoush on an initial loan.

Sky Sports News understands a £60m obligation to buy has been inserted in the deal and the fee is split into a £50m guaranteed payment, plus £10m in add-ons.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at Omar Marmoush's goals for Manchester City in the Premier League and Carabao Cup

Eintracht Frankfurt, who sold Marmoush to City in January 2025, do not have a sell-on clause, contrary to reports.

The German club received their desired guaranteed fee at the time, plus additional bonuses.

There were also very few instalments, meaning all payment obligations to Frankfurt have been fulfilled by City.

Marmoush, who will wear the No 22 at Spurs, now follows former City teammate Savio to join Roberto De Zerbi's squad, after the Brazil winger completed an £85m move to Spurs on Tuesday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Savio scores 11 minutes into his Spurs debut against Charlton

Savio made his debut for the club during Wednesday's 5-1 win against Charlton in the Carabao Cup, where he scored and assisted Ben Davies in the victory.

De Zerbi: Marmoush can take our attack to next level

De Zerbi believes the addition of Marmoush to his squad can take their attacking play to the "next level" with the pace, intelligence and threat he offers in front of goal.

"Omar is exactly the kind of player we want at this club - ambitious, hungry and determined to make a difference," De Zerbi said.

"He has incredible attacking quality but what I also love is his desire to improve and to win.

Sports.title: Kim joins Rangers in £8.5m deal
Sports.content:
Rangers have signed winger Minsu Kim in an £8.5m deal from Spanish side Girona.

The 20-year-old has put pen to paper on an initial four-year contract, with the option of a further 12 months.

Kim is Rangers' 12th summer signing, with striker Kevin Kelsy expected to follow after the Ibrox side agreed a £9.2m deal with his club, Portland Timbers, ahead of the transfer deadline on September 3.

As the South Korean international is not in Rangers' Conference League squad ahead of tonight's play-off second leg against Jablonec, he could make his debut at Aberdeen on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

He joined Girona in 2022 and, after impressing with the B team, made his La Liga debut in October 2024, before featuring in the Champions League the following month.

Last season he scored six goals and provided four assists while on loan at La Liga 2 club Andorra.

Image: Kim has joined Rangers on an initial four-year deal

Kim said: "I'm so happy to sign for Rangers. I know it's a big club with great, great fans.

"I want to help the team to be better every day, to be a good person, and to do everything I can to help the team win everything that comes our way.

"I have a lot of excitement and I believe I have the mentality of a winner. I want to face whatever comes next head-on and I'm going to give the club what it deserves."

Manager Derek McInnes added: "We are delighted to welcome Minsu to Rangers. Strengthening our options in the forward areas has been a real target and focus for us throughout this window, and we believe he will add another exciting dimension to the squad.

"Minsu is a talented young player with excellent technical ability, energy and a real desire to develop, and we are looking forward to working with him."

Raskin transfer interest ramps up

Image: Nicolas Raskin could be set to leave Rangers

Meanwhile, McInnes has confirmed Nicolas Raskin has not travelled to the Czech Republic for the club's Conference League play-off second leg due to growing transfer interest in the midfielder.

Sky Sports News reported on Monday that clubs from across Europe and England were keen on the Belgium international, having previously confirmed that the likes of Atalanta and Real Betis had shown interest earlier in the transfer window.

It is thought interest has been shown in the 25-year-old from teams in Spain, Italy, France and England.

Raskin has two years left on his contract at Ibrox.

Rangers have a 1-0 lead ahead of their play-off second leg against Jablonec, as the clubs battle for a spot in the Conference League.

Image: McInnes' side are in the Czech Republic as they bid to qualify for the Conference League

McInnes said: "Nico hasn't travelled. Nothing to do with injury or anything like that, just the potential of a transfer, potentially. I just think we're so late in the window, maybe it's something the club's looking at. He's trained this morning but has been left back in Glasgow.

"When I came into the job, it was quite clear that there was going to be an opportunity for Nico. There's been plenty of interest in him. We believe that interest has stepped up over the last couple of days, so something may or may not happen.

"If Nico stays beyond the window, then it would be great to work with him. But if he doesn't, we wish him well."

When asked if Rangers might move for another midfielder if Raskin departs - having already added three players in that area this summer - McInnes added: "In certain areas of the pitch, we're a bit stronger than others. I think everything moves on.

Image: Cammy Devlin (L) and Dan Neil (R) are among the midfielders to join Rangers this summer

"Nico served the club well. There's obviously an opportunity for him and the club to capitalise on that for a transfer fee. I don't really want to say too much about Nico at the minute until, if and when, something happens.

"It's still an if rather than a certainty. So maybe we can comment a bit more on that if something happens."

Sports.title: 'London or Madrid' - Alvarez's Arsenal ultimatum explained
Sports.content:
Atletico Madrid say they will not enter into negotiations with Barcelona for striker Julian Alvarez, who is considering a move to Arsenal.

Alvarez did not train on Wednesday and Thursday because of illness after a poor night's sleep on Tuesday, not because of anything related to his future.

The 26-year-old wants to join Barcelona, who again went public with their desire to sign him on Wednesday in an interview with president Joan Laporta.

However, Atletico have now publicly said they won't engage with Barcelona over a transfer for Alvarez.

"Atletico de Madrid is open to standard transfer market negotiations when conducted in a professional, ethical and respectful manner," the club said on Thursday.

"We fully stand behind the club's previously communicated position that FC Barcelona failed to meet these requirements and, as a result, there will not be any negotiation and there is zero consideration of an Alvarez transfer to Barcelona.

"Atletico de Madrid trust that our player will understand the decision and will remain focused on helping the club achieve its goals, just as he has done during the two seasons he has been defending our colours."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Friday Night Football panel discuss whether Arsenal are still shy of a world-class attacker that would see them get over the line to win their first UEFA Champions League title

Marca, Spain's biggest sports newspaper, had previously received on-the-record quotes from the club saying: "The player is being portrayed as the victim, but we are the only victims in this case.

"[Barcelona] have harmed us both financially and socially. There is a zero-per-cent chance of selling him to Barcelona - it's not about money, it's about dignity."

'London or Madrid for Alvarez'

The situation around Alvarez's future has become "extremely tense", according to Atletico expert and journalist Ruben Uria.

Alvarez's public desire to leave has made him so unpopular with the club's supporters that they booed him off the pitch after their 2-2 draw with Villarreal on Sunday and he is understood to be starting to consider whether a potential move to Arsenal would be right for him.

Uria now believes the striker has two options. He said: "My interpretation of the statement is that Atletico is making it public that it will not negotiate with Barcelona under any circumstances, and that this is not only the CEO's position, but also that of the club and, above all, its majority shareholder, Apollo, one of the largest private equity funds in the world.

"Absolute support. It's a clear message for Julian: 'Either you go to London, or you stay. We will never negotiate with Barcelona.' It's very clear, Julian decides. London or staying in Madrid."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the Transfer Talk podcast, Sam Tighe and Daniel Storey debate whether Arsenal should gamble on signing Julian Alvarez despite the striker clearly wanting to sign for Barcelona

What is Arsenal's position on Alvarez?

As far as Arsenal are concerned, nothing has changed. They still believe signing Alvarez is very unlikely before the deadline and would need strong encouragement from the player to start negotiations with Atletico.

There is ongoing dialogue between Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta and Atletico CEO Miguel Angel Gil Marin, but this has been the case all summer. They used to work together at Atletico Madrid and remain close.

Atletico are already making contingency plans and are exploring the possibility of bringing in a new striker. Interestingly, one of the players on their radar is Arsenal's Viktor Gyokeres, with the Spanish club keen to gauge how open Arsenal would be to selling the Sweden international.

They were also keen on Nicolas Jackson, but he is heading to Aston Villa.

The next 24 to 48 hours have been described as crucial to understanding Alvarez's wishes: whether to stay at Atletico and regain his position among the fans and the club, or to push for an exit. Atletico do not want the situation to drag on until the final day of the window.

Could Arsenal be stepping stone to Barca?

South American football expert Tim Vickery speaking on Sky Sports News:

"It is up to Atletico. They have two options: do they want to keep a player who doesn't want to be there? Or do they want to cash in?

"Clearly, they wouldn't sell to Barcelona and wouldn't sell to Real Madrid if they were interested. That does not leave them with many options; who else could afford him?

"The other options are in the Premier League. I'm not sure he was wildly happy during his time in England. He has got himself in a place where there are not many options.

"Arsenal would give a fantastic narrative. Why not try to be part of the first Champions League at Arsenal?

"Why not be a part of that? And, depending on the terms of the contract, Arsenal could be a stepping stone to Barcelona. But it is up to Atletico.

"I am told that the fans would probably take him back if he has to go back to Atletico. He is a wonderful player, a striker with the soul of a midfielder."

Sports.title: Boxing's Bane warns Dubois: 'I was raised in the darkness'
Sports.content:
Think darkness is your ally? Amelia Moore was born in it, moulded by it. And she plans to demonstrate as much against Caroline Dubois on Saturday night.

Sure, it is all very Christopher Nolan, all very caped crusader, all very masked man, but the American shoulders her own hardship as immunity to retreat across life both in and out of the ring.

The 36-year-old carries a young professional record of 4-0 as she, in the words of champion Dubois this week, comes 'back onto the radar' to challenge for the Londoner's WBC and WBO lightweight world titles.

From childhood emancipation to Olympic heartbreak, she is well versed in resilience. She will keep coming, like she always has done. Ask Moore and she might tell you she has always been on the radar.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer, Chantelle Cameron, Caroline Dubois and Amelia Moore face off ahead of their MVP 06 clashes on Saturday

"I had a fight a couple of years ago, I got headbutted and it broke my nose," Moore tells Sky Sports. "I took a punch and shattered my nose, I was bleeding everywhere and it just did not matter.

"There's something inside of me that, in a lot of the time those dark places that people get, I feel like I've been here before.

"It's like in Batman with Bane, he goes, 'I was raised in the darkness'. And I think that's when you are truly comfortable being in uncomfortable places, it's normal to you.

"No matter what, you dig deep, you believe in yourself and you push through."

Moore grew up on a farm in Maine before being emancipated at the age of 16, later working two jobs to fund her life throughout high school, which is where she would also first begin boxing.

Financial circumstances saw her turn towards military opportunities as opposed to the conventional college route, with Moore eventually joining the U.S. Naval Academy. Having been recruited to run track, she also trained in boxing, wrestling and swimming until being medically discharged following her diagnosis of Crohn's disease.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Caroline Dubois says she is looking forward to encountering Alycia Baumgardner at Thursday's press conference and has already won their verbal sparring on social media

"I didn't know what an allowance was, there was responsibilities that required your attention, and that sacrifice and selflessness was kind of built into me at a really young age," she explains of her childhood.

"My life has been obstacle and challenge, perseverance, and I've created it. I've created that, who I am and who I've become has had to be my effort. There's been no artificial push. There's been no handouts.

"There are times where things get so tough and you think to yourself, why me? You get older and you look back and you're like, thank God it was me. You become resilient, you become creative, you become all of these facets that without a stressor you would never be able to adapt and change and grow."

Moore was previously part of Team USA for three Olympic cycles having reached the 2016 Summer Games qualifying tournament after just 14 official fights.

She was subsequently forced to withdraw through illness, before also missing out on travelling to Tokyo as an alternate in 2020 as a result of COVID restrictions.

On the surface her professional record may speak to that of an unproven, unknown underdog in the face of a greatness-chasing Dubois, but Moore deems her vast amateur pedigree and accompanying tribulations as evidence of her worth on this weekend's platform.

With it comes a chance to tear up the narrative.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Caroline Dubois is determined to fight rival Alycia Baumgardner sooner rather than later

"There's a line that I love in a song, it says it's not about a matter of luck, it's just about a matter of time. The timeline isn't what we think it is," she adds. "2020 really broke my heart because I knew that I felt ready, but there was something else meant for me. So you just have to sit with it keep building."

"If you keep persevering eventually you get to this point where it's about being undeniable, and eventually the door opens and opportunity comes, but you have to be ready. I'm ready, I'm ready for this moment.

"We'd all love to be spoon fed and live in a padded world, but those people that don't experience life don't change the world. You can't be bitter, you just have to be better."

While Moore has been gearing up for the biggest test of her career to date, she has also watched on as opponent Dubois continues to be linked to a clash with WBA, IBF, WBO and The Ring super featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner.

Not so fast.

"Everything that's been going on in the background, and then the announcement of the fight between Baumgardner and Elif Nur Turhan, there's already been news articles talking about Caroline's next fight," said Moore.

"Everyone's talking about beyond me. Let them. Go ahead. Come Saturday night, it's just she and I. So that's totally fine.

"Go ahead and keep thinking beyond me, but I know where I am, and I'm still focused on what I need to do."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer says if she reproduces her form from training camp she may shock the pundits who are calling this a close contest and win by knockout

Moore has trained in martial arts since childhood, she is a former Elite National Championships and National PAL gold medallist, a seasoned Team USA athlete, she is a ringside analyst, she is writing a book, she is an advanced Emergency Medical Technician and she bakes a mean sourdough bread.

A multi-faceted, multi-talented life and career also sees her rub shoulders with boxing's best, Moore having notably worked with undefeated great Terence Crawford in Colorado Springs.

"His entire team has been a great integral part into not only just like my development, but the amount of things that I've learned from Bud," she says.

"I remember the first time I trained with him, I always felt like I was the crazy one. I trained really hard, I don't know if I've ever met anybody that trains harder than I do, or is as dedicated and as crazy disciplined, and then I met him and was like oh my gosh, he's a lot like me.

"I was blown away. All of his team, all of his coaches, they're amazing."

To be fair, the pots do seem to be well structured – so there’s not a huge range between the best- and worst-case scenarios. And given English teams snagged five of the top eight places last year, it’s not unreasonable to suggest that the Premier League quintet are the ones the rest will want to avoid. Share

1h ago 11.39 EDT The pots and how it works The draw is pretty straightforward. Each team is allocated eight opponents, with four home games and four away games. Two opponents are taken from each seeding pot and teams cannot meet a team from their own country. Then we have the matches, played between September and January. Goals are scored, hearts are broken, stuff happens. When it’s all said and done, the top eight teams in the 36-team table go straight through to the last 16. The 16 teams ranked ninth to 24 go into a playoff round, with the eight winners going through to the last 16. The bottom eight are eliminated and will be taunted and booed until our throats are sore. Pot 1: Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Liverpool, Inter, Manchester City, Arsenal, Barcelona, Atlético Madrid. Pot 2: Borussia Dortmund, Roma, Sporting Lisbon, Aston Villa, Porto, Manchester United, Club Brugge, Real Betis, PSV. Pot 3: Feyenoord, Lille, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Fenerbahce, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray, Bodø/Glimt.
