Sports.title: UEFA threaten legal action against Gianni Infantino as part of efforts to oust FIFA president following failed plan to sell the World Cup
Sports.content:
UEFA is threatening to seek criminal proceedings against Gianni Infantino as they continue their efforts to oust the FIFA president.

In an explosive statement, European football's governing body says it is 'preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino' along with other FIFA officials following the now-dropped secret plans to sell of stakes in the World Cup.

UEFA say they will use Swiss criminal code with regards to the 'secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing' of the controversial plans.

They have filed two filings with the US District Court - one relating to FIFA and the other to Thrive Capital - headed by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law.

They may also ask the authorities to establish whether Infantino, who is clinging to power, came up with a 'fraudulently off-market price' promoted 'for his own benefit'.

The move comes after UEFA withdrew its plans to boycott FIFA tournaments in protest at the proposals having been given assurances there will be no repeat of the sell-off from Infantino, who is up for re-election next year.

UEFA is threatening to seek criminal proceedings against FIFA president Gianni Infantino

UEFA also point out that the Swiss code states that anyone entrusted with the management of property who is in breach of their duties and causes or permits others to sustain financial loss should be subject to a custodial sentence not exceeding three years. They add that should the offender be found to have acted with the intention of 'securing unlawful gain for themselves or another' a custodial sentence 'not exceeding five years' is among the potential punishments.

Meanwhile, national association representatives serving on UEFA's executive committee met to discuss the situation in Monaco ahead of the Champions League draw.

Following the summit, UEFA said those present 'unanimously mandated the UEFA President and Administration to pursue every available institutional, political and legal avenue necessary to secure fundamental reform, restore proper limits on presidential authority and ensure that FIFA is once again governed as an institution – not around one individual'.

A statement added that 'FIFA cannot investigate itself', said that the trust in Infantino was 'broken' and that trust could not be restored. It also vowed to seek a 'credible alternative' should he stand for re-election.

UEFA added that FIFA had 'billions of dollars in reserves' which 'belongs to the Member Associations' and vowed to explore the 'responsible release' of some of those reserves to associations across the world, in a move clearly aimed at drumming up support for such an alternative.

'The abandonment of FFE does not erase the deception, intimidation and abuse of power that made it possible,' it added. 'Nor does it restore the confidence that has been lost.'

'FIFA must once again be governed as an institution serving football – not operate as an instrument of individual power.'

Sports.title: LIV and left to die? Inside the rebel tour's collapse after Saudi exit - and what's next for stars such as Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm with nine-figure contracts to be paid, hundreds of staff laid off and rival tours' revenge
Sports.content:
Had things worked out differently, the staff of LIV Golf would be in Michigan today for what was meant to be their season-ending team championship. Instead, the vast majority were informed on Monday that they would be laid off.

By then, it was not a surprise. That tournament in Michigan, once slated to begin on August 27, was cancelled earlier this month, but it was dead in the water before any formal announcement and the prognosis for LIV’s staff has been bleak for even longer.

The league employs around 300 staff, many of them talented and hard-working, and well over half will leave in the coming weeks. There remains a possibility some will be taken back if the circuit survives to a 2027 season, but that is one of the biggest ‘ifs’ in sport.

For now, LIV has only the faintest of pulses and the hopes of a drastically scaled-back LIV 2.0 are tethered to fresh investors seeing value in what was left behind by the Saudis, who fled in April.

LIV CEO Scott O’Neil thinks he can pull it off, but the next month will be decisive at a time when players are searching for off-ramps, bankruptcy is being considered, vendors are suing for millions in unpaid work, and LIV’s rivals are mobilising their tanks.

Here, Daily Mail Sport assesses O’Neil’s chances as he sizes up the toughest shot in golf.

LIV Golf stars such as Bryson DeChambeau are facing a hugely uncertain future following the withdrawal of Saudi investment

LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil is adamant that the rebel tour can survive

What comes next?

In the broadest sense, that depends very much on a London-based investment firm. BC Capital is widely understood to be the private equity group cited by O’Neil in July, when he announced a saviour had potentially been found. His words: ‘A lead investor has signed a term sheet approved by our board, which will carry and fund LIV going forward.’

Seeking between $250-350million to keep the party alive after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund departed, O’Neil was bullish in his optimism that the tour would be backed through 2030. But a term sheet is not remotely the same as a done deal.

There remains no clarity on the conditions needed to cement the arrangement, but golf insiders are clear on one thing – LIV surely need to keep their best players to get it over the line. Of LIV’s cast, Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm stand head and shoulders above the rest in terms of competitive relevance and profile. The likes of Tyrrell Hatton and Joaquin Niemann stand among the prime-age players on the next rung down.

For his part, DeChambeau wants to stay, but as of the premature conclusion of the LIV season in Indianapolis last weekend, he is now out of contract. Rahm, meanwhile, has offered no public reassurances of a desire to remain and multiple sources insist the Spaniard wants out of a contract that is believed to run through the 2028 campaign.

The complication here is obvious – do BC Capital finalise a deal when the best assets are less than secure? And how can the players possibly commit before the money is definitively in place? Unless those issues are solved, it is hard to see how the investment materialises.

Jon Rahm has offered no public reassurances of a desire to remain and multiple sources insist the Spaniard wants out of a contract that is believed to run through the 2028 campaign

What are the options for players who want to break their contract?

It's a waiting game. Prominent sources in the sport, and those connected to many of the players, are of the view that the ideal scenario for wantaway stars is for LIV to breach their contracts first, clearing the way for a less messy separation.

For Rahm, the considerations are vast. He signed a contract worth around $300million in late 2023 and a vast amount remains unpaid.

Brooks Koepka's LIV signing fee in 2022 was understood to be around $150million and after the five-time major winner walked away in January, Daily Mail Sport revealed that only half of that sum was paid up front, with the remainder paid in $15million installments over the five years of his deal.

By skipping the final season of his contract, he would have forfeited $15million plus any penalties potentially incurred by breaking his arrangement to rejoin the PGA Tour. In Rahm’s case, with two full seasons left he is estimated to be owed a nine-figure fee – not the kind of money even a wealthy man gives up lightly.

Daily Mail Sport has been told that agents are studying whether any forthcoming, downscaled version of LIV 2.0 would amount to a breach of contract. In other words, if LIV breached it first, all ties are off.

Brooks Koepka (centre) got a $150m signing fee in 2022 and after the five-time major winner walked away in January, Daily Mail Sport revealed that only half of that sum was paid up front

How might that look?

One key area of change is the proposed terms and rewards of a 2027 season, if it even happens. Prime among O’Neil’s plans is to scale back from 14 tournaments to 10 - split evenly between the US and the rest of the world - and with far less money up for grabs.

Under the Saudis, the latter ran to absurdly unsustainable levels, with purses of $30m a tournament, but it is understood LIV 2.0 tournaments would pay out between $6-$10million. Clearly, that is not what the bigger beasts signed up for.

Are any departures on the horizon?

As it stands, the players and their management are still waiting on information. One agent I consulted has been scathing of the lack of communication from LIV during this process, dating back to April when the Saudis confirmed their intention to go. That agent explained how the league became exasperated by ‘mole’ leaks to the media, which led to representatives being kept out of some of the player meetings.

As for the players, many have been actively exploring options at different tours. This includes DeChambeau, as previously reported. But he does want to stay, even if the days of nine-figure signing bonuses are over. Daily Mail Sport revealed in May that equity in the league could be one sweetener for those who stay loyal, yet you have to query the value of any size of stake in LIV 2.0. Given the PGA Tour are not bending over backwards to offer him a route back, his hand has been significantly lessened.

Meanwhile, Hatton raised a few eyebrows at the final LIV event last week, when he chose Queen’s I Want to Break Free as his walk-on music. As members of the DP World Tour, having settled an assortment of fines in the past year, Hatton, Rahm, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter and a number of others have kept open the option of jumping ship, but none has yet stated that as a preference.

Speaking this week at the British Masters, a DP World Tour event, Hatton said: ‘I would expect there to be LIV next season. I know they've worked really hard to get the funding stuff in place and it's full steam ahead on that front.’ That being said, sources on the traditional tours are confident Hatton would want to return.

For anyone looking to leave, one key staging post in the process could come if LIV file for bankruptcy. Sources say that such a filing could be made in the first couple of weeks of September. When O’Neil was asked about it this month, he said: ‘I don’t think we would rule out any option.’

LIV's creditors are many and varied, from vendors of tournament infrastructures to multimillionaire players still owed money in their contracts. Sources believe it is possible the latter might argue that attempts to reduce those amounts to cents on the dollar could be a breach of contract.

Tyrrell Hatton raised a few eyebrows at the final LIV event last week, when he chose Queen’s I Want to Break Free as his walk-on music

While sympathy for LIV rebels might be limited in a bankruptcy scenario, greater thought should go to those behind the scenes. That brings us to the vendors. One of them, Mobii Systems Group, a Canadian company that supplied technology for LIV broadcasts, is pursuing a claim for more than $1.1million and Fresh Tape Media, a relatively small content production agency, are also trying to recoup more than $1.2million. Fresh Tape claim LIV sent a letter earlier this year saying it would be able to pay only $200,000 towards its remaining bill. That offer was later reduced to $150,000.

The agency’s founder, Jared Kleinstein, posted on social media: ‘When a small business does the work, it deserves to be paid for it.’ O’Neil said earlier this month: ‘We’re doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed, and I hope we can.’

Have the players been caught up in cash-flow issues since the Saudis pulled out?

According to one well-placed agent, yes. They told Daily Mail Sport that there was no issue with prize money arriving on time at tournaments for individual placings, with the sums arriving typically within a week, but money from team placements was ‘two to three weeks late’ after the British LIV stop in July. That only exacerbated the uncertainty from the playing field.

What are the rival tours doing about all this?

The facetious answer would be that they are stuffing their faces with popcorn. But there has been a turning of the screw – never underestimate the threat placed on the DP World Tour and PGA Tour by LIV’s arrival. Even now, those traditional tours are paying unsustainable prize money as a legacy of changes LIV brought to the market for their super-sized fees. With LIV taking on water, they have struck back.

One measure adopted by the DP World Tour has been a re-tightening of their ‘conditional release’ protocols around dual members playing in LIV tournaments that conflict with one of their own. Tour sources have said it is ‘highly likely’ that six-figure fines would be reintroduced after being shelved for a number of players this year, such as Rahm and Hatton.

If stars stay with LIV and wish to retain their Ryder Cup status, they’d be hit hard in the pocket

It is an unenviable task facing O'Neil - and if more marquee players defect, LIV’s status will presumably shrink from desperate to either calamitous or non-existent

In short, if they stay with LIV and wish to retain their Ryder Cup status, they’d be hit hard in the pocket. That mechanism might be interpreted with some plausibility as a means of applying pressure to quit LIV.

Roads back to the PGA Tour remain tricky. Tour bosses Stateside have doubled down on their stance that a one-year period, commencing with a golfer’s last LIV event, would have to elapse before they can return. Patrick Reed took that one on the chin when his LIV deal expired and he will almost certainly play on the PGA Tour next season after a successful 2026 on the DP World Tour.

If more marquee players adopt that route, LIV’s status will presumably shrink from desperate to either calamitous or non-existent.

Sports.title: The 'boss', the 'brain', the 'general' - and now the 'next Rodri': The making of Ayyoub Bouaddi, Man City's £85.7m gem who has terrified opponents since he was 11 and wowed Brigitte Macron with his debating skills
Sports.content:
The 'boss', the 'brain', the 'general' - and now the 'next Rodri': The making of Ayyoub Bouaddi, Man City's £85.7m gem who has terrified opponents since he was 11 and wowed Brigitte Macron with his debating skills

Unlock more from our team inside the Manchester City camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

There’s a one in 13 gradient in the hills above Creil, 40 miles north of Paris where Ayyoub Bouaddi was brought up, and the story they tell there of him easing up it on his bicycle while his class-mates struggled with their gear ratios belongs to a wider narrative of the 18-year-old, who Manchester City have signed for £85.7million, being a genuinely exceptional boy.

The scouts and the academy managers always say that a strong family background helps dictate the trajectory of a football career and the young midfielder certainly has that. It was his father, a Moroccan-born bank executive, handball player and deputy mayor of Creil in the 2010s, who put him into gymnastics at the age of three and got him swimming and playing tennis before football took over. His mother, an HR manager in the aeronautical industry, was another constant presence.

He and his three sisters all excelled academically and skipped grades. ‘Ah, the Bouaddis! A name to make you smile! We teachers used to fight to attract them to our classes,' the headteacher of the local Creil primary school told L’Equipe some years back, when they came looking for the roots of a player who was proving to be a prodigy for Lille.

But familial influence cannot entirely explain the quality which – briefly at least, until Liverpool seal their £120million deal for Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola – has made him the most expensive export in French club history.

Other talents have blended academic intelligence with sport in the same way as Bouaddi, who is pursuing a degree in mathematics after excelling in his baccalaureate exams because, as he has put it: ’It's part of how I was raised and it keeps my mind sharp.’ Others have also displayed the articulacy which took him to the opulent setting of the Elysee Palace three years ago at the age of 15, to participate in a national debating competition for which, in the presence of Brigitte Macron, he declaimed on the topic ‘does the end always justify the means?’

But the intelligence of Bouaddi’s football – his capacity to ‘see the pictures’ as Graeme Souness often describes the visionary quality required in the deep-lying midfield position which he will take up at City – can’t be entirely rationalised in a process of cause and effect.

It was clear from an early age that Manchester City's new £85.7million man Ayyoub Bouaddi is an exceptional young man

The fee paid to Lille makes Bouaddi the most expensive export in French club football history,

At the levels of football he has accelerated up through, he has always seemed to have that split-second more time than anyone else. Everyone says this. From staff on the Jean-Mace primary school team – ‘he was the best because he varied his positioning and his shots, unlike the other kids who shot like bulls,’ his games teacher there observed – to coaches at AFC Creil, the eighth-tier French side who had him in their academy for nine years from the age of five. 'He was always playing above his age group because he understood immediately where to position himself, how to play, all the while remaining calm,’ said Malek Kismoune, one of the club’s officials.

When an Under 11s coach at the club suggested to the Under 15s coach that he was ready to play in that team, he was greeted with scepticism but that cognitive faculty made him an organiser of the boys four years higher up. ‘He was the general, and below him were soldiers he organised around him,’ the older boys' coach, Arman Doue Diop, said. Those extra seconds at his disposal gave Bouaddi what Diop calls an ‘emotional control’.

The boy’s reputation spread across the region so that opposition coaches would arrive at Creil, in the valley of the river Oise, and ask the home team, 'is your little guy with the headband here today?’ Diop nicknamed his protege ‘El Jefe’ (‘the boss’). Others called him ‘the brain’.

Lille, the top-flight team two hours’ drive away, first saw Bouaddi in Creil’s Under 10s and were relentless to ensure they signed him. The trajectory was maintained. His debut in the UEFA Conference League for Lille, at 16 years and three days old, made him the youngest player ever fielded in a European match. His Ligue 1 debut came 18 days later.

His first Champions League match against Real Madrid in October 2024 – a 1-0 victory in which he misplaced only one pass out of 44 – was a signature moment, sending him up against Luka Modric, one of several in his position he has adored. ‘The use of the outside of the boot, his vision, his intelligent positioning... he’s at the very highest level,’ Bouaddi has said of Modric.

The concern among many in France is whether, despite his prodigious talent, natural intelligence and command of English, Bouaddi is heading for the Premier League a year or two too soon, especially with that price tag and the expectation that he will be ‘the next Rodri’. All City have to go on are his three seasons in Ligue 1: not a huge body of evidence.

From a perceived value of £50million before the World Cup, where he excelled for Morocco against Brazil in the group stage, the asking price has almost doubled. Lille president Olivier Letang was keen to keep the player for another season at Lille on loan, but City knew they were losing Rodri and that there was stiff competition to sign him, so have paid an immense premium to bring him to Manchester now.

‘I just hope he doesn’t get burned and that it’s not too soon for him. It does seem early and a huge ask,’ says a British source who has brought many players to the Premier League. In a debate on the L’Equipe du Soir programme on Tuesday night entitled ‘Could Bouaddi be weighed down by the price of his transfer?’ the France Football analyst Dave Appadoo cautioned: ‘It’s not a good moment for Manchester City. Pep Guardiola has gone and they are under construction.’ But Bouaddi, for his part, told the French press that it’s ‘the perfect time to take the plunge’.

From a perceived value of £50million before the World Cup, where he excelled for Morocco against Brazil in the group stage, the asking price has almost doubled

His first Champions League match against Real Madrid in October 2024 – a 1-0 victory in which he misplaced only one pass out of 44 – was a signature moment

A national inquest is under way about the loss of France-born Bouaddi, who played at all the age levels, to the Morocco national side

Some at the top of the French game feel he will immediately prosper. ‘His intelligence serves him well on many levels,' says France Under 21s coach Gerald Baticle. ‘On the pitch, it allows him to simplify the game and clarify it by playing with one or two touches. It allows him to read the game in all midfield positions and gives him great versatility.'

A national inquest is under way about the loss of France-born Bouaddi, who played at all the age levels, to the Morocco national side, whose coach Mohamed Ouahbi courted him far more assiduously before the World Cup than outgoing France boss Didier Deschamps.

In the hills of Creil, they feel their fresh-faced boy will flourish wherever he goes and the local club now stands to earn an additional half a million euros (£430,000) in development fees for those nine years of work with him, under UEFA rules.

‘Even as a young child, he was a fan of English football, and Kevin De Bruyne was his role model,’ club president Slimane Layadi said of Bouaddi this week. ‘It feels completely surreal, and yet we knew he possessed immense talent that could take him to the very top.’

Sports.title: Aryna Sabalenka is the face of Gucci, wears £160k worth of diamonds on court and has a history of success in New York... now she must rediscover her 'tiger power' to end 2026 with a Slam
Sports.content:
A Hollywood film of Aryna Sabalenka’s 2025 US Open win might have had the subtitle: The Great Escape. Now, the world No1 must prepare for the sequel.

Last year, the Belarusian star had one last chance to win a major in New York at the third attempt, or else suffer the indignity of being the best player in the women’s game without winning a Grand Slam trophy in the calendar year. It took two sets to topple Amanda Anisimova, and after the deciding tiebreak, Sabalenka retained her crown on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Now Sabalenka finds herself back in a familiar position. Only this time the challenge is two-fold: defend her title and keep hold of her world No1 ranking.

This year’s task is an almighty gambit. Victory at Flushing Meadows is the only way for the Belarusian to assure a firm grip on the top spot, with closest rival Elena Rybakina snapping at her heels.

Rybakina may have beaten Sabalenka at the Australian Open in January, but she is far from the sole challenger. In-form home favourites Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula are both capable of causing trouble for Sabalenka, with the former having beaten her in two Slam finals – including the 2022 US Open.

Defeat to Rybakina at the start of the year preceded a remarkable run of form where Sabalenka became only the fifth woman to win the Sunshine Double of Indian Wells and Miami Open.

But then something snapped. Perhaps it was defeat in her Rome quarter-final against Hailey Baptiste that started the slide, ending not just her 15-match winning streak, but her incredible record of 19 straight victories in tie-breaks.

Aryna Sabalenka knows how to play the crowd and appeal to New York's celebrity culture - but can she claim another Grand Slam?

The tennis star is looking to retain her world No 1 status and also grow herself as a brand

An upturn in fortunes threatened briefly at the French Open with Sabalenka one set and 4-1 up in the second set of her quarter-final against Diana Schnaider. But the Belarusian disintegrated in spectacular fashion to lose the third to love.

At Wimbledon, she couldn’t make it past Naomi Osaka, who ended her run in the fourth round, her earliest Grand Slam exit since 2022. By now, Sabalenka’s season had entered crisis mode.

When Sabalenka is on song, her opponents feel as though they have been blasted off the court, caught up in the tornado of her aggression and left confused by the whip-cracking serves and bullets sent down from the baseline. Players who can’t absorb her power haven’t got a hope.

But when things aren’t going her way, Sabalenka has found it difficult to adjust her game plan mid-match, continuing to try to muscle her way through her problems and watching the unforced errors stack up.

Sabalenka has also become increasingly vulnerable to the best of her peers. Since April, she has only beaten six opponents ranked inside the top 40, and lost to seven of them.

There are no easy conclusions to draw on as to why Sabalenka is experiencing such a shift in her game. No public injury concerns, disruptions to her coaching team or changes in her personal life she has shared.

Instead, her level has dropped and she has been punished by the constant grind of the tour.

She has been a special guest of Gucci and Vogue in New York City this week

Her relationship with Brazilian entrepreneuer Georgios Frangulis is sure to make headlines

Sabalenka wore an exquisite set of Material Good jewellery at the French Open

The 28-year-old is increasingly becoming known for her fashion choices alongside tennis

Repeated collapses in deciding sets have forced Sabalenka's hand. She has chosen to work on her mental game, re-hiring the sports psychologist she dropped in 2022. Then, Sabalenka hired biomechanics specialist Gavin MacMillan in his place, who reworked her serve and helped her to win her first major at Australia in 2023. The 28-year-old described herself as her ‘own psychologist’ before claiming that title. Three years later, she needs a second opinion.

’It’s good to have someone back who knows you well, who can just say a couple things that are going to completely flip the page,’ Sabalenka told TIME this month, a ‘shocking reminder’ of the approach she knows she should have.

There have been suggestions that attempts to keep her cool on-court have blunted the ‘tiger power’ (she has a tattoo of the animal on her arm and decorates her Nike shoes with its stripes) key to her bombastic style.

When asked whether she felt that had been the case in her defeat to Osaka at Wimbledon, Sabalenka’s ‘no’ could hardly have been shorter or more dismissive. But watching her huff with obvious frustration during her defeat to Bejlek will not have eased concerns that her on-court state of mind is unusually unsettled.

After all, Sabalenka likes to be the best. She's used to it too, having sat No1 in the world for 96 consecutive weeks. Being the best has brought her magazine cover shoots, high-profile sponsors like Gucci and Audemars Piguet, exclusive Nike kits and her own Tiger Edition Wilson racquet. Sporting over £160,000-worth of rubies, emeralds, and diamonds on-court, as Sabalenka has done at all three Grand Slams this year as part of her deal with New York jeweller Material Good, is harder to pull off as world No7.

It’s fitting then, that once again, New York is the backdrop to Sabalenka’s last shot at glory in 2026.

The US Open is American to its core; bigger, brasher, and bolder than Melbourne, Paris, or London, sprinkled with the celebrity stardust that has turned the tournament into the hottest ticket in town for two weeks every year. Players who can harness the crowd’s energy, particularly during its floodlit night matches, come alive in the Big Apple.

Sabalenka's power has earned her the nickname 'the tiger' and she has a tattoo of the animal on her left forearm

Sabalenka's tiger tattoo pictured in 2023 in a Wimbledon first-round clash

And Sabalenka is nothing if not an entertainer. Two years ago, she offered spectators a round of drinks in exchange for their support through the tournament and she returns this year as their defending champion for a second time. With the crowd likely on her side again – at least until she faces a local talent – there is no better backdrop for Sabalenka to regain her form at a tournament that must rank as one of, if not, her favourite.

What remains beyond dispute is Sabalenka’s talent. The form storm will surely pass. There will likely be more Grand Slam titles in the future – and you would be a fool to write off Sabalenka from delivering a blockbuster curtain call in New York.

Sports.title: Tottenham defender Jan Paul van Hecke appears to blame pre-season trip to Australia and New Zealand for spate of injuries
Sports.content:
Tottenham defender Jan Paul van Hecke appears to blame pre-season trip to Australia and New Zealand for spate of injuries

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jan Paul van Hecke has revealed details of his hectic summer schedule which will fuel the theory that a pre-season tour Down Under seriously damaged Tottenham's preparations for the new Premier League season.

Van Hecke had a break of less than three weeks between defeat in the last 32 of the World Cup with the Netherlands in North America and taking off on the flight to New Zealand and Australia.

The Spurs centre-half, signed for £54million from Brighton, was eager to start on the latest chapter of his career, working again with Roberto De Zerbi.

Like all elite modern footballers, he appreciates the commercial and emotional value of connecting with the club's global fanbase, but he admits the travel has had a draining physical impact.

'Everyone knows it's the other side of the world,' said Van Hecke. 'To go there and see all the people, you see they love football, they love Tottenham, that also gives you a really good feeling.

'But for physical-wise, of course, it impacts your body. I also struggled for one or two weeks after and that's not ideal.'

Jan Paul van Hecke has suggested that Tottenham's pre-season trip to New Zealand and Australia has led to their injuries

Van Hecke played in every minute of the four Netherlands games in the World Cup, which ended in defeat after extra time and penalties against Morocco on June 30 in Mexico.

By July 24, he was landing in New Zealand with Spurs for a friendly in Auckland and two friendlies in Australia. Van Hecke's first appearance came in the final game of the tour against Chelsea in Sydney.

'I only had, like, two weeks, two-and-a-half weeks, it was a really short break, to be honest,' said Van Hecke. 'My first days were in New Zealand and Australia on the trip. But that's what you want. You want to play football, especially in a new club. I didn't want to miss anything in pre-season.'

New Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, on an identical schedule, did not play in pre-season after picking up an injury during the tour.

'He suffered a problem during the pre-season in Australia,' said De Zerbi last week. 'I don't know, the flight, I don't know, something, not a big problem, but not right to work.'

Van de Ven returned as a second-half substitute as Spurs beat Charlton 5-1 in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

Others, including £85m signing Mateus Fernandes, James Maddison, Dominic Solanke, Kevin Danso and Destiny Udogie suffered minor pre-season injuries which limited their fitness work.

Maddison, who missed most of last season with a cruciate knee ligament injury, then damaged a shoulder when he came on as a sub during the 3-0 defeat at Brentford on the opening day of the Premier League season and will be out for a couple of weeks more.

Micky van de Ven did not play in pre-season after picking up an injury on tour, but returned as Spurs thrashed Charlton 5-1 on Tuesday night

After the sobering Brentford defeat, De Zerbi said Van Hecke, Marcos Senesi and new £100m midfielder Sandro Tonali had for different reasons not been in the right physical condition.

Senesi played for Argentina in the World Cup final on July 19 and was not on the Spurs tour. Nor were Pedro Porro, who also played in the final, or Rodrigo Bentancur who was granted extended summer leave.

'At the beginning of Australia we played every three days,' said De Zerbi when asked why Tonali, who was neither at the World Cup nor injured, was behind the curve on fitness. 'The trip was 25/26 hours and the day after we couldn't work in the right condition.

'When we came here [back to London], we couldn't work immediately because there was a friendly game against Getafe. In the last two weeks, the players from the World Cup came and we worked in different situations, but I think he needs more time like JP.'

Tonali and Senesi were spared the Carabao Cup tie against Charlton to spend Tuesday working on an intense physical session. De Zerbi confirmed Tonali will start against Newcastle on Saturday.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher faces being declared bankrupt: HMRC take action over Sky Sports pundit's unpaid tax bill which could be in 'region of up to £800,000'
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher faces being declared bankrupt: HMRC take action over Sky Sports pundit's unpaid tax bill which could be in 'region of up to £800,000'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jamie Carragher faces being declared bankrupt over an unpaid tax bill which is reported to be in the region of £700,000 to £800,000.

HMRC filed a petition at the High Court in London on Wednesday to have the Sky Sports pundit and former England footballer declared bankrupt.

A spokesperson for HMRC told Daily Mail Sport: 'We take a supportive approach to dealing with customers who have tax debts and do everything we can to help those who engage with us to get out of debt, such as offering instalment plans. We only petition for bankruptcy as a last resort.'

HMRC added that it does not comment on individual cases.

Carragher, 48, is listed as a director at four firms and as a LLP Member for another. He is currently a regular pundit on the Premier League for Sky Sports and on the Champions League for US network CBS Sports.

He is also a regular on the Stick To Football podcast, run by Gary Neville's media business The Overlap.

Jamie Carragher, pictured with his wife Nicola, faces being declared bankrupt

The former Liverpool and England defender could be declared bankrupt over an unpaid tax bill

A spokesperson for Carragher told Daily Mail Sport: 'This is a private tax matter that should have been resolved sooner, and the appropriate steps are being taken today to settle it.

'It is understood that the matter will not proceed any further and will be resolved imminently.'

The BBC reported that the bill is around £700,000 to £800,000.

Carragher played for Liverpool throughout his club career, making 737 appearances and only scoring four goals – though he almost added a remarkable long-range fifth in his final game against QPR in 2013.

The centre-back played every second of Liverpool's iconic Champions League final comeback against AC Milan and is regarded as a club legend. His annual salary with the Reds is believed to have peaked at around £5million per year.

He also tallied 38 caps for England and went to the 2004 Euros, as well as the 2006 and 2010 World Cups.

The Bootle-born personality is the founder of the 23 Foundation, an organisation aiming to help young people in Merseyside, and is a co-founder of Football For Change, which helps to tackle child poverty through education, sport and training.

He is married to his wife of 21 years, Nicola, and together they have two children: James, 23, who plays as a defender for League One club Wigan Athletic, and actress and model Mia, 22.

Jamie and Nicola got married in 2005 at a 17th-century stately home on the Staffordshire-Shropshire border after their initial dream venue, Allerton Castle in Yorkshire, was partially destroyed by a fire.

Carragher has been married to his wife Nicola for 21 years and they have been together for 30

'We’ve been together for the best part of 30 years now and I’m really proud of that. It doesn’t always happen in football or if you’ve got a bit of a profile,' Carragher told The Times earlier this year.

'When I was a young lad I used to look at couples who had been together for years and think that would never be me. But here we are. Nicola is not just my wife, she’s also my best mate.

'I’ll admit I’ve been dead lucky; my professional life was full of amazing moments: playing for England, Liverpool’s 2001 treble, that amazing comeback in the 2005 Champions League final - from absolute despair to absolute joy, the stuff you dream of when you’re a kid.

'But it doesn’t matter what I’ve achieved or what you’re going to offer me, there is only one person I want by my side.'

Carragher also joined sixth-tier Merseyside club Marine in May to help out in an advisory capacity.

‘Marine is a proper community football club with good people involved and a clear vision for where it wants to go,’ said Carragher in a statement.

‘I’ve enjoyed watching the progress the club has made over recent years and I’m pleased to be able to support the club in an advisory capacity going forward.’

Carragher has built a successful career as a pundit but that wasn't always a guarantee - particularly after he accidentally spat in a 14-year-old girl's face, having been taunted by her father, in 2018.

Carragher's son, James, 23, plays as a defender for Wigan Athletic in League One

His daughter, Mia Carragher, 22, is an actress and model who has performed in The Hunger Games On Stage

He admitted that the controversy 'knocked me for six months' after being suspended as a pundit by Sky Sports, with the Liverpool legend revealing he saw a psychologist to help him deal with the episode.

There were widespread calls for Carragher to be sacked after his spit hit the 14-year-old girl, but he left his role at Sky briefly before returning six months later having reached out to the two involved to apologise.

He said he 'wasn't himself' during his period out of work and ended up visiting former Liverpool and England psychologist Steve Peters.

'Coming home from Old Trafford and then when I lost my job at Sky - I'm someone who's quite on the front foot, if someone attacks me,' he told Gary Neville on his YouTube show The Overlap.

'But that knocked me for six months. For a good six months I wasn't myself. I'd get up in the morning and just have that pain in my stomach, oh that did happen.

'I went to see Steve Peters after it. I felt really bad, embarrassed, my family, my Mum or Dad. And the kids. I remember getting back to the house that night when I'd been at Sky. I haven't seen the kids, they're at school, and you just get back and we all sat together and it was tough.

'Even though we're in the public eye, we're not the royals, [David] Beckham, big stars. You read them on the front page. When it's you, everywhere I went it felt like people were looking at me.'

Sports.title: Arsenal push for Julian Alvarez transfer as Atletico Madrid hand star brutal ultimatum
Sports.content:
Arsenal push for Julian Alvarez transfer as Atletico Madrid hand star brutal ultimatum

Arsenal are willing to go to the wire for Atletico Madrid strike Julian Alvarez, who has once again been told that his dream transfer to Barcelona remains off the table

View 3 Images The Julian Alvarez saga has taken a fresh twist (Image: Getty Images)

Arsenal transfer target Julian Alvarez has been told there is 'zero chance' Atletico Madrid will negotiate with Barcelona. The Argentine marksman was absent from training again, for the second successive day, on Thursday due to 'illness'.

‌



Tensions are threatening to reach boiling point at the Metropolitano after Atleti's board of directors once again blasted Barca, reminding them in another strongly-worded statement that a deal is totally off the table.

‌



It leaves Alvarez with two options: stay and potentially face a season of toxic fan scrutiny or sign for the Premier League champions. If the player opts to stay put, Atletico would ideally like the centre-forward to publicly address the club's supporters to smooth relations, following a turbulent summer.

‌



But one source close to the former Manchester City frontman feels the ugliness of the saga has reached the point of no return. Alvarez's personal frustration with Atletico started at the back end of last season when he received a pain-numbing injection in his ankle so that he could play in the Champions League semi-final second leg against Arsenal.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



The issue took time to heal, impacting his World Cup preparations and there's an underlying feeling that Alvarez's sacrifice was never truly valued by Atletico. Since then, the relationship has soured drastically.

Atleti are still prepared to do business with Arsenal, provided their valuation is met. Director of football Mateu Alemany was in London last week and is believed to have held direct talks with the Gunners.

Arsenal are willing to be patient and pull out all the stops to land the 26-year-old. They are prepared to raise cash by selling Gabriel Jesus and Gabriel Martinelli to help finance a move, however, the idea that they're on their knees and persistently pressing Alvarez for an answer is inaccurate.

‌



In fact, the legwork has long been done according to well-placed sources and a final decision remains firmly in the player's hands. The main stumbling block is believed to be around family logistics, plus Alvarez's desire to remain in Spain, ideally with Barcelona given he has already conquered England with Manchester City.

Should Julian Alvarez join Arsenal? Have your say in the comments section.

View 3 Images Julian Alvarez wants to leave Atletico Madrid - but only for Barcelona (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Jesus is no longer training alongside his team-mates while Martinelli is mulling over a mega-money switch to Al-Hilal. There's a sense Barcelona could yet turn attention to Viktor Gyokeres, who was an unused substitute against Coventry, after all remaining hope of signing Alvarez went up in smoke.

Mikel Arteta has told Arsenal's attackers to knock on his door if they require clarity over their future. He said when asked about the challenge of keeping everyone happy: "Very simple. Whatever you read, if you have a question, come and knock on my door, and I will tell you whether it is true or not.

"Because if, I don't know, in any position, if they read it, we now put a catalogue [of rumours] on all of these walls about all the players that we wanted in the last three months, I think we need the whole building to put it on.

‌



"So I think they know that there's so much speculation with a lot of players. If ever they feel the doubt of what we think of them and if we're going to recruit a player, I tell them straight away."

View 3 Images Julian Alvarez played with an injection against Arsenal in the Champions League semi-final second leg last season (Image: Getty )

Arteta was asked whether there was any substance to Spanish reports Alvarez had not answered his recent phone calls, responding: "You know I'm not going to make comments on that publicly, that would be doing a different job."

‌



The Spaniard insisted that personal circumstances sometimes dictate whether it's viable to land elite players, adding: "They come with a team, whether it's a family, with people that work with them. So, I think that whole ecosystem of the player has to be understood. And I think everybody around it, as well, has to feel that it's the right thing to do."

Arteta said of Martinelli's future: "It's another personal situation that we are dealing with, I think everyone knows and recognises, whatever the outcome it is, it's because everyone has agreed to that."

Sports.title: UEFA release punchy statement after threatening criminal proceedings against Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
UEFA release punchy statement after threatening criminal proceedings against Gianni Infantino

UEFA and their member associations met in Monaco on Thursday to discuss the fallout from the FIFA scandal and their continuing attempts to oust Gianni Infantino from power

View 3 Images UEFA still want to oust Gianni Infantino (Image: Chris Brunskill/Getty Images)

UEFA have released a lengthy statement confirming the decision to abandon a boycott of FIFA tournaments, but reaffirming their desire to oust Gianni Infantino from his position.

‌



UEFA and their 55 delegations met in Monaco on Thursday ahead of the Champions League draw. They have agreed that, while a boycott of FIFA tournaments is no longer necessary, the removal of Infantino as FIFA president remains paramount.

‌



The news comes on the same day that UEFA considered launching criminal proceedings against Infantino. European football's governing body is subpoenaing FIFA and the financial institutions involved in the failed plot to sell shares in tournaments in an attempt to obtain documents ahead of possible legal action in Switzerland.

‌



UEFA has now decided to seek a "responsible release of part of FIFA’s reserves" in an effort to increase the pressure on Infantino, who remains determined to seek re-election next year.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

UEFA's statement read: "The meeting reviewed the fallout from the FIFA President’s aborted attempt to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup to outside investors – a scheme which exposed a profound failure of judgement, an abuse of presidential power and a conception of leadership incompatible with the duties of the highest office in world football.

‌



"Those present unanimously mandated the UEFA President and Administration to pursue every available institutional, political and legal avenue necessary to secure fundamental reform, restore proper limits on presidential authority and ensure that FIFA is once again governed as an institution – not around one individual.

"The first step must be a genuinely independent external review of FIFA Forward Enterprise, with full access to all relevant documents, communications and decision-making records. FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino faces an uncertain future at FIFA with Aleksander Ceferin determined to oust him (Image: Harry Murphy/UEFA via Getty Images)

‌



"But the consequences of this crisis go beyond governance. The trust required to exercise the office of FIFA President has been broken and cannot be restored by withdrawing one proposal, issuing assurances or promising reform after the event. World football now needs new leadership capable of rebuilding that trust.

"UEFA will therefore continue working with Confederations, Member Associations and the wider football community – including fans, players, clubs, leagues and others – to shape the future of FIFA. Should the current FIFA President nevertheless seek another mandate, UEFA will join forces with its partner confederations to ensure that Member Associations are offered a credible alternative – one committed to integrity, accountability, development and genuine institutional change.

"FIFA has currently billions of dollars in reserves. This money belongs to the Member Associations. Together with other Confederations, UEFA will jointly explore a responsible release of part of FIFA’s reserves for the benefit of the Member Associations – while at the same time ensuring that any proposal preserves FIFA’s financial stability. The question is therefore why the FIFA President believed he needed outside investors to expand development funding.

‌



"The delegates were also informed that FIFA has now confirmed in writing to UEFA that the FIFA Forward Enterprise project has been 'irrevocably and permanently withdrawn' and that it 'will not re-appear in any other shape, construction, name or form'.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino is still clinging onto power (Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/FIFA via Getty Images)

"Having now secured the two assurances it required from FIFA on 30 July, and following consultation with its National Associations, UEFA has therefore agreed to suspend, on a provisional basis, the withdrawal by European teams from FIFA competitions in the coming season, including the Women’s U20 World Cup, U17 World Cup and the Women’s U17 World Cup. This position will remain under constant review and may be reconsidered immediately if circumstances so require.

‌



"While the immediate question of participation has now been resolved, the underlying crisis has not. The abandonment of FFE does not erase the deception, intimidation and abuse of power that made it possible. Nor does it restore the confidence that has been lost.

"This is not a choice between good governance and football development. Nor is this about Europe seeking greater power within FIFA. It is simply about ensuring that no part of world football – large or small, those with more and those with less – is dependent on the power of one individual.

"FIFA has a fundamental responsibility to support every Member Association and this responsibility must be strengthened, not weakened. But development is an institutional obligation – not a presidential favour – and no Member Association should ever have to choose between the resources to which it is entitled and the freedom to exercise its own judgement.

Article continues below

"UEFA’s position remains unequivocal: whether it is the World Cup or an Under-15 tournament, FIFA’s competitions are not for sale. Neither is the governance of our game. FIFA’s development resources must likewise never become instruments of personal or political influence. They belong to world football and must be protected by transparent, objective rules.

"FIFA must once again be governed as an institution serving football – not operate as an instrument of individual power."

Sports.title: Moses Itauma slams Filip Hrgovic's 'schoolboy banter' after rival's brutal promise
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma slams Filip Hrgovic's 'schoolboy banter' after rival's brutal promise

Filip Hrgovic has attempted to get under Moses Itauma's skin throughout the week, but the young Brit refuses to engage in all of the pre-fight theatrics

View Image Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic face off ahead of their fight (Image: Queensberry)

Moses Itauma is unfazed by Filip Hrgovic's trash talk after the Croatian promised to send the youngster “back to high school."

‌



The pair will meet for the vacant IBF heavyweight title in a mouthwatering showdown at the O2 Arena in London on Saturday night. Itauma, 21, will be looking to make history this weekend by becoming the second youngest heavyweight world champion of all time.

‌



But Hrgovic will prove to be the Brit's toughest challenge to date. Throughout fight week, the Croatian brawler has decided to poke the bear in a bid to get under Itauma's skin. The 34-year-old believes a win for Itauma on fight night will be terrible for his soul, while also labelling his upcoming foe as 'delusional.'

‌



Itauma admitted to reporters, including Mirror Fighting, on Tuesday evening that his antics were starting to get on his nerves just a tad. The two hard-hitters came face-to-face on Thursday afternoon for a pre-fight press conference in London - with Hrgovic trying his best to spark a reaction from the Chatham scrapper.

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

But Itauma refused to engage with any pre-fight theatrics. When asked if his rival had rattled him, the 21-year-old replied: “Nah man. At the end of the day talk is cheap. He has just got schoolboy banter and that’s it. You’ve got to keep rolling.”

‌



Olympic medalist Hrgovic was quick to hit back by vowing to send Itauma back to school, stating: “I am just telling you facts. I am not playing any games. I just tell you what I think in the moment. Like I said, I am not so smart to play these mind games. I think he is a kid, he is not mature enough and I think I am the man. I am a much better age, much more experience and yeah, that is it. No mind games. God willing you know I will beat him, I’ll smash the kid on Saturday and send him back to high school.

“He has said he wants some props but I have come here to London, on his territory, this kid everyone is avoiding. I have come here for a fight and – against all the odds – I believe in myself. I am fighting the guy they call ‘The next Mike Tyson.’ So give me some props, I am going to smash the kid.”

Anthony Joshua informed of crucial mistake made before Tyson Fury fight READ MORE :

Boxing fans backed to boycott Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight READ MORE :

Despite all the talk of creating history with a win, Itauma has put such remarks to one side, unbothered by the accolades and is solely focused on becoming the second man to topple Hrgovic. “I want to first address that I am not trying to become the second youngest heavyweight champion of the world, I am trying to beat Filip Hrgovic,” he explained.

Article continues below

“Second of all, this fight is what I wanted. I asked Queensberry for so long. I think it is a style match-up I reckon I can thrive on, the pressure I can thrive on and it is just waiting to fight. Obviously the world title is an achievement and an accolade. And that is a plus one, but my sole focus is Hrgovic.

“If I ain’t going to beat Hrgovic, it doesn’t matter about the world title and it doesn’t matter about the noise or nothing. My job is to be victorious on fight night. I am ready to rock and roll.”

Sports.title: Jockey disqualified for five years for betting makes comeback with new name
Sports.content:
Jockey disqualified for five years for betting makes comeback with new name

Terry Treichel, who rode over 1,200 winners, pleaded guilty to 32 rule breaches, including 30 which involved betting, when he was banned

View Image Jockey Terry Treichel will return to the saddle under his legal name of Daniel Smith (Image: DAN PELED/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock)

A jockey who was disqualified for five years for betting offences is to return to the saddle under a new name.

‌



Terry Treichel has ridden over 1,200 winners in Australia and is a former champion in the Northern Territory where he was latterly based.

‌



In 2021 he pleaded guilty to 32 rule breaches, including 30 which involved betting for which he was subsequently banned. He was originally banned for eight years but served five. During an investigation into allegations of betting activity, Thoroughbred Racing Northern Territory stewards discovered Treichel had changed his name by deed poll to Daniel Jack Smith.

‌



Willie Mullins announces retirement of dual Gold Cup hero Galopin Des Champs READ MORE :

He had betting accounts under the name Smith with a number of bookmakers through which he placed 27 bets on races he was riding in as Terry Treichel and 168 on other races.

The 46-year-old pleaded guilty to all the charges issued against him while a licensed jockey between July 2019 and December 2020. These included falsely declaring in his licence application that his name was Terry Treichel when in fact he had changed his identity.

Article continues below

The inquiry notice said at the time: “This is a unique set of circumstances not seen before in Australian racing. The covering of a change of identity and a subsequent volume of betting whilst licensed as a jockey is unprecedented.”

The ban, backdated to start from December 2020, was completed in December last year and the jockey applied to be relicensed under his legal name, Daniel Jack Smith, in New South Wales where he rode earlier in his career.

RacingNSW announced on Thursday: “Daniel Smith, who formerly rode under his previous name of Terry Treichel, has been passed to resume riding in races and has accepted rides at the Taree race meeting on Monday 31 August.”

Sports.title: Bradley Barcola 'farce' continues trend that has transformed Liverpool's reputation
Sports.content:
Bradley Barcola 'farce' continues trend that has transformed Liverpool's reputation

Liverpool once had a reputation of being one of the shrewdest recruitment teams in world football - but a change of approach has led to some very differing results

View 4 Images Bradley Barcola is closing in on a massive transfer to Liverpool (Image: Getty)

Liverpool have long since judged their standards alongside those belonging to bitter rivals Manchester United.

‌



European Cups, league title wins and the talents of managers and footballers alike have been barometers the two English giants like to measure themselves against.

‌



Liverpool have held the upper hand in recent times. The Merseysiders have been English champions twice since United last managed the feat in 2013.

‌



And have also won a sixth Champions League/European Cup, which is now double the amount of times United have lifted club football's biggest trophy.

And it wasn't too long ago Liverpool's owners were sitting back and watching United spend cash like it was going out of fashion, on expensive signings who turned out to be a complete waste of money.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

There is no point listing them. We don't have enough time.

In that same period, Liverpool conducted their own business with ruthless stealth. Big targets were kept under the radar, until a deal was so close to being completed it would be made public.

‌



This happened with the likes of Virgil Van Dijk, Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson and Luis Diaz, to name but a few.

Liverpool resembled a well-oiled machine who got the job done - and on their terms. But times have changed.

View 4 Images Liverpool were once heralded as the transfer kings - but in recent years their crown has slipped (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

‌



Because in recent seasons Liverpool have decided to take a change of tact, not to mention a leaf out of United's soiled book.

We know new investor Jeff Bezos has more dollars than sense, but he's not been around long enough to be blamed for what can only be described as a haphazard approach to luring new talent to Anfield.

Last summer Liverpool broke the British transfer record not once, but twice in a matter of weeks. Florian Wirtz arrived for £116m, before Alexander Isak followed suit at a cost of £125m.

‌



Both have been huge disappointments. And fast forward 12 months and Liverpool could be about to break their own record again.

Negotiations are taking place with PSG about a deal for Bradley Barcola, with a deal likely to come close to the fee paid to Newcastle for Isak.

View 4 Images Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak both struggled in their first seasons with Liverpool

‌



Under normal circumstances, such a move would leave supporters feeling overwhelmed excitement.

The problem is, Liverpool have turned to Barcola in desperation less than a week before the transfer window closes, having pulled out of the bidding for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh.

Liverpool bid £60m, but Brighton wanted £80m. Brighton's track record of making profit on previously unheralded talent is second to none.

‌



But despite this, Brighton knew on this occasion at least, how desperate Liverpool had become - and looked to take full advantage. This isn't Brighton's fault. It's Liverpool's.

Liverpool have created a situation where every selling club now knows how keen they are to make quick signings. Millions will be added to the value of a target.

‌



What makes the scenario even more baffling is that Liverpool knew in March Mo Salah would be leaving. How has it taken this long for them to attempt to sign another right winger?

The gaps in the squad are clear for all to see. New manager Andoni Iraola needs a new winger, defensive midfielder and forward.

But Liverpool have still not signed a player they've been negotiating for since the end of the World Cup. The situation is farcical.

‌



But perhaps the most negligible aspect of the whole shambles is how owners FSG have allowed sporting director Richard Hughes to continue in charge of signings, despite the fact he's expected to leave in the coming weeks?

View 4 Images Richard Hughes remains in charge, despite the fact he is set to leave Anfield (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Should he have not been put on gardening leave instead?

‌



Liverpool finished fifth in the table last season, 25 points behind champions Arsenal. And nothing they've done this summer suggests this gap is going to be closed anytime soon.

Liverpool can change their squad all they like. But it's a change of approach to how this is done, which is needed the most.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
