Sports.title: Why McLaren thinks Norris is even better now than his F1 title-winning year
Sports.content:
Just over a month ago, it seemed pretty clear that McLaren was going to be unable to successfully defend the Formula 1 drivers’ title in 2026.

Coming into the Hungarian Grand Prix, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli led the standings with 204 points to his name, while the papaya drivers combined couldn’t even match that tally – Lando Norris was on 103, Oscar Piastri on 92.

However, McLaren introduced a substantial upgrade package at the Hungaroring, focusing on front and rear corner bodywork as well as introducing a floor and rear wing.

The consequence was immediate: Norris won from pole and repeated the feat in Zandvoort, courtesy of a round-the-outside move on challenger Antonelli in Turn 1. He is now ‘just’ 83 points adrift of the championship lead.

The straightforward conclusion would be that McLaren’s updates simply delivered, but team principal Andrea Stella is adamant that Norris is consistently extracting the most from the MCL40 – even hinting at the Briton outperforming his machinery.

“Lando is driving and operating at a very high level, in absolute sense, in relation to a Formula 1 world champion,” Stella commented following the Dutch Grand Prix. “He's driving at the level of a world champion.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“And like I always say for Lando, what I like the most of his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving. And especially after the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but is a way of working with Lando, for Lando, and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular. And this approach has led Lando to continuous improvements.

“So it's almost like I see Lando stronger and stronger race by race. Because this weekend was nowhere near a weekend in which we could fight for the victory for granted, especially after having seen the performance in the sprint.

“But we invested in trying to understand where was the opportunity from a tyre exploitation point of view, and car improvement. Actually, both drivers improved from this point of view, but unfortunately a question mark remains as to the behaviour of the second stint of Oscar.

“So there's overall a positive trajectory for both, but at the moment Lando is capable of maximising the performance in qualifying trim. If we think the start of 2025, this had become a bit of a concern that he overcame. And then, when you have conditions in which the car slides in the race, there's not much grip, he is the master in this kind of conditions.”

Qualifying performance indeed is a key point to look at.

Over the course of the 2025 season, the McLaren drivers were evenly matched on one lap, with their qualifying head-to-head (including sprint qualifying) a perfect 15-15 split.

As F1 switched to new machinery in 2026, Norris was down 3-1 going into the unexpected April break. But since then, the reigning champion has thrashed his team-mate 12-1, with Piastri quicker in Monaco only. The average gap between them is not huge – 0.128s – but it is consistently to Norris’ advantage, amid the Australian’s latest struggles.

Lando Norris' move on Kimi Antonelli Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT Images via Getty Images

Yet, Stella reckons what really has been making the difference is Norris’ enhanced state of mind, leading to perfected racecraft.

“If you want to look at Lando from another angle, I would say that definitely he is now expressing a higher level of assertiveness as he drives,” the Italian pointed out. “You know, the manoeuvre to pass Antonelli today is a really good demonstration of that. He's demonstrating more self-confidence.

“This is interesting, and I quite like it – the self-confidence sometimes is not demonstrated by being the most aggressive. Sometimes you are self-confident when you think like, ‘You know what? I'm not going to have a fight now because I may lose in this fight. It's a very long race. See you at the end of the race.’

“It's this confidence in your means, in your strength, that I quite like. Which means that sometimes you are actually the one backing off when the situation becomes too risky.

“We need to remember that in the last couple of races that he won, he didn't defend the pole position. He was actually second at the end of the first lap. But I did not hear or perceive any decay in his confidence, as to the fact that he was fast and he was just preparing his opportunity to then cash in on his competitiveness. So I think assertiveness and confidence are probably the two characteristics that he has improved the most from a non-technical, non-operational point of view.”

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording and Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: Alpine completes F1 2027 line-up with Colapinto renewal
Sports.content:
Alpine has retained Franco Colapinto for the 2027 Formula 1 season, signing a new deal with the Argentinian for a second full-time campaign.

The 23-year-old will remain alongside Alpine’s lead driver Pierre Gasly, who has been Colapinto’s team-mate since he joined the French marque for round seven of 2025.

Colapinto faced a big 2026 season as he aimed to impress team executive Flavio Briatore after an up and down 2025 campaign.

But he rose to the challenge with more consistent performances aboard Alpine's vastly improved car, which allowed him to add 19 points to Gasly's tally of 44.

Colapinto took his career best result in Montreal, where he finished sixth, and currently holds 12th in the drivers' standings after 12 rounds of this year.

"I am very pleased to remain with this team in 2027. I feel very happy and very settled here and it's been even better that we have made significant progress this year compared to last," Colapinto said.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine, Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"We have a lot more milestones to reach and I know the team is working so hard in finding performance and making the car better and better. Our long-term goals are obvious – to compete and win - and I am grateful to the team, Flavio and Steve [Nielsen], for the trust placed in me to be one of its drivers going into the future. I'm looking forward to seeing how everything plays out and focusing on my job on-track first and foremost.”

Following a nine-race debut stint with Williams in 2024, replacing Logan Sargeant, Colapinto was brought on board by Alpine for 2025 as part of a suite of reserve drivers behind Gasly and rookie Jack Doohan.

But Doohan was jettisoned after the Miami Grand Prix in favour of Colapinto, who initially struggled to perform much better than the Australian as Alpine slid towards the rear of the field.

Yet his promising underlying pace and generous backing from Argentinian sponsors helped keep Colapinto in the seat for 2026.

"We are very happy to confirm our driver line-up for 2027 with Franco staying as a race driver alongside Pierre," Briatore added. "For me, having consistency is very important.

"We are now settled from a driver point of view and I have said many times that, while this is an important piece of the puzzle, the most significant we have to get right is designing and building a fast race car which absolutely remains our number one priority.

"We have seen Franco truly grow and mature into a great driver this year. His results in Miami and Montreal especially confirmed what I already knew: Franco belongs in Formula 1 and he belongs at this team. I expect both Franco, and Pierre, to continue doing a fantastic job on track and for the entire team to push relentlessly until we are fighting, and winning, at the front end of this sport."

Sports.title: Why Gasly’s Monaco case is so complex – and why the outcome could take weeks
Sports.content:
Almost three months after the Monaco Grand Prix, the result of Formula 1’s most prestigious race is still not definitive.

Pierre Gasly’s penalty for pitlane speeding was overturned in the week after the race, restoring him to third place at the expense of Isack Hadjar, but that was far from the end of the matter.

McLaren and Red Bull have since challenged the decision before the FIA’s International Court of Appeal (ICA), with the hearing taking place on Wednesday.

However, all parties have indicated that a verdict should not be expected in the immediate future. A decision - or at least an explanation of that decision - could take another two to three weeks, which is standard procedure for an ICA case.

What was more unusual was that the hearing lasted the entire day. The ICA heard the arguments from all sides, but it will take time to reach a considered judgement. This is due to the complexity of the legal arguments involved, but also the wider implications for F1, which McLaren in particular has explicitly linked to some general 'principles of fairness'.

Hadjar and Oscar Piastri both lost positions and therefore championship points as a result of Gasly’s time penalty being overturned, but according to both teams, there is a lot more at stake. Both have portrayed the events in Monaco as setting a dangerous precedent.

Gasly has been handed Hadjar's trophy, but nearly three months later he still doesn't know whether he is allowed to keep it Photo by: Erik Junius

Team principal Andrea Stella spoke at Zandvoort of a "double intent" behind his team’s appeal, with the matter extending beyond the points lost in both championships.

"We think that the process that happened after the race in Monaco is a process that needs to be reviewed from a fairness [point of view] for all competitors. The fact that the penalty was removed introduces some significant elements of concern," McLaren’s team principal said.

"There's obviously more related to this case. It can go into the technical aspects of how the pit limiter speed was calculated. But for me, at a high level, it's more the fairness and the principle that needs to be clarified and possibly reinstated. I think what happened sets some significant concerns."

Those final words refer to the precedent that drivers and teams could in future be encouraged not to serve time penalties on track, but instead challenge them after the chequered flag.

By not doing so, Piastri and George Russell were among those who ended up paying the price in Monaco.

The Mercedes driver unsuccessfully attempted to serve his time penalty, incurring an additional drive-through penalty in the process. It ultimately left him without points in the principality, and with no opportunity to do anything about it afterwards – even though Mercedes explored the options.

Furthermore, the teams feel that as long as the measurements have been incorrect for everyone, accepting that the system has certain flaws is part of the responsibility that comes with competing in a championship – so as not to open a can of worms.

According to McLaren and Red Bull, the appeal also concerns the wider implications and the fairness of the sport Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

According to McLaren and Red Bull, that sets a precedent, although the ICA judges are effectively faced with choosing between two evils. It must be said that an ideal solution for the Monaco race is no longer really available.

After the Monaco GP, it was established that the pitlane measurement was inaccurate, with a discrepancy of 77cm in the distance between two timing loops. This meant the speed measurements were incorrect and that it could not be proven that drivers such as Gasly had actually exceeded the limit.

Knowing that the measurement was wrong makes it difficult, with the benefit of hindsight, to reinstate Gasly’s time penalty once more.

At the same time, however, other drivers who may have been wrongly penalised cannot get that lost time back, meaning that getting to a fair result for all parties is virtually impossible, no matter what the ICA’s decision will be.

Sports.title: Why Red Bull has F1's top-ranked engine, and what it reveals about ADUO
Sports.content:
The FIA’s ADUO announcement – the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities for Formula 1 power units – had been a long time coming. In fact, after the results of the first period were shared with all teams and manufacturers at the Monaco Grand Prix, the press release was ready to go in exactly this form. The only thing missing was the sentence about the second period.

The long wait was due to Red Bull expressing considerable dissatisfaction with the outcome of the first period behind the scenes, with even Oliver Mintzlaff getting involved.

However, Red Bull had very few ways to challenge the result. The system undeniably has its weaknesses – more on those later – but the teams and manufacturers themselves agreed to it last year.

Red Bull Ford Powertrains could therefore only request a factual review, but that did not change the outcome either. FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis said the governing body’s measurements had proved correct, despite Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies arguing that there was "not a single data point" showing that Red Bull had the best engine.

Among other things, Red Bull pointed to its deficit at power-sensitive tracks. According to Mekies, that deficit was greater than at circuits such as Monaco and the Hungaroring, where the power units play a less significant role. In reality, that picture is also related to energy management at energy-starved tracks and how good – or not – a power unit is in that respect.

Those are factors the FIA does not take into account, as the ADUO ranking only measures the power output of the internal combustion engine. The FIA cannot publicly reveal too much about the exact measurement methods and data, not least because they involve intellectual property and confidential information.

"Due to the confidential nature of this information, no further details on power unit performance index measurements will be communicated," the FIA statement reads.

The ADUO system was intended to help manufacturers lagging far behind, such as Honda, but has become a political battleground in F1 Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

As a result, the press release merely states that Mercedes falls into the 2%-4% deficit category, which earns it one upgrade opportunity in 2026 and another in 2027. Ferrari, Audi and Honda all fall into the plus-4% deficit category, which gives them two new homologations – and therefore updates – in the current season and two more next year.

In addition, all of these manufacturers receive extra financial headroom under the budget cap for power unit manufacturers. For Mercedes High Performance Powertrains, that means a cost cap allowance of up to $3m, while Ferrari receives up to $4.65m.

Notably, an additional safety net has been introduced specifically for manufacturers in serious trouble – such as Honda. A manufacturer more than 10% behind the best ICE would receive a cost cap allowance of up to $11m per ADUO period, plus an additional $8m for 2026 as a whole, but it was understood after the first period that Honda did not fully meet the criteria for that back then.

The Japanese manufacturer can nevertheless live with the outcome of the FIA’s analysis.

"I think the number we received from the FIA looks reasonable. I would say that number is fair. And also, thanks to ADUO, we are now working hard to develop our engine," chief engineer Shintaro Orihara told Autosport.

FIA wanted to factor in championship standings – has Red Bull’s stance backfired?

The second period subsequently did not result in any additional tokens being handed out, indicating that the picture has not changed significantly.

For Red Bull, this could theoretically mean one of two things: either the newcomer is still right at the top of the ICE ranking, or its deficit is less than 2%. The latter scenario would not yield a token either.

However, Autosport understands that the ranking and the gaps between the manufacturers remain broadly the same. This means Red Bull Ford Powertrains is indeed rated by the FIA as having the best internal combustion engine in F1.

Mercedes has the best power unit in F1, as Toto Wolff also acknowledged, but has nevertheless received a token Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has acknowledged that the Silver Arrow has the best power unit, but as is well known, ADUO only looks at the internal combustion engine. This immediately highlights one of the system’s weaknesses: the measurement only concerns the ICE, but the upgrade opportunities consequently awarded go much further and also cover the electrical components.

Red Bull is still lacking on the electrical side, but because it has the most powerful ICE, it cannot do anything about that. And so the newcomer is effectively checkmated.

It is a weakness of the system, but the FIA cannot fully be blamed for it. Tombazis has told media that he was open to taking more parameters into account, but teams and manufacturers pushed to keep the system as simple as possible.

That includes the size of the turbo, an aspect Tombazis wanted to factor in. In practice, that did not happen, allowing Ferrari to benefit. The Italian manufacturer had an advantage off the line at the start of this year, thanks to its smaller turbo, but paid a price in terms of power. ADUO does, however, allow Ferrari to work on that, especially now that it has received two tokens.

It raises the question of whether that is fair given that these are deliberate design choices, but that is simply how the system works.

Moreover, the FIA intended to take the championship standings into account. After all, ADUO was not designed to give the dominant force even more upgrade opportunities, but according to insiders, Red Bull was among those opposed to factoring in the championship standings.

That was understandable based on what was known at the time, but in the current reality it has come back to bite Red Bull. When the discussions took place last year, it was not unreasonable for Red Bull to think as follows: 'As a newcomer, we are probably going to be more than 2% behind, but if the chassis is good, we could still be relatively high up in the championship standings. In that case, it would logically be advantageous if the FIA did not take that aspect into account.'

Red Bull’s chassis has proved to be below par, which means, with hindsight, it would have been better for them had the championship standings been taken into account Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

In practice, however, the situation is the opposite: Red Bull’s ICE is highly competitive, but its chassis was below par at the start of this year, meaning the championship standings do not make for pretty reading from Red Bull’s perspective and could actually have provided a lifeline.

FIA acknowledges weaknesses in ADUO system – what’s next?

All of this explains why Red Bull is the only manufacturer not allowed to work on its power unit during the season. There is still one opportunity to change that: the third period, which ends after the Mexican Grand Prix.

Red Bull, however, does not control its own fate, which instead depends on its rivals. If they do not use their upgrades on the ICE – Mercedes in particular – and do not suddenly, for whatever reason, extract more from it than they have so far, Red Bull will remain checkmated.

The ADUO results have therefore not only revealed something about Red Bull, but also exposed some weaknesses of the system. The FIA readily acknowledges that as well, for example when Autosport asked Tombazis in Hungary whether the system was currently working as it should.

"I think our measurement, in my opinion, has proven to be very accurate," he replied. "With that said, has everything worked fine? No, because obviously people are not happy and so on. Do we need to think about improvements in the future? Yes, I would say so."

When announcing the results, Tombazis once again indicated that the system may need to be overhauled for the coming years: "This is the first year of ADUO so naturally there are areas which we may evolve over time, in discussion with all the PU manufacturers."

ADUO will be assess for a third time after the Mexican GP Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Behind the scenes, however, that process is not yet very advanced and will need to lead to more concrete proposals in the coming months.

In that respect, the current outcome is perhaps the clearest possible illustration of some of the system’s weaknesses: the manufacturer with the best overall power unit in F1 does receive development opportunities based on its ICE deficit, while a manufacturer that is lacking on the electrical side is not allowed to do anything about it because of the ADUO figures.

It provides food for thought for the longer term, but for now the manufacturers and teams – including Red Bull – also need to look in the mirror, given that they agreed to this system last year.

Sports.title: Red Bull officially named F1's best engine as FIA makes ADUO results public
Sports.content:
The FIA has published the results of the latest Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) evaluation for Formula 1 power units - with Red Bull-Ford still considered the benchmark.

According to the governing body’s analysis, which is inclusive of all races from the Melbourne season opener to round 11 at Budapest, the Red Bull-Ford internal combustion engine is the most powerful in F1.

Mercedes is 2-4% down on power, while Audi, Ferrari and Honda are more than 4% adrift; the Japanese manufacturer’s new powertrain, which was introduced at last weekend’s Dutch Grand Prix, was not taken into account.

After the first quarter of the 2026 season, Mercedes had been granted one additional homologation for 2026 and 2027 each, while Audi, Ferrari and Honda received two each for this year and next year too. This consists in additional cost cap allowance and further dyno tests.

However, no official announcement had been made. While the FIA did confirm the ADUO ranking today on Wednesday 26 August, no additional homologations have been awarded this time.

“The FIA has undertaken thorough and exhaustive analysis as part of our ADUO review process,” said the FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“With the release of the findings of Period 2, we are confident that, based on the quality of the data, its analysis is incredibly robust, giving us a high level of confidence in our findings.

“We also have to respect the confidentiality and intellectual property of the teams and their power unit manufacturers in disseminating any details from the findings.

“This is the first year of ADUO so naturally there are areas which we may evolve over time, in discussion with all the PU manufacturers.”

ADUO has been at the receiving end of criticism with an obvious drawback being that it only considers the internal combustion engine, which is not the only performance differentiator in F1’s current hybrid power units.

Mercedes, not Red Bull-Ford, has widely been considered to have the most powerful engine, which even Silver Arrows boss Toto Wolff admitted - though he perhaps let his guard down when he made that comment, given he wasn’t referring to ADUO.

Red Bull in particular has been dismayed by the lack of opportunities afforded by the current ranking, requesting a review of the post-Canada results - which was unsuccessful.

“Toto is right. I also think that they have the most powerful power unit,” said Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies after the Belgian Grand Prix. “And certainly they had a sizeable advantage on the straight this weekend again.

“But it's not the first weekend. They have an advantage on the straight most weekends and this weekend a bit more with the track sensitivity. As you said, the second period closing in Budapest in a week's time. We'll see what's happening.”

Sports.title: McLaren rejects Mercedes claim it cannot afford aggressive upgrades in F1 2026
Sports.content:
McLaren Formula 1 team principal Andrea Stella is sceptical about his Mercedes counterpart Toto Wolff's claims that Mercedes doesn't have the available budget to fast-track car upgrades.

In recent weeks Ferrari and especially McLaren have made drastic improvements to their 2026 cars, allowing them to take two wins apiece and put significant pressure on the erstwhile dominant Mercedes team.

Compared to its rivals, Mercedes has only trickled out a minimal quantity of aero upgrades, planning to bring a bigger package to October's Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia.

That delay exposes Mercedes to further damage over the next three September rounds in Italy, Spain and Azerbaijan. But when asked by Autosport after the Dutch Grand Prix if those development decisions are now starting to become increasingly uncomfortable in light of McLaren's rapid progress, Wolff said his team's hands are tied with how Brackley has partitioned its $215m cost cap allowance.

"We haven't got the money to put developments on the car. I said before that we are trying to evenly split that through the season based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimising the championship points. But we just can't do what we can't do," the Austrian said.

"You will see towards the end of the season whether they are going to be able to deploy as much stuff onto the car as they do now. Someone might have a different strategy in spending more at the beginning and the middle of the year than towards the end."

When those comments were put to McLaren chief Stella, he replied: "I would like to believe you, but I actually don't believe you."

Andrea Stella cast doubt on Mercedes' claims Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

Stella was sceptical because the changes to the 2027 power unit regulations, which move F1 towards a 57-43 split between combustion power and electrical energy, but also affect certain areas of the car design, come with an additional $3m cost cap allowance to be used in 2026 or 2027 to help teams prepare for the changes.

If Mercedes really wanted to, Stella said, it could use that allowance to put upgraded car parts into production.

"All teams will have an allowance in their reporting for the cost cap," Stella said. "And if I'm not wrong, it's like three million that you can use in the 2026 reporting for cost cap calculations. And I'm sure that Mercedes, having seen that their rivals are kind of elevating the game, I'm sure they will now cash in on their development that surely is happening in the ground.

"I'm sure the car in the wind tunnel is quite a bit faster than the car they have on track and they will want to now convert some of this potential into upgrades that make it to the real car. So, I'm just pretty sure that they will have upgrades. Obviously, it would be good if not, but I don't even want to think about it..."

Sports.title: Hamilton claims Dutch GP radio outbursts weren't "the best version of me"
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says his Dutch Grand Prix frustration "wasn’t the best version of me" as he apologised to his Ferrari Formula 1 team for it boiling over on team radio.

During the second half of the race, Hamilton grew increasingly frustrated at the lack of strategy updates from Ferrari, especially once he got stuck behind team-mate Charles Leclerc, who was slower than the Briton on older tyres.

“Great way of wasting time guys, good job,” a sarcastic Hamilton fired over on the airwaves once Leclerc finally pitted on lap 43.

After the race, Hamilton said Ferrari still had steps to make on race weekend execution, pointing to Mercedes' much slicker swap between George Russell and Kimi Antonelli as a source of inspiration.

But for Ferrari, the picture was a little bit more complicated than that, as the team was planning to pit Leclerc earlier but had to extend his stint for another lap to avoid traffic.

At the same time, the plan for Hamilton was to stay on track until the end of the race, but team principal Fred Vasseur explained Ferrari didn't want to alert its rivals to its strategy, so it decided not to communicate it straight away.

Charles Leclerc leading Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Taking to social media, Hamilton has now apologised to his team for his heated radio exchanges.

"I’ve listened back to some of my radio and TV comments. In the heat of the moment frustration can come out, especially when you care as deeply as I do," Hamilton wrote. "But that wasn’t the best version of me. I take responsibility for that, and I’ll be better.

"That passion comes from believing in this team, the people in it, and what we’re building together. The direction is clear. The belief is there. And the fight is absolutely still on."

Hamilton was buoyed by Ferrari's recent progress as its relentless car upgrade programme has allowed both him and Leclerc to win a grand prix, with Hamilton holding third in the drivers' championship on equal points with second-placed Russell.

"I’m incredibly proud of everyone back at the factory who continues to bring updates, find performance and push us forward," the seven-time world champion added.

"To the team at the track, thank you. The commitment and effort never go unnoticed. We still have work to do, particularly over one lap, but we’ll keep digging in, learning and improving together."

Eventually, a late virtual safety car helped Mercedes' Russell defend third place, with both Hamilton and Leclerc stranding off the podium in fourth and fifth.

Sports.title: No changes as FIA completes second ADUO power unit development analysis | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA has confirmed the results of its second analysis of Formula 1 engine performance under its Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity regulations.

The sport’s governing body has decided not to allow any further development opportunities beyond those announced following its first analysis. The first analysis followed the Canadian Grand Prix and the second concluded following the Hungarian Grand Prix at the beginning of the summer break.

Under the first analysis, all power unit manufacturers except Red Bull-Ford were given extra opportunities to introduce upgrades.

“The FIA has undertaken thorough and exhaustive analysis as part of our ADUO review process,” said Nikolas Tombazis, the director of the FIA’s single-seater division. “With the release of the findings of period two, we are confident that, based on the quality of the data, its analysis is incredibly robust, giving us a high level of confidence in our findings.

“We also have to respect the confidentiality and intellectual property of the teams and their Power Unit Manufacturers in disseminating any details from the findings.

“This is the first year of ADUO so naturally there are areas which we may evolve over time, in discussion with all the PU manufacturers.”

The third ADUO period will cover last weekend’s Dutch Grand Prix up to the Mexican Grand Prix in November.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: When Schumacher returned to karting – against Hamilton | Brief

Four-times Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen will compete in a special kart race next month against 100 competitors of varying abilities.

This promoted several readers to recall the times another multiple champion, Michael Schumacher, returned to his karting roots in 2001 – while he was still racing in Formula 1 – and in 2009:

Schumacher did a round of the karting world champs in 2001. He was was mid-grid pace for most of the weekend, until it rained (and thus had somewhat home track knowledge advantage) and he got a podium in the second final. Lewis Hamilton was racing, but was similarly kinda off the pace. 2001 wasn’t his best season, but it is FSA and was the top echelon of karting back then. It is crazy thinking back he did this considering his position at Ferrari at the time, you have to give him so much respect to be that brave.

Schumacher also did the SKUSA Supernats in 2009. I was there in the middle of the circuit reporting. He was there with Buemi and Piquet Jnr. They were all spanked though by the top guys. Bas Lammers was next level good (a deaf racer for those who don’t know). Schumacher had a respectable finish in the final with a few retirements ahead. He had a good dual with Ron White. They were going proper toe-to-toe.

Sports.title: Stats: McLaren win Formula 1’s last Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort – again | 2026 Dutch Grand Prix stats and facts
Sports.content:
The Dutch Grand Prix became a Max Verstappen stronghold when it returned to the calendar six years ago. The Red Bull driver won each of the first three grands prix at his home track.

However the final three editions of the race were all won by McLaren. Lando Norris claimed back-to-back wins either side of the summer break.

This was the last Dutch Grand Prix for the foreseeable future as Zandvoort does not have a deal for F1 to return. Just as when it hosted the last race of its previous stint as an F1 venue in 1985, McLaren won the final race.

On that occasion Niki Lauda claimed his 25th and, as it turned out, final victory. He had announced his retirement plans at his home event one week earlier.

Norris’s win was his 13th, giving him as many as two-times world champion Alberto Ascari and David Coulthard. He also took his 18th pole position, giving him as many as Mario Andretti, Kimi Raikkonen and Rene Arnoux.

Although Ferrari failed to win on the modern Zandvoort layout, they remain the most successful team at the track with eight wins to McLaren’s six. Ferrari’s last win came courtesy of Arnoux in 1983. Mercedes also did not manage to win at Zandvoort during its return; their only victory at the track remains Juan Manuel Fangio’s 1955 triumph.

Charles Leclerc denied Norris a hat-trick by recording the 13th fastest lap of his career. He now has as many as 1983 world champion Alan Jones, plus Jacky Ickx and Riccardo Patrese.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Regardless of how the weekend turned out, Andrea Kimi Antonelli was always going to go to his home race next week as the world championship leader. With a 59-point lead, he is now guaranteed to head the standings when F1 departs Europe for the final nine ‘flyaway’ rounds.

George Russell claimed his fourth sprint race victory but failed to make any inroads on Antonelli’s points lead after following his team mate home in the grand prix.

Liam Lawson made his 50th appearance at a grand prix weekend back at the team he made his 15th and 16th participations with at the beginning of last year. His second stint at Red Bull was much more successful than his first as he finished seventh, despite a 10-second time penalty.

His return to Red Bull came about due to Isack Hadjar’s unfortunate injury. This also prevented Hadjar extending his run of seven consecutive points-scoring finishes.

Verstappen’s first-lap retirement meant Lawson was the only driver to score points for Red Bull. Prior to that Verstappen had never failed to finish outside the top two places at Zandvoort.

He has now gone 12 rounds without a grand prix victory. This is the second-longest win-less streak of his career, only behind the 30-race spell between his first and second grand prix victories in 2016 and 2017.

Yuki Tsunoda returned and finished one place outside of the points. Had he reached 10th he would have tied Kamui Kobayashi as Japan’s all-time top points-scorer.

The second half of 2026 ha begun much more brightly for Aston Martin following their upgrades in the last two races. Fernando Alonso took ninth place, their best result of the season so far. Team mate Lance Stroll remains one of only three drivers yet to score this year, along with the Cadillac duo, but he must fancy his chances now.

Sports.title: Domenicali hopeful Verstappen’s new deal will end talk of F1 exit | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Stefano Domenicali hopes Max Verstappen’s new Red Bull contract will put an end to claims he could leave Formula 1.

The Red Bull driver, who is one of the strongest critics of F1’s current regulations, said his uncertainty over agreeing a new deal with his team had been “mainly about actually continuing in Formula 1.”

Speaking ahead of Sunday’s Dutch Grand Prix, Domenicali said “the news of Max staying in Red Bull for the next couple of years is a cherry on the cake for this weekend.”

“It’s great news, [I’m] very proud and happy because Max is a world champion, world class person that has a great personality in the sport and I cannot see [imagine] Formula 1 without him.”

In May, Verstappen said it was “mentally not doable for me to stay” if F1 did not alter the power balance between the combustion and electrical parts of its engines next year. It subsequently announced changes will be introduced over the next two years.

“The rules are slowly getting a bit better and, let’s say, I’m willing to live with it,” said Verstappen. “Hopefully by 2030 it opens up another opportunity, potentially with V8 engines coming in, to look again.”

Domenicali hopes Verstappen’s new deal will quieten speculation the popular four-times champion will leave F1. “[I’m] very happy that this news now is official and all these talks that have been happening so far will be out of place,” he said. “Now I’m sure that the focus [will be] for the team to be as good as possible to give Max the best car that he can.”

Doubt continues to hang over the status of F1’s final two rounds this season, which will be held in the Middle East. The conflict in the region has already led F1 to abandon its plans to race in Saudi Arabia in Bahrain this year and arranged for the latter event to take place in Malaysia instead.

Domenicali indicated no decision has yet been taken to cancel the final two rounds in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. “The calendar, as I said, is confirmed, so there are still a few tickets to be sold in Abu Dhabi,” he said. “Everything is progressing well, and we stay focused on delivering the calendar we promised at the beginning of the year.”

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Lenient response to drivers passing red light sets bad precedent | Brief
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s stewarding guidelines state drivers should receive 10-second stop-and-go penalties if they pass a red light at the pit lane exit during the grand prix.

However the stewards opted for much more lenient penalties when Oliver Bearman and Gabriel Bortoleto broke the rule at Zandvoort last weekend. Reader @Alianora-La-Canta says this sets a bad precedent:

The drivers had no way to know that no dangerous situations would be created by ignoring the red light. Therefore a penalty should have been issued that involved a sporting disadvantage. Even mitigating the penalty would be risky, if understandable (due to the point of the procedure, I recognise the risk should have been much lower than usual). Now people are going to ignore the red light if they think it’s under a red flag and they think there’s an advantage in doing so, which is dangerous because the drivers do not have the information the FIA does.

Sports.title: Verstappen to race 100 drivers at once in karts at Silverstone | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen will take on 100 drivers in a special go-kart race at Silverstone, Red Bull has announced.

The four-times world champion will start at the back of the grid with 100 rivals ahead of him.

“In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking,” said Verstappen. “Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it’s always nice to return.

“It’s about understanding the grip of the go-kart. I’ve done so many years in go-karting that you quite naturally get back into things. I will be looking forward to just seeing the carnage unfold in front of me.”

Red Bull say Verstappen’s rivals will be drawn “from every corner of sport and culture: from Red Bull athletes and celebrities to content creators, personalities and everyday fans invited from around the world.”

The event will take place on September 16th, three days after the Spanish Grand Prix, at a specially designed track at the home of the British Grand Prix.

“Creating a track for 100 drivers at the same time has never been done, never been seen,” said circuit designer and race director David Terrien. “So it’s very exciting.

“When you have Max Verstappen chasing everyone, I think that’s going to be the experience of a lifetime for all the drivers. You’re going to have Max showcasing all these skills of looking through the traffic, trying to prepare and plan where he can overtake people, and going through the traffic at the fastest speed he can because he doesn’t want to let the drivers at the front pull away.”

The event will be broadcast in some territories on Disney Plus and the ESPN app.

Sports.title: Dmitrii Bivol And Callum Smith Agree WBO Title Fight
Sports.content:
“Please be advised that the WBO World Championship Committee has received written confirmation from RCC Boxing, on behalf of WBO Light Heavyweight Champion Dmitrii Bivol, and Matchroom Boxing, on behalf of Mandatory Challenger Callum Smith, confirming that the parties have reached terms, including an agreed date and venue for the WBO Light Heavyweight Mandatory Championship Contest. The WBO respectfully defers to the parties to formally announce the date, venue, and event details in due course,” said Olivieri on X.

Smith, 36, is finally getting the title opportunity he has waited for, but the financial value remains unknown. Bivol’s two fights with Artur Beterbiev were backed by Turki Alalshikh and carried undisputed championship status. A mandatory defense does not have the same commercial weight.

The venue will reveal more. Saudi involvement may turn the event into another major payday. If RCC Boxing and Matchroom are financing it without that support, Smith may receive considerably less than Bivol and Beterbiev earned from their two meetings.

Inactivity presents another concern for the challenger. He has not competed since going through a 12-round war with Joshua Buatsi in February 2025 and has boxed only twice since suffering a seventh-round knockout against Beterbiev in January 2024.

Bivol, 35, underwent back surgery after his questionable majority decision over Beterbiev in February 2025. He returned in May 2026 and defeated IBF mandatory Michael Eifert by a wide unanimous decision before undergoing surgery on his injured left elbow in July.

The champion has therefore boxed only once since the Beterbiev rematch and must now return from a second operation. Smith has been inactive longer, but neither man enters under ideal conditions. Bivol must show that his elbow permits him to throw combinations freely, while his challenger must overcome approximately 18 months outside the ring.

Those two Beterbiev bouts supplied Smith with a blueprint for troubling Bivol. Sustained aggression denied him room to settle, made him expend energy, and reduced the time available for his accurate combinations.

During the opening six rounds of their rematch, Beterbiev looked capable of breaking Bivol. His work rate dropped from the seventh through the 11th, however. Once he increased the pace in round 12, Bivol again looked vulnerable and close to being stopped.

Smith cannot afford similar quiet stretches. He must cut off the ring, attack the body and maintain the pace instead of following Bivol while absorbing straight punches. Knowing the plan and executing it for an entire championship bout are very different tasks.

At six feet three inches with a 78-inch reach, Smith owns major physical advantages but has not always used them effectively. He often retreats in straight lines before settling behind a static high guard near the ropes. That habit would give Bivol the stationary target he wants for his quick multi-punch combinations.

A counter left hook remains Smith’s best chance of changing the contest with one punch. Landing it cleanly will be difficult because Bivol maintains a disciplined defensive position while jabbing and rarely leaves his chin exposed for the shot that Smith used to stop Gilbert Castillo and Mathieu Bauderlique.

High guards also give Bivol opportunities rather than discouraging him. He can split the gloves with straight punches, attack around them with hooks and leave the pocket before the counter arrives. Canelo Alvarez and Gilberto Ramirez struggled to interrupt that rhythm once he began controlling the distance.

Their common opponents underline the size of Smith’s task. Bivol neutralized Canelo over 12 rounds and divided two close decisions with Beterbiev. Smith suffered a one-sided decision against Canelo before Beterbiev dropped him twice and stopped him in the seventh. Those results do not decide this contest, but they show that the champion has handled the elite opposition that overwhelmed his mandatory challenger.

At 36, this may be Smith’s final opportunity to win a world title in a second division. That urgency may force him to take risks, yet passive pursuit will not be enough. He needs to use his reach to push Bivol backward, work the body and prevent him from resetting without becoming trapped behind his guard.

Waiting preserved Smith’s mandatory position but took away valuable time near the end of his career. He finally has the opportunity he wanted. Now he must carry out an exhausting tactical blueprint against one of boxing’s most accurate technicians after approximately 18 months without competition.

Sports.title: Oscar Collazo Takes Major Flyweight Risk Against Sandoval
Sports.content:
Entering only his second fight at flyweight, Collazo is coming off a two-round stoppage of late replacement Neider Valdez. The 5-foot-2 unified minimumweight champion will give away four inches in height to the 5-foot-6 Sandoval while moving directly from a trial fight in the division to arguably its best fighter.

Sandoval earned the WBA and WBC titles by traveling to Japan and defeating Kenshiro Teraji by split decision in July 2025. He survived a fifth-round knockdown and recovered well enough to outwork Teraji across the later rounds.

That victory showed the difficulty of the task facing Collazo. The champion is larger, experienced against top opposition and capable of maintaining his output over 12 rounds. Collazo dominated at minimumweight, but beating fighters closer to his own size does not guarantee that his pressure and punching power will carry into a fight against a full-sized flyweight.

The seven-pound move from 105 to 112 represents nearly seven percent of Collazo’s former weight limit. He bypassed the 108-pound division entirely, although the Valdez bout gave him one short appearance at flyweight before challenging Sandoval. Two rounds against a late replacement could not show how his power, stamina and punch resistance will hold up against a natural 112-pound champion.

Their methods create a clear contest between precision and activity. Collazo uses timing, lateral movement and accurate body combinations, while Sandoval applied enough pressure and maintained sufficient output to defeat Teraji. The challenger must land with enough force to reduce that activity. Without earning Sandoval’s respect, the smaller man may struggle to control the pace over 12 rounds.

“Sandoval is a challenge that motivates me and my team. I was looking to make history and prove that there are no limits when you know what you’re capable of doing,” Collazo said. “This isn’t just for me. This is for Puerto Rico and to raise the level of Puerto Rican boxing.”

The southpaw stance gives Collazo a route inside. His rear left hand can reach Sandoval’s body from an angle, but he must cross the taller champion’s punching range to deliver it. Sandoval’s straight right hand and uppercut will be available whenever Collazo lowers himself or steps forward. Much may depend on how often the challenger reaches the body without taking a clean counter on his way inside.

Sandoval’s recovery against Teraji creates another question. He got up from a fifth-round knockdown and fought effectively enough over the remaining rounds to win the titles. Collazo carried useful power at 105 pounds, but hurting an established flyweight is a different physical test. Failure to slow the champion early may force him to match Sandoval’s activity deep into the contest.

His brief appearance against Valdez offered little evidence because it lasted less than two rounds. Collazo overwhelmed an opponent brought in on short notice, but Sandoval represents an entirely different level of resistance.

Rather than spending several fights adjusting to the division, Collazo is going directly after two flyweight championships while retaining his WBA and WBO minimumweight belts. Winning would give him recognized titles in two divisions simultaneously. This is far more than a ceremonial opportunity for a successful champion moving up in weight.

Sports.title: Janibek Wants Sheeraz Belt For Canelo Fight
Sports.content:
That complaint cannot conceal the competitive danger involved. Janibek is a former unified middleweight champion and the most accomplished available contender in the WBO’s top 15. Canelo is occupied with Christian Mbilli, while Diego Pacheco is pursuing another title. The WBO had few credible alternatives.

The speed of Janibek’s return still gives Sheeraz a legitimate complaint. His suspension was terminated on July 10, and he was installed as mandatory little more than a month later, allowing him to move above active super middleweights without first competing in the division. That decision favored proven championship credentials over activity at 168. Sheeraz can question that policy without claiming Janibek was still suspended when the order was issued.

Sheeraz Received A Comfortable Route

Sheeraz was given a high super middleweight ranking after his controversial draw against WBC middleweight champion Carlos Adames. His first three opponents at 168 were Edgar Berlanga, Alem Begic, and Simon Zachenhuber.

Berlanga had been heavily promoted without beating a leading super middleweight. He lost when he finally faced Canelo, returned against limited opposition, and was then stopped by Sheeraz. Begic was largely unknown when he fought for the vacant WBO title. Zachenhuber had little international profile before serving as the opponent for Sheeraz’s first defense. Neither had accomplished anything comparable to Janibek.

Placed alongside those three opponents, the former unified middleweight champion looks like gold. Moving up without a previous appearance at 168 is unusual, but it does not make Begic or Zachenhuber more qualified.

This run at super middleweight has been carefully managed. The Janibek order is the first time Sheeraz has been required to face someone with an established championship record and a realistic chance of beating him.

The styles explain some of the reluctance. Sheeraz has used his height, long jab, and right hand to control less sophisticated opponents from a distance. Janibek is a southpaw with sharper footwork, educated counters, and the experience to attack from angles Begic and Zachenhuber could not create. This is not merely a larger name. It is a considerable increase in tactical difficulty.

The Belt Comes With Responsibilities

Despite his criticism, Sheeraz has stopped short of refusing the defense. He told IFL TV that “if this is the fight, this is the fight,” while leaving the decision to his team. He also said they would examine how to make it most beneficial for him.

However, his repeated criticism makes it clear that Janibek is not the opponent Sheeraz and Queensberry wanted next. They now must decide how much they value the WBO title.

Negotiations also place Queensberry in a difficult promotional position. Allowing the defense to reach a purse bid could give another promoter control of the venue, broadcast arrangements, and conditions surrounding one of its most valuable fighters. Vacating would preserve matchmaking control but remove the championship leverage Sheeraz hopes to carry into negotiations with Canelo.

A similar issue can be seen in Teofimo Lopez’s reaction to inheriting Jack Catterall as his WBA welterweight mandatory. Teofimo wants Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn rather than a dangerous challenger carrying less commercial value. The two mandatories present the same basic inconvenience. Janibek and Catterall can defeat the champions, but neither supplies the enormous payday needed to make that danger appealing.

A decisive Janibek win could remove Sheeraz from the Canelo sweepstakes. Canelo is 36 and approaching the end of his career. If his October 31 fight with Mbilli goes badly, that opportunity may disappear before Sheeraz can rebuild from a damaging loss.

Holding the WBO belt does not guarantee Sheeraz a Canelo fight, but it supplies a unification storyline and separates him from Pacheco and other contenders pursuing the same opportunity.

That is not a reason for the organization to protect him. If boxing is going to operate as a sport instead of a popularity contest, champions must face qualified mandatories rather than selecting opponents entirely by commercial value.

The choice is simple: defend the title or surrender it. Sheeraz should not receive the championship status needed to pursue Canelo without accepting the difficult defense attached to that status.

Sports.title: George Foreman’s Drugged Water Claim Against Ali Resurfaces
Sports.content:
“It’s a theory that the fight was tampered with. For the older boxing guys what do yall think?” Prograis posted on X.

Foreman’s own account is more valuable than the theory raised by Prograis. The former heavyweight champion described receiving suspicious-tasting water shortly before the fight in his 2007 memoir, God in My Corner.

“Just before the fight with Ali, my trainer handed me a glass of liquid and said, ‘Here’s your water,’” Foreman wrote. “As I took a swig, I almost spit it out. ‘Hey, this water tastes like it has medicine in it.’”

Trainer Dick Sadler assured Foreman that it was the same water he had always received. The medicinal taste, Foreman said, remained when he went to the ring.

“After the third round, I was as tired as if I had fought 15 rounds,” Foreman wrote. “What’s going on here? Did someone slip a drug in my water?”

No test results or other evidence ever supported his account. Sadler died in 2003 and was unable to answer the version Foreman publicized four years later.

Ali Forced Foreman Beyond His Usual Script

Foreman had destroyed Joe Frazier in two rounds to win the heavyweight championship and stopped Ken Norton in the second. Those performances encouraged him to attack Ali with the same expectation of an early finish. Kinshasa produced a different fight. Foreman threw heavy punches from the opening bell, while Ali blocked shots with his arms, leaned away from others and struck him repeatedly with straight right hands. Many of Foreman’s widest punches either missed or landed without their full force.

Loose ropes helped Ali lean farther back, but the idea that Angelo Dundee deliberately loosened them remains disputed. Dundee complained about their condition and attempted to have them tightened. Ali still recognized how they could be used once the fight began.

That fatigue has a physical and tactical explanation without introducing an unidentified substance. Foreman maintained a knockout pace against an opponent who refused to disappear, forcing him to work longer than Frazier or Norton had.

Over time, his explanations for the loss included the loose ropes, referee Zack Clayton’s count and dissatisfaction with his corner. The drugged-water story later became the most serious of them.

By the eighth round, Foreman’s punches had lost much of their force. Ali landed a fast combination and dropped him for the knockout. Prograis has revived an old piece of boxing folklore, but the film continues to show Ali winning through cleaner punching, patience and control of Foreman’s aggression.

Muhammad Ali watches as George Foreman lies on the canvas during their heavyweight championship fight in Kinshasa, Zaire, on October 30, 1974. Foreman later alleged that his pre-fight water contained an unidentified substance. Photo: El Gráfico/Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

Sports.title: Vergil Ortiz Jr. Botches Ennis Fight, Leaves 154
Sports.content:
“Boots is part of the plan, but it doesn’t have to be next,” De La Hoya said in January. “Eddie, since you’re so desperate to make this fight, let’s do this: 60/40 for Vergil and 5% to the winner because I’m generous, and I’m not moving off those numbers.”

Golden Boy treated Ortiz like the established attraction, even though Ennis had been a two-belt titlist at welterweight and proven his ability to sell tickets on the East Coast. Ortiz had never headlined a major pay-per-view or generated comparable gate revenue.

The WBC interim belt gave Ortiz Jr. a negotiating tool, but it did not make him the commercial leader of the division. Golden Boy tried to turn temporary sanctioning body status into promotional dominance. Once Ennis accepted the smaller share, the biggest obstacle should have been gone. The fight still did not happen.

A breach of contract lawsuit against Golden Boy tied up much of Ortiz’s year before the dispute was settled in July. During that lost period, Ennis moved on and accepted the type of risk Ortiz’s side had avoided. He faced unified super welterweight champion Xander Zayas as the B side, helped draw 15,000 fans to Barclays Center and came away with two belts.

Their career choices produced opposite results. Ennis accepted the subordinate role because beating Zayas offered him a route to the top. Ortiz’s team fought over contractual and financial positioning before he had beaten the opponent needed to justify it.

Ennis now has everything Ortiz Jr. was trying to negotiate without fighting him: championship status, greater leverage and command of the division’s biggest fights. A bout against Josh Kelly is planned for later this year. If Ennis and WBC champion Sebastian Fundora continue winning, an undisputed fight between them can be made in 2027. Staying at 154 has placed Ennis inside a valuable series of title fights.

By moving to middleweight, Vergil Jr. has removed himself from that group. The change may reduce the strain of making 154 pounds, but the division offers fewer major names. Team Ortiz Jr. is pursuing possible fights against Jermell Charlo and Tim Tszyu, although both men have expressed interest in facing each other. If Charlo and Tszyu meet, Ortiz Jr. may find himself at 160 lacking a major opponent, a full world title or the large payday he missed against Ennis. Beating lower-profile middleweights would keep him active, but it would not replace the attention available in fights with Ennis or Fundora.

Leaving junior middleweight means Ortiz Jr. departs without getting either man or turning his interim status into full championship recognition. He spent months protecting an A side designation that brought him nothing. There was no larger purse against Ennis because there was no fight, and his bargaining position never became a championship opportunity.

Middleweight gives Ortiz a new starting point, but it also confirms how badly the Ennis negotiations were handled. Ennis took unfavorable terms, backed himself against a champion and took over at 154. Ortiz demanded control, missed the fight and abandoned the division empty handed.

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Changes Style for Christian Mbilli
Sports.content:
Eight years later, Canelo operates at a much slower pace and needs longer recovery periods between attacks. He normally conserves energy by holding his ground, making small defensive movements and waiting for opportunities to land hard single counters. That approach gives Mbilli exactly what he wants.

The WBC champion enters behind punches, stays on the front foot and continues throwing after his opening shots have been blocked. Canelo cannot remain behind a stationary guard and expect Mbilli to stop after one or two punches. He will have to escape before those attacks turn into sustained combinations to the head and body.

Using the ring may delay Mbilli’s offense, but it creates another physical drain. Canelo landed 99 of 338 punches in the Terence Crawford fight, averaging only 28.2 attempts and 8.3 connects per round. Despite throwing so little, he still tired during the championship rounds.

That performance raises serious doubts about his ability to keep circling Mbilli. Changing direction and defending extended combinations consume stamina without showing up in Canelo’s punch totals. Mbilli will force him to work during the portions of rounds when he normally rests. Munguia offers useful preparation because he brings size, aggression and combination punching. He does not reproduce Mbilli’s nonstop pace or compact attacks, however. Canelo is caught between two exhausting options. Staying on his toes may leave his legs depleted before the late rounds.

Remaining near the ropes allows Mbilli to overwhelm him with activity. Canelo may need to hurt the younger champion early because a prolonged fight conducted at Mbilli’s pace favors Mbilli taking control.

Sports.title: Turki Hasn’t Answered Joshua’s Fury Addendum
Sports.content:
The dispute now includes money owed from Joshua’s July knockout of Kristian Prenga. BoxingScene learned that his purse was due on fight night, but Joshua has yet to receive the full amount.

That detail is significant because delayed payment can sometimes be permitted under a fighter’s contract. Pugmire referenced another boxer whose representative complained about an unpaid purse before accepting that the agreement allowed payment within 45 days. Joshua’s contract did not contain that same waiting period.

Silence Weakens the New York Plan

“No change,” Hearn said when asked about the response to his addendum.

Leaving the document unanswered creates pressure without formally rejecting Joshua’s terms. The closer the event moves toward its promotional deadline, the harder it becomes for Hearn to insist on Britain without being accused of costing Joshua the Fury payday. Alalshikh’s side can gain negotiating leverage simply by waiting, although that tactic also makes Madison Square Garden harder to deliver.

Frank Warren and Fury have publicly urged the parties to finish the deal, but those appeals do not resolve the contractual issues. Joshua signed for a UK fight and is being asked to accept a different country, reduced earnings after taxes and added obligations.

The unpaid Prenga money changes the character of Hearn’s demands. Ticketing, security and compensation might otherwise look like routine bargaining over a venue switch. Asking Joshua to accept new obligations before the previous purse has been completed gives Matchroom a practical reason to demand everything in writing. The issue is no longer only how much Joshua receives for New York, but how much trust remains between the parties.

Claims that Hearn is delaying the event over unrelated payments involving snooker and darts have also circulated. Pugmire’s report gives his position considerably more weight. The dispute concerns money contractually due from Joshua’s own bout, not another sport’s unpaid bill being used to extract a larger purse.

Joshua’s sporting position and contractual position are not the same. He no longer holds three heavyweight belts or commands the leverage he carried when 90,000 spectators watched him defeat Wladimir Klitschko at Wembley in 2017. Losses to Oleksandr Usyk and Daniel Dubois, followed by two knockdowns against Kristian Prenga, have weakened Hearn’s ability to demand premium treatment. None of that erases the UK clause or Joshua’s right to receive money already due.

Madison Square Garden supplies prestige, and a US prime-time window for Netflix, but the location serves the broadcaster more clearly than it serves the rivalry. Fury and Joshua built their drawing power in Britain, and their shared history carries greater emotional value at Wembley than in New York. Moving the event across the Atlantic trades domestic atmosphere and gate certainty for American visibility, making financial protection for both fighters a reasonable part of the negotiation.

Time is working against the organizers. A November 20 event requires venue confirmation, travel arrangements, media dates and a full Netflix promotional campaign. Each week without an answer reduces the time available to sell a fight whose commercial value depends heavily on the names and history involved.

Hearn still risks overplaying the protection supplied by the contract. Alalshikh and Sela control the financing, and Joshua has no alternative event approaching the commercial value of Fury. If the backers decide that New York cannot be delivered under Joshua’s revised terms, enforcing the UK clause may leave him legally justified but without the largest payday remaining in his career.

That is the pressure created by the unanswered addendum. Joshua has enough contractual leverage to resist the venue change, but not enough current value to assume the organizers will keep increasing their offer. Hearn must protect him without turning a favorable clause into the reason the event disappears.

Sports.title: Teofimo Lopez Claims Catterall Deadline No Longer Applies
Sports.content:
Catterall defeated Shakhram Giyasov on May 23 to get the WBA’s secondary welterweight belt. The organization then required Romero to face the winner within 180 days. Catterall maintains that the WBA has told him he is next and that promoter Eddie Hearn has written to WBA president Gilberto Mendoza requesting an immediate order.

Lopez’s legal team can argue that the original directive named Romero, but a mandatory requirement issued by a sanctioning body is not simply a private contract that binds only the two fighters named in it. The WBA committee can transfer the obligation, modify the deadline, or grant Lopez another fight. Until it makes that decision, Lopez cannot declare on his own that the process has restarted.

The new champion also cited the cut over his right eyebrow and his resulting medical suspension.

“I’m suspended by all commissions right now due to the cut over my right eye. Until I get my license back from the commission, we don’t need to talk about any mandatories at this particular time.”

That suspension prevents Teofimo from returning to the ring until he receives medical clearance. It does not prevent the WBA from confirming Catterall’s status or ordering negotiations for a later date.

Nobody is asking Lopez to defend the belt before the cut heals. The dispute concerns who receives his next defense after he is cleared. Catterall says the WBA has already given him that answer, while Lopez is trying to persuade the committee to give him a different one.

Mannix: Teofimo Lopez Knows Ryan Garcia Is Next

Chris Mannix says Teofimo Lopez and his team already know Ryan Garcia is likely to be his next opponent. Their confidence suggests they do not regard Jack Catterall’s mandatory WBA title consolidation as an obstacle that will stop the fight.

“Ryan Garcia is the name that is at the top of everybody’s list. Ryan Garcia is the name that Teofimo Lopez and his team know that they’re likely going to face,” Mannix said on his DAZN show with Sergio Mora. “In fact, win or lose this fight against Conor Benn, I think Ryan Garcia is going to be next for Teofimo.”

A Garcia victory over Benn on September 12 would allow Lopez to request permission for a WBA-WBC unification. The organization could authorize that fight, give Catterall another deadline and argue that consolidating championships took priority over immediately eliminating its own secondary title.

Losing to Benn would remove that justification. Garcia would no longer bring the WBC belt, leaving Lopez to choose a commercially valuable voluntary defense over a mandated consolidation. Allowing it would amount to the WBA discarding its order because Lopez found a more profitable opponent.

Catterall is not merely a contender waiting after winning an eliminator. He captured the WBA Regular welterweight title by defeating Shakhram Giyasov and was promised a fight against the primary champion within 180 days. Lopez inherited that obligation when he took the WBA title from Rolando Romero.

The sanctioning body must now decide how much its own order is worth. A Garcia unification would produce greater attention and a larger sanctioning fee, but another postponement would further reduce the value of holding its Regular title. Fighters are asked to compete for that belt, pay sanctioning fees and trust that victory will lead to the primary champion.

Lopez’s apparent freedom to plan around Catterall shows that commercial appeal may defeat enforcement. If the WBA permits Garcia to go first, especially after a loss to Benn, it will make itself look second-rate by showing that its orders apply only when champions have nothing richer available.

Matchroom Presses WBA To Force Teofimo Lopez vs. Jack Catterall

Jack Catterall confirmed Tuesday that Eddie Hearn and Matchroom sent a letter to the WBA in an attempt to get his title fight with Teofimo Lopez enforced.

“Letter was sent to them yesterday by Eddie and Matchroom,” Catterall posted on X in response to a supporter asking his team to act.

Catterall also revealed that WBA president Gilberto Mendoza personally promised him that the 180-day commitment would remain in place regardless of who held the Super title.

“When I met Gilberto Mendoza in Egypt, I shook his hand and he gave me his word if I beat Giyasov, someone who was avoided and waited for his shot for two years, I will get my shot within 180 days regardless who has the belt. So I believe the WBA will do the correct thing,” Catterall posted.

That account removes much of the uncertainty about what the WBA intended. Its published resolution named Rolando Romero, but its president allegedly told Catterall that the commitment followed the title. Lopez still has a technical argument based on the written wording, yet the WBA would have to break Mendoza’s personal promise to let him move on.

The dispute began after Lopez openly denied that Catterall was his mandatory during Monday’s Inside the Ring show. Lopez plans to pursue the three additional titles he needs to become the undisputed welterweight champion, beginning with the winner of Ryan Garcia versus Conor Benn on September 12.

That pursuit leaves no place for Catterall, but the secondary WBA champion has rejected the easiest negotiated solution.

“There’s not $1 that can persuade me to step aside to allow a unification bout to happen. I’m here to fight,” Catterall said.

His refusal means Matchroom cannot be paid to wait while Lopez pursues the Garcia vs. Benn winner. The WBA must enforce the consolidation fight, permit a unification first, or allow its two welterweight champions to remain separated.

The 180-day period expires on November 19, based on Catterall’s May 23 victory over Shakhram Giyasov. That leaves less than three months to settle the dispute. The cut Lopez suffered over his right eyebrow against Rolando Romero places more strain on the schedule, although there has been no indication that it will keep him out for an extended period.

Teofimo may believe the WBA will permit a unification to take priority over its internal consolidation fight. Sanctioning bodies regularly move mandatory obligations aside when champions pursue another belt, giving his team a stronger argument than the wording omission alone.

Catterall brings tactical risk with little financial reward. His awkward southpaw style and sharp counterpunching deny opponents clean offensive opportunities. Ryan Garcia, Conor Benn and Devin Haney generate massive paydays. Catterall brings no comparable commercial appeal, only a genuine threat to expose Lopez inside the ring.

WBA Loophole Gives Teofimo Lopez Easy Out On Jack Catterall

A review of the WBA’s published rulings supports part of Teofimo Lopez’s argument. No public order currently names Jack Catterall as the mandatory challenger for Lopez’s newly acquired Super welterweight title.

The May 21 ruling required Rolando Romero to face the Catterall-Shakhram Giyasov winner within 180 days. Its language named Romero specifically. It did not say the obligation would transfer to Romero’s successor if the title changed hands.

That omission gives Lopez a technical basis for denying that Catterall has been formally assigned to him. The WBA would need to issue another ruling, clarify that the original order followed the championship, or designate Catterall as Lopez’s challenger.

Teofimo still goes too far by claiming Catterall was lied to. The WBA sanctioned the Giyasov bout and publicly stated that its winner would receive Romero within 180 days. Catterall’s expectation came directly from the organization, not from an invented promise by his team.

The real issue is poor wording from the WBA. It created two champions and ordered them to meet, yet attached the obligation to Romero by name rather than clearly attaching it to the Super title. Lopez is now using that opening to pursue the Garcia-Benn winner while Catterall waits for the WBA to explain what its own ruling means.

Teofimo Lopez Denies Jack Catterall Mandatory Status

Teofimo Lopez claims Jack Catterall is not his WBA mandatory and says the British contender was lied to about his right to challenge for the welterweight title.

During today’s Inside the Ring show, Catterall confronted the new WBA champion after Lopez discussed facing the Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn winner and eventually meeting Devin Haney for the undisputed championship.

“He’s not. He’s not my mandatory,” Lopez said when Catterall was identified as next in line. “By the sanctioning rules, he’s not my mandatory, and I think they lied. I think they lied to him.”

“It’s in the contract,” Catterall answered.

Teofimo’s denial conflicts with the WBA’s own published ruling. When the organization elevated Rolando Romero to Super champion in May, it sanctioned Catterall’s bout with Shakhram Giyasov for the vacant secondary title and stated that Romero had to face the winner within 180 days.

Catterall defeated Giyasov and now holds that belt. Lopez may argue that the ruling named Romero rather than whoever defeated him, or that no separate order has been issued since Saturday. Neither explanation supports his claim that Catterall was lied to. The WBA publicly connected the two titles and imposed a deadline for bringing them together.

The exchange became entertaining because Lopez tried to rewrite the situation while Catterall was on the screen looking directly at him. Rather than explain the supposed sanctioning rule, Teofimo declared that the obligation did not exist and blamed unnamed people for misleading Catterall.

After making that denial, the new champion returned to the familiar claim that he will face anyone.

“I’m always willing to fight anybody and everybody,” Lopez said.

“I’m glad you won on the weekend because I know you don’t duck nobody,” Catterall replied. “It would have been more difficult to get Rolly into the ring. I’m happy for you, but we’ve got to get it on.”

Catterall played the interaction perfectly. He congratulated Lopez, reminded him that Romero would have been harder to bring into the ring and declined to turn the conversation into a shouting match. That left Teofimo arguing against a contract he had not seen while Catterall calmly insisted the terms were already written down.

There was also some clever pressure inside Catterall’s praise. Telling Lopez, “I know you don’t duck nobody,” gave the champion little room to reject the fight without contradicting the reputation Catterall had just assigned to him.

The WBA now needs to explain the status of its own ruling. It can grant Lopez permission to pursue a unification, arrange a step-aside payment or order the title consolidation. What it cannot credibly do is remain silent while its new champion claims the other titleholder was fooled.

Lopez is clearly trying to look past the mandatory to chase the massive paydays against the Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn winner or a unification with Devin Haney. Catterall holds the regular belt after beating Shakhram Giyasov, which, in standard WBA procedure, makes him the direct mandatory to unify the titles.

Ghana News.title: Education Ministry to amend law to restore faith-based representation on GES Council
Ghana News.content:
Dr Clement Apaak — Deputy Education Minister

The Ministry of Education says it will initiate steps to amend the Pre-Tertiary Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049), to ensure appropriate representation of recognised faith-based organisations on the Ghana Education Service (GES) Council.

The announcement follows concerns raised by the Ghana Catholic Bishops’ Conference over its exclusion from the current GES Council.

The Deputy Minister of Education, Dr Clement Apak, in a statement on Thursday, August 27, said the concerns were receiving due consideration.

The Ministry acknowledged the significant contribution of faith-based institutions to the development of Ghana’s educational system and would ensure their representation to address the growing indiscipline in the educational sector.

It explained that the Ghana Education Service Act, 1995 (Act 506), provided for three representatives of faith-based organisations on the GES Council.

However, the subsequent Pre-Tertiary Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049), reduced the provision to one representative.

The statement said the change created what it described as “an anomaly in the representation of faith-based organisations.”

“When constituting the GES Council in 2025, it recognised the inadequacy of the provision and decided to hold on to the arrangement pending an amendment to the law,” it said.

The proposed amendment would take into account the government’s decentralisation policy on education, the statement said, adding that it had been engaging relevant stakeholders on the matter.

The Ministry reiterated its commitment to an inclusive and consultative approach to education governance and said it would continue engaging stakeholders to strengthen the education sector.

It also acknowledged the contribution of the Ghana Catholic Bishops’ Conference and other faith-based organisations to education in Ghana and called on them to work with the Government to address the “growing indiscipline in the education sector while the legislative review was being pursued.”
