World.title: Canada-U.S. trade minister welcomes U.S. decision 'withdrawing positions' on language, culture
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says the federal government "welcomes" the United States "withdrawing" its positions on the French language and culture after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CBC News Canada's streaming laws are not a "red line" for the American side.

"Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labelling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions," LeBlanc said in a statement posted on X.

"We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty."

WATCH | U.S. trade rep disputes why talks fell apart | Canadian exclusive: U.S. trade rep disputes why talks fell apart | Canadian exclusive | Duration 16:53 In a Canadian exclusive interview, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer disputed Canada’s explanation about why trade talks fell apart, and told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton there’s currently no ‘open channels’ to get both sides back to the negotiating table.

Last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney told his negotiators to walk away from the table after the Trump administration introduced demands on culture, autos and sovereignty.

The prime minister said the U.S. had issues with Canada's subsidies for French culture, the prevalence of French-language media online and even the requirement to have bilingual labels on products sold in Canada.

"It was unacceptable right from the start, but the Americans kept trying and trying, and we said no," Carney said at a press conference on Saturday.

"Ultimately, it's simple. That was never on the table for Canada and it would not have been acceptable to Canadians."

Modifying position on culture, language

In an interview with CBC News's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that aired Wednesday evening, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer appeared to modify the U.S. position on culture and language.

On the issue of discoverability of French content on streaming services, Greer told Barton it had been "highlighted" by the White House, but not as a dealbreaker.

"President Trump, myself and the U.S. government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada, in Quebec, in the Maritimes and some [other] areas. We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important," he said of French-language protections.

"There is no way we would let a good deal go by for something like this. This is not something where we push hard or condition or red-line. It's like the farthest thing from a red line."

When the talks fell apart, U.S. tariffs of 50 per cent were slapped on a wide range of Canadian products, impacting about $27-billion worth of Canadian goods.

The Americans' modified position comes two days after Canada announced its own dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on more than 700 different U.S. imports.

While the position on language and culture is good news for the prospect of a deal between the two countries, Greer told Barton that as of now, talks had all but broken down.

He said it wasn't clear when the two countries might return to the negotiation table, confirming he and LeBlanc were not in contact as of Wednesday.

"I would say we don't have open channels right now," Greer said. "I have a good relationship with Minister LeBlanc, but right now, I think the Canadian side is talking about their next steps."

World.title: Police investigating suspected arson after car at Liberal MP's home torched
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police are investigating a suspected arson at the home of a Scarborough MP after multiple cars were torched early Thursday, her office has confirmed.

In a written statement Thursday, Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East MP Salma Zahid said an "individual" set her car and another vehicle on fire overnight.

"Both vehicles were destroyed. There was no damage to the home. My family and I are all safe," her statement said.

"I don't want to speculate on a possible motive. We will await the results of the investigation," she said.

Zahid, a Liberal backbencher, has been an MP for Scarborough Centre since 2015. (CBC News)

Toronto police say a total of three cars were damaged as a result of a fire in the area of Bellamy Road N. and Lawrence Avenue E. around 1:20 a.m. Police did not confirm a connection to Zahid.

In an emailed update Thursday, Toronto police spokesperson Stephanie Miceli said officers are canvassing for video surveillance and looking to speak with witnesses. Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

Zahid, a Liberal backbencher, has been an MP for Scarborough Centre since 2015. She currently chairs the standing committee on science and research and is the vice-chair of the Canada-China legislative association.

World.title: Raptors to raise Kyle Lowry's No. 7 to rafters in January retirement ceremony
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Toronto Raptors will retire Kyle Lowry's No. 7 following their Jan. 10 game against the Philadelphia 76ers.

Lowry will become the second player in franchise history to have his number raised to the rafters at Scotiabank Arena, joining Vince Carter.

The 40-year-old guard retired in July after signing a one-day contract with Toronto to end his 20-year NBA career as a Raptor.

"I've been looking forward to this moment for years. I always said that Toronto is home, and that I'd retire a Raptor, and to see my No. 7 go up in that building is going to mean everything to me," Lowry said in a statement.

"We built something special here — my teammates, the organization, the city and the fans, and all of Canada. We became champions together, and to be able to share this night with all of them, and with my family, is going to mean a lot to me."

Lowry spent nine seasons in Toronto and helped the Raptors win their first NBA championship in 2019.

The six-time all-star is the franchise's career leader in assists, steals and three-pointers.

World.title: Consumers say 'resolve is strengthened' to buy Canadian, bringing patriotic shopping movement back to life
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Since the U.S. first imposed tariffs on Canada in early 2025, Francine Pich é has made a point not to buy American products.

"The rule in our house," said the Burlington, Ont., resident, "is Canada first, non-U.S. second, and never American, if we can avoid it."

Pich é has switched her personal care product brands, cancelled her Amazon membership and abandoned plans for a trip to New York in an effort not to give her dollars to the States, except when she can't find another alternative.

But after the most recent round of trade talks fell through and new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs came into force, Pich é says she won't be making any more exceptions.

Her family now plans to cancel the last of their American streaming service subscriptions once those come up for renewal. And Pich é plans to say goodbye to some of the gluten-free foods she enjoys that are made in the U.S., even though she hasn't been able to find alternatives.

"My resolve is strengthened," Pich é said. "That's the only way that I can fight back."

After consumers first walked away from American products more than a year ago, renewed trade threats from the U.S. have sparked the Buy Canadian movement to come roaring back, as some consumers pivot even harder to Canadian products.

WATCH | Trade war sparks 'Buy Canadian' resurgence: Trade war sparks 'Buy Canadian' resurgence | Duration 2:04 A renewed trade war with the U.S. has sparked a resurgence of calls for consumers to buy Canadian products, but the higher costs can be a challenge for businesses and shoppers alike.

Traffic skyrockets for Buy Canadian apps, sites

That's meant an influx of newcomers to the Made in Canada Facebook group, where more than 1.4 million members were already sharing information about Canadian-made products or alternatives to American ones.

Their page saw about a 300 per cent increase in views so far in August compared to June 2026, and there are more than 1,000 people currently waiting to join the group, according to administrator Jayne Little, who says that's way more than usual.

Little, from Glen Morris, Ont., says the conversations happening in the Facebook group right now seem more sophisticated and thoughtful than those she saw in 2025, when people were mostly discussing plans to switch to Canadian brands for basics like ketchup.

"They're really looking at what … their fall shopping habits are going to be and trying to find Canadian sources for that."

Little says others in the group seem to be digging deeper and talking about revisiting certain subscriptions or even their use of American-owned social media platforms.

Other platforms and apps that give information about Canadian products have also noticed an increase in traffic lately.

Web developer Ryan Checora says his app that allows shoppers to scan barcodes or search products and get information about their country of origin — aptly named O SCANada — was downloaded more than 4,000 times over the weekend.

"It's continuing to go, it seems," Checora said. "Traction really is picking up again for it."

Ryan Checora and his mom, Cathy, co-developed the O SCANada app in February 2025 when the U.S. first imposed heightened tariffs on Canada. They wanted to help Canadians figure out where the products they loved came from. (Submitted by Ryan Checora)

He says an initial boom of about 100,000 new downloads when the app first debuted had eventually slowed to a trickle about a month before this recent spike.

Checora says he's glad to see more Canadians showing interest in where the products they buy come from.

"You can almost get complacent with, you know, the new normal of things," Checora said. "I think it's important that we realize that … we need to stick together and support each other."

Price vs. Canadian pride

But for some, the price point still outweighs where products come from despite the increasing trade hostilities between Canada and the U.S.

Outside a fruit market in Vancouver, Lauren Hung says cost is still her main concern when shopping for groceries.

"I obviously want to [opt] for B.C. berries, but sometimes the price tag is just pretty high," she said.

WATCH | 'Buy Canadian' website traffic surges: ‘Buy Canadian’ website sees traffic surge 300% after U.S. trade talks collapse | Duration 4:41 Traffic to Canadian e-commerce marketplace Common Goods has surged 300 per cent since Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, according to owner Valerie Crisp. She says the response shows continued interest in buying Canadian, even as consumers navigate the complexities of the new tariffs.

David Hardisty, an associate professor of marketing at the University of British Columbia's Sauder School of Business, says consumers might be more likely to avoid American products or purchases for discretionary items that don't need to be bought so urgently.

Travel is a good example, he says, and could be a reason why the travel boycott to the U.S. by Canadians has held so strong for more than a year. Despite a slight uptick in travel south of the border in recent months , return trips from the U.S. by Canadians are still way down compared to pre-trade war levels.

"But for everyday staples, if you're trying to feed your family, you're struggling to get by," Hardisty said, "definitely for some people that may not be realistic" to buy Canadian.

Nonetheless, some Canadian brands, like Antigonish, N.S.-based Peace by Chocolate, have instead enjoyed a bump.

Tareq Hadhad, the chocolate company's founder and CEO says lots of Canadians have been happy to spend the extra dollars and energy to support home grown businesses like his — both in the last 18 months, and in recent days.

The company proudly displays the maple leaf on their packaging and has a line of chocolate bars featuring Canadiana-phrases like "Strong and Free" and "Elbows Up," which have been major sellers since the Buy Canadian movement began.

The Nova Scotia-based Peace by Chocolate company has Health Canada's front-of-package nutrition label on some of its chocolate bars. The food industry has until Jan. 1, 2026, to comply. (Anjuli Patil/CBC)

Hadhad credits the movement's resurgence for a 500 per cent increase in web traffic to their website over the last few days. And while it's still too early to tell if that will translate to higher sales, he expects it will mean a boost for his business.

"It is a spike in the support for Canadian brands," Hadhad said. "It is a spike for the showcasing of love for Canada from customers in every community across this country."

He's stopped shipping products to the U.S. amid the trade war, in part because of the uncertainty of tariffs and in part because he says it's the "right thing to do right now." That's made support from non-American customers all the more important.

LISTEN | What retaliatory tariffs and moving forward without a deal looks like for Canada: Front Burner 29:58 How will the new tariffs hit Canada's economy?

And while the attention of the Buy Canadian movement never fully faded for his company, Hadhad says this round feels different.

He says consumers have learned how impactful their spending habits can be in the last 18 months, and doesn't think Canadians are in the mood to give the administration south of the border a second chance.

"They can put a tariff on what Canada makes, but they will never be able to put a tariff on what Canada is made of."

World.title: The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Like a fox trying to bring down a moose, Canada's retaliation against the latest U.S. tariffs is a classic case of asymmetrical warfare.

That's because the U.S. economy is about 12 times larger than Canada's, says economist Trevor Tombe.

"It's incredibly hard for a small country to move the needle in aggregate in the United States. That's why it's important to zoom in on specific states where possible. But even in these heavily affected states, the effects are small," he said.

Not only is the U.S. much bigger than Canada, it's also much less dependent on international trade, because its internal market consumes so much of what it produces.

WATCH | Canada mounts response to U.S. tariffs: Canadian counter-tariffs target appliances, fish, cosmetics | Duration 3:13 The federal government laid out Canada's plan to strike back at the U.S., announcing billions in counter-tariffs on hundreds of America products including fish, cosmetics and furniture.

And so with its counter-tariffs set to take effect after Labour Day, Canada must maximize every conceivable advantage if its tariff jiu-jitsu is going to throw its heavier opponent off balance.

But it's not as simple as just looking for maximum pain points in the U.S.

"You have to be very conscious of limiting self harm against our own importers and exporters," said Brian Clow, who was chief of staff to International Trade Minister Chrystia Freeland during Canada's last tariff war with the U.S. and chief adviser to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau on Canada-U.S. relations.

"There were a whole bunch of categories that it looks like the Canadian government didn't touch precisely for that reason."

Canada's tariffs need to be politically targeted, reciprocal and proportionate, said Clow.

Change behaviour or go home

There are three main objectives when selecting a target, says Tombe.

The first, what he says is most important, "is changing the behaviour on the part of the target country."

Second, he says, it has to come at a cost to the U.S. — something "difficult for a smaller country to do." It makes little sense to tariff products where Canadians make up only a small part of the overall export market for U.S. producers, Tombe says.

WATCH | NDP leader says trade war should hurt Trump: 'This trade war could and should hurt President Trump,' says NDP Leader Avi Lewis | Duration 11:50 Opposition leaders from the Conservative Party, NDP and Bloc Québécois all met with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday to discuss the government’s response to the latest 50 per cent U.S. tariffs. Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis says he 'was struck' by the prime minister's tone regarding the likelihood of a deal while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Third, he said the target must be a product where Canadians have options at home or beyond the U.S.

"You want to go after areas of the country that will cause the business community in the United States to speak up, and therefore cause politicians in those areas to speak up, and try to influence the president and his team," Clow says.

He pointed to how Canada went hard on Kentucky in 2018, the home state of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, who was the majority leader at the time.

"Kentucky was a big target, but we definitely targeted Pennsylvania, Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin, some of those key swing states that elected Donald Trump as president," Clow said.

States at play in midterms big exporters to Canada

The federal government hasn't explicitly said the counter-tariffs are designed to make an impact on the U.S. midterms. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said on Tuesday that Canada's response is "proportionate, targeted and strategic."

If swing states seem to be even more of a target today, that's probably just because the 2026 midterm battlegrounds happen to fall in some of the northern states that trade most with Canada.

Two in particular, Michigan and Maine, send about 40 per cent of their exports to Canada, and both have tight election campaigns underway that are critical to the Republicans' continued control of the U.S. Senate.

Tombe estimates Canada's planned retaliatory tariffs on Michigan exports amount to about 0.3 per cent of the state's economy, similar in percentage terms to the latest U.S. tariffs' impact on Canada's GDP — and far greater than the overall hit to the U.S. economy.

WATCH | How federal supports will work amid trade war: How Canada's federal supports will help workers amid the Canada-U.S. trade war | Duration 8:21 U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff onslaught looms over Canada’s economy. Tyler Meredith, head of economic policy for former prime minister Justin Trudeau, says the current government is trying to 'keep people connected to work as long as possible.'

Clow says the goal of influencing swing states is why some food products are on Canada's retaliatory list — even though those tariffs will likely lead to higher prices at the grocery store.

Seafood — a significant export from Maine and Alaska — was originally on Canada's counter-tariff list. But late Wednesday, the Finance Department announced seafood and fish products were removed to "protect against broader economic harms."

Tit-for-tat on some sectors

Reciprocity is clearly a motivation behind many of the tariff choices — increasing targeted industries' share of the Canadian domestic market to offset export losses.

That explains why nearly half of the volume of the Canadian counter-tariffs targets American metals and metal products. Those are typically products where Canada both imports and exports, and a Canadian substitute is generally available.

If tariffs are applied to harder to replace items, "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," then putting a tariff on it merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, said Tombe.

This is particularly important because the need to offset U.S. tariffs means that a high proportion of Canada's tariffs are aimed at intermediate inputs and capital goods (such as metalworking tools, railway switches and industrial robots), even though Canada usually prefers to tariff consumer-facing goods (such as bread ovens, heat pumps and kitchen utensils) in order to minimize disruption to Canadian manufacturers.

LISTEN | Front Burner on the trade war view from the U.S.: Front Burner 30:20 How the trade war is registering in America

But Tombe says it's not really possible to create a domestic market equivalent to the one lost in the U.S.

"What's much more important, in terms of the protection that these tariffs provide for businesses and workers, is not changing Canadian buyer decisions, but financing the large support package that the government has also announced."

He estimates the counter-tariffs could bring in about $1 billion a month.

"So there's a mechanism to pay for the supports that we'll be providing to affected workers and businesses," he said. "That's going to matter a lot more than any indirect protection our tariffs might provide."

He said strong support for the individuals and companies most affected by the trade war is key to maintaining unity. He says he also sees signs that the counter-tariff package was structured in such a way as to minimize sticker shock for Canadian shoppers.

"A list of retaliatory items that Canada would target to minimize the broader economic costs in Canada would have been a lot more consumer goods and food," Tombe said.

Canada's goal should be to maintain cohesion within the country, while encouraging division and recriminations in the U.S., he said.

Talking while tariffing

The communications strategy that goes with tariffs is important, says Tombe, in steering American anger away from Canada and back toward the White House.

"Love him or hate him, when [Ontario Premier] Doug Ford is on U.S. news networks, that's part of trying to influence the nature of the political response there to retaliation," Tombe said.

But Clow says Americans already know who's to blame.

WATCH | Ford makes rounds on U.S. programs: Doug Ford softens trade war message on U.S. TV | Duration 2:04 A day after hurling insults at U.S. President Donald Trump, Ontario Premier Doug Ford took a more measured approach while discussing the trade war during appearances on American TV. Meanwhile, Canadian officials rebuffed Trump’s threat to change Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

"Folks know where this trade war started and they know how it's going to be solved," he said.

"If you're a U.S. business that's hit by Canada's retaliation, you know that the person you need to call to lobby is on the U.S. side of the border, in the Trump administration."

While Clow says that Canada's unity and determination gives it strength out of proportion to its size, the massive weight of the U.S. economy makes it difficult to imagine going through multiple rounds of escalation.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CBC News on Wednesday that the White House is "not going to just sit down and take" the planned counter-tariffs.

"This will be a very tough judgment call for the prime minister and his team," Clow said.

The best tariffs — the ones that hurt the U.S. most with the least blowback for Canada — have been used this round, say the experts.

"My own estimates suggest that if you were to narrow yourself down to areas where Canada represents a majority of U.S. sales and where they are a minority of our imports, and we're talking about swing states only," said Tombe, "you have a few billion dollars' worth of trade that could be targeted."

Any subsequent round of tariffs would involve more pain for less gain.

World.title: Peter Cullen, Canadian voice of Eeyore, Optimus Prime, dead at 85
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Peter Cullen, the Canadian voice actor behind Eeyore in Winnie the Pooh and Optimus Prime in the Transformers franchise, has died.

His agent Kevin Motley confirmed to CBC News that Cullen died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 85.

The Montreal-born actor honed his chops on the radio, first on CKGM, and later on television as the announcer for The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour on CBS f rom 1967 to 1969.

In the 1976 remake of King Kong, Cullen was the voice of the giant ape. He also was responsible for the terrifying sounds that emerged from the monster in Predator in 198 7.

Millennials may recognize Cullen's voice from the 1988-91 series The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh, where he began voicing the the donkey Eeyore. He continued to play the role in the 2002 film Winnie the Pooh: A Very Merry Pooh Year and other shows and videos.

But his biggest role was the talking truck transformer, Optimus Prime, who he played starting in the early '80s.

The leader of the Autobots was so beloved that in 1986, there was huge fan backlash to Optimus Prime dying in a duel with the evil Megatron in The Transformers: The Movie.

Producers brought the character back to life in 1987 with The Transformers: The Return of Optimus Prime.

Although Cullen hadn't played the character for two decades, director Michael Bay rehired him in 2007 for his science fiction action film Transformers, alongside stars Shia LaBeouf, Megan Fox and Josh Duhamel.

At the Calgary Comic Expo in 2015, Cullen explained how his brother Larry inspired the voice. Larry was a U.S. Marine who had fought in battle. He had seen real action and received medals for his valour.

So when Cullen was standing in the voice booth for the first time and looking at his script, he remembered Larry said a real hero was "strong enough to be gentle."

Cullen's family referenced that moment today, when they announced his death in a statement.

They said Cullen will be "held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide," and they asked the public to "honor his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity and loyalty and always remember, 'Be strong enough to be gentle.'"

World.title: Conservatives want the Liberals to release the rejected U.S. trade deal. Should they?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservatives are calling on the Liberals to release the text of the U.S. tariff agreement that the federal government ultimately rejected last week. While one expert argues there is some merit to showing that level of transparency for the sake of national unity, others suggest it would ultimately hurt Canada's negotiation position.

U.S. President Donald Trump slapped 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian imports over the weekend after negotiators failed to secure some form of trade agreement — even though there were indications that progress was being made.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Americans "asked too much and offered too little" for the government to settle on a final agreement.

Conservative MPs have been calling on Carney to be fully transparent about the details in the agreement that the government turned down.

"Canadians deserve to know what is the deal that the prime minister at first planned to accept and later decided to reject. Release the proposed text," Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a news conference on Tuesday.

"Canadians deserve to know what was on the table so all of us can know what we are fighting for and what we are fighting against."

WATCH | ‘Canadians deserve to see’ dead U.S. trade deal, Poilievre says: ‘Canadians deserve to see’ dead U.S. trade deal: Poilievre | Duration 1:05 Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to release the details of the proposed trade agreement between Ottawa and Washington that caused Carney to order his delegation to walk away from the bargaining table on Aug. 21. Poilievre also called on Carney to recall Parliament, for more transparency on incoming counter-tariffs and a new plan that ‘jolts’ Canada’s economy.

For his part, Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said in a French-language interview with Radio-Canada's Midi info that he's not against the government releasing those details.

"I'm open to it, but it's not an imperative for me as it would have been the case if a deal would have been reached," Blanchet told host Alec Castonguay on Wednesday.

Lawrence Herman, a trade lawyer and senior fellow with the C.D. Howe Institute, told CBC News that it would "be a total mistake" for any government to release that level of detail around trade talks.

"Trade negotiations are highly delicate matters that have to be dealt with behind closed doors. It's just the way the world works when we're dealing with trade talks," he said.

Herman suggested that putting out full details of what was on offer would tip the government's hand in future talks.

"We may be sitting down with the Americans, I think, at some point in the future and talking to them again. You don't want to have all kinds of political gamesmanship surrounding papers that Canada might have put on the table during the suspended negotiations."

WATCH | U.S. trade representative disputes why talks fell apart: U.S. trade rep disputes why talks fell apart | Canadian exclusive | Duration 16:53 In a Canadian exclusive interview, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer disputed Canada’s explanation about why trade talks fell apart, and told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton there’s currently no ‘open channels’ to get both sides back to the negotiating table.

But Carlo Dade, the international policy director and head of the New North America Initiative at the University of Calgary, said there is merit to being fully transparent given that much of what the U.S. is asking from Canada had been put on the table with other countries.

"The Americans aren't constructing a whole new set of negotiations and demands for us. They're resetting the global trade agenda," Dade told CBC news.

"This is not just about Canada. This is a larger global process and as we continue to think about this only as Canada, we miss the forest for the tree that we're looking at right now."

WATCH | Feds announce 'dollar-for-dollar' counter-tariffs on billions in U.S. imports: Feds announce 'dollar-for-dollar' counter-tariffs on billions in U.S. imports | Duration 1:15 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Canada will match the latest round of U.S. tariffs in a 'proportionate, targeted and strategic' way. Champagne says the tariffs, which will impact more than $27 billion in U.S. goods, are 'all about fairness.'

Asked about Poilievre's call to release a draft of the deal, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne argued that key details had been publicly reported in the media.

"This is probably the most publicly advertised negotiation of a trade agreement I can recall," he told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.

"In terms of transparency I think Canadians have been able to follow that on a daily basis."

'No national secrets,' Poilievre says

On Tuesday, Poilievre argued that if the two sides were close to an agreement, American negotiators would have seen much of what Canada was offering at this point.

"There are no national secrets in that text. It's already been shown to the United States' administration." Poilievre said.

But Jason Kenney, a former Conservative cabinet minister and Alberta premier, told CBC Radio's The Current that it might not be that simple.

"There wouldn't be a final text that was subject to negotiations," Kenney told guest host Susan Ormiston.

"In contexts like this, there are lots of different texts flying back and forth, different versions, a lot of it is happening verbally."

WATCH | California governor says Carney is ‘playing this well’ in Trump trade fight: California governor says Carney is ‘playing this well’ in Trump trade fight | Duration 10:23 California Gov. Gavin Newsom responds to the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade talks, telling CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that Prime Minister Mark Carney is ‘playing this well’ because Donald Trump doesn’t respect weakness.

Kenney also suggested that negotiations should remain confidential, although he agreed with Poilievre's suggestion that Parliament be recalled to discuss the ongoing trade dispute.

Even though Herman argued that trade talks need to remain largely confidential, he said the government does need to have some level of transparency. He specifically said the government needs to lay out its broad goals for trade talks, but added that he thinks the current government has done that.

While Dade thinks the government should release the details of the talks, he did agree that Canada is in a unique circumstance compared to other countries because the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement is still subject to review.

Be transparent, expert says

But Dade suggested the CUSMA review might be a "minor point" given that Canada is also the only country subject to tariffs under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, or the Smoot-Hawley Act.

Section 338 is what Trump used to impose the latest round of tariffs and Dade suggested they can be used as a "divide and conquer" tactic.

A CBC News analysis of the goods that now have a 50 per cent tariff suggests the levies are hitting provinces to various degrees. But Dade said that Section 338 can also be used to level tariffs against a specific good from one province while leaving it off another province.

"The administration [could] decide it has the authority under Section 338 to say liquor from B.C. and Ontario, no [tariffs]. Wine from Nova Scotia, yes [tariffs]. So that creates a further potential for the Americans to divide and conquer," he said.

"Under that scenario, national unity is more important than it is with your normal trade negotiation."

Dade argued that, according to his own research, the government needs to be transparent about what each province would need to give up in a successful negotiation or suffer through if a deal isn't reached to ensure the U.S. can't set jurisdictions against one another.

"By not providing details, we create the fuel for division. We create the fuel for uncertainty in Canada and it's uncertainty that leads to division between the provinces" if the government isn't transparent, Dade said.

World.title: Conrad Black: This is an opportunity Carney, don’t squander it
World.content:
Article content

Before we embark altogether in Carney’s war-canoe, we should verify the Liberal claim that they did everything possible to secure an acceptable accord: I find it hard to believe that the Americans considered bilingual packaging a non-negotiable issue, (Trump has already called this a lie from a “weak and ineffective” Carney). If our side of this commercial war is going to be anything other than mawkish Churchillian posturing, we need a real breakout from the purblindness and paralysis of the last decade. The prime minister is making worrisome and incoherent noises about automobile production by Japanese companies being pushed into the U.S. and replaced with imports from China, while fumbling General Motors truck production in Canada, a St. Vitus’ dance for our beleaguered auto industry. Despite his commendable efforts, Carney has really only completed two new trade deals, and their significance is negligible. There is still no evidence that pipelines are going to be built and we should have pipelines to both oceans and increased refining capacity as quickly as we can build them. If Mark Carney has outgrown his former self as a social market eco-geek and Davosian secular cleric, he can be a historic leader of this country. This is a greater opportunity than a challenge and we must not fail or squander it.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Media concentration in Colombia
World.content:
Listen to this episode on Spotify

Colombia’s corporate media have played a dubious role in the history of the country and have concentrated an immense power for their owners.
