World.title: What’s the latest on the security situation in Mexicali?
World.content:
The U.S. government issued a security alert late Monday due to a potential “August 25 threat in Mexicali,” but no major security incidents were reported in the northern border city on Tuesday.

The U.S. Mission to Mexico issued the alert, announcing that due to “threat information,” U.S. government activities in, and travel to, Mexicali had been suspended for Aug. 25.

The diplomatic mission advised U.S. citizens to “avoid government buildings in Mexicali” on Tuesday and “seek shelter in the event of an incident.” It didn’t specify the nature of the potential threat.

On Tuesday morning, President Claudia Sheinbaum said the U.S. security alert was issued due to the possibility that a criminal group could pose a danger in Mexicali, the capital of Baja California. The criminal group was identified as “Los Rusos,” which is affiliated with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Mexican authorities recently seized a large quantity of fentanyl from a property in Mexicali linked to “Los Rusos,” leading to fears that the criminal group could carry out a retaliatory attack in the city. Journalist Luis Chaparro said in a social media post on Tuesday that he obtained information from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration in San Diego that confirmed that the security alert was issued after that agency intercepted “at least one call” in which members of “Los Rusos” spoke of plans to attack buildings in Mexicali occupied by municipal police and the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

No such attacks eventuated on Tuesday, and no major security incidents occurred in Mexicali, located opposite the city of Calexico, California. A Mexico News Daily reader who lives in Mexicali commented on an MND article that the city wasn’t “shut down or impacted in any way” after the U.S. security alert was issued. He wrote that his experience in Mexicali on Tuesday was “business as usual.”

Authorities did bolster security in the city in light of the U.S alert, which was acknowledged and endorsed by the government of Canada. That included increasing surveillance of public buildings and “strategic points” of the Baja California capital, the newspaper Milenio reported. The Baja California-based news outlet En Contraste News reported that there were fewer visitors than normal to public buildings in Mexicali on Tuesday. It also noted that state and federal judicial authorities suspended activities. The border between Mexicali and Calexico remained open.

US Northern Command ‘applauds’ Mexico’s success against ‘Los Rusos’

In a social media post on Tuesday, the U.S. Northern Command, one of 11 “unified combatant commands” of the U.S. Department of Defense, wrote:

“USNORTHCOM applauds the Government of Mexico’s success against ‘Los Rusos.’ Mexico’s whole-of-government commitment to countering cartels is reducing illicit trafficking at the Southern Border. #USNORTHCOM, through @JIATFCC [Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel], continues to identify, disrupt, and dismantle cartel operations posing a threat to the United States along the U.S.-Mexico border.”

USNORTHCOM applauds the Government of Mexico’s success against “Los Rusos.” Mexico’s whole-of-government commitment to countering cartels is reducing illicit trafficking at the Southern Border. #USNORTHCOM, through @JIATFCC, continues to identify, disrupt, and dismantle cartel… https://t.co/dPLwClDtRT pic.twitter.com/wjsYD4DaQ1 — U.S. Northern Command (@USNorthernCmd) August 25, 2026

Included in the same post was Mexican Security Minister Omar García Harfuch’s Aug. 20 post to X in which he announced a fentanyl bust — the very bust that U.S. authorities reportedly suspected could lead to a retaliatory attack by “Los Rusos,” a group said to be linked to the “Los Mayos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel.

In his post, García Harfuch wrote:

“Derived from the exchange of information with @DEAHQ and from intelligence and investigative work by Mexican authorities in Mexicali, Baja California, … [federal security forces] and state authorities carried out an operational action at a property linked to the criminal group known as ‘Los Rusos.’ During the operation, 120 kilos of fentanyl pills, equivalent to more than 4 million doses, a firearm and vehicles were seized. International cooperation, accompanied by the investigation and operational capacity of Mexican institutions, allows information to be translated into concrete results against criminal organizations and their logistical structures.”

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson shared García Harfuch’s post to his X account last Thursday.

Above the security minister’s post, Johnson wrote: “Information shared becomes action taken. More than 4 million potentially deadly doses of fentanyl kept off our streets and away from our families. This is what results-driven cooperation looks like: sharing information, acting on it, and putting real pressure on the cartels. That’s the partnership @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein are driving.”

With reports from La Jornada and Milenio

World.title: Bárcena presents bill to put environmental justice at heart of Mexican law
World.content:
The Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) presented an initiative today to reform the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection (LGEEPA), which is Mexico’s main environmental legal framework.

The proposal, spearheaded by Minister Alicia Bárcena, aims to update a regulation created in 1988 in response to new challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, pressure on water resources and conflicts arising from infrastructure, industry and urban development projects.

Presented at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference, the bill includes 10 policy principles that seek to prevent and repair ecological damage, protect communities and make economic development compatible with environmental justice and nature conservation.

According to Sheinbaum, the objective is “to strengthen the capacities of the Mexican state to protect, care for, conserve and restore the environment and natural resources.”

What are the new principles?

With environmental justice as the bill’s central focus, Semarnat aims to deepen the link between the protection of ecosystems and natural resources with social well-being, citizen participation and respect for the rights of Mexico’s Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

It also proposes that authorities, in collaboration with private companies, assess the possible ecological consequences of works and productive activities further in advance (currently, a company can request an Environmental Impact Assessment (MIA) at any time prior to the onset of construction), and assume partial responsibility if and when the work causes eventual deterioration.

Bárcena explained that the reform takes a “proactive” approach by requiring developers of large-scale projects to carry out a strategic environmental assessment over a longer time frame and prohibiting them from fragmenting projects to avoid a comprehensive assessment of their regional impact.

The bill incorporates new tools to address current environmental challenges, including an ecological restoration program, new mechanisms to address climate change and provisions to strengthen the prevention, repair and remediation of environmental damage.

The plan also includes promoting ecological restoration programs, focusing on rivers, mangroves, coastlines, forest ecosystems and other degraded areas.

Bárcena said that the enhanced protection of native species will be paramount, including the Mexican wolf, the condor, the blue whale and dolphins.

Moreover, the law proposes a specific chapter dedicated to those who defend the environment and public goods, incorporating a new platform for “payment for environmental services” (PSA) and facilitating compensation for communities that protect their natural resources.

Bárcena added that the bill incorporates scientific advances, innovation and new technologies, as well as the recognition of the ancestral knowledge of Indigenous peoples as tools for the protection of biodiversity.

“We cannot do science without recognizing the wisdom of our Indigenous peoples,” Bárcena said.

Overall, the bill proposes that economic development must honor nature’s limits while promoting shared well-being.

World.title: The MND Economy Index™ for June 2026
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND ECONOMY INDEX™

Providing broad insight into the Mexican economy

MND Intelligence · Fourth edition

Welcome to the fourth edition of the MND Economy Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products from Mexico News Daily.

The MND Economy Index™ is a 10-pillar, 19-indicator composite index that compiles a broad range of economic data into a single score between 0 and 100, giving Mexico News Daily readers a clear, accessible picture of how the Mexican economy is performing across multiple dimensions.

In the inaugural MND Economy Index™ article, published in late May, we not only analyzed the index score — 63.4 out of 100 — but also explained what the index is, why we developed it and how it works. Click here to read (or re-read) those explanations.

In this August edition of the MND Economy Index™ — which uses economic data primarily from the month of June — the index score is 66.9, a decrease of 1.7 points compared to the previous score.

The score for June is above the neutral benchmark of 60, but there is still significant room for improvement.

Before we look more closely at the latest index result, and the index trend in the first half of 2026, here is a short guide to what the overall index score means.

85–100: Exceptional — the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Strong — broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern.

— broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern. 60–74: Above neutral — meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement.

— meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement. 50–59: Mixed — passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below.

— passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

The MND Economy Index™ trend between February and June

The first two MND Economy Index™ scores we calculated for 2026 — both corresponding to the first quarter of the year — were very similar.

The first index score we calculated for 2026 was 63.7, a number derived mainly from economic data for the month of February. The index score declined slightly to 63.4 based on a calculation using data that was primarily for the month of March.

While there was little variation in the index score across those two editions, there were some significant changes in individual pillar scores, including the inflation one and the sovereign risk one (see more details here).

In April, we saw the first significant movement of the year in the overall MND Economy Index™ score. In the space of a month, the score rose 4.16 points to 67.55, a clear indication that the Mexican economy was gaining strength. What was particularly encouraging was that the biggest contributor to the increase was the economic growth pillar, as the Mexican economy expanded 2.2% in April compared to just 0.5% in May.

While economic growth moderated to 2% in May, there were encouraging signs in other data related to the Mexican economy for that month, allowing the MND Economy Index™ score to increase for a second consecutive month to reach 68.6.

In June, the MND Economy Index™ declined for the first time since March. Among the reasons why the index score fell in June compared to May were lower annual economic growth and a year-over-year contraction in manufacturing output.

The August edition of the MND Economy Index™ (based mainly on June data) As noted above, the MND Economy Index™ score for this August edition — based mainly on data for June 2026 — is 66.9, a decrease of 1.7 percentage points compared to the previous score. Below you will see the score for each of the ten pillars that make up the index, expressed out of 10 to reflect each pillar’s exact contribution to the final composite score. Pillars are color-coded using a traffic light system: green (a score above 7.5) indicates strong performance; yellow (5.0–7.5) signals decent performance but with room for improvement; and red (below 5.0) flags a pillar that is falling short of its benchmark. Where a pillar score has improved compared to the previous month, an upward arrow appears alongside its corresponding traffic light; a downward arrow indicates deterioration; and a pause symbol denotes no change.

As you’ll see below, scores for five of the ten MND Economy Index™ pillars decreased in June compared to the previous month. Scores for four pillars increased while one stayed the same.

🟢 ⬇️ MONETARY POLICY (9.57):

The score for this pillar declined to 9.57 in June from 9.86 in May. The Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate remained at 6.50% in June after a 25-basis-point cut to that level took effect on May 8. Therefore, there was no change in the interest rate component of the pillar score.

The deterioration in the pillar score was due to an increase in Mexico’s real interest rate in June — i.e., the Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate minus the annual headline inflation rate. The real interest rate in June was 3.13%, a reading 0.43 points above the 2.7% neutral midpoint. The real interest rate in May, at 2.56%, was closer to the neutral midpoint than the reading in June.

Despite the decline in the monetary policy score, this pillar remained the index’s top performer in June 2026.

🟢 ⬆️ INFLATION (9.33):

The score for this pillar increased to 9.33 in June from 9.06 in May.

Inflation eased to 3.37% in June from 3.94% in May, causing an increase in the score for the current inflation component of the pillar.

The score for the pillar component that considers the 12-month forward inflation forecast declined as the Bank of Mexico now anticipates an annual rate of 3.3% in the second quarter of 2027, which, of course, includes the month of June. The central bank previously predicted an inflation rate of 3% in the second quarter of next year.

The increase in the inflation component score was greater than the decrease in the inflation forecast score, allowing the overall pillar score to rise.

The inflation pillar score is poised to improve again in the next edition of the MND Economy Index™ as inflation fell again in July, settling at 3.12%. In addition, the Bank of Mexico is currently forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.2% in the third quarter of 2027. Therefore, the score for that component of the pillar should increase slightly in our next index.

🟡 ⬇️ SOVEREIGN RISK (7.43)

The score for this pillar was 7.43 in June, down slightly from 7.45 in May.

The score for the sovereign credit ratings component of the pillar remained unchanged in June, as there were no month-over-month changes to the Mexico ratings of Moodys (Baa3/stable); S&P (BBB/negative); and Fitch (BBB-/stable).

The slight decline in the overall pillar score was due to a modest widening in Mexico’s 5-year credit default swap spread. The credit default swap spread was 86.87 basis points at the end of June, up from 86.03 basis points at the end of May. The increase reflected a slight rise in the market-implied cost of insuring against a Mexican sovereign default.

🟡 ⬇️ MANUFACTURING SECTOR HEALTH (6.9)

The score for this pillar declined in June, falling to 6.9 from 7.48 in May.

The exports component of the pillar remained at the maximum score due to a 34.4% annual increase in export revenue in June, well above the 16.7% threshold needed for a perfect ten. Official data shows that 91.3% of Mexico’s export revenue between January and June came from the shipment abroad of manufactured goods.

The decrease in the overall pillar score was due to a 2.4% annual contraction in manufacturing output in June. Manufacturing output also declined in annual terms in May, but the contraction that month was much smaller at 0.1%.

🟡 ⬆️ CURRENCY STABILITY: (6.8)

The score for this pillar rose to 6.8 in June from 6.77 in May.

The standard deviation of daily exchange rate movements increased to 0.49% in June from 0.42% in May, leading to a slight decrease in the score for that component of the pillar.

The increase in the pillar score in June was due to a higher spot rate score. The score for that component increased because the peso weakened against the US dollar in June to trade at 17.50 to the greenback at the end of the month, a depreciation of 0.7% compared to the end of April.

The exchange rate was thus closer to the index’s 19.00 USD:MXN baseline, which is based on the 2025 average rate. This pillar penalizes significant deviation from the 19.00 USD:MXN baseline in either direction, recognizing that a peso that has strengthened too far from this benchmark can erode export competitiveness and reduce the purchasing power of remittances, just as a weakening peso raises import costs.

🟡 ⬇️ INVESTMENT CLIMATE (6.56)

The score for this pillar fell to 6.56 in June from 8.25 in May.

In part, the decline was due to lower — but still strong — annual growth on the S&P/BMV FIBRAS Total Return Index, which tracks the performance of Mexico’s listed real estate investment trusts. The index grew 27.1% annually to the end of June.

The score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar also declined as the Economy Ministry published data this week showing that foreign direct investment in Mexico increased 2.1% annually in the first six months of 2026. That result is significantly weaker than the 10.4% year-over-year growth recorded in the first quarter of the year.

🟡 ⬆️ EXTERNAL INCOME (6.52)

The score for this pillar increased in June, rising to 6.52 from 5.53 a month earlier.

Incoming remittances grew 4.2% year-on-year — an increase compared to the 3.8% increase in May.

Thus, the score for the remittances component of the pillar increased. However, the 4.2% annual growth rate is still well below the 16.67% increase required for a perfect score.

The pillar score also improved in June as tourism revenue increased 5.9% annually, a welcome development after a 0.3% year-over-year contraction in May.

🟡 ⬆️ LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT (6.21):

The score for this pillar increased to 6.21 in June from 6.02 in May. Scores for two of the three pillar components increased, allowing the overall score to edge up.

In June, there was a 2% annual increase in the number of people in formal sector jobs, up from a 1.5% increase in May. Therefore, there was an increase in the score for that component of the pillar.

Nominal wages rose 6.4% year-on-year in June — down slightly from 6.6% in May, but still well above the 3.5% benchmark.

Year-over-year growth in Mexico’s informality rate was only 0.2 percentage points in May, down from an annual increase of 0.3 points in May. In June, 55% of all Mexican workers worked in the informal economy. Lowering that rate is a major challenge for the Mexican government.

🔴 ⬇️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (4.4)

The score for this pillar fell to 4.4 in June from 5 in May.

The decrease was due to a lower annual economic growth rate in June. The annual growth rate in June was 1.7%, according to final data published by INEGI this week, whereas the rate in May was slightly higher at 2%.

While Economic Growth remains one of the index’s worst-performing pillars, the performance of the Mexican economy did improve in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the first quarter. INEGI reported this week that the economy grew 1.4% on a quarter-over-quarter basis between April and June, while the annual expansion was 1.9%. The economy contracted 0.3% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the previous two months, while annual growth was just 0.4% in that period.

🔴 ⏸️ PRODUCTIVITY (3.2):

The score for this pillar remained at 3.2 in May after plummeting to that level in April from an already low 4.8 in March.

Data published by the national statistics agency INEGI in June showed that the IGPLE — INEGI’s quarterly productivity measure — increased only 0.1% annually in the first quarter of 2026. That level of productivity growth was significantly weaker than the 0.9% reading in the final quarter of 2025.

An annual productivity growth rate of 0.1% is well below the 1.0% neutral benchmark, and thus, the score for this pillar is very low.

INEGI will publish productivity data for the second quarter of 2026 in early September. We will use that data for the next edition of the MND Economy Index™.

Mexico News Daily

Who Is YOUNITE

YOUNITE debuted in April 2022 under Brand New Music with the EP YOUNI-BIRTH, a nine-member group built on synchronized performance and an all-rounder concept.

The group’s catalog runs through a fast release cycle typical of K-pop, with the mini-album Another and its title track GEEKIN as the most recent chapter.

Covers and stages across Korean music shows built their reputation as a performance-first group — the format Brazilian fans will see live.

The INYUN Tour and Brazil’s K-Pop Moment

The INYUN tour extends a relationship the group has been building with Brazil, following a 2025 run through the country with dates beyond the Rio–São Paulo axis.

Brazil has consolidated as one of K-pop’s strongest markets outside Asia, with fandom infrastructure — fanbases, cup-sleeve events, dance cover groups — in every major city.

Porto Alegre’s fan community is among the country’s most organized, which is exactly why tours like this one now route through the south.

Bar Opinião: The Room

Few venues in Brazil carry Bar Opinião’s weight: since the 1980s, the Cidade Baixa room has been Porto Alegre’s temple of live music, from MPB and rock to today’s pop circuit.

The address, Rua José do Patrocínio, 834, sits in the city’s traditional nightlife district, dense with bars and restaurants for before and after the show.

For K-pop, whose productions usually aim at clubs and theaters in Brazil, the room’s scale fits the genre’s close-contact fan culture.

Tickets and Fan Culture

Tickets are sold through Sympla’s official event channels; K-pop dates in Brazil typically sell in tiers, with fan packages announced by the producer.

Expect the genre’s standard rituals outside the venue: lightsticks, banner projects and fan-organized queues.

As with most K-pop shows, doors open well before the 19:30 start — early arrival is part of the experience.

One of Brazil’s longest-running independent festivals has its date and first names: No Ar Coquetel Molotov returns on November 28 to its traditional home at the Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, in Recife.

A Festival Older Than the Format

Long before Brazil had a festival circuit, Recife had Coquetel Molotov: born in 2003 on the university campus, it helped define what an independent Brazilian festival could be.

The 23rd edition keeps the classic recipe — one day, multiple stages, and a lineup that refuses to separate generations or genres.

The UFPE campus remains its home, a setting that has hosted everything from manguebeat legends to global indie acts.

Fernanda Abreu Heads the Bill

The first confirmed name is a statement: Fernanda Abreu, the Rio singer who fused funk, dance music and MPB into hits like Rio 40 Graus.

Festival organizers highlight that the date brings her to Recife in a rare headline appearance for the city.

Her set anchors the cross-generational bet: a 1990s dance icon on the same bill as the new Pernambuco scene.

Recife’s Own on the Lineup

Cidadão Instigado, the band of guitarist Fernando Catatau — a foundational figure of the manguebeat movement through Nação Zumbi — carries the city’s experimental rock flag.

Katy da Voz e as Abusadas represent Recife’s rock and punk memory, one of the names that defined the city’s underground.

Nanda Tsunami and Bia Soull complete the confirmed list, extending the lineup toward the state’s new generation of voices.

Why the Festival Matters Beyond Music

Coquetel Molotov has doubled as a talent platform: acts that played its early editions went on to national careers, and its curation still works as a map of Brazil’s independent scene.

Its tradition of free or low-cost entry made it a rare point of access in the festival economy — a policy that shaped Recife’s live-music culture.

The November date also closes the region’s festival season, after a calendar that runs from Carnaval through São João.

Planning Ahead

The festival takes place on Saturday, November 28, at the UFPE campus in Recife’s Cidade Universitária.

Organizers are releasing the lineup in waves; the first confirmed names are out, with more to come as the date approaches.

Follow the festival’s official channels for entry format, tickets and the full program.

Florianópolis opens its gates to the pampa this weekend: the city’s first Acampamento Farroupilha runs Friday through Sunday, August 28–30, at Arena Floripa, with free entry.

The Pampa Comes to the Island

The Acampamento Farroupilha is the signature format of Rio Grande do Sul’s traditionalist movement: a camp of piquetes, stages and barbecue fires celebrating gaúcho identity.

This weekend the format debuts in Florianópolis, a city with a large community of gaúchos who migrated north to Santa Catarina.

For three days, Arena Floripa becomes a slice of the pampa, with families, CTGs — the traditional gaúcho centers — artists and exhibitors.

Music From the Tradition’s Front Line

The lineup is led by Mano Lima, one of the most popular voices of música gaúcha, whose romantic, storytelling style fills dances across the south.

Garotos de Ouro, a veteran traditionalist group with decades on the road, brings the classics of the genre.

Around the headliners, the program mixes dance presentations, religious observance and the food of the gaúcho table.

What the Farroupilha Name Means

The celebrations honor the Farroupilha Revolution of 1835–1845, the decade-long war in which Rio Grande do Sul declared itself a republic.

September 20, the revolution’s date, is the high holiday of gaúcho tradition — and acampamentos across the south and beyond mark the season.

Florianópolis’ first edition lands at the start of that season, effectively opening the Farroupilha calendar in Santa Catarina.

A Community Event at Heart

Beyond the stage, the acampamento format is built on participation: CTG stands, typical gastronomy and spaces for families and exhibitors.

Churrasco, chimarrão and traditional dress — bombachas, boots and scarves — are as much the attraction as the music.

For expats and visitors, it is the most accessible window into a culture that defines Brazil’s southern identity.

Planning the Weekend

The event runs Friday to Sunday, August 28–30, at Arena Floripa; entry is free across the three days.

Organizers recommend arriving early for the headline shows, especially Mano Lima’s set.

Arena Floripa sits in the northern part of the island; ride-hailing and car are the practical options from the center and beaches.

Belo Horizonte’s weekend starts early and downtown: on Friday, August 28, the Espaço Popular do Centro receives Mumuzinho from 18:00 for a night of samba and pagode, the headline of the city’s cultural agenda this week.

Samba Takes the Center

The Espaço Popular do Centro, the city-run venue in downtown Belo Horizonte, hosts Friday’s headline night with programming from 18:00.

Mumuzinho tops the bill with the catalog that made him one of the most-streamed names in Brazilian samba and pagode.

The downtown setting puts the show within walking distance of the central market and the Praça da Estação cultural circuit.

The Man Behind the Resenha

Mumuzinho built his career inside Rio’s pagode circuit, championed early on by Zeca Pagodinho and Dudu Nobre.

His album Resenha do Mumu earned a Latin Grammy nomination in 2023, and the 2024 DVD Conectado became his biggest project to date.

With nine albums and more than two billion streams, he now anchors lineups that mix pagode tradition with arena-size crowds.

A Weekend Beyond Samba

G1’s weekly guide pairs the Mumuzinho night with roots music of a different register: Chico Lobo, one of Minas Gerais’ great viola caipira players.

The project Cancioneiros do Meio do Mundo also features in the city’s programming this week, extending the agenda beyond the concert circuit.

The mix is typical of BH’s calendar: samba, caipira music and independent projects sharing the same weekend.

Why the Downtown Stage Matters

City venues like the Espaço Popular have become the anchor of Belo Horizonte’s policy to bring major acts back to the center.

Friday-night programming from 18:00 is designed for the after-work crowd, turning the center into the weekend’s first stop.

For visitors staying in Savassi or Lourdes, the venue is a short ride — and a different Belo Horizonte from the bar circuit.

Planning the Night

The program at Espaço Popular starts at 18:00 on Friday; arriving early is recommended for downtown events.

The venue sits in the central district, best reached by metro or ride-hailing, with limited parking around.

FITPAR 2026 was officially launched on August 26 in Asunción: the 21st Feria Internacional de Turismo del Paraguay runs October 16–18 at the Centro de Convenciones Mariscal, with the Dominican Republic confirmed as guest country.

The Fair That Opens Paraguay’s Season

FITPAR is the country’s main tourism marketplace, the week when Paraguay’s travel trade compresses its year into three days of business rounds, destination launches and consumer offers.

The 2026 edition, the 21st, keeps the established format: trade meetings and seminars for professionals, plus public days with promotions for travelers planning their next trips.

The fair was launched on August 26 at the Unión Industrial Paraguaya, doubling as the celebration of organizer ASATUR’s 67th anniversary.

A Caribbean Guest of Honor

The Dominican Republic attends as guest country, with destination operators in direct contact with local companies and the public across all three days.

The designation reflects the Dominican Republic’s weight as the Caribbean’s leading destination for Paraguayan travelers.

The partnership was formalized in a letter of intent between the Dominican tourism ministry and Paraguay’s SENATUR, signed in the framework of UN Tourism cooperation.

Institutional Weight

FITPAR carries official backing: SENATUR declared it of National Tourist Interest, and both chambers of Paraguay’s congress moved declarations of National Interest for the 21st edition.

That status matters for exhibitors, who treat the fair as the sector’s official showcase rather than a private expo.

For a landlocked country selling itself on rivers, wetlands and Jesuit missions, the fair is the main shop window.

What Paraguay Sells

The host destination uses FITPAR to push its own product: the Costanera and historic center of Asunción, the Jesuit missions of Trinidad and Jesús, the Itaipu dam and the Triple Frontier, and the Chaco’s wilderness.

Regional integration is the fair’s stated mission, with strong Mercosur participation from Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia.

Organizers expect the usual mix of roughly 6,000 visitors across trade and public days.

Regional Context

FITPAR sits in the Southern Cone’s busy fair season: Buenos Aires’ FIT runs in late September, São Paulo’s ABAV Expo right after, and FITPAR closes the circuit in mid-October.

That sequencing lets international exhibitors work all three markets in one trip — a selling point ASATUR actively promotes.

For travelers, the public days are the practical draw: airlines, agencies and operators traditionally launch their season’s promotions at the fair.

Curitiba has a new concert room, and it opened with the heaviest name in Brazilian music: Caetano Veloso inaugurated the Cine Lido on Wednesday, August 26, in an intimate format far from the arenas of his recent tours.

A Venue Born With a Classic

New venues rarely get to open with a legend. Curitiba’s Cine Lido did, welcoming Caetano Veloso as its first-ever headliner on August 26.

The room, on Rua Desembargador Ermelino de Leão in the city center, was designed for close listening: around 1,650 capacity between the premium floor and the upper seating.

Tickets ran from R$450 to R$1,300 at full price — arena money for a club-scale night, and the market absorbed it.

The Intimate Caetano

After years of stadiums and festivals — including the massive joint tour with his sister Maria Bethânia — Caetano framed the Cine Lido date as a return to proximity.

The set drew on six decades of song: Sozinho, Leãozinho, Sampa, Oração ao Tempo, Alegria Alegria and the rest of a catalog Brazilians carry by heart.

It is the format his live reputation was built on: classics reworked in real time, spoken asides, and a band that leaves him room to improvise.

A Career Still Moving

Caetano turned 84 on August 7 and keeps a schedule artists half his age would refuse.

This year added another Grammy to the shelf: the live album of the tour with Bethânia won Best Global Music Album at the 2026 awards.

His calendar continues through December, with São Paulo’s Espaço Unimed on November 21, Rio’s Festival Clássicos do Brasil on December 6 and Florianópolis’ Festival Saravá on December 13.

What Cine Lido Wants to Be

The venue’s opening week laid out its thesis: historic artists in a room built for listening rather than spectacle.

Marisa Monte followed Caetano on August 27, confirming a curation aimed at the MPB canon and its inheritors.

For Curitiba, long criticized for losing mid-size shows to São Paulo and Porto Alegre, the house fills a structural gap in the touring circuit.

Context for Visitors

Cine Lido sits in central Curitiba, a short ride from the Batel and São Francisco districts where most visitors stay.

The venue operates with digital tickets and assigned sectors; doors open three hours before showtime.

Curitiba’s winter evenings are cold by Brazilian standards — the city’s August nights regularly drop below 10°C, so dress for the queue.

Florianópolis opens September as an open-air gallery: the third Festival Street Art Tour runs from the 1st to the 7th, spreading murals and concerts across the island city under the theme Conexões Lusófonas.

A City Repainted in a Week

The Festival Street Art Tour has become Florianópolis’ largest urban art event, and its third edition is the most ambitious yet.

Between September 1 and 7, more than 100 artists intervene on walls across the Centro, Córrego Grande, Estreito, Mariquinha and the university district.

For the first time, the festival crosses the city’s borders, taking interventions beyond the island capital.

The Lusophone Connection

This edition’s theme, Conexões Lusófonas, traces the cultural lines linking Brazil to Portugal, Angola, Cape Verde and the wider Portuguese-speaking world.

The music program embodies it: Cape Verdean-born, Lisbon-based Dino D’Santiago shares the bill with Brazilian names like Criolo and Amaro Freitas.

Melly, Stefanie, Makalister and MC Versa complete a lineup mixing rap, jazz-inflected piano and Afro-Atlantic sounds.

From Walking Tours to a Festival

Street art touring is already part of Florianópolis’ visitor economy: guided walks through the center cover murals honoring local history, from poet Cruz e Sousa to the island’s fishing communities.

The festival scales that logic up — instead of explaining finished walls, the city watches them being made.

Organizers treat the city as a permanent gallery, with each edition adding a new layer of works that outlast the event.

Why Urban Art Fits Floripa

Florianópolis built its tourism brand on beaches and nature; the street art scene adds an urban counterpoint that keeps the center relevant year-round.

Independent collectives seeded the scene years before the festival, painting light boxes, facades and full buildings downtown.

The Lusophone theme plugs the city into an international circuit of mural festivals, from Lisbon to Luanda.

Planning the Week

Interventions and events run daily from September 1 to 7, spread across neighborhoods — check the festival’s official channels for the map and concert schedule.

The Centro and Córrego Grande host the densest clusters of new walls, both easily reached by bus or bike from most of the island.

Most mural viewing is free by definition; concerts may require tickets, so confirm formats per event.

Two exhibitions bookending Brazilian art — popular sculpture from the sertão and contemporary work from the Amazon — anchor Rio’s cultural calendar this season.

A Retrospective for Véio

Véio — Cícero Alves dos Santos, from Nossa Senhora da Glória, in Sergipe — is one of the masters of Brazilian popular sculpture, famous for transforming gnarled wood into a bestiary of creatures.

The Museu do Pontal retrospective, curated by Angela Mascelani and Lucas Van de Beuque, assembles more than 300 works produced across six decades.

It is the largest institutional survey yet of an artist who spent most of his career far from the gallery circuit, in the sertão of Sergipe.

Fifty Years of the Museu do Pontal

The museum, founded from the collection of French designer Jacques Van de Beuque, holds the country’s most important folk art collection, in Recreio dos Bandeirantes.

The Véio retrospective is the centerpiece of its 50th-anniversary program — a deliberate statement that popular art remains the institution’s core mission.

For many visitors, the show doubles as an introduction to a museum that sits off Rio’s beaten tourist track and rewards the trip.

Amazônicas at CCBB Rio

From September 2 to November 16, CCBB Rio hosts Amazônicas: Poéticas Femininas, a visual arts project built around women creators of the Amazon.

The exhibition gathers around 65 works by approximately 25 artists from Pará, Acre and Amazonas, opening in the week of the Day of the Amazon.

The Rio run follows a season at CCBB Brasília, extending one of the year’s most discussed regional exhibitions to the city’s busiest cultural center.

Why These Two Shows Belong Together

Both exhibitions argue the same point from opposite directions: Brazil’s art map is incomplete if it only covers the Rio–São Paulo axis.

Véio’s carved animals come from the northeastern sertão; the Amazônicas artists work from the rainforest states — territories the national circuit has historically treated as periphery.

That two major institutions program them simultaneously suggests the correction is underway, at least in exhibition terms.

Planning the Visits

The Museu do Pontal sits in Recreio dos Bandeirantes, in Rio’s west zone — best reached by car or BRT, and easily paired with a beach afternoon.

CCBB Rio occupies a historic building on Rua Primeiro de Março, downtown, a short walk from the Candelária and Uruguaiana metro stations.

Amazônicas runs September 2 to November 16; check both institutions’ sites for hours and free-entry days before visiting.
