World.title: Yayoi Kusama dies at 97, weeks before Amsterdam show
World.content:
Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, whose polka dots, pumpkins and mirrored infinity rooms made her one of the world’s most famous contemporary artists, has died at the age of 97.

Her death comes just over two weeks before a major retrospective of her work opens at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, turning the show into a posthumous tribute.

From hallucinations to art

Born in Matsumoto in 1929, Kusama began drawing as a child, channelling troubling visions and hallucinations into the repeated nets, dots and other forms that would define her work. She moved to New York in the late 1950s and became a central figure in the city’s avant-garde art scene.

She returned to Japan in 1973 and, in 1977, voluntarily took up residence in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she lived for the rest of her life while working daily in a studio nearby.

Amsterdam retrospective

The Stedelijk exhibition, which opens on September 11 and runs until January 17, is the final stop of a European tour that began at the Fondation Beyeler near Basel and passed through Cologne’s Museum Ludwig.

It brings together more than 300 works spanning over 70 years, including pieces never shown in Europe before and new installations made for the show.

“She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush,” her studio said.

World.title: Srebrenica war criminal Ratko Mladić dies in The Hague
World.content:
Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, has died aged 84 in the United Nations detention unit in The Hague, a UN official has confirmed.

It was Mladić’s forces who overran Srebrenica – a UN “safe area” guarded by lightly armed Dutch peacekeepers known as Dutchbat – and killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995. It was the worst mass killing in Europe since the Second World War.

Mladić had been held in the UN detention unit in Scheveningen since his arrest in Serbia in 2011, after 16 years on the run. Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, he had been in poor health for years and reportedly suffered another stroke over the summer.

An international tribunal convicted him in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and jailed him for life; the verdict was upheld on appeal in 2021. He showed no remorse during his trial.

His death comes days after the tribunal rejected a request from his defence team, backed by the Serbian government, to release him on humanitarian grounds so he could spend his final days in Serbia.

Dutch guilt and apologies

For the Netherlands, the memory of Srebrenica is an open wound. Dutchbat’s failure to protect the victims led to a 2002 inquiry whose findings pushed the government at the time to resign, and to years of court action by survivors against the state.

Prime minister Mark Rutte apologised to Dutchbat veterans in 2022, saying they had been sent on an impossible mission and unfairly blamed for the killings. The government also repeated its “deepest apologies” to survivors in 2025.

Thousands gathered in Srebrenica to mark 30 years since the genocide last year. In the Netherlands, campaigners are still pressing for a national monument to the victims in The Hague.

World.title: Arsonists target planned asylum shelter for teen refugees
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Someone tried to set fire to a building in Valkenswaard in Noord-Brabant, which is being prepared as a shelter for teenage refugees, police have said.

The fire was started at two points on the former business premises on Leenderweg late on Wednesday, several windows were also broken.

Police said on Thursday that they were treating the incident as arson. A flammable liquid may have been thrown against the building, according to reports.

News emerged less than two weeks ago that COA, the refugee settlement agency, had approved a plan to house 40 unaccompanied minors aged 14 to 18 at the site for up to five years, a term that could be extended to 10.

Valkenswaard council stressed that no final decision had yet been taken, and that it would work through the details with COA over the coming months.

Run of attacks

The arson is the latest in a wave of vandalism, fires and bomb scares at sites earmarked for asylum seekers. In June, explosives were found at a planned centre in nearby Nuenen.

Earlier in the year, an explosion damaged a building in Den Bosch earmarked for teenage refugees, and a disused town hall in Loosdrecht was targeted during weeks of riots and arson.

The domestic security service AIVD is still investigating whether organised groups are behind the unrest.

World.title: Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell
World.content:
Small private landlords are selling off cheap, shared housing that students depend on, new figures from the land registry Kadaster show.

Across the Dutch cities with a university, these private landlords cut the number of homes they rent out by 19% on average over three years, according to NRC, which reported the figures.

Bigger property companies bought and built enough to keep the total number of rental homes almost steady, and student cities are attractive to investors, but these tend to be smaller studios rather than shared houses.

For a student hunting a room, that means there are likely fewer affordable shared rooms and more competition.

Hardest on internationals

International students are hardest hit by this, as they cannot join the years-long waiting lists for social housing, which the Kadaster figures don’t include, and often have to rent from abroad without seeing the room first.

That leaves them relying on the private market, which is shrinking, and more exposed to scams and overcharging.

It is not the same everywhere though – the number of rental homes actually rose in Amsterdam, Leiden and Eindhoven, while The Hague and Utrecht saw the steepest falls.

The national shortage stood at 21,500 rooms last year, and more students are giving up the search and staying with their parents, according to student housing centre Kences, which has linked the sell-off to lost rooms. Its next report is due on September 3.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan this week asked councils to be more flexible about shared student houses, after 10 students in Groningen faced eviction because their council would not treat them as one household.

World.title: Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema wants to decriminalise sleeping outdoors, despite objections from residents of the Plantage neighbourhood in the east of the city.

Residents have launched a petition to prevent that from happening, according to AT5. Sleeping on the street or in parks is technically a fineable offence, although in practice no one has been fined over the past year. The mayor now wants it to become official policy.

Plantage resident Dennis de Vreede, who supports the petition, said he fears scrapping criminal liability will lead to more people sleeping outdoors, more nuisance and less possibilities for official action – despite acknowledging that fines are pointless.

“These people cannot afford it and might end up in even more debt trouble,” he told AT5. “But the entire legal framework collapses, meaning the police can no longer take action at all.”

“Shameful” fines

Halsema called fining sleeping homeless people “shameful” in 2021 and has said the measure doesn’t even work. “The intention is that the fine will bring about a change in behaviour,” she wrote, but she questioned whether it actually reduces nuisance.

From 2021 to 2024, fines were only issued for nuisance resulting from sleeping outdoors. Some 1,800 fines were handed out in that period.

But Bianca Koster of the Rainbow Group agrees that fining has little effect. “It helps to address the visibility, but not the core of the problem,” she said.

What needs to be addressed, she said, is why people end up on the streets. She called for more shelters, more care and more housing.

“I understand that when it gets visibly worse, people think we have to do something,” she said. “But punishing people is not the way.”

World.title: Back to the office: learning Dutch at work is the new perk
World.content:
With working from home increasingly out of favour with employers, offering in-company Dutch courses can be a great way of getting your international staff back on location.

Earlier this month financial services group ABN Amro said it wanted its staff to come into the office for at least three days a week. The move was necessary, the bank said, to increase creativity, encourage contacts between staff and improve the differentiation between their work and private lives. It would also, the bank said, make it easier to integrate new colleagues into their jobs.

It’s a trend that is becoming increasingly apparent across Dutch industry. After all, work is about more than just sitting at a desk or being part of an online meeting. It is about interacting with colleagues, sharing experiences and learning something new. And this is one reason why in-company language courses are growing in popularity. They help people to develop skills together while strengthening intra-team communications. And they are also proving a popular perk!

“We’ve noticed that an increasing number of companies are offering Dutch courses at their offices,” says Margreet van ‘t Haaff, owner of language school Taalthuis, which recently expanded to Amstelveen, Rotterdam and Eindhoven and now offers lessons in 10 different cities.

From online to in-company

Taalthuis pioneered the development of online lessons during the coronavirus pandemic and found an enthusiastic market for learning Dutch when people were confined to their homes. Now, however, in-company lessons are becoming increasingly popular as employers seek ways of improving contacts between staff – and helping their foreign workforce settle into the Netherlands more quickly.

“Employers see language lessons as a way of encouraging people to reduce the amount of time they work at home as well as to boost team spirit,” says Margreet. “It’s not a question of forcing people to go back to the office, but of making it more attractive to do so. And of course, learning Dutch helps you to feel more at home as well as getting to know your colleagues.”

Dutch as teamwork

Taalthuis’s dedicated teachers come to the company itself to provide the lessons – either 14-week courses tailored to fit their students’ language level, or tailor-made conversation sessions to meet a particular need on a month-by-month basis. Every student is given a test to find out their Dutch level before they start.

The courses themselves cover beginners to C1 and emphasise conversation skills, which, says Margreet, are perfect for boosting chats between colleagues over lunch or during brainstorming sessions.

The lessons include discussion about typical Dutch themes such as Koningsdag, cycling culture and, of course, food. You will learn about the delights of bitterballen at the vrijmibo, and how to explain your disappointment to your colleagues when faced with a broodje kaas for lunch in the bedrijfsrestaurant.

Learn Dutch during office hours

Many classroom-based Dutch courses take place during office hours, and people who have been struggling to learn Dutch often say that they find it difficult to combine work with lessons and family duties. Offering lessons at the office is another way of getting round that hurdle.

One Taalthuis client, for example, offers its workers lunch combined with a Dutch language course. Others offer lessons towards the end of the day, but in company time, such as a session at 4.30pm, allowing staff to still go home at 6.15pm.

Engineering group Haskoning began offering Taalthuis language courses to its employees in Delft about two years ago and continues to do so. “We recognised a growing need among our international colleagues in the Netherlands to feel more integrated into Dutch society and workplace culture,” says Sofia Aguero from the company’s HR department.

Strengthening teamwork

“From a company perspective the Taalthuis courses strengthen team cohesion, support retention, and enhance our inclusive culture. And given all the positive feedback from students and a growing interest from other employees, we’re already planning future sessions and exploring ways to expand access.”

“Learning Dutch makes it more fun to go to the gym or to have a chat with your colleagues at the coffee machine,” says Taalthuis teacher Floortje, who specialises in in-company courses. “You can talk about the weather, your weekend, what you want to drink… it just makes it easier to have personal contact.”

If you are an employer who would like to offer your staff Dutch lessons, feel free to contact Taalthuis. And if you are a worker who would like your company to offer Dutch lessons at the office, ask your HR department to get in touch.

World.title: Heavy thunderstorms expected this evening
World.content:
Following Thursday’s oppressive daytime humidity and heat – with temperatures ranging between 25° and 30° – the night will see rain and thunderstorms in the south of the country moving north, reports the KNMI weather service.

“During the showers, wind gusts of up to 60 km/h are possible,” said the weather service, and “there is a chance of hail up to 2 cm and heavy rain may fall in a short time”.

While no official warnings have currently been issued, KNMI said there’s a possibility of wind gusts, downed trees and local flooding.

The weather service has just launched a thunderstorm notification app to alert people of local storms happening within 15 minutes of where they are. Currently operating as a beta test through August 31 in the KNMI app, you can download it here and provide feedback later.

World.title: New agreement secures healthcare for 20,000 refugee children
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The national refugee settlement agency COA has secured a three-year contract with public health body GGD to ensure that the nearly 20,000 children living in Dutch asylum centres will continue to receive uninterrupted healthcare.

The current contract was due to expire in October while another with a separate health body wouldn’t come into effect until June 2027, leaving a potential 8-month gap that led six children’s ombudsmen to brand “a serious violation of children’s rights”.

“The decision to award GGD GHOR Nederland a new three-year contract brings stability and clarity,” said André Rouvoet, chairman of GGD GHOR Nederland.

“Accessible youth healthcare is of great importance for asylum-seeking children. With this period, we can continue to do what is necessary: ​​provide accessible, expert, and preventive care.”

Children’s rights organizations were concerned that a gap in care could lead to lower levels of vaccination and a decrease in flagging health and mental health issues.

While regular medical and emergency care are available to refugees, without the new funding, preventative care – which also includes consultations, growth checks and developmental assessments – could have fallen through the cracks.

World.title: Polish Olympic Committee chief detained over links to collapsed crypto firm
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee (PKOl), Radosław Piesiewicz, has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland’s Olympic team. The development comes a day after Waldemar Żurek, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, revealed that prosecutors are investigating possible crimes relating to Zondacrypto’s financing of various individuals and organisations, including PKOl, Piesiewicz, and figures from Poland’s right-wing opposition. Dziś w ramach śledztwa w sprawie ZondaCrypto zatrzymany został Radosław P. Prokuratura będzie przekazywała dalsze informacje po zakończeniu czynności z jego udziałem, prowadzonych w Śląskim Wydziale PZ PK. — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) August 27, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, Żurek announced that Piesiewicz had been detained and would be charged. He said he was unable to reveal what the charges would be, but confirmed that prosecutors are investigating a €40,000 watch reportedly given to Piesiewicz by the former head of Zondacrypto, Przemysław Kral. Under Piesiewicz’s leadership, PKOl signed an agreement in 2025 with Zondacrypto that made the crypto firm the main sponsor of the Polish team at this year’s Winter Olympics in Italy. However, in April, Zondacrypto began to come under scrutiny after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. The firm subsequently collapsed and Kral went into hiding abroad. Prosecutors estimate losses to its clients of at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million). At a press conference today, Żurek confirmed that Piesiewicz had been detained in connection with the investigation into Zondacrypto, which concerns suspected large-scale fraud and other criminal activity. The development comes days after two leading media outlets, Wirtualna Polska and TVN, published a joint investigation in which they alleged that Piesiewicz received a watch worth €40,000 and other gifts from Kral. The gifts were allegedly given in exchange for Piesiewicz intervening on behalf of Zondacrypto with Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK. Piesiewicz denies the allegations and says he bought the watch with his own money, with Kral simply helping facilitate the purchase. 🔴Szef Zondacrypto, prezes PKOl i złoty zegarek za 40 tysięcy euro Prezes Polskiego Komitetu Olimpijskiego Radosław Piesiewicz dostał od szefa Zondacrypto Przemysława Krala zegarek Patek Philippe wart 40 tysięcy euro oraz inne prezenty – wynika z ustaleń wspólnego śledztwa… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 24, 2026 Piesiewicz, who became head of PKOl in 2023 under Poland’s former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, has long been a controversial figure. In 2024, after PiS had lost power, he publicly clashed with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s new government following Poland’s poor performance at the Paris Olympics, where the Polish team finished with its lowest medal haul since 1956. This year, as Zondocrypto fell into crisis, it emerged that the company had failed to provide promised bonuses to Polish athletes following the Winter Olympics. In May, 82 of the 106 members of the Polish Olympic Committee supported a motion calling for an extraordinary meeting at which the sole item on the agenda was the dismissal of Piesiewicz from his position. He has so far refused to convene the meeting. Poland has finished @Paris2024 with just one gold and 10 medals in total – its worst result since 1956. The prime minister has suggested there are failings in how Polish sport is managed. But the head of the Olympic committee has blamed the government https://t.co/iS9OqF1RuB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2024 On Wednesday, Piesiewicz and PKOl were among a list of individuals and organisations Żurek announced were being investigated by prosecutors over potential crimes relating to financing they had received from Zondacrypo. Most of them are linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. They included the foundations of Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, and Przemysław Wipler, a former PiS politician now associated with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja); conservative broadcaster Republika and its head, Tomasz Sakiewicz; and the Polish version of the American CPAC conference. Earlier this year, Tusk claimed that Zondacrypto’s financial success was “rooted not only in Russian money linked to…one of Russia’s most powerful mafia groups, but also to the Russian security services”. His ruling coalition has three times passed a bill to introduce tougher regulation of the crypto market. However, each time, it has been vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argues that the measures are too restrictive. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk wrote on social media that “we now know why Nawrocki and PiS have blocked the cryptocurrency bill like maniacs”. “Cash for watches worth €40,000 euros, [financing] for media, election parties, foundations of right-wing politicians,” he continued. “And the ‘Zonda’ show is just getting started.” PiS figures have, however, denied any wrongdoing in relation to Zondacrypto. “I’m outraged by the suggestion that PiS was involved in anything illegal,” one of the party’s MPs, Piotr Kaleta, told news website Interia. He noted that no evidence had been presented and no indictments made against PiS politicians. “Instead, we have ministers threatening to hold others accountable, and nothing has happened. This is simply meant to cover up the incompetence of the current government.” Teraz już wiemy, dlaczego z uporem maniaka @NawrockiKn i PiS blokowali ustawę o kryptowalutach. World.title: Poland asks EU to fine Meta €250m over scam Facebook ads
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally requested that the European Commission fine Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, €250 million (1.1 billion zloty) for failing to tackle fraudulent advertising on its platforms. Its decision follows a high-profile campaign by Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire owner of Polish delivery giant InPost, over scam adverts on Facebook that exploit fake images of him and other prominent Polish public figures, including President Karol Nawrocki. Platformy cyfrowe muszą ponosić pełną odpowiedzialność za swoje działania i dlatego zawnioskowałem o nałożenie na Metę kary w wysokości miliarda złotych. Po analizie materiałów, w tym tych otrzymanych od Meta, a także kolejnych doniesień medialnych o braku kontroli nad… pic.twitter.com/1zSZg8MGf4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 27, 2026 On Thursday morning, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski announced that he had sent a request to the European Commission to take action against Meta, including fining it €250 million. “Inaction and ineffectiveness in combating harmful s and fraudulent content targeting Poles will not be tolerated,” wrote Gawkowski. “I expect the European Commission to conduct the proceedings swiftly and impose the fine. There is more than enough evidence.” The minister also called on Meta itself to “immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, fake s, and the promotion of illegal applications. This Wild West on the platform must come to an end”. Gawkowski shared an image of the first page of a letter he had sent to Henna Virkkunen, the European commissioner for technological sovereignty, security and democracy, in which he argued that Meta’s failure to combat fraud may violate the EU’s Digital Services Act. He pointed to a study by CERT Polska, a Polish state IT security body, which found that, of 122 adverts reported to Meta as being fraudulent, in 106 cases the company rejected requests to remove them. Gawkowski noted that the European Consumer Organisation has reported similar concerns to the EU. On Wednesday, Gawkowski also shared copies of correspondence he had exchanged with Meta earlier this month. In response to the minister’s concerns, the tech firm had argued that it “does not seek to profit from” fraudulent advertising and outlined steps it was taking to address the problem. Meta disclosed that, between July 2025 and June 2026, it had, in Poland alone, removed 380,000 examples of content and 137,000 adverts for violating its policies on fraudulent practices. It noted that the vast majority were removed before users even reported them. Meta przesłała odpowiedź o działaniach związanych ze zwalczaniem scamów i wskazuje, że niektóre dane przekazuje z zachowaniem ścisłej poufności. W państwie szanującym obywatela takie dane muszą być jawne i dlatego podjąłem decyzję o ujawnieniu treści pisma. W piśmie Meta… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 26, 2026 Gawkowski’s intervention follows a high-profile campaign by Brzoska, one of Poland’s richest people and who, along with his wife, former TV presenter and businesswoman Omenaa Mensah, is a prominent public figure. Brzoska and Mensah have long complained about the unauthorised use of their likenesses in fraudulent social-media advertising, especially on Facebook. In 2024, Poland’s data protection authority ordered Meta to stop displaying adverts that featured false reports of Mensah’s death to promote scams. Earlier this month, Brzoska renewed his campaign, highlighting an example of a scam on Facebook that used a fake image of him being handcuffed by police in his home. Tak działa koncern @Meta w Polsce-nieustająco tolerując fake newsy na mój i wiele innych publicznych osób temat… Może innym to nie przeszkadza, ale jeśli moje małoletnie dzieciaki wysyłają mi te screeny pytając "o co chodzi Tato?", to jak się polskiemu zarządowi tej gównianej… pic.twitter.com/rp4CUscah1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 14, 2026 Brzoska – who also pointed to examples of Facebook running fake adverts featuring other prominent Polish figures, including President Nawrocki – launched a petition calling for platforms that run scam adverts to be fined 150% of the revenue they received from them. The petition – which, at the time of writing, has been signed by almost 91,000 people – cited leaked data, reported by Reuters last year, indicating that Meta estimated 10% of its sales in 2024, around €16 billion, came from advertising scams or illegal products and services. In comments to Reuters, Meta said at the time that the estimate was “rough and overly inclusive” and that the actual figure was lower. But it declined to provide an updated figure. Nowy dzień i nowy scam serwowany bez żadnych oporów przez @Meta z Prezydentem @NawrockiKn w roli głównej. Ale to managerowie Meta (Robert Bednarski, Jakub Turowski,Tomasz Parfjanowicz i Ewa Tumanow) mówią,że nic nie mogą w tej sprawie. Jeśli chcemy temu powiedzieć stanowcze… pic.twitter.com/ZVZl04yYY1 — Rafał Brzoska (@RBrzoska) August 24, 2026 This week, Brzoska welcomed Gawkowski’s moves against Meta. He also noted that, while the minister’s letter to Meta had been addressed to Jakub Turowski, Meta’s director of public policy for Central and Eastern Europe, the firm’s response to him was unsigned. “First-class cowardice,” declared Brzoska, who has repeatedly published the names of four of Meta’s senior Polish managers, including Turowski. World.title: US provides equipment and training to protect Polish border from migratory pressures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The United States has donated $2.1 million worth of equipment for border protection, including drones and thermal imaging cameras, to Poland under an agreement signed on Tuesday. The Polish border guard says that the package is part of a wider US programme, worth an estimated €12 million, to support Poland and the Baltic states in response to the migration crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus on their borders. Stronger border security strengthens our shared security. Today in Warsaw, the United States and Poland marked the donation of more than $2 million in U.S.-funded equipment to the Polish Border Guard @Straz_Graniczna . The donation, funded by the State Department’s @StateINL and… pic.twitter.com/8Mh1eHLo0t — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) August 25, 2026 “Stronger border security strengthens our shared security,” declared the US embassy in Warsaw, announcing the donation of equipment, which includes 45 drones and nine advanced thermal imaging cameras. “This is just the next step in our security partnership,” they added. “Additional equipment, training, and expertise will follow.” The Polish border guard also confirmed that the support includes training packages and bilateral study visits, as well as the delivery of 15 snowmobiles to Poland next year. On Tuesday, it also hosted a delegation of senior figures from the US Border Patrol and US Customs and Border Protection for talks on “exchanging experiences, strengthening cooperation, and implementing advanced technologies in response to migratory pressures”. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging and assisting migrants – mainly from Africa and Asia – to attempt to irregularly cross into the European Union over its borders with Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Tens of thousands of attempted crossings have been reported each year. In response, Poland has strengthened physical and electronic barriers along the border with Belarus. It has also eased rules on the use of firearms by uniformed officers to protect the border, and has temporarily banned asylum applications by people who irregularly cross from Belarus. As a result of such efforts, attempted illegal crossings are down 98% so far this year, while Poland also claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who do manage to cross. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 After meeting with American officials on Tuesday, the Polish border guard said that the head of the US delegation, Jason E. Schneider, acting chief patrol agent for the US Border Patrol’s Rio Grande Valley sector, had praised Poland as a “model and benchmark” for dealing with migratory pressures. It also noted that Stephanie Holmes, the deputy chief of mission at the US embassy, had noted Poland’s role “protecting the entire eastern flank of NATO and [acting] as a guarantor of transatlantic security”. Belarus is a close ally of Russia, and the migration crisis engineered by Minsk on the EU and NATO’s eastern flank is seen as one element of the so-called “hybrid warfare” being waged by Moscow against the West. 🤝 Polska i USA wspólnie dbają o bezpieczne granice i stabilność całego regionu! 🇵🇱🇺🇸 W Warszawie odbyło się spotkanie kierownictwa polskich i amerykańskich służb, w tym U.S. Border Patrol. Wydarzeniu towarzyszyło podpisanie umowy z Departamentem Stanu USA, dzięki której na… pic.twitter.com/rN9umTfPfU — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) August 25, 2026 The Polish border guard reported that, as well as donating equipment, the US has since 2024 been providing and funding “advanced tactical and technical training”, including “courses in border protection tactics”, for Polish officers. Next month, they will provide training in operating the newly donated drones, which are being provided as part of a broader $12 million US programme to support Poland and the Baltic states in “direct response…to the situation on the Belarusian border”, said the Polish border guard. In January this year, Polish officials also conducted study visits to El Paso and Detroit in the United States to “learn about methods used for counteracting illegal migration on the US borders with Mexico and Canada”. A further visit to the southern US border is scheduled for November. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 In 2024, the EU itself announced that it would allocate €170 million to help member states neighbouring Russia and Belarus “counter hybrid threats from the weaponisation of migration”, which it said was being used “as a political tool to destabilise EU society”. Poland was allocated the largest share of the fund, with €52 million. Last year, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked Warsaw for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” being orchestrated by Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom she called a “predator”. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year, of organisations and individuals linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. Among those named in an announcement by prosecutor general Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as justice minister, are Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party, and the Polish edition of CPAC, an American conservative political conference. Meanwhile, a lawyer representing Przemysław Kral, who was Zondacrypto’s head when it collapsed, has revealed that his client is cooperating with prosecutors. That lawyer, Roman Giertych, is also a prominent politician in Poland’s main ruling party, Civic Coalition (KO). Mamy przełom w śledztwie dotyczącym ZondaCrypto. Połączyliśmy w jedno wielowątkowe postępowanie sprawy oszukanych inwestorów oraz sprawę zaginięcia S. Suszka, prześwietlając nielegalne strumienie finansowe płynące w stronę polityków i powiązanych z nimi podmiotów. Więcej w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) August 25, 2026 Zondacrypto came under scrutiny in April after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. By late July, prosecutors had received several thousand notifications of suspected criminal activity connected with the exchange. Potential losses have been estimated at at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million). In a statement published on Tuesday, Żurek said investigators had secured extensive evidence, questioned numerous witnesses, and carried out proceedings involving suspects who have already been formally charged, though he declined to identify them or disclose the charges. However, he added that there had now been a “breakthrough in the investigation”, including “looking into illegal financial flows towards politicians and entities associated with them”. Polish prosecutors have so far identified hundreds of possible victims and potential losses of at least 350m zloty relating to troubled crypto exchange Zondacrypto. The firm's oversight board resigned last week and many users say they cannot access funds https://t.co/ib4bGhzg2m — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 21, 2026 Żurek revealed that, “based on the evidence secured in the case, the prosecutor’s office is verifying information…regarding the possibility of crimes being committed in connection with the financing by Zondacrypto of” individuals and entities associated with the right-wing opposition. They included the foundations of Ziobro and Przemysław Wipler, a former PiS politician now associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group; conservative broadcaster Republika and its head, Tomasz Sakiewicz; the CPAC conference; and Radosław Piesiewicz, head of the Polish Olympic Committee. CPAC and the Olympic committee were previously sponsored by Zondacrypto, while Republika sold extensive advertising space to the crypto firm. Żurek also said they were investigating potential financing by Zondacrypto of actions taken by individuals who helped fugitive former PiS deputy justice minister Marcin Romanowski. Both Ziobro, who served as justice minister when PiS was in power, and Romanowski are currently on the run from criminal charges in a separate case. They were initially given asylum by Hungary, then in May Ziobro fled to the United States. Romanowski’s current location is not confirmed, but he is believed to be in Transnistria, the pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Giertych confirmed that he was the defence counsel for Kral, who reportedly fled Poland after reports of wrongdoing at Zondacrytpo began to emerge. In an interview with state broadcaster TVP, Giertych said that his client is “cooperating with the justice system as best he can” and that his “motive is to mitigate his sentence”. Giertych is himself an MP for KO, the centrist party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Giertych has previously acted as a lawyer for Tusk as well as members of his family. Kral had previously been represented by Bartosz Lewandowski, a lawyer who represents Ziobro and Romanowski. Giertych told TVP that he had been representing Kral pro bono since May. “I made a commitment to my voters that I would hold PiS to account,” he said. “Drawing people out from that side is the most effective way of holding them to account.” 🗣️ "Ta afera ujawni, czym było PiS. Czym była ta zorganizowana w moim przekonaniu grupa przestępcza, która podzieliła sobie kraj i kradła. (…) To ujawnienie zakończy mit patriotów, którzy walczyli o Polskę z Bogiem na ustach"@GiertychRoman w rozmowie z @DorotaWSch ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/1hVJafmRwQ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 25, 2026 In response to yesterday’s developments, Ziobro, in an interview with Niezależna, a news website also run by Sakiewicz, confirmed that his foundation had received 450,000 zloty from Kral’s law firm. “Zondcrypto collaborated with major media outlets, sports clubs, social organisations and other reputable entities…All of this created the image of a large, legally operating enterprise,” said Ziobro, adding that he refused to accept any further money when public doubts arose about the company. Ziobro accused the current authorities of being too lenient towards Kral because he had “become politically useful”. “This is the desperation of a regime fighting for its own future impunity…This is being done even at the expense of the victims and the recovery of their money,” Ziobro said. On Tuesday, Sakiewicz noted that, while Zondacrypto had bought advertising on Republika, it had also done so with many other media outlets. He claimed that Kral was now “under the thumb of the current authorities” and “will say whatever is convenient” to get out of his “difficult situation”. Czy pod pozorem rozliczania jednej afery Tusk z Giertychem właśnie tworzą kolejną? O tym mówię w wywiadzie. https://t.co/7Suu9SbCS3 — Zbigniew Ziobro | SP (@ZiobroPL) August 25, 2026 The Zondacrypto case has become entangled in a wider political dispute, with senior government officials alleging that the company had links to illicit financial networks and that money associated with it was used to support political and public initiatives connected to the right-wing opposition. During a speech in parliament in April, Prime Minister Donald Tusk alleged that the company’s financial success was “rooted not only in Russian money linked to…one of Russia’s most powerful mafia groups, but also to the Russian security services”. The allegations have fed into a broader dispute over cryptocurrency regulation. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed government legislation aimed at introducing tighter regulation of the crypto market three times. The president argued that the bill threatened citizens’ freedoms and could drive Polish companies abroad. The government, however, said the lack of regulation left consumers vulnerable to unscrupulous operators and without adequate protection. President Nawrocki has for the second time vetoed a government bill aiming to regulate the crypto-assets market in Poland He argues that the measures are too onerous but the government says they are necessary to protect consumers and for national security https://t.co/1phQCiXlfO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish far-right leader charged with Holocaust denial for calling Auschwitz gas chambers “fake”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. The charges relate to statements last year in which Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, suggested that the gas chambers at Auschwitz, which was the Nazis’ main killing centre during the Holocaust, are “fake”. Komunikat o przedstawieniu posłowi do Parlamentu Europejskiego zarzutów publicznego i wbrew faktom zaprzeczania zbrodniom ludobójstwa popełnionym w niemieckim nazistowskim obozie koncentracyjnym i zagłady KL Auschwitz-Birkenau w Oświęcimiu. https://t.co/nLq3XKnXCK — IPN Kraków (@ipn_krakow) August 25, 2026 On Tuesday morning, Braun was summoned to appear as a suspect at the Kraków branch of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when Poland was under Nazi and communist rule. A group of his followers gathered outside the building to express their support for Braun, who finished fourth in last year’s presidential elections. Since then, his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party has risen to around 9% in polls, making it a potential kingmaker after next year’s parliamentary elections. After meeting with Braun, IPN prosecutor Robert Janicki announced that they had presented him with charges for “publicly and contrary to the facts denying the crimes of genocide committed by officers of the Third Reich in the German concentration and extermination camp KL Auschwitz-Birkenau”. The charges relate to two interviews Braun gave in July last year. He declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake” and said that claims about the use of gas chambers are part of a “propaganda narrative” supporting a “quasi-religious cult”. In fact, gas chambers were used at Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, to kill around 900,000 people, the vast majority of them Jews. Janicki noted that Braun’s remarks “clearly contradict common historical knowledge based on documents, witness accounts, perpetrators’ statements and findings from past criminal proceedings”. Far-right leader Grzegorz Braun says the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake” and it is a “fact” that Jews have committed ritual murder. Prosecutors have launched an investigation into whether he violated Poland's law against denying Nazi crimes https://t.co/7UUKzH5ndG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2025 When Braun originally made his remarks, they were widely condemned in Poland, which suffered enormously under German occupation during World War Two. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek asked the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, to lift his legal immunity so he could be charged. “For me, it is a scandal that, in a country that suffered such enormous war losses, there is a politician who can deny historical facts that are so painful for Poles,” said Żurek at the time, quoted by the Onet news website. “I won’t let this go. We must bring such people to justice.” In March, the European Parliament approved Żurek’s request, allowing Braun to face charges in relation to his Auschwitz comments, as well as for other alleged crimes. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 On Friday last week, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw charged Braun with those other crimes, including the theft of Ukrainian and EU flags he tore down and vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition being displayed in parliament. In a separate case, in February this year, Żurek also asked the European Parliament to strip Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes over another incident in which he called the gas chambers at both Auschwitz and Majdanek, another Nazi-German camp in occupied Poland, “fake”. Meanwhile, Braun is already on trial in Poland for four other alleged crimes, including using a fire extinguisher to attack a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony in the Polish parliament in December 2023. The trial of Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun for his attacks on a Hanukkah celebration in parliament and a Holocaust lecture has begun. He declared in court that he was facing trial because he had "dared to defend myself against Jewish supremacy" https://t.co/NRZLw7yzyo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 8, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish state defence firm Mesko has signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.9 billion) agreement to supply its Piorun man-portable air-defence systems to the armed forces of Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia. The deal is being financed through the European Union’s SAFE mechanism. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. World.title: Historic Invalidovna Building in Prague Begins Major Reconstruction
World.content:
The long-awaited reconstruction of Prague’s Invalidovna has officially begun.

The Baroque complex in Karlín will undergo a major renovation costing CZK 2.15 billion, with work scheduled for completion in 2030.

The project is the largest investment in the history of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ). Alongside the restoration of the historic building, two new extensions will be constructed on the southern side of the complex.



One will provide facilities for the Prague Philharmonic Choir, while the other will house technical infrastructure needed to operate the site.

Much of Invalidovna will remain open to the public

Once the reconstruction is complete, the NPÚ will use part of the complex for restoration workshops, laboratories, archives and study rooms.

An underground garage with space for 50 vehicles is also planned.

Around 80 percent of the complex is expected to remain accessible to the public. The restored site will include exhibition and conference spaces, visitor routes through the Baroque interiors, a café and facilities for children’s groups operated by Prague 8.

A new multi-purpose hall in one of the extensions will be suitable for concerts, conferences and other events. The modern section will also contain technical facilities that cannot be accommodated inside the protected historic building.

The courtyard and gardens will be opened through the original entrances.

A Baroque complex with a long military history

Invalidovna was built between 1731 and 1737 based on plans by Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer, one of the leading architects of the Czech Baroque. The institution provided accommodation and care for war veterans and their families until 1935.

The original complex was designed at a time when European armies were beginning to develop more systematic forms of care for soldiers who had been wounded or disabled in war.

Military campaigns were often accompanied by outbreaks of diseases such as cholera and typhus, which could kill even soldiers whose battlefield injuries were not life-threatening. Separate psychiatric institutions were later established for veterans suffering severe mental trauma after their military service.

World.title: PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP Returns to Holešovice Market on September 3
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will turn into a one-day celebration of Italian food next Thursday, September 3, with the fourth edition of PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP.

The event will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., with more than two dozen food and drink businesses serving pizza, pinsa, pasta, arancini, Italian desserts, coffee and drinks. Admission is free.



Among the returning participants will be Pizza Metro, Mate’s PIZZA TRUCK, PIZZA Therapy, Pinsa Al Forno, HOLY PASTA, La Mia Spitzeria, Spojka Karlín, ŝam.ŝam.Piaggio, PIZZAKOLEM, Picoška, Vege Stará Placka, Naše maso and Cukrárna U Moučků.

This year will also bring a new style of pizza to the event. Third Coast Pizza will serve Detroit-style pizza, alongside the wide selection of Neapolitan pizza available from other vendors.

Visitors looking for something beyond pizza can try fresh pasta, pinsa, arancini and Italian sweets.

Drinks will include prosecco, beer, cocktails and coffee, with Gin Twist, Aperol Ape, Milujemě Prosecco, Pivovar Chroust and Garage 22 running various bars and stands. Garage 22 will also operate a negroni bar.

Bovelii Caffé will arrive in its red Piaggio, serving coffee roasted in Parma, Italy.

The programme will include music and Italian lessons from Lingua Nostra. Beads & Lemons will also be at the market with jewellery inspired by life by the sea.

PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP has been held at Holešovice Market for four years, bringing together restaurants, food producers and other businesses focused on Italian cuisine. This year’s edition will feature more participants than last year, including both returning vendors and newcomers.

World.title: Manifesto Market’s Craft Beer Returns for Its Third Edition
World.content:
Prague’s beer lovers can look forward to one of the city’s biggest beer events of the year as Manifesto Market brings back its annual beer festival for a third edition.

The two-day event will bring together some of the Czech Republic’s best-known craft breweries, alongside a guest brewery from Berlin, with more than 40 beers available to taste throughout the weekend.

Zichovec, Sibeeria, Chroust, MadCat, Fracek, Pivovar VIK and Berlin-based BRLO will each have their own pop-up tent, giving visitors the chance to explore a wide range of beer styles directly from the breweries.



More breweries are expected to be announced ahead of the event.

One of the highlights will be the festival’s limited-edition glass. It serves as the ticket for accessing the festival specials and can also be taken home as a souvenir.

The beer will be accompanied by food from more than 10 international kitchens at Manifesto. Visitors can expect everything from juicy burgers and tacos to spicy ramen and authentic Chinese roast duck, making it possible to turn the beer tasting into a full weekend meal.

World.title: More Czechs Are Living Paycheck to Paycheck, New Survey Finds
World.content:
The number of Czechs who have nothing left from their paycheck at the end of the month is rising.

This year, 13 percent say they have no money left after covering their expenses, up from 9 percent last year. Meanwhile, 84 percent have at least a small amount left over, five percentage points less than in 2025.

The findings come from a May survey conducted by loan provider Provident Financial among 1,000 respondents.



According to the survey, Czechs’ ability to save is declining. Only 43 percent of respondents have at least 20 percent of their monthly income left after covering their expenses, down nine percentage points from last year. Almost half of Czechs nevertheless regularly set aside part of their paycheck each month.

At the same time, their overall financial resilience appears to be improving. More than a quarter of respondents have enough savings to cover their expenses for more than a year, compared with just 15 percent last year. The share of people with no financial reserve at all has also fallen, from 18 percent in 2025 to 13 percent this year.

The gap between men and women in the amount of money left at the end of the month has also narrowed. This year, 45 percent of men have at least 20 percent of their paycheck left after expenses, compared with 59 percent last year. Among women, the figure has fallen from 45 percent to 39 percent.

The share of Czechs with enough savings to cover 12 months without their main source of income has increased sharply this year, rising by 11 percentage points compared with 2025. At the same time, the proportion of respondents whose savings would last less than three months fell to 12 percent, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Men are considerably more likely than women to report having enough savings to cover at least six months of expenses. The figure is 63 percent among men, compared with 39 percent among women.

Education also appears to play an important role in financial preparedness. Seven in ten respondents with a university degree say they have enough savings to cover at least six months, compared with 43 percent among people with lower levels of education.

World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: GALLERY: Light Installation “Synapse” Coming to Florenc Metro Station
World.content:
Jan Poš light installation Synapse will go on display in the Florenc Line C metro passage at the end of September.

The artwork will track passengers’ movements and complement the existing Battle of Sokolovo mosaic. Prague city councillors approved around CZK 1.38 million in funding to complete and install the artwork.

“Synapse” is a light-based installation by visual artist Jan Poš (1996) and the winning entry in the “Light for the Metro” competition held in 2023.



The aim was to create a light artwork for the passage connecting the north and south concourses of Florenc metro station. A total of 23 artists and teams submitted proposals, with four advancing to the final stage, which was conducted as a competitive dialogue.

The five-member jury considered the artwork’s long-term maintenance and its ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

According to Poš, the artwork, installed on the wall opposite the underpass’s main staircase, comes into view as metro passengers ascend or descend the stairs.

It becomes part of their daily journey while remaining elegantly set apart, creating a space where it can stand on its own and offer a moment of respite from the hustle and bustle.

Poš says the work’s format and style enliven and build on the Battle of Sokolovo mosaic, creating a bridge between the past and present of the city.

The artwork was originally due to be installed alongside the completion of the reconstruction of the station’s ceiling slab. Prague’s public transport operator, DPP, has been repairing the structure since 2022 due to corrosion.

World.title: Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%
World.content:
Hungary’s new government has set its sights on adopting the euro by 2030, with Finance Minister András Kármán revealing how and when the country could bring its budget deficit below the EU’s key 3% threshold. The government says it will tackle the country’s huge fiscal gap without imposing austerity measures on households.

Hungary targets euro adoption by 2030

The new government plans to meet the Maastricht criteria required for euro adoption by the end of the current parliamentary term in 2030, Kármán said in an interview with Hungarian public broadcaster Kossuth Radio. One of the most important conditions is bringing the budget deficit below 3% of GDP. The target is particularly challenging given the fiscal situation inherited by the new administration following the spring 2026 election.

According to Portfolio, Kármán said the government would submit a new medium-term programme by the end of October, alongside next year’s budget. This will set out the path towards meeting the criteria for joining the euro area by 2030. The government argues that adopting the common currency would eliminate Hungary’s exchange-rate risk and contribute to permanently lower inflation and interest rates, providing greater stability and predictability for households and businesses.

Finance Minister András Kármán. Photo: Facebook/Kármán András

Deficit was much worse than expected

According to Kármán, the previous government’s 2026 budget had initially been based on a deficit target of just 3.7% of GDP. However, a review carried out after the change of government found that the deficit could have reached 8.3% without intervention. The finance minister said the previous budget had relied on unrealistic economic growth assumptions and that numerous unfunded spending commitments had been made before the election.

He also pointed to hidden financial obligations and projects whose actual costs under existing contracts were significantly higher than the amounts included in the official budget. The revised 2026 budget now targets a deficit of 7.5% of GDP.

If you missed it: Another severe food price surge is taking shape: prices could start rising in the autumn, with 2027 bringing the greatest pain

Government promises no household austerity

Rather than raising the burden on households, the government says it plans to close the fiscal gap by cutting wasteful state spending and renegotiating or cancelling overpriced contracts. Kármán said the government had already saved around HUF 400 billion (EUR 1.1 billion) this year by terminating or renegotiating unfavourable state contracts. A further HUF 300 billion in excessive spending is expected to be reversed by the end of the year.

Among the measures cited by the minister are the abolition of the Sovereignty Protection Office, cuts to MPs’ remuneration and the cancellation of an operating contract for part of the M6 motorway. The latter was reportedly reassigned to another operator at around one-third of the previous price, which the government estimates will save approximately HUF 100 billion over the next 11 years.
