Targeted support instead of blanket benefits

Kármán said the government’s economic policy would also place greater emphasis on means-tested social support and transparent management of public funds. The new administration has introduced a HUF 100,000 school-starting allowance, removed VAT from prescription medicines and increased the social firewood allowance, he said.

A similar targeted approach is expected for pensions and potential additional benefits, such as a proposed pensioners’ SZÉP Card. According to Kármán, support should primarily reach those who genuinely need it. Following Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s subsequent announcement that the lowest old-age pensions would be raised to HUF 120,000, Kármán added that the lowest pensions would be increased further on a tiered basis.

Kármán’s interview can be listened to below (only in Hungarian):

New tax scheme could replace KATA

The Finance Ministry is also working on a new simplified tax regime with minimal administration, aimed at self-employed people and small businesses. The scheme is intended to provide an alternative to the former KATA small-business tax system, which was significantly restricted in 2022. For the government, the aim is to combine a simpler tax environment for small businesses with a more sustainable fiscal framework.

Can Hungary really join the euro by 2030?

The 2030 target represents a significant shift in Hungary’s economic policy. Meeting the Maastricht criteria would require a substantial improvement in public finances, particularly given the current 7.5% deficit target.

Kármán stressed that EU rules allow a new government following a change of government to present a fresh medium-term fiscal programme. The new administration now plans to use that opportunity to set out a path towards getting the deficit below 3% and fulfilling the conditions for euro adoption by 2030.

World.title: Former Hungary international footballer Buzsáky missing, concern grows in England
World.content:
The disappearance of former Hungary international footballer Ákos Buzsáky has sparked concern both in Hungary and England, where the midfielder spent much of his career. The 44-year-old has been reported missing by Hungarian authorities, while his former club Queens Park Rangers has said it is praying for his safe return.

Former QPR star reported missing

Buzsáky’s disappearance was first reported in Hungary on Tuesday by Blikk, when it emerged that police were searching for the former international as a missing person. His current whereabouts remain unknown, and reports suggest that even members of his family and people close to him have been unable to establish contact with him.

The news has now attracted attention in England, where Buzsáky is a familiar name to football supporters. The Sun and Daily Mail have both reported on the case, highlighting his time in English football and the concerns surrounding his disappearance.

Queens Park Rangers, one of Buzsáky’s former clubs, has also reacted to the news.

“The club are concerned to learn that R’s favourite Ákos Buzsáky has been reported missing. We’re all praying he’s found safe and well,” the club said.

From Porto success to English football

Buzsáky enjoyed an impressive playing career. After establishing himself at MTK and with Hungary’s Under-21 side, he moved abroad in 2002, joining Portuguese giants FC Porto. Although he struggled to establish himself in Porto’s first team, he was part of a hugely successful squad that won the Portuguese league and cup as well as the UEFA Cup.

He subsequently moved to England, initially joining Plymouth Argyle. Buzsáky quickly became a favourite with supporters, with then-manager Ian Holloway praising his creativity and ability to surprise opponents. In 2007, he moved to QPR, where he played in the Premier League as well as the Championship. He later represented Portsmouth and Barnsley before returning to Hungary and joining Ferencváros.

Persistent injuries eventually brought his playing career to an end in 2015.

If you missed it: The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget

A difficult period after retirement

Buzsáky later moved into coaching, working as sporting director and manager at III. Kerületi TVE before subsequently taking charge of BVSC. However, his post-playing career was overshadowed by personal difficulties.

In previous interviews, the former footballer spoke openly about struggling to adjust to life after professional football and developing an addiction.

He explained that the end of his playing career had left him in a difficult psychological state and that he had eventually become dependent on one of the forms of addiction he had previously been able to keep away from.

Buzsáky also said that professional football had provided him with an extremely disciplined lifestyle and that, after leaving the game, he struggled to find the same sense of purpose and enjoyment.

Business interests in Greece add to the questions

Buzsáky earned 20 caps for Hungary during his international career. His former clubs and fans are now hoping for news that the popular midfielder has been found safe.

World.title: Would you work in Hungary for this median salary? Half of the Hungarians earn even less
World.content:
In June, the gross average earnings of full-time employees stood at 754,700 forints, while net average earnings reached 529,700 forints. Gross average earnings rose by 7.1 per cent, net average earnings by 9.4 per cent and real earnings by 7.6 per cent compared with the same month a year earlier, the Central Statistical Office (KSH) reported on Thursday. However, the median salary was much lower.

Median salary shows reality

Gross median earnings reached 617,900 forints, while net median earnings stood at 438,000 forints (EUR 1201) – increases of 8.8 per cent and 10.9 per cent respectively since June last year. Compared with May, gross earnings fell by 9,339 forints and net earnings by 6,137 forints.

The KSH noted that the rise in net average earnings outpaced the increase in gross average earnings partly because of the expansion of the family tax allowance and tax concessions available to mothers.

Regular gross average earnings, excluding bonuses, rewards and one-month special payments, stood at 708,600 forints, up 7.9 per cent on the same period a year earlier. Regular gross average earnings were 700,800 forints in the business sector, 717,600 forints in the public budget sector and 757,600 forints in the non-profit sector, representing annual increases of 7.5 per cent, 9.0 per cent and 8.3 per cent respectively.

Gross average may be tempting

In June, gross average earnings stood at 788,000 forints in manufacturing, 613,000 in construction and 589,000 in agriculture. Monthly gross earnings reached 1.204 million forints in telecommunications and information technology, and 1.181 million in the financial and insurance sector.

During the first half of the year, gross average earnings rose by 11.5 per cent year on year to 772,800 forints, while net average earnings increased by 13.7 per cent to 541,200 forints.

World.title: One of Hungary’s top five construction companies, Orbán-linked Bayer Construct, could go bankrupt
World.content:
Bayer Construct Ltd. has filed a request with the court to initiate insolvency proceedings, Attila Balázs, the owner of the Bayer Group, told employees yesterday. According to the company chief, developments over recent months have left the business facing serious financial exposure. He cited regulatory changes affecting projects under way, the Government’s decision concerning Zugló City Centre and adverse market conditions.

A minor technicality may have derailed a supposedly fixed mega-project

The most pressing problem is likely to be the Zugló City Centre development being built behind Bosnyák Square. The state bought the office complex in November 2023, but for the sale to be completed, entries relating to pre-emption rights had to be removed from certain title deeds. That did not happen, and the new Magyar Government announced on 3 August that it was withdrawing from the purchase of the office complex.

The new Zugló City Centre built by Bayer Construct: nobody wants it. Photo: Facebook/Velkey György László

The Zugló office complex had already attracted considerable controversy. Critics have argued that it is unnecessary, cannot be properly utilised and makes little sense from a public-transport perspective. They have also warned that the geothermal energy it consumes could deplete the wells supplying Budapest’s thermal baths.

Geothermal heating of Zugló city centre could deliver fatal blow to Budapest’s thermal baths

Bayer Construct disputed the Government’s decision and had previously threatened legal action, Telex reports. Meanwhile, the Zugló municipal council could also sue the company if the council approves a proposal to that effect on 3 September.

Bankruptcy on the horizon

It is important to note that insolvency proceedings do not automatically mean that a company is about to collapse. On the contrary, the purpose of the legal procedure is to give a business facing payment difficulties time to reach an agreement with its creditors and stabilise its operations. Bayer Construct says it will continue operating during the proceedings, complete its projects under way and settle claims made by its partners.

Bayer Construct did not become one of the construction industry’s leading players overnight. The group has more than two decades of history and operates not only in Hungary but also in Romania.

Its Hungarian portfolio includes the Hungaroring, the Zenit shopping centre, Waberer’s Ecser Logistics Centre, Kincsem Residential Park and the Láng Quarter. Alongside residential and office buildings, the group is involved in civil engineering and water-management projects, structural construction, steel fabrication, prefabrication and geothermal developments. The Zugló City Centre was the group’s largest project to date.

The company is also involved in the development of Epres Liget in Debrecen, while its Budapest portfolio includes the Szilas Liget residential project. In Romania, the Bayer Group is primarily engaged in construction work and the sale of products, particularly in Transylvania. Its Romanian subsidiary, Bayer Strada, builds residential and non-residential properties.

One of Orbán’s biggest business allies could be forced to shut up shop

In 2025, Bayer Construct recorded net sales of approximately HUF 217 billion and after-tax profit of HUF 13.2 billion, while employing 1,340 people. By revenue, the company ranks among the largest players in Hungary’s construction industry, placing around the top five in publicly available rankings for 2025.

In Hungarian public life, Bayer Construct is regularly described as a company close to the NER, chiefly because of the business links between Attila Balázs and István Tiborcz, Viktor Orbán’s son-in-law, as well as the group’s substantial volume of state contracts. According to an earlier summary by Telex, Attila Balázs is a business associate of István Tiborcz, while Bayer has signed state agreements and received public contracts worth several hundred billion forints in recent years. These deals effectively propelled it into the top five of Hungary’s construction market.

Attila Balázs was also the man who urged his employees on 12 April to vote for Fidesz. “Anyone who disagrees with this, please do not take part in our team,” he added. He later apologised for the letter.

World.title: Magyar government to raise minimum old-age pension, but it will still remain very low
World.content:
From 1 January, the minimum state pension will rise to HUF 120,000 (EUR 330), Péter Magyar, the Prime Minister, announced on Thursday, outlining the Government’s decision taken the previous day on his Facebook page.

In a video, Péter Magyar pointed out that the measure would bring a substantial increase for several hundred thousand elderly people, doubling the pensions of many recipients. He recalled that the minimum old-age pension had remained unchanged at HUF 28,500 (EUR 78) since 2008, MTI wrote.

Péter Magyar delivering his speech at Kossuth Square. Photo: MTI/Bruzák Noémi

“There are debts that cannot be repaid in forints. One such debt is owed by the nation to those who worked for decades, raised children, cared for their parents and helped Hungary through its most difficult periods,” the Prime Minister said. He added that the debt could never be repaid in full, but every government could demonstrate through its decisions how much it valued older people.

“During the Orbán government’s 15 years in office, we have reached the point where nearly one million of our elderly compatriots are living in severe deprivation,” Péter Magyar said. He recalled that, before the election, the Tisza Party had already pledged to raise the minimum pension to HUF 120,000 and to increase the lowest pensions in a targeted manner.

He added that exempting prescription medicines from VAT and cutting the VAT rate on firewood from 27 per cent to 5 per cent would also help hundreds of thousands of “our most forgotten elderly compatriots” to live a life of dignity. The Tisza Party made further pledges concerning older people and pensions, and preparations for fulfilling them have already begun, the Prime Minister said.

“The Orbán government left Hungary in a tragic economic and financial state. We inherited a huge deficit and a ruined, drained budget. In such circumstances, a humane country begins by offering help where it is most needed,” Péter Magyar said. He stressed that a pension was neither a gift nor a favour. “After a lifetime of work, our elderly compatriots are entitled to security, respect and dignity.”

World.title: Shocking tragedy: former Hungarian world and European champion kayaker dies aged just 42
World.content:
Gergely Boros, a former world and European champion kayaker and ex-professional director of the Hungarian Canoe Federation, has died in tragic circumstances at the age of 42. News of the sportsman’s death sent shockwaves through Hungary’s canoeing community.

Hungarian kayaker champion dies at a tragically young age

Boros’s death was announced by the Hungarian Canoe Federation, although its statement did not disclose what had led to the tragedy. It later emerged that the 42-year-old had been killed in an industrial accident in Paks. The incident took place near Vácika Street, close to the tennis courts of Paks SE, Blikk wrote.

Police were already at the scene on Wednesday evening after a local news agency reported that a 42-year-old man from Paks had died in what was believed to have been a workplace accident. The authorities said they would provide further details at a later stage.

Further information emerged on Thursday morning, when police confirmed that proceedings had been opened over the death at the construction site on Vácika Street. The investigation is examining suspicions of negligent endangerment in the course of an occupation resulting in death.

Gergely Boros more than 10 years ago in Moscow. Photo: Facebook/Magyar Kajak-Kenu Szövetség



He was building a padel court

The tragedy occurred during the construction of a padel court. According to information obtained by Index, a large glass wall fell on Boros.

Boros was born in Paks and began kayaking with ASE before going on to become one of the most influential figures in Hungarian canoeing. He served as the federation’s professional director from 2018 to 2024. His former club remembered him as a cheerful, energetic, dependable and highly motivated man.

World.title: Will Budapest become safer? New measures to tackle ‘drug zombies’, traffic offenders and dangerous junctions
World.content:
The government has accepted proposals submitted by district mayors to improve public safety in Budapest in the foreseeable future, the mayors of five inner districts said in a joint statement on Wednesday.

Elevated police presence in Budapest

The statement was signed by district 9 mayor Krisztina Baranyi, district 7 mayor Péter Niedermüller, district 8 mayor András Pikó, district 6 mayor Tamás Soproni and district 13 mayor József Tóth.

In a statement posted by Tóth on his Facebook page, they said that on 15 July, the mayors of Budapest’s inner districts had appealed to the government, calling for immediate measures to improve public safety in the capital. At that time, a 30-day period of heightened police patrols was launched, and now Minister of the Interior Gábor Pósfai said that their further proposals had also been accepted, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

These include permanent police presence at Budapest’s most problematic junctions, so concentrated police presence will be provided at 19 permanent and 90 ‘recurring’ locations in the capital.

Regarding a Budapest allowance the mayors had proposed, Posfai said that the issue of introducing a pay supplement taking into account the specific nature of law enforcement officers’ duties in the capital was on the government’s agenda.

New rule concerning tobacconists

Additionally, the minister supports the proposal that local authorities should be granted regulatory powers to regulate the operation of tobacconists. The mayors are requesting that the districts be granted regulatory powers enabling local authorities to restrict the night-time opening hours of tobacconists and to suspend their operations in the event of serious breaches of the law.

A National Tobacco Shop (Nemzeti Dohánybolt) in Budapest. Photo: depositphotos.com

If you missed: Budapest no-go zones? 5 areas where tourists should be more cautious

The mayors said the minister also supported the proposal for fines for traffic violations imposed and collected by public space surveillance authorities to be transferred to the local authorities concerned.

Additionally, they said the government would examine their proposals regarding the operating procedures of night shelters. The minister for the interior indicated that this would be the task of a social working group to be set up by the government.

World.title: Péter Magyar’s candidate for powerful new prosecution agency named – and the strongest criticism levelled at her
World.content:
The National Assembly’s Justice and Constitutional Affairs Committee has nominated Anna Róza Unger to head the National Office for the Recovery and Protection of National Assets (NVVH). The NVVH is Hungary’s new, almighty prosecution agency entrusted to protect public assets and to trace and recover state property that has been unlawfully managed, misappropriated, or used.

Gábor Török: Unger believes Hungary was under dictatorship from 2010 to 2026

At its meeting on Thursday, the committee also nominated Katalin Tasnádi as deputy head responsible for investigations. However, following the hearings, it declared the application process for the deputy head responsible for public finances unsuccessful, MTI wrote.

After Unger’s hearing, political analyst Gábor Török wrote that she was “a theoretical expert removed from the practical realities of the subject” who, “as before, essentially started from the premise that Hungary was governed by a dictatorship – an authoritarian system – before 2026, and regards preventing their return as a central political objective”.

Unger is a political scientist by training, a lecturer at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest and a corruption researcher who has studied the subject extensively over the past decade. Her specialist fields include electoral systems and the functioning of democratic institutions. That means Unger is not a legal expert although she will lead Hungary’s exceptionally powerful prosecution agency.

Parliament will decide on the nominee at Friday’s sitting, although the vote is now little more than a formality: Tisza has 141 MPs in the 199-member chamber. Fidesz, the largest opposition party, is not taking part in the selection process.

No final verdicts any time soon

At an earlier hearing before a parliamentary committee, Unger dismissed as nonsense the suggestion that final, legally binding verdicts would be delivered in cases uncovered by the new institution during its future leader’s first six-year term.

She told the Justice and Constitutional Affairs Committee that six years would be enough to uncover “down to the last nail” what had happened in Hungary, MTI wrote.

Photo: MTI

She explained that this would provide sufficient time to launch proceedings and bring every person responsible before the courts, “whether they are powerful or insignificant, from Budapest or the countryside”. This would include both those who committed the offences and those who allowed them to be committed, she said, adding that Hungarian society must finally understand and learn what had happened so that it could never happen again.

She wants to map the entire corruption structure

Unger stressed that the National Office for the Recovery and Protection of National Assets would not be tasked merely with uncovering individual corruption cases. Its purpose, she said, would be to map the system that had created and sustained corruption, and to show how it had operated, so that the “newly emerging Hungarian democracy” could develop an immune system capable of making a recurrence impossible once the country had been consolidated.

If you missed: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes

Individual corruption cases can also be uncovered by the Integrity Authority, the prosecution service and the police, while the Hungarian Competition Authority and the State Audit Office can raise the alarm. But the system itself must be “pieced together”; “they put it together once”, and now it was time for “us to put it together too, and make Hungarian voters understand” what had happened, she said.

New prosecution agency’s structure presented

She indicated that the office would initially employ roughly 150 people. Each of the four deputy heads would oversee a quasi-directorate, with investigative work expected to require the greatest number of staff, she said.

She also stressed that, once the office had been established, it would need to review as quickly as possible high-value state contracts signed less than a year earlier, since these could still be challenged.

World.title: iMapp Bucharest 2026 to feature seven digital art shows, Nadia Comăneci tribute
World.content:
The 11th edition of iMapp Bucharest will take place in Constituției Square on September 19 and 20 under the theme PAST. FORWARD. The free event will feature seven international video mapping competition winners and a special moment celebrating Romanian gymnastics legend Nadia Comăneci.

The façade of the Palace of Parliament, covering approximately 23,000 square meters, will once again be transformed through large-scale digital projections.

This year’s theme explores the relationship between past and future through memory, heritage, technology, and imagination, the organizers said. Each of the seven works in the competition will offer a different perspective on time and memory while incorporating the Palace of Parliament into its narrative.

“The fact that iMapp Bucharest has reached its 11th edition says something important about how the city’s public has come to view the event: not only as a large-scale show, but as a cultural landmark,” ARCUB director Mihaela Păun said. “Over 11 years, iMapp has managed to create a tradition around digital art and bring new perspectives and artists into dialogue with a very broad audience.”

The seven artists and studios competing in the Winners League were selected through partner festivals in Hungary, Japan, Germany, France, China, the United States, and Brazil.

An international jury will select the winner of the Jury Prize, while spectators can vote for their favorite work by sending a standard-rate text message to 1755. The entry receiving the most votes will win the Audience Award.

The 2026 edition will also include a special video mapping show marking 50 years since Nadia Comăneci’s historic performance at the 1976 Montreal Olympic Games and highlighting her impact on international sport.

The two-day program will also feature music, entertainment, and outdoor experiences, with the participating performers due to be announced later.

Organized by Bucharest City Hall through ARCUB as part of Bucharest Days, iMapp Bucharest is open to the public free of charge.

World.title: Cambridge School of Bucharest celebrates exceptional examination results across IBDP, IGCSE, AS and A Level
World.content:
News from Companies

Cambridge School of Bucharest is celebrating another outstanding year of academic achievement, with impressive results across its two internationally recognised pathways: Cambridge International Education (CIE) qualifications and the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IBDP).

Founded in 1994, CSB has a long-established history in Romania and has helped generations of students graduate with internationally recognised CIE qualifications for more than two decades. This year's achievements continue that tradition while marking an exceptional beginning for the school's first IBDP cohort.



Students completing CIE qualifications achieved strong results across IGCSE, AS Level and A Level. At A Level, 15% of grades were awarded at A*, while 36% were between A* and A. At AS Level, 36% of grades were awarded at A, the highest possible grade at this stage.



IGCSE students achieved equally impressive outcomes, with 60% of grades awarded between A* and A and 96% between A* and C. These results provide a strong foundation as students progress into Sixth Form, where they can choose between A Levels and the IBDP.



CSB's first IBDP cohort also achieved exceptional results. The Class of 2026 attained an average score of 39 points out of 45, compared with the worldwide average of 30.88 points for the May 2026 examination cycle. The school's highest-performing student received the maximum score of 45 points, and the entire cohort achieved a 100% pass rate.



These results demonstrate what is possible when academic expertise, individual support, and student ambition come together. They celebrate the determination of the students, the dedication of their teachers, and the encouragement of the families who supported them throughout their educational journeys.



High-quality teaching sits at the heart of the CSB educational experience. Students are guided by teachers who bring specialist subject knowledge, strong academic backgrounds, and a genuine commitment to helping each learner fulfil their potential.



This academic ambition is accompanied by a strong emphasis on well-being and belonging. Students learn within a community where they are known and valued, and where success is understood as something broader than a final grade. Confidence, Success, and Belonging are central to school life, shaping how students learn, collaborate, and prepare for the future.



For many members of the graduating class, these results represent the culmination of an educational journey that began at CSB in Nursery, when they were just three years old. Their progress from the earliest years of education to internationally recognised qualifications demonstrates the value of a continuous learning experience that develops knowledge, character, independence, and personal responsibility.



As students progress through the school, the curriculum allows them to discover their strengths, develop their abilities, and choose the pathway best suited to their interests and ambitions. Critical thinking, independent enquiry, and meaningful discussion are embedded throughout the learning experience, helping students become confident and articulate learners.



Examination preparation is one part of this wider journey. Dedicated university and careers guidance helps students explore international study options, understand application processes and make informed decisions about their next steps.



An extensive supercurricular and extracurricular programme also allows students to take their learning further. These are classed as activities or academic pursuits that explore a specific subject beyond the standard school curriculum, such as competitions, societies, and further learning.



Through academic enrichment, leadership, sport, the creative arts, and community service, students deepen their interests, develop new skills and build the confidence to participate fully in university life and beyond. Supercurricular activities also strengthen applications to leading universities by demonstrating intellectual curiosity and engagement beyond the curriculum.



This approach has enabled CSB graduates to progress to highly regarded universities around the world. UK destinations have included the University of Cambridge, the University of St Andrews, the University of Warwick, and the London School of Economics and Political Science, alongside other leading Russell Group universities.



Across Europe, graduates have continued their studies at institutions including Bocconi University, IE University, LUISS University, Delft University of Technology, Eindhoven University of Technology, Ecole Polytechnique, and Erasmus University Rotterdam. Students have also secured places at respected universities in the United States, Canada, Hong Kong, Australia, and the United Arab Emirates, reflecting the international outlook of the school community.



The next chapter for CSB promises to be equally exciting. Two new buildings will open during the coming academic year, expanding the opportunities available to students. New spaces for science and technology, sport and the creative arts will encourage further experimentation, discovery, collaboration, and creativity.



These facilities will build upon the elements behind this year's achievements: inspiring teachers, ambitious students, a future-focused curriculum, and a community in which every learner can belong.



Families are invited to book a visit, experience the school community and discover the Cambridge School of Bucharest formula for success.

World.title: Interim PM Ilie Bolojan hails Romania-Moldova ties as Chisinau marks 35 years of independence
World.content:
Romanian interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan sent a message on Thursday, August 27, marking 35 years after the proclamation of the Republic of Moldova’s independence, saying that Romania has been and will remain “the closest partner.”

The prime minister recalled that Romania was the first state to recognize the independence of the Republic of Moldova, on August 27, 1991.

“Happy birthday, Moldova! Happy birthday, Bessarabian brothers!” Bolojan said in a Facebook post. The official emphasized that Romanians and Bessarabians are bound by “the same language, a shared history and a common destiny.”

Several festivities are taking place in Chisinau, including a military parade and a concert, to mark the Independence Day of the Republic of Moldova, celebrated on August 27.

Nicușor Dan on visit to Moldova

Romanian president Nicușor Dan is also currently in the Moldovan capital, where he will be received by President Maia Sandu and attend the military parade organized for the occasion. At the same time, Nicușor Dan will hold a trilateral meeting with Maia Sandu and the president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, according to the president’s official agenda.

In the evening, Maia Sandu, Nicușor Dan and Volodymyr Zelensky will address citizens in Great National Assembly Square, where a concert dedicated to Independence Day will take place, featuring established artists and musical bands from the Republic of Moldova. The event is part of the national program “Independence that unites us. Moldova-35.”

The program includes a total of more than 20 cultural, educational, commemorative, and festive events taking place throughout the year.

Message from Marco Rubio

United States state secretary Marco Rubio also sent a message marking the 35th anniversary of Moldova’s independence. “On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Moldova on the anniversary of their independence,” he said at the beginning of the message.

“The United States is proud to continue strengthening our partnership with Moldova. Over the past year, our two countries have deepened cooperation across a range of shared priorities. We have expanded economic ties, strengthened border security, and worked together to promote stability in the region,” the message continued.

In conclusion, the US official promised continued support for the “Moldovan people’s sovereignty and independence.”

World.title: Record 180 museums in Romania and Republic of Moldova to participate in Night of Museums in Villages
World.content:
Over 180 museums and rural heritage collections from Romania and the Republic of Moldova are set to participate in the fourth edition of the Night of Museums in Villages.

The sites, spread over a diverse area of rural heritage, will be open to the public with free admission on Saturday, August 29, 2026.

Unlike its sister event, the Night of Museums, the Night of Museums in Villages also features multiple types of sites. Visitors can explore wooden churches and fortified churches, fortified manor houses and mansions, traditional houses and peasant households, mills and ovens, workshops and collections of old objects, archaeological sites, memorial houses, traditional households, cultural centers, village schools, inns, parks, creative barns, narrow-gauge steam trains, contemporary art collections, orchards with sculptures, castles and palaces, gastronomic points, mausoleums, arboretums and fishing villages.

This year’s edition also brings a first: 14 sites from the Republic of Moldova are participating in Night of Museums in Villages for the first time. These include traditional houses, village museums, ethnographic collections, traditional gatherings and handicraft circles.

“180 participants means 180 reasons to hit the road on August 29. The fact that we have reached such a large number of participants and that, for the first time, we have such a strong presence from the Republic of Moldova shows us that Night of Museums in Villages has become more than just an event. It is a network that grows year after year and connects people, communities and places that need to be seen,” said Dragoș Neamu, initiator of Night of Museums in Villages and project manager.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Cordia analysis: Bucharest gaining attention of regional investors thanks to its affordability
World.content:
Bucharest is increasingly standing out on the residential investment map of Central and Eastern Europe as its new-build home prices remain more affordable than in Budapest, while rental yields are comparable to those seen on the Polish market, according to an analysis by Cordia, one of Europe’s largest residential developers and investors.

More homebuyers and investors are looking beyond the simple price per square meter. Total investment cost, rental potential, and long-term market prospects are becoming increasingly important considerations. From this perspective, Bucharest is emerging as one of the region’s most attractive residential markets. While the average price of new-build homes in Budapest has exceeded EUR 5,200 per square meter and prices in Warsaw are approaching EUR 4,700 per square metre for unfinished units, the average price of new homes in Bucharest has remained below EUR 3,600 per square meter, even after significant growth over the past year.

“These price differences, which can be substantial in some cases, may also attract the attention of Hungarian investors. For our cross-border projects, we naturally assist buyers wishing to purchase a new-build home either elsewhere in the region,” said Áron Görög, Head of Sales at Cordia.

At the same time, gross rental yields in Bucharest stand at approximately 5-6%, a level comparable to that seen across major residential markets in Poland.

The analysis also shows that residential markets across Central and Eastern Europe cannot be compared solely based on headline prices. For example, unlike in Romania and Hungary, developers in Warsaw traditionally sell homes in an unfinished condition, which means buyers face significant additional fit- out costs before moving in.

At the same time, construction costs for an average residential project in Bucharest or Warsaw are approximately 25-30% lower than in Budapest, while land prices per square meter in the Polish capital are more than twice as high as in either Bucharest or Budapest.

Differences between tax systems are also important. In Hungary, VAT on newly built homes is currently 5% and can be reclaimed for homes located in designated brownfield regeneration areas. In Poland, the VAT rate is 8% for residential properties up to 150 square meters, while any floor area above that threshold is taxed at 23%. In Romania, following a period of reduced taxation, VAT returned to 21% in August 2026.

“Prices are strongly influenced not only by differences in underlying costs, but also by the complexity of administrative processes, varying levels of demand and the range of government support schemes available to buyers,” added Áron Görög.

World.title: Fire breaks out in southeastern Romania after alleged drone explosion
World.content:
A fire broke out on Wednesday, August 26, and spread over 2,000 square meters in Tulcea County, southeastern Romania, after a drone allegedly exploded.

The fire was quickly extinguished by the local authorities, and investigations are ongoing to determine the exact cause.

“The most likely cause of the fire, according to the testimony of residents, appears to be the explosion of a drone,” said representatives of Romania’s forest authority Romsilva.

The drone was spotted by residents of the locality of Plauru, situated 2 kilometers from the forest.

The Tulcea Inspectorate for Emergency Situations is carrying out checks to determine the cause of the fire, and a team of EOD specialists from the Ministry of National Defence is heading to the area to conduct an on-site investigation.

“The area was secured, the vegetation fire was extinguished by the structures of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the local authorities, and a Border Police crew secured the perimeter during the night,” MApN representatives said.

However, the Defense Ministry noted that no incursions into national airspace had been reported for the same day.

According to the same source, Romania has seen 63 attacks near its borders with Ukraine since the start of the year, and 25 unauthorized entries in its airspace. Four drones were also brought down by Romanian or allied fighter jets after infringing the national airspace.

World.title: Romanian IT company Arctic Stream posts EUR 1.32 mln consolidated net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
Romanian IT infrastructure and cybersecurity integrator Arctic Stream recorded a consolidated net profit of RON 6.95 million (EUR 1.32 million) in the first half of 2026. The consolidated operating revenue more than tripled year-on-year to RON 96.3 million (EUR 18.3 million).

The consolidated operating expenses rose by 180% to RON 89.7 million.

The consolidated figures include the results of companies in the Arctic Stream ecosystem, namely Data Core Systems, Optimizor, and Cyber Arena. The company attributed the net profit mainly to the contribution of Data Core Systems, in which it holds a 23% stake.

On a standalone basis, Arctic Stream reported a net profit of RON 5.51 million (EUR 1.05 million) and an operating profit of RON 6.11 million (EUR 1.16 million).

Its standalone operating revenue increased by 202% to RON 91.7 million, compared with RON 30.4 million in the first half of 2025. The operating expenses rose at a slower rate of 172%, reaching RON 85.6 million.

“The results from the first half of this year confirm the positive dynamics of Arctic Stream’s business and our ability to turn market opportunities into successful projects and increasingly strong results,” CEO Florin Mărginean said.

He attributed the performance to efforts made during the previous year to expand the company’s customer base and secure major contracts.

Looking ahead, Mărginean said Arctic Stream expected to continue operating amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty and potential technological disruptions.

“I am convinced that the strategic partnerships within the Arctic Stream ecosystem - Data Core Systems, IT Prepared (Optimizor), Cyber Arena and Faur.ai - will continue to provide complementary expertise and differentiate us in the market,” he added.

Since its previous financial report, Arctic Stream has signed a RON 17.3 million contract to supply and commission communications systems, computing equipment, and other IT components. The project is scheduled for completion by December 2026.

The company also completed a share buyback program under which it purchased 82,645 AST shares at an average price of RON 21.8644 per share.

The Financial Supervisory Authority has approved another offer covering up to 50,000 shares, equivalent to 1.1553% of the company’s share capital. The offer will run from August 27 to September 9 at RON 23 per share.

Founded in 2017, Arctic Stream is listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange under the AST ticker. Its activities include IT infrastructure, cybersecurity, managed IT services, and locally deployed artificial intelligence solutions.

World.title: New classical music festival brings 11 weekends of concerts to Constanța Casino
World.content:
The first edition of the Cazino Music Festival will take place at Constanța Casino this fall, between September 12 and November 22. The program will bring international musicians and ensembles to the Black Sea city for 11 consecutive weekends.

Held under the artistic direction of Ioan Holender, who led the Vienna State Opera for almost two decades, the festival will feature chamber music, vocal recitals, jazz, and crossover performances.

“The most important thing is for what happens inside the Casino to match what the building represents on the outside. Quality must remain the common thread,” Holender said.

“Music should not be approached with the preconception that you first need to understand it to enjoy it. You can come without knowing, but you must come with an open mind and be curious enough to stay,” he added.

The festival will open on September 12 and 13 with the Janoska Ensemble, comprising brothers Ondrej, Roman, and František Janoska and double bassist Julius Darvas. Their program will combine classical works by Johann Strauss, Brahms, Bizet, Bartók, and Vivaldi with music by the Beatles and Astor Piazzolla.

Then, Italian ensemble I Solisti Veneti will perform on September 19 and 20, presenting works by Albinoni, Händel, Vivaldi, and Tartini.

Austrian baritone Liviu Holender and soprano Adriana González will take the stage on September 26 and 27 with a program ranging from Mozart, Verdi, and Leoncavallo to Bernstein, Gershwin, and American musical theater.

The lineup for October and November also includes CrossNova, Romana Amerling & The Henry Love Group, Hugo Wolf Quartett, Eddie Luis 5, sisters Ania and Sophie Druml, and Romania’s Arcadia Quartet. Soprano Adela Zaharia and baritone Ionuț Pascu will join Ioan Holender for two special recital and discussion evenings.

The festival is organized by Constanța Casino in partnership with the Mamaia-Constanța Destination Management Organization. It is intended to attract visitors to the seaside outside the traditional summer season.

“Culture can build a tourist season that continues long after summer,” organization president George Măndilă said. “A concert featuring international-level artists in a Casino that many Romanians want to see after its restoration can become the starting point for an entire weekend by the sea.”

Tickets are available through the Casino’s official website, its ticket office, and ticket machines located on the seafront.

The restored Art Nouveau landmark has reopened to the public and is now also being used as a cultural venue.

World.title: North Macedonia, Serbia Sign Pipeline Agreement to Enable Regional Gas Link
World.content:
The signing of the new gas interconnector agreement between North Macedonia and Serbia in Skopje. Photo: Government of the Republic of North Macedonia.

North Macedonia’s gas network could be connected with Serbia’s system as early as 2028, under an agreement signed by the two countries in Skopje on Thursday. The project involves the construction of a 67-kilometre pipeline, which should be completed by 2027.

It is part of a broader effort to knit together the gas networks of Southeast Europe and enable diversification for a region that has historically relied heavily on Russian supplies.

The new link will be developed alongside a separate North Macedonia-Greece interconnector, which is expected to be operational in 2027.

At the signing event, North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hrisitijan Mickoski said that together, the two projects would grant his country “full vertical energy connectivity”.

The pipelines may also turn North Macedonia from a largely end-point market into a key part of a south-north transit route, allowing gas entering from Greece to move towards Serbia and potentially further into Central Europe.

The Alexandroupolis terminal is particularly important to this strategy. Its floating LNG facility can receive gas from global suppliers and feed it into Greece’s transmission system, giving countries in the region access to supplies beyond traditional pipeline sources.

The European Union and the countries involved have been promoting the new infrastructure as part of the wider Vertical Gas Corridor linking LNG infrastructure and gas networks across Southeast and Central Europe.

Mickoski has also framed the project in geopolitical terms, saying the planned route could carry US LNG from Alexandroupolis through North Macedonia and Serbia towards Hungary and Austria. He added that he hopes North Macedonia’s other Northern neighbor, Kosovo, would build a similar interconnector with his country.

LNG from other sources – such as Azerbaijan – could also use the route, creating more options for the region. Mickoski estimates the eventual capacity could be between three and six billion cubic metres annually, making it a potential competitor to Russian gas supplies in the region.

Serbia, in particular, remains strongly dependent on Russian gas. In 2025, Serbia imported around 2.76 billion cubic metres of gaseous natural gas. Of that, 2.45 billion cubic metres were imported from Russia, 232 million cubic metres from Azerbaijan, and 112.5 million cubic metres from the EU.

However, Belgrade has increasingly been seeking alternative sources and routes. It has already reserved 300 million cubic metres of capacity at the Alexandroupolis LNG terminal for the next 10 years.

The timing of this new infrastructure also reflects a fundamental shift in Europe’s energy map. The EU formally adopted legislation this year to phase out the use of Russian natural gas. LNG imports will be subject to a full ban from the start of 2027, with pipeline imports to follow in the autumn.

Serbia is making links with North Macedonia and Romania a priority for diversifying its supply routes. Meanwhile, the Energy Community – which includes all six Western Balkans countries as well as EU member states – says stronger cross-border infrastructure will improve the security of supply across Southeast and Eastern Europe.

World.title: Kosovo Judicial Council Rejects Serb Judges’ Reinstation
World.content:
Kosovo Judicial Council meeting on August 27, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Judicial Council.

The Kosovo Judicial Council, KJC, on Thursday denied the requests of several Serb judges and court administrative staff to return to their posts, nearly four years after Kosovo Serbs staged a mass resignation from Kosovo institutions in 2022.

The KJC will send the names of the judges to acting President Albulena Haxhiu, who will formally confirm the original resignations.

Haxhiu posted on Facebook that she “welcomes the proposal by the Kosovo Judicial Council to relieve the Serbian judges who resigned in 2022 of their duties”, confirming she would “take action to relieve them of their duties”.

The decision follows a similar ruling in July by the Kosovo Prosecutorial Council, KPC. It denied requests by several Serb prosecutors to return to the posts from which they had resigned in 2022. Media in Kosovo reported that five prosecutors and 15 administrative staff members had asked to return.

The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, OSCE, has warned that Pristina must ensure Serb participation in Kosovo’s juducial institutions. It said the KJC should “promptly fill the vacant positions through transparent, inclusive, and merit-based recruitment,” adding that “a judicial system that reflects the communities it serves is essential to ensuring equal and effective access to justice for all”.

Most Serbs in Kosovo’s four Serb-majority northern municipalities who were working in Kosovo state institutions resigned on November 5, 2022, in protest at Pristina’s failure to implement EU-mediated agreements between Serbia and Kosovo.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party Srpska Lista coordinated the resignations. The party’s then leader, Goran Rakic, said the boycott would remain in force until Pristina fulfilled its commitment under the 2013 Brussels Agreement to establish an Association of Serb-Majority Municipalities.

Kosovo Serb voters also boycotted the extraordinary elections in April 2023, resulting in extremely low turnouts and the election of ethnic Albanian mayors in majority-Serb municipalities. Their installation triggered violence between protesters and members of NATO’s KFOR peacekeeping force who had formed cordons around the municipal buildings. Kosovo authorities also later shut down a number of institutions serving Kosovo Serbs, claiming they were illegal.

Brussels blamed Pristina for inflaming ethnic tensions and imposed sanctions in June 2023. Those measures were not lifted until March this year, following the return of Serb mayors in December 2025.

Ahead of that, Srpska Lista admitted that urging Serbs to abandon Kosovo institutions had been a mistake. It still maintained that the move had successfully attracted the international community’s attention.

World.title: Ratko Mladic: Genocide Convict Who Left Trail of Blood Across Bosnia
World.content:
Mladic was convicted of genocide of Bosniaks in the eastern town of Srebrenica in 1995, the persecution and extermination of Bosniaks and Croats across the country, terrorising the population of Sarajevo with a campaign of shelling and sniper attacks, and taking UN peacekeepers hostage.

But he was acquitted of committing genocide in six other Bosnian municipalities in 1992.

It is for Srebrenica – the systematic killings of Bosniak men and boys and the subsequent cover-up operation – that Mladic will be remembered by history. According to the ICTY’s indictment, “more than 7,000 prisoners captured in the area around Srebrenica were summarily executed from 13 July to 19 July 1995. The killings continued thereafter.”

The Bosnian Serb Army and Serb paramilitary formations tried to hide the extent of the crimes by burying victims in mass graves. A total of 95 mass graves have been discovered around the Srebrenica area; seven were primary mass graves, where bodies were initially buried. The rest of them were secondary or tertiary grave, to which bodies were moved in subsequent cover-up attempts.

The ICTY rejected Mladic’s appeal against his conviction in June 2021, finally bringing some kind of justice to thousands of families of people who were killed.

Refija Hadzibulic, one of the mothers of the victims of the Srebrenica genocide, said at the time that the final verdict was a recognition of their suffering.

“It means a lot to us to know that there was a genocide, that they committed genocide. Because they always deny it. And now they can’t deny it, the whole world sees what happened and what they did,” Hadzibulic said.

But Bosnian Serb political leaders still see Mladic as a hero who fought to defend Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated entity of the country that was established, with Radovan Karadzic as its leader, just before the war erupted in 1992.

Milorad Dodik, who has long been the most powerful Bosnian Serb politician, said that the Mladic verdict had “nothing to do with law and justice”.

Dodik claimed that the trial was held in order to “Satanise” Serbs, and complained that “an attempt is being made to create a myth about the genocide in Srebrenica, which did not happen”.

A family legacy of war

World.title: US Army Selects Croatian Company Orqa to Supply FPV Drones
World.content:
Srdjan Kovacevic, one of the three founders of Orqa. Photo: Orqa.

The Croatian company Orqa, which produces first-person-view (FPV) drones, has been selected as a supplier for the US Army. The company, headquartered in Osijek in eastern Croatia, announced the news on its LinkedIn profile on Thursday.

The company confirmed that the US Army’s 2nd Infantry Division had selected Orqa following an assessment of several suppliers.

“Orqa is delighted to announce that the US Army’s 2nd Infantry Division has confirmed an agreement to procure our FPV drones after a focused evaluation of multiple suppliers,” the company said in a LinkedIn post.

“Orqa emerged as the chosen provider based on the proven performance of its systems in the field,” it company added.

However, details of the agreement have not been disclosed. It is not known how many drones are involved and what the value of the entire deal is.

The announcement comes as the US military continues to expand its use and evaluation of small FPV drone systems for tactical applications.

The 2nd Infantry Division has also been developing its drone capabilities on the Korean Peninsula, including through recent training involving FPV systems.

Founded in Osijek in 2018 by Srdjan Kovacevic, Ivan Jelusic and Vlatko Matijevic, Orqa develops FPV drones and advanced remote-reality technology.

The three founders started as enthusiasts involved in FPV drone racing and have since built a company that produces tens of thousands of technologically advanced products.

The latest development highlights the growing international role of Croatian-developed drone technology at a time when unmanned systems are becoming increasingly important to modern military operations.

In May, Orqa announced that, in cooperation with US cyber and defence solutions provider By Light Professional IT Services, it had established Orqa US, a company focused on drone production for the US market. The move was a strategic response to the requirements of new US Department of Defence programmes, including the Drone Dominance plan, Orqa said at the time.

Building on its capacity to produce up to 280,000 drones annually in Osijek, Orqa has been extending this model globally through an international manufacturing network. Orqa US is headquartered in Palo Alto, in Silicon Valley, and has a 17,000-square-metre production facility in Florida.

The company has already established manufacturing partnerships in North America, Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

World.title: Ratko Mladic, Convicted Bosnian Serb War Criminal, Has Died
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Ratko Mladic waiting for his appeal judgment in The Hague, June 2021. Photo: EPA-EFE/Jerry Lampen/Pool.

Ratko Mladic, wartime commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, died on Thursday at the age of 84 at the UN Detention Centre in The Hague.

Mladic was was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Demo Berisa, Serbia’s Minister for Human and Minority Rights, confirmed to BIRN that “it is true that Ratko Mladic has died”.

Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic told Srna news agency that his ministry will handle the transfer of the body to Serbia, saying that Mladic’s family and the ministry are now “waiting for instructions” from the UN court.

A statement later on Thursday from the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals officially confirmed that Mladic “passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague” and that the Dutch authorities have “commenced the standard procedures and investigations required under Dutch national law”.

As head of the Bosnian Serb Army, Mladic oversaw the mass executions of over 8,000 mainly Bosniak men and boys around Srebrenica in 1995 after his forces overran the town – a crime classified by international courts as genocide.

The UN court in The Hague confirmed his conviction and life sentence after an appeal in 2021.

Emir Suljagic, director of the Srebrenica Memorial Centre, where thousands of victims are buried, saying that the fact of Mladic’s death does not change the historical evidence or erase the consequences of the genocide of Bosniaks by Bosnian Serb forces in July 1995.

“The people he sent to their deaths did not get the chance to grow old. That is the only fact about his death that matters to me,” Suljagic said.

Mladic, who had been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011, had suffered serious health problems in recent years. The UN court stated last week that he was approaching the end of his life.

World.title: Serbia’s Competition Commission Approves Acquisition of Critical Media Outlets
World.content:
Amid a process that has raised questions about media pluralism and independence, Serbia’s competition regulator told BIRN on Thursday that it had given the green light to the sale of the country’s most prominent government-critical media outlets.

As a result, the N1 and Nova S television stations, Danas newspaper and Radar magazine will come under the same ownership umbrella as Euronews, whose majority owner is Alpac Capital, a Portuguese investment firm.

“The concentration involving European Future Media Investments S.C.S. and Adra News S.a r.l. was notified to the Commission for Protection of Competition on 8 June 2026. Following the conducted proceedings, the notified concentration was approved,” it is said.

The decision has yet to be published on the Commission’s website.

United Group told BIRN late on Wednesday that it had transferred its news businesses in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Slovenia to European Future Media, a Luxembourg-based fund backed by Alpac Capital.

“The remaining steps, including the transfer of the Luxembourg licences for the N1 and Nova S channels and the transfer of certain United Group interests in Montenegro, will follow in line with the terms of the agreement conditional upon the receipt of requisite regulatory approvals,” United Group said.

Montenegro’s Commercial Court in mid-August temporarily blocked planned changes to the ownership and management structure of TV Vijesti.

On Tuesday, Alpac Capital’s CEO Pedro Vargas David said that his company had received all the required permits from the Bosnian authorities for the acquisition of the N1 and Nova outlets there.

Serbian website Raskrikavanje reported on Wednesday that United Group stated in an internal memo to management that the sale of several media outlets was “substantially implemented” on August 24.

On August 18, before the ownership was transferred, Pedro Vargas Santos David was registered as director of four companies – Adria News, United Media Digital, Adria News Nova S, and Dan Graf, the companies that run N1 and other media outlets in Serbia. The sitting directors were dismissed.

The European Federation of Journalists and Serbian civil society organisations have all voiced concerns about the sale of the media outlets, with the EFJ warning of a potential impact on “media pluralism, editorial independence [and] public opinion”.

The timing of the sale, with the parliamentary elections in Serbia likely before the end of the year, has also triggered alarms. United Group’s outlets had been among the few which published critical opinions of President Aleksandar Vucic and his governing Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

Alpac Capital acquired a majority stake in the pan-European news channel Euronews in 2022. French newspaper Le Monde reported in 2024 that this takeover was partly financed by funds linked to the then Hungarian leader Viktor Orban.

Alpac CEO Vargas David’s comments on Wednesday will not have reassured those who would like the former United Group outlets to continue their robust, government-critical editorial line. In an open letter to Serbia’s Information and Telecommunications Minister Boris Bratina, Vargas David wrote that he wanted a return to “non-activist” journalism.

“When news organisations believe that they are the news, and their mission is not to report on the news but to be the news, they enter the arena; they become part of the game. With this come the attacks from politicians, the boycotts, the aggressiveness. When journalists use their platform to share an agenda, they change the nature of their profession,” Vargas David wrote.

Vargas David’s letter followed a call by Serbian minister Bratina for Alpac Capital to register its new acquisitions with Serbia’s media regulator, REM.

World.title: Albanian Businessman Arrested in Information Agency Tenders Corruption Case
World.content:
Albanian businessman Ergys Agasi in front of the SPAK organised crime and corruption prosecution office in Tirana. Photo: LSA.

Albanian businessman Ergys Agasi, arrested on Wednesday in Durres, is suspected of being part of a scheme that utilised organised crime to manipulate and extort public procurement procedures valued at approximately 59 million euros.

Albania’s organised crime and corruption prosecution SPAK confirmed the arrest in a statement saying saying that “at the time of the arrest, this individual (Ergys Agasi) was accompanied by U. Sh., a former police officer, who was arrested immediately for the criminal offence of ‘aiding the perpetrator of a crime’.”

Agasi is accused of forming a structured criminal group with another businessman, Ermal Beqiraj, to rig and extort tenders from the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, including through the use of violence and hostage-taking.

Agasi denies the allegations. His lawyer Maksim Haxhia told media on Thursday that “it is a fact that he has not touched public funds, as he has never held a position of authority involving the management of public finances, nor has he participated in any tenders.”

His alleged partner in the scheme, Beqiraj, was arrested in France on July 24 while flying a light aircraft through restricted airspace over the Penly nuclear power plant. He was escorted by air force units until he landed at the Albert airfield in the Somme region of northern France.

According to SPAK, further investigations by French authorities identified assets belonging to Beqiraj in France that are suspected to be of criminal origin. SPAK alleges that Beqiraj transferred a portion of his illicit proceeds to France, using the funds to purchase a château, two apartments, and motor vehicles, while also depositing over 2 million euros into bank accounts.

Beqiraj has not commented publicly on the allegations so far.

SPAK initially charged Agasi and Beqiraj with “illegal competition through violence”, “illegal deprivation of liberty”, “violation of equality in tenders”, involvement in a “structured criminal group” and “laundering of the proceeds of a criminal offence”, in December last year.

AKSHI coordinates the development of state information systems and digitalisation procedures, and administers the state public services portal, e-Albania. For over a decade, the agency managed a massive budget; in just 19 procedures investigated by SPAK, the estimated total value (limit fund) amounted to 5.9 billion lek (approximately 59 million euros).

The SPAK investigation alleges that AKSHI director Mirlinda Karcanaj and her deputy, Hava Delibashi, placed these funds in the hands of a group linked to organised crime, pre-selecting winners and ensuring the diversion of tens of millions of euros into the accounts of IT businessman Beqiraj and Agasi.

Karcanaj and Delibashi have both denied the allegations.

World.title: Study Finds CEE’s Outsourcing Sector Primed for AI Age
World.content:
The rankings show which destinations are best positioned for AI-augmented outsourcing work, with Hungary in 4th place, Czechia in 7th, Bulgaria in 9th, Poland in 11th and Romania in 13th, out of a total of 25 countries surveyed.

The CEE region averaged 63.9 out of 100 in AI readiness across its five outsourcing destinations, ranking second among outsourcing regions behind only Southeast Asia (68.6), and ahead of Latin America (62.4), South Asia (48.1) and Africa (42.6). The spread across CEE’s five destinations was just 9.7 points, the tightest regional clustering of any outsourcing block.

“The typical outsourcing conversation centres on Asia [but] new data on AI readiness suggests the region building the deepest AI talent pipeline is somewhere else entirely,” says George Atuahene, founder of Ataraxis, referring to CEE.

Looking in more detail at Ataraxis’s findings, CEE led every outsourcing region on the AI education pipeline by a wide margin, suggesting it is ahead in producing the next generation of AI-capable workers. CEE’s average AI education pipeline score was 70.4, more than 16 points above the global destination average of 54.1. Two of the top five AI education pipeline scores among outsourcing destinations belong to CEE: Czechia ranked 3rd with 81, and Poland ranked 5th with 74.

CEE held the two highest population AI adoption scores of any outsourcing destination in the world. Hungary ranked 1st among outsourcing destinations on population AI adoption (86) and Bulgaria ranked 2nd (82). The region’s average of 71 led the global outsourcing destination average by 10.9 points, the region’s largest single advantage over the rest of the outsourcing world. Poland ranked 4th among the top 25 outsourcing destinations on workforce AI literacy (70).

Experts say such AI preparedness is crucial for the CEE region, whose countries were the major beneficiaries of offshoring and integration into Western European – particularly German – production networks, helping to reshape entire economies and provide one of CEE’s main engines of growth.

But AI is now impacting what customers expect from outsourcing and it is set to destroy the old model of outsourcing, “the one built on labour arbitrage, offshore scale, rate cards, and long-duration contracts measured largely by headcount and service levels”, according to Abhinav Agrawal, a partner and managing director in AlixPartners’s digital practice, writing in the Harvard Business Review.

“For more than three decades, outsourcing has rested on a simple economic idea: If work can be defined, standardized, monitored, and moved to a lower-cost labour market, someone else can often do it more cheaply. That idea no longer works,” Agrawal said.

As Ataraxis’ Atuahene explains to BIRN: “Being AI-prepared is what lets the region move up the value chain, from providing cost-effective labour to providing genuinely high-skill, AI-augmented work. The markets that get this right will be positioned to capture a large part of outsourcing demand. The ones that don’t risk being left behind.”

World.title: The Secret Real Estate and Maritime Rights Only Croatian Citizenship Unlocks
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – There’s a hack to the complicated and bureaucratic minefield of Croatian real estate and maritime rights, and that is possessing Croatian citizenship. It might sound obvious, but there’s far more to it than you might imagine.

Croatia’s administration is full of red tape. Anyone who has had any experience with it will know that bureaucracy is rife and one area in which this is particularly true is when it comes to real estate laws and maritime rights. In this sense, your passport matters more than you might think it would, and the key to bypassing a lot of the drama is holding Croatian citizenship. That trusty little blue passport allows you to purchase any type of real estate or land you like, without needing to make additional applications, seek extra permissions or adhere to zoning.

If you are an American of Croatian descent, you’ll likely have already read about our extensive coverage of the lifestyle perks of reclaiming your heritage. It spans from making entering and travelling around the EU more easily, to reconnecting with your roots in a concrete way, to providing your children and even grandchildren with an open door to not only Croatian but EU education and career opportunities. The list of benefits to turning the hands of the clock backwards through time to allow you to be granted Croatian citizenship is not only extensive but surprising, and extends far beyond the obvious. Even if you’re not considering doing anything like moving to Croatia or setting up a business there, long, hot summers on the Adriatic, the slower pace of life, and the security of a EU passport is often enough of a reason to explore the route in and of itself.

if you’re looking to purchase property, land, or spend a significant amount of time on the adriatic sea, there are barriers for non-citizens…

If you are looking to buy land, property, invest in a piece of land, or spend significant time sailing on the Adriatic Sea, there is an enormous legal barrier that an American passport simply cannot (and likely will never) be able to cross. To truly unlock the Croatian coastline and islands in a totally unbridled way, you’ll need to move past the tourist visa and the constantly ticking Schengen clock. Here’s exactly how obtaining your Croatian citizenship (more specifically your Domovnica) fundamentally alters and upgrades your legal rights when it comes to real estate and maritime ownership.

Many in the Croatian diaspora dream of buying that classic, traditional old stone house with an attached olive grove, a little vineyard, or a piece of forested land handed down through generations. Dreaming about it is often where it ends for those who don’t seek citizenship. Here is the cold, bureaucratic reality: Third-country nationals (which US citizens are) are extremely heavily restricted from buying agricultural land (known legally as poljoprivredno zemljište) or what is listed as a protected nature zone anywhere in Croatia.

While the EU moratorium on foreign ownership of agricultural land has officially expired, strict reciprocity laws and complex local bureaucracy mean that as a US citizen, your purchase is tied up (or rather tangled up) in ministry approvals for months on end, or outright denied from the get-go, as the case often is.

if you’re a croatian national, the bureaucratic headache vanishes

The second you hold a Croatian passport, you have the absolute, unrestricted right to buy any piece of agricultural land, OPG (family farm), or forestry anywhere in the country. You completely bypass the Ministry of Justice approvals, allowing you to secure that dream vineyard or piece of agricultural land with the exact same ease as a local.

What makes this so monumental is that an absolutely massive percentage of the Croatian diaspora technically owns land right now, they just don’t legally have their name on it. Millions of parcels of land dotted up and down the coast and in the hinterlands are tied up in multi-generational legal limbo, still registered to great-grandparents who emigrated to the US a century ago and have long since passed away. In fact, this is a bit of a Croatian right of way. Arguing with family members over ancient, falling apart houses for decades is a joke many Croats will smirk at, as they’ve likely been involved with it. Trying to clean up a messy land title (which is aptly named gruntovnica) or claim your rightful inheritance as a foreign national is an extremely expensive, bureaucratic nightmare. There are also unscrupulous lawyers who will look at a naive person entering into this proverbial ring with dollar signs flashing in their eyes, knowing from the start that there’s no way around this without a passport.

the citizenship application gives you an official way in

When you apply for Croatian citizenship, you officially enter the system. You get a Croatian personal identification number (OIB) and the ball gets rolling. As a citizen, you have the legal standing to easily interact with all of the municipal courts, hire local representation to clear up multi-generational titles, and officially claim ancestral property without facing the discriminatory tax rates or legal hurdles aimed at foreign buyers. You also bypass the aforementioned lawyers who will be more than happy to “help” a US citizen without a Croatian passport just to get absolutely nowhere.

croatian maritime laws and the citizenship golden egg

For many, the ultimate goal of spending time in Croatia is spending long, lazy periods of time sailing the Adriatic and exploring the 1,000 islands. However, all that comes grinding to a violent halt when Croatia’s ultra-complicated maritime laws are delved into. Croatia is very fiercely protective of its waters, and navigating them as an American boat owner is both highly restricted and incredibly expensive.

As a Croatian citizen, however, you can legally register a vessel under the Croatian flag (and by extension, the flag of the European Union). This allows for much, much lower mooring and marina fees reserved for local residents and EU citizens, and the legal right to apply for highly coveted communal berths (known as a komunalni vez), which is a privilege protected and reserved just for citizens. It also unlocks the ability to legally charter or monetise your vessel on the wider EU market without facing third-country commercial bans.

there’s no need for reciprocal agreements

When an American buys a standard residential property in Croatia, the sale cannot legally close straight away. The purchase is subjected to a “reciprocity check” by the Ministry of Justice to ensure a Croatian citizen could buy the equivalent property in the buyer’s home US state. This process can take anywhere from six months to a year, leaving your deposit in limbo and sellers (rightfully) frustrated. Knowing this, many Croatian sellers simply avoid American passport holders like the plague, which greatly limits your ability to do anything at all.

As touched on previously, Croatian citizenship totally eliminates any need for any kind of Ministry of Justice review. Your property transaction can close in mere days rather than months and months, making you a far more attractive buyer to local sellers who don’t want to wait on government paperwork.

that window might not be open forever…

Croatia’s current citizenship laws (specifically Article 11 for Croatian citizenship by ethnicity) are among the most generous in not only the EU but in Europe as a whole. Currently, diaspora applicants do not have to pass a Croatian language test or a culture exam to reclaim their citizenship and lock in all of these benefits. However, it does need to be stated that the Croatian property market has faced a massive boom and EU immigration policies are forever tightening up, meaning that these legal windows very rarely stay open forever. You only have to look at how neighbouring Italy suddenly opted to make it extremely difficult for Italian-Americans to get their foot in the door administratively in Italy. Croatia isn’t immune to making such a move. Therefore, if your long-term plan involves owning a piece of the Adriatic coast or captaining a boat in Croatian waters without the need to worry about limits, fines and bans, getting your Domovnica and your Croatian passport isn’t just a sentimental nod to your heritage or a way to bypass long airport queues, it’s a critical financial and legal tool.

here’s how croatianbydescent can help you get the ball rolling

Croatian by Descent is a service aimed at US citizens who have Croatian roots and are on the hunt for Croatian citizenship. The administrative pathway to being granted citizenship in Croatia, while arguably easier than in many other countries, is still burdened with administrative pitfalls, delays, paperwork upon paperwork and very little help (if any at all) from the Interior Ministry (MUP), which handles applications.

Acting as your guide, a free consultation with them will allow you to see the situation in a more structured and less overwhelming way. Founded by members of the Croatian diaspora, they know the situation you’re facing better than anyone else, and have navigated this process personally in their own lives and with their own loved ones. With fair pricing and genuine guidance, applying for Croatian citizenship as an ethnic Croat is made easier and clearer, without the worry of the infamous fali ti još jedan papir (you’re missing another paper) that so many who have opted to try to go it alone have heard repeatedly.
