World.title: Live: Nepal-Tibet flood kills 392, as Australians remain among hundreds missing
World.content:
The big concern going into today is the possibility of a second flood along the same river.

Two barrier lakes have been formed as a result of Wednesday's disaster, one in Nepal and one in China.

The worry, according to officials in both countries, is that either or both are expected to continue filling with water and then overflow, leading to a second debris flow down the same river, and through the same disaster-hit communities.

Nepal's disaster authority issued a notice on Thursday warning that a lake formed by debris blocking a river at the flood site is rising and at risk of bursting.

Meanwhile, China is warning that 3 million cubic metres of water are expected to flow into an already dammed lake on its side of the border within the next three days.

There's also further rainfall forecast, according to Chinese state media, and this is what the lake looks like as of Thursday, according to Chinese state broadcaster Xinhua.

World.title: Ratko Mladic, ex-general convicted of Bosnia genocide, dies in prison
World.content:
Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic — who was was serving a life sentence for his role in the 1992-95 war in Bosnia — has died, a United Nations official has said.

The octogenarian former general, nicknamed "the Butcher of Bosnia", had been in ill health in the last few years and was hospitalised repeatedly. He had been in the UN detention centre since his arrest in 2011.

Mladic was convicted of genocide in 2016 for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in a UN-designated "safe area" of Bosnia, widely considered Europe's worst atrocity since World War II.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017.

According to his son, documents gave Mladic's date of birth at March 12, 1942, but he was actually born on March 8, 1943.

'Butcher of Bosnia'

A mural of Ratko Mladic seen in Belgrade, Serbia, in 2021. (Reuters: Zorana Jevtic)

The son of a World War II partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladic was an officer in the old communist Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia's disintegration began in 1991.

When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia's Muslim-led secession, Mladic was picked to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70 per cent of the landlocked country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down as 22,000 troops of the UN Protection Force stood by more or less helplessly, with orders not to take sides.

The army Mladic created to fight in Bosnia was a model of ruthlessness, daring and brutality in the Serb warrior tradition — once prized in the life-or-death partisan struggle against the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia in World War II.

In some of the most horrific examples, prisoners suffocated in the heat after being forced to eat salt and denied water, were starved and raped in prison camps, were made to jump off a bridge and shot, and were gunned down at night by the hundreds after being driven out of detention with chemical gas.

Mladic had a cameraman film the blitz on the encircled enclave of Srebrenica, to show him extolling his "lads" and haranguing Dutch UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands. Srebrenica supposedly had "safe area" status, meant to protect civilians from ethnic cleansing.

Mladic's forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for execution.

Mladic's capture took nearly two decades

A combination of Western pressure, covert American arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladic's army. Determined NATO strikes did the rest.

When NATO tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited air strikes, his troops defiantly seized UN peacekeepers as human shields — chaining them to likely targets.

In November 1996, Mladic and top generals gave in to strong Western pressure that he step down as ordered by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who succeeded Karadzic and was later jailed for her role in war crimes.

Despite Western appeals, the reformists ruling Serbia after Milosevic's fall did not dare move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

Mladic attempted to appeal his conviction for genocide at the Hague. (AP: Peter Dejong)

Mladic topped the wanted list for years at the UN International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), alongside Karadzic — also convicted of genocide.

Sporadic sightings put him at a Belgrade horse race or a soccer match. In 2004, NATO said he had toasted hard-drinking old comrades at his former bunker in Han Pijesak, Bosnia.

When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. His right arm was lame, the apparent result of an untreated stroke. He looked nothing like the burly general in camouflage who ruffled the hair of a Srebrenica boy in 1995.

He suffered a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.

In his few court appearances, he wavered between self-pity, smiling defiance and vague distraction.

"I am a very sick man," Mladic pleaded to the court.

In 2019, Mladic told the judges that he was too ill to participate in outdoor exercises and requested leave to visit the graves of family members in Serbia. The request was denied.

His appeal against conviction was rejected in 2021, as were repeated requests for his release on compassionate grounds.

In August 2026, a UN doctor found Mladic's death "may occur at any time," possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected as not in the interests of justice.

Reuters

World.title: Voluntary assisted dying legal nation-wide after laws pass NT parliament
World.content:
The Northern Territory Parliament has passed a bill legalising voluntary assisted dying (VAD) in the NT, with significant restrictions on accessing, and initiating conversations about, the practice.

The NT is now both the first and last Australian jurisdiction to legislate for VAD after a watershed 1995 law was overturned by the Commonwealth two years later.

A gag clause preventing medical professionals from starting conversations about VAD will remain in the legislation after government members voted down two attempts to remove it.

Recipients of VAD will be required to have an end-of-life prognosis no greater than 12 months before accessing the service, after proposed amendments to change the eligibility criteria were also rejected.

Tanzil Rahman says the law should no longer be called "Rights of the Terminally Ill". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Several Country Liberal Party (CLP) backbenchers split from their government colleagues throughout the two days of debate, siding with the Labor Opposition and independent Member for Johnston Justine Davis in pushing for the gag clause and prognosis period to be amended.

"These are meaningful changes and if we're just obstinate about it, if we just dig our heads in the sand, I don't think you can really call this a 'Rights of the Terminally Ill' bill anymore," CLP Member for Fong Lim Tanzil Rahman said.

Member for Fannie Bay Laurie Zio also appealed to her CLP colleagues to consider the amendments, at one point reminding them they were not expected to vote along party lines.

"It is a conscience vote, nobody's going to get in trouble if you're voting one way or the other, please have a think about what your electorate wants," she said.

Attempts to remove the gag clause were ultimately rejected by a majority of government members, including Member for Blain Matthew Kerle, who had last week voiced support for the amendments.

Laurie Zio urged her parliamentary colleagues to "think about what your electorate wants". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Dr Rahman, Ms Zio and member for Karama Brian O’Gallagher all supported the changes, joined by independent Justine Davis and all participating Labor Opposition members but the bill still had enough support to pass unamended.

Labor Member for Gwoja Chansey Paech abstained from the debate.

An amendment to the 12-month prognosis period was also rejected by a majority of government members, including Mr O’Gallagher, despite the Member for Karama previously seeking to extend the time frame to two years.

Righting the 'greatest wrong’

The passage of the bill marks the second time voluntary assisted dying has been legislated in the Northern Territory, after the federal parliament moved to disallow the 1995 law.

Speaking outside parliament after tonight’s debate, Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the moment was a long time coming for Territorians who had been wronged by the Commonwealth.

"It's a very surreal moment," she said.

" I remember as a young girl watching this debate unfold, watching the news of Marshall [Perron] walking out of the parliament. "

"Tonight we have righted the greatest wrong in delivering this important reform for Territorians."

Lia Finocchiaro says the bill's passage was "a very surreal moment". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Mrs Finocchiaro denied suggestions CLP members had been pressured into toeing the party line, despite all cabinet members and a majority of backbenchers voting in lockstep.

Labor Opposition Leader Selena Uibo said while it was disappointing the amendments were rejected, she was glad to see Territorians put on the same footing as the rest of the country.

"It's important Territorians know their voices have been heard," she said.

"While the bill has passed tonight, and I think many Territorians will absolutely welcome that, it has exposed even more division within the CLP government."

Gag order scrutinised

The NT joins South Australia as the only two Australian jurisdictions with a VAD gag clause, after Victoria's parliament removed a similar provision late last year.

Ms Uibo seized on a response to questions from other MLAs tonight in which Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby revealed the gag did not extend to administrative officers and receptionists.

"Effectively, [it] could be worked around and overridden if a GP has an administrative officer or an assistant who provides information to a patient," Ms Uibo said.

Selena Uibo says the gag clause "could be worked around and overridden". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The back-and-forth also revealed the bill did not outline a clear means of enforcing the gag, with Dr Rahman saying it was "raising more questions than answers now".

As debate continued into the evening, MLAs including the CLP's Mr O'Gallagher said the clause undermined the work of doctors across the territory.

"It's not the doctor making the choice, the doctor is only discussing information," he said.

" If we can trust them to talk to families about the option of turning life support on and off, I'm sure I can trust them to have a good conversation with patients. "

Supporters of the gag clause spoke with concern about its impacts for vulnerable Indigenous Territorians.

Yingiya Guyula says VAD could lead people in remote communities to "blame the clinics for early deaths". (ABC News: Ian Redfearn)

Health Minister and Minister for Aboriginal Affairs Steve Edgington said removing it ran the risk of causing fear and mistrust in remote communities.

CLP fielding VAD bill amendments A week out from a conscience vote on voluntary assisted dying in the NT, several CLP backbenchers have proposed amendments to the bill.

Treasurer Bill Yan read from an email sent by former member for Mulka Yingiya Guyula in his contribution to the debate before resigning from parliament last week.

"If VAD is introduced to our communities and initiated by visiting nurses and doctors, there's a possibility many people will fear the clinics and blame the clinics for early deaths," he read.

Meanwhile, Labor Member for Daly Dheran Young argued for removing the clause after previously voicing concerns about how VAD may be received in Indigenous communities.

"I'm quite confident that removing the gag clause won't impede upon Aboriginal people in remote communities," he said.

The amendments were ultimately defeated by eight votes to 15.

World.title: Israeli commander defends ordering strike that killed Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
An Israeli commander who ordered a deadly drone strike on an aid convoy in Gaza, killing Australian woman Zomi Frankcom, says he still stands by his decision to launch the attack and did not intend to harm aid workers.

This interview was conducted in October 2025, before last week's decision by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) not to prosecute those involved in the strike.

Zomi Frankcom, 43, was working for World Central Kitchen (WCK) when she was killed in April 2024, along with six of her colleagues.

The commander who ordered the attack, Colonel Nochi Mendel, was sacked from his role as chief of staff for the Israeli military's Nahal infantry brigade.

Colonel Nochi Mendel ordered the Israeli drone strike that killed seven aid workers in 2024. File photo. (Supplied: Israel Defense Forces)

The IDF said the attack was a grave mistake, arising from mis-identification of the occupants of the convoy as Hamas members due to the presence of armed security.

However, Colonel Mendel was dismissed because of what the IDF described as a series of failures that occurred that night, including a violation of the IDF's rules of engagement and standard operating procedure.

The interview with Colonel Mendel was conducted with the help of an interpreter, and his responses have been translated.

"I'm the commander, and I'm the one who gave the order to carry out the operation. I didn't run away from the situation. I said I gave the order; don't look for anyone else," he said.

Colonel Mendel said he did not mean to kill any of the WCK employees, but said: "I'm not sorry for what I did."

Last week, the IDF said it would not pursue a criminal investigation or take additional measures against anyone involved in the incident.

The seven aid workers who died had been delivering food to a warehouse in central Gaza. (AP Photo: World Central Kitchen)

That decision was criticised by the Frankcom family, the Albanese government and World Central Kitchen.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said that "we still have not had a satisfactory explanation of why the strike occurred in a humanitarian fire control zone, and after High Command had directed the brigade commander not to engage the convoy."

The ABC's Unravel podcast is working on an investigation into the incident, which will be released later this year.

'We didn't intend to kill anyone from the WCK'

In the interview, Colonel Mendel said that he did not have any intention of harming the WCK aid workers when he ordered the attack.

But he claimed he was compelled to act by developments on the ground, for which he primarily blames a complex operational environment in Gaza, and errors made by WCK.

Colonel Mendel blamed what he viewed as "an intermingling between the WCK and Hamas operatives" that occurred on the evening.

"Of course we didn't intend to kill anyone from the WCK; their connection with Hamas was a deviation from the plan," he said.

One of the three World Central Kitchen vehicles destroyed in Gaza on April 1, 2024. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

He says later, after the incident, he became aware of what he claims were links between WCK and Hamas.

"So the WCK, too — unfortunately, they aren't really a neutral organisation. Not really an organisation you can say is innocent and completely clean.

"It had ties to Hamas."

In the interview, Colonel Mendel pointed to reports that WCK let go of some staff members in December 2024, after they were accused by Israel of links to Hamas.

However, he said he was not aware of this at the time of the strike, and those claims have been refuted by WCK, which stated at the time that because Israel does not share its intelligence, the dismissals "should not be taken as a conclusion by WCK that the individuals are affiliated with any terror organisation."

Israel accused Zomi Frankcom's organisation of having links to terrorists. (Supplied)

In response to Colonel Mendel's public comments, WCK said it rejected the allegations, calling them "false and outrageous."

"This is the latest attempt to shift blame away from the IDF's own actions," a spokesperson told the ABC.

"The individual making these slanderous claims has no credibility.

"He was directly involved in the decisions that led to the April 1 strikes and was immediately removed from his post for serious failures and breaches of standard operating procedure.

"We demand truth and justice for our seven colleagues who were killed, through a full, independent investigation into the attack."

In his words: the night of the strike

For the first time, Colonel Mendel has publicly detailed the sequence of events leading up to the strike, from his perspective.

Stationed at a control centre within the Sde Teiman defence facility in southern Israel, Colonel Mendel said he was watching a live feed from an Israeli drone hovering above the convoy travelling through central Gaza towards a warehouse in Deir al Balah.

The drone was being controlled by the Israeli air force from a separate base closer to Tel Aviv, known as Palmachim.

One of the three World Central Kitchen vehicles attacked by an Israeli air strike on April 1, 2024. (AP: Ismael Abu Dayyah)

Colonel Mendel said he had oversight of the drone feed, and open communications with the pilots in Palmachim.

"I can see [a] continuous video feed. I can see the trucks moving," he said.

Colonel Mendel said he saw several armed men, which he described as "terrorists", climbing onto the trucks that were being escorted by WCK cars in convoy.

"We can clearly see armed terrorists getting out and firing from the trucks."

Soon after, the convoy arrived at a warehouse to unload the aid. Colonel Mendel claimed that the live drone footage he was observing showed the armed men and the aid workers intermingling.

"We see them all mixed together — both the WCK guys and the Hamas terrorists with weapons," he said.

"We can see them right next to each other, and they're not trying to distance themselves from one another."

Colonel Mendel said that he decided not to attack the gunmen at this stage, despite asserting that he would have been justified to do so.

"There was a good enough reason for me to kill them, but because they were with the WCK, we didn't attack them at that stage," he said.

"I saw terrorists clearly; I didn't kill them so as not to harm the WCK."

Colonel Mendel says he observed armed men and aid workers intermingling, via live drone footage, before ordering the attack. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

However, a 2024 Australian investigation by Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin found that during this time, Colonel Mendel and an IDF brigade fire support commander classified several gunmen who were moving around the escort vehicles at the warehouse as Hamas and sought permission to engage the escort vehicles outside the warehouse.

Colonel Mendel's request to engage was denied by higher command due to the vehicles being deemed too close to the humanitarian aid convoy.

In his interview, Colonel Mendel said the military made contact with WCK to ask them about the presence of the gunmen.

According to Colonel Mendel, a WCK representative in Europe advised that there were not meant to be armed guards present in the convoy.

"They tell us there aren't supposed to be armed guards," he said.

After the aid was unloaded, the trucks stayed at the warehouse, while the WCK vehicles departed.

Colonel Mendel claimed that at this stage, World Central Kitchen deviated from the prearranged route they had coordinated with the IDF, which he said was meant to head to accommodation north of the warehouse.

Instead, the convoy separated, with some vehicles heading south towards Rafah.

However, according to the Binskin investigation, the decision to strike had already been finalised before the convoy made that turn, suggesting it could not have contributed to the decision.

Colonel Mendel further claimed that he identified an armed man entering one of the vehicles and insisted that the presence of a gunman in the vehicles heading south was confirmed to him by "professionals" at Palmachim air base, from where the drone was being operated.

"They definitely confirm that they identified an armed terrorist in the vehicle," he said.

Colonel Mendel revealed that was when he made the call to strike.

"I attacked the vehicle where an armed terrorist boarded with the weapon, and it's southbound."

An investigation by Australia's Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin diverges from the account given by Colonel Mendel. (AP: Abdel Kareem Hana)

In its initial response to the incident, published on their website shortly after the attack, the IDF stated that this was a "mis-identification."

And in briefings with journalists in the days following the attack, the military stated that the weapon seen as someone was entering a vehicle, was actually a bag.

Authorising the attack

The attack consisted of three separate strikes on three different vehicles over four minutes.

According to the Binskin report, these strikes were authorised despite an order from the division commander that "no more strikes around humanitarian convoys were to occur that night."

All three aid vehicles were hit along a coastal road, heading south. (ABC News Source: Bellingcat)

However, the report noted that "it was not stated how this direction was given and whether it was deemed a formal order," and the brigade staff had assessed that after the vehicles left the warehouse the "situation had now changed and they had now become targetable".

When asked by the ABC whether he had successfully killed any terrorists in the strike, Colonel Mendel was inconclusive.

"Maybe one, or maybe none were killed," he said.

While Colonel Mendel said he did not intend to harm anyone from the WCK, ultimately, he said he did not regret the decisions he made that night, despite the outcome, and was disappointed by the IDF's decision to dismiss him from his position in the army.

"It's a matter of it being painful because you're fighting a very complex situation," he said.

"We came here to win, to eradicate this evil for the whole world, not just for ourselves."

Colonel Mendel defends the decisions he made that led to the deaths of aid workers. File photo. (Supplied: Israel Defense Forces)

Referring to his dismissal from the army, he said: "In the end, in a very difficult situation, I'm paying the price."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is demanding Israel commission an independent investigation into the incident.

The family of Zomi Frankcom has repeatedly criticised the IDF for refusing to provide a copy of the drone audio that could help to resolve conflicting accounts of the evening.

World.title: Death in custody investigation launched after rural Darwin police pursuit
World.content:
Northern Territory Police have launched a death in custody investigation after a 43-year-old man died following a police pursuit in Darwin's rural area yesterday.

Addressing the media in Darwin today, Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the man died after reportedly self-harming during a confrontation with police in scrubland near the Stuart Highway.

Acting Assistant Commissioner Malley said the rural area local had stolen a vehicle from Adelaide River which he then abandoned near Acacia Hills, south of Humpty Doo.

"He went to take a vehicle, but there was children in the vehicle, and he was directed to another vehicle that had keys in it, so he drove away in that one," he said.

Police said the man then stole another vehicle from an address on Colton Road.

Police said the man stole a vehicle from an address on Colton Road during the incident. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The ABC spoke to residents at that address, who said they were left rattled by the incident, with the vehicle stolen from the property while a mother and child were at home.

Pursuit in vehicle and then on foot

A pursuit reportedly then ensued in the area between police and the stolen vehicle.

The man reportedly abandoned the vehicle at the Acacia Quarry, then fled on foot.

When confronted by officers, police said the man self-harmed.

"An officer deployed a taser in an attempt to prevent the man from further harming himself," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Police say the man abandoned one of the vehicles at the Acacia Quarry. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Officers provided immediate first aid and St John Ambulance arrived at the scene soon after, but the man succumbed to his injuries and was declared deceased at the scene."

Acting Assistant Commissioner Malley said he backed the action of officers at the scene but investigations were ongoing.

"It's a death in custody investigation declared, and major crime have it, with oversight from professional standards command," he said.

The officers involved have also been offered welfare support following the incident.

World.title: Hopes dashed as search for elderly man with dementia scaled back
World.content:
A multi-agency search for a missing 87-year-old man in Western Australia's Wheatbelt region has been scaled back, six days after he failed to return from his morning walk.

James Ballantyne, who lives with dementia, was last seen near Leonora Street in Wagin, about 230 kilometres south-east of Perth, on Saturday.

His disappearance sparked an extensive land and air search, with dozens of volunteers joining police to try to find him.

Their hopes were all but dashed on Thursday, with authorities significantly scaling back the operation.

Extensive search

Police used drones, a helicopter and plane to search for Mr Ballantyne, while his family organised tracker dogs and a private plane.

State Emergency Service volunteers from as far as Perth and Bunbury joined in, while others supported the search teams with food and supplies.

Acting Inspector Wasley said the community response was "absolutely amazing". (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

A large image of Mr Ballantyne was projected onto a sign in the middle of the town to try to elicit information about his whereabouts.

A small farming community, Wagin has a population of about 1,400 people with locals and those in surrounding areas quick to jump into action.

"The community was just absolutely amazing, searching outside their houses, sheds, laneways," Great Southern Acting Inspector Craig Wasley told the ABC.

Residents have been out in force searching for missing Wagin man James Ballantyne. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Shire of Wagin acting president Bryan Kilpatrick similarly praised the support from the community.

"The good majority of the community has been involved in some way or another, whether it's been searching, providing food, providing support," he said.

" It's just been overwhelming support by all community. "

Community rocked

Mr Kilpatrick said it was "devastating" to have no answers six days into Mr Ballantyne's disappearance.

"It really rocks a community like this," he said.

Mr Ballantyne is a beloved member of the Wagin community. (Supplied: WA Police)

"Mr Ballantyne was a loved part of the community and his family are an important part of the shire, so it certainly has an impact."

Mr Ballantyne's family declined to speak to media, but passed on a message via Acting Inspector Wasley who said they wished to thank everyone involved with the search.

"They're aware of the effort that has been put in, the people that have been involved, and they are absolutely amazed and appreciate the effort that everyone has put in, including the community," he said.

Scaling back

Acting Inspector Wasley said police and SES had searched the target area to a "high degree" and would be pulling back external resources.

"Air wing, police horses, all of those resources have returned to Perth, SES have returned to their home locations," he said.

Authorities still hope to find Mr Ballantyne, though they have all but lost hope that he will be found alive.

"Look, the prospect of Jim being alive is probably not there anymore," Acting Inspector Wasley said.

"The family are aware of that and they accept that.

"Our aim is to find Jim and we will continue to search for him.

"The battle now becomes a local inquiry, so Wagin Police will continue with inquiries."

Anyone with information about Mr Ballantyne's whereabouts is urged to contact police.

World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta CEO steps aside weeks from grand opening
World.content:
Powerhouse Parramatta CEO Lisa Havilah has stepped aside 10 weeks before the cultural institution opens in Western Sydney.

The decision was announced in a statement from the office of Minister for Arts John Graham on Thursday, which said she had stood aside while "investigations into governance and procurement" were underway.

In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for the Department of Creative Industries said the matters were "complex and involve multiple lines of inquiry".

"The Department has a responsibility to address these matters with due diligence and procedural fairness," the spokesperson said.

The museum will be open to the public in November. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)



"As the investigation is continuing and no formal findings or conclusions have been made, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment at this stage." "As the investigation is continuing and no formal findings or conclusions have been made, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment at this stage."

'Challenging time'

President of the Powerhouse Trust David Borger told 702 ABC Sydney the announcement came at a challenging time.

"I think obviously, it's challenging…these things are always somewhat surprising," he said.

"Obviously it's not an ideal situation this close to the opening."

He also confirmed the opening date would not be impacted.

"A 100 per cent the curtains are going to rise on the November 7….and there's no changing that," he said.

Ms Havilah was tasked with overseeing the $915 million build of Powerhouse Parramatta following her appointment in 2018.

The development is the city's most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.

David Borger reacted to the news of Ms Havilah leaving the CEO role. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Interim team to lead opening

Ahead of the museum's November opening, an interim team to oversee the organisation has been established.

From September 1, NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin will step in as CEO and former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron has been named strategic advisor.

Mr Graham's office described Ms Galvin as "an experienced senior executive with significant experience across the public, infrastructure and cultural sectors".

Ms Havilah has been the chief executive of the Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences (MAAS) for more than seven years and previously oversaw the significant expansion of the Carriageworks multi-arts hub in Redfern.

But in March this year, Ms Havilah was grilled over "budget blowouts" for the Powerhouse Parramatta by upper house MP Chris Rath.

"I know there have been budget blowouts from years and years gone by, but are we expecting any further cost blowouts from the relocation, or has it all basically been accounted for now in the budget?" he said.

Powerhouse Parramatta faced accusations of a budget blowout. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Ms Havilah denied any such budget blowouts.

"There haven't been any budget overruns on Powerhouse Parramatta or the revitalisation of the Powerhouse Museum in Ultimo. They're both being delivered within the allocated budget," she said.

The ABC has contacted Ms Havilah for comment.

Speaking to the ABC earlier this month, Ms Havilah said she was eager to attend the opening.

"I won't be holding the scissors, but I'm looking forward to watching that ribbon being cut," she said.

She also confirmed NSW Treasury executive Cassandra Wilkinson's sudden appointment to the Powerhouse as Chief Operating Officer in July.

"She [Ms Wilkinson] is acting in the COO role, and she's continuing that work and has been a great member of the team," she said.

World.title: 'There was no fanfare': Broncos criticised for Reynolds farewell in Storm rout
World.content:
The Melbourne Storm have handed Brisbane another miserable night at Lang Park, scoring eight tries in a 46-20 demolition as the Broncos farewell a number of departing players in disappointing fashion.

Captain Adam Reynolds was one of a number of Broncos waving goodbye to his adopted home ground, doing so from the sidelines after being ruled out by injury.

A number of fans criticised a pre-game tribute to him and other players bound for new clubs or retirement in 2027 after it was cut short by an  on the big screen.

Retiring player Adam Reynolds waves goodbye at Lang Park. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"You didn't even know there was a send-off, that's how bad it was," former Queensland Maroon Billy Moore said in commentary for ABC Sport.

It comes after their was controversy over the decision for Reynolds to sit out the final two games of the season, despite the halfback saying he felt like he could have played at least part of one of the games.

It overshadowed the lead-up to what should have been a celebration of a two-time premiership winner and the man who led the team to their first trophy in 19 years less than 12 months ago.

"Regardless whether he was playing or not, the Broncos could've done something to send him off," Parramatta great Nathan Hindmarsh said on Fox League.

"They had a bit of a clap pre-game in the middle of the pitch and that was about it. There was no fanfare. It just doesn't seem there was enough build-up.

"He's a champion player and to not really have a big build-up … there needed to be something special."

The Broncos' final game is against the Eels at Parramatta Stadium, while the Storm travel to Shark Park to take on Cronulla.

World.title: From controversy to calamity: Where do Broncos go from ninth-straight implosion?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 From controversy to calamity: Where do Broncos go from ninth-straight implosion? Nick Wright August 27, 2026 — 10:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A week of frustrations and more headlines for the Brisbane Broncos as their season fell further into the doldrums has ended in calamity – suffering a humiliating 46-20 defeat to the Melbourne Storm to mark their ninth-straight loss at Suncorp Stadium. Even as retiring skipper Adam Reynolds completed a lap of honour around Suncorp Stadium, the speculation surrounding the nature of his omission for the rest of the season seemed to be too much of a distraction to overcome. A Jordan Riki push on Jahrome Hughes seemed to typify Brisbane’s frustrations. Getty Images While the official line he could not fight beyond a calf issue eventually came out, it took several turns. First Reynolds declared himself eager to play, before then insisting he had withdrawn himself from the remaining contests. Coach Michael Maguire repeated the latter, but not before Ben Hunt expressed his disappointment at the situation on radio, and an ill-fated social media ‘like’ by Reece Walsh on a post which condemned the captain’s treatment was issued. It typified a season of woes: from premiers, to barely avoiding the wooden spoon.



Neither Brisbane nor Melbourne had much to play for, given they will not factor in the finals, but the goal-line defence of the Broncos in their final outing at home this year would have done little to give their fans a promise of what 2027 may bring. Related Article NRL 2026 ‘The message Nathan would always give me’: How Cleary planted seeds for Dolphins Melbourne’s first try was described in commentary as “under-7s stuff” – Stefano Utoikamanu shrugging off four defenders, Payne Haas and Pat Carrigan among them, to reach out and score straight from a penalty tap 10 metres out. While a Shawn Blore knock on gave Brisbane the chance to strike back through Kotoni Staggs, a Billy Walters’ mistake opened the door for Tryan Wishart to latch onto a short pass from Cameron Munster and fend off two more defenders to score. Nick Meaney soon sliced through with ease, Haas and Ezra Mam getting nowhere near him, while Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown bullied his way beyond Josiah Karapani and over the top of Deine Mariner to cross.



Not even a Mam intercept try could settle the carnage that was being inflicted upon Brisbane. On the stroke of halftime, the Storm showcased some razzle-dazzle – Harry Grant’s chip over the top straight from a scrum leading to Wishart’s second. By halftime, trailing 30-10, the Broncos had missed 27 tackles to Melbourne’s seven. Loading It took a one-man advantage following Moses Leo’s sin binning for a forceful high shot – and a play of madness which featured kicks from Hunt, Staggs and Mam for Hunt to eventually score – for Brisbane to get back in the contest after the break. But all that did was delay the inevitable, and gave fans the chance to see the NRL’s first trial of the kick-off rule change in which the team to concede a try determines who kicks off. That Hunt try was the only instance where the scoring team took the kick.



What does the future hold for Brisbane? They still have a round to play – a trip to Accor Stadium next Thursday to face the Bulldogs – but there are growing concerns for just how the Broncos can bounce back in 2027. True when they last missed the finals they won the premiership the following year, but the nature of this campaign’s derailing has been particularly concerning. Sweeping changes will go through the squad – Reynolds, Payne Haas, Corey Jensen, Gehamat Shibasaki, Jesse Arthars and Grant Anderson all departing. Mitch Barnett, Dane Gagai, Jonah Pezet and Blore will arrive at Red Hill with an uphill battle to steady the ship. Adam Reynolds and Michael Maguire after Brisbane’s premiership victory last year. Getty Images



But there is no replacing the game’s best prop in Haas. Nor can the likes of Pezet and Tom Duffy be expected to fill Reynolds’ halfback void. The problems at Brisbane go beyond personnel. In the opening half of Thursday’s defeat, the first four tries they conceded were all directly from errors or needless penalties – Jordan Riki’s push on Jahrome Hughes as the halfback put up a kick seemingly a sign of the side’s frustrations. Heading into the clash, no outfit had conceded more penalties than the Broncos (128). The Melbourne clash was the 12th time in 2026 they had conceded 30 or more points. A team which boasts Walsh – sidelined with a syndesmosis injury – Mam, Staggs and Carrigan should possess enough talent to go deep into the year. An offseason of serious soul-searching is on the cards, not just for the players, but for how coach Michael Maguire unites this dressing room. What does the future hold for Melbourne?



Not since 2010 have the Storm not featured in finals football. On that occasion, it was due to the infamous salary cap scandal. This time around, it came on the back of their most inconsistent performances witnessed under Craig Bellamy’s tutelage – a seven-game losing streak at the start of the season one they were never quite able to recover from, despite winning eight of their past 14 games. News Bellamy had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative condition hardly would have aided their cause, nor did the fate of star edge forward Eli Katoa; who missed the entire campaign after undergoing surgery on a brain bleed suffered in the Pacific Championships last year. Melbourne were emphatic on Thursday night, spearheaded by their all-star spine. Getty Images But while they will lose Wishart, Meaney (Bears), Blore (Broncos) and injured winger Will Warbrick (Warriors) for 2027, their all-star spine of Grant, Munster, Hughes and Sua Fa’alogo – who all had some lethal touches against the Broncos – will enter next year as one of the best play-making combinations in the competition.



Munster’s decision in the second half to put in an early grubber for Fa’alogo to break any chance of a Brisbane comeback summed up just how potent this spine can be, with the quartet combing for six try assists. Tuimalatu-Brown’s length-of-the-field intercept try, before leaping above Karapani to score his hat-trick, was the icing on the cake. It has been far from the envisioned season for Melbourne, but they have the troops and coach to ensure this campaign is an aberration News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Dress code loophole revealed
World.content:
Jeff Apter of Keiraville reflects on the bare facts of dress codes (C8): “During my lively youth, a group of us were on a coastal holiday, and were advised a collared shirt was required to attend the local club. No problem, my friend figured, and that night he duly strolled through the door wearing nothing but a collared shirt and a broad smile. He didn’t last long inside, but he did turn a few heads.”

“In the early ’80s, a trip to Karumba revealed the local pub had two bars: The Animal Bar and The Suave Bar,” recalls Les Montgomery of Whian Whian. “On asking, we were told the Suave Bar insisted that footwear be worn, but that thongs would suffice. There were no other dress rules for either bar.”

Paul Hunt of Engadine has a bit of Chatswood Charles (C8) folklore: “I, too, used to frequent that popular place, which was famous for having one of the longest bars in Australia as well as booking some top entertainers. It was late on a Saturday night as the band took up their places on stage in front of a capacity audience. The excitement was palpable, the enthusiasm spectacular. There was no formal introduction, just a few notes that immediately conveyed who they were. The song? Spicks and Specs. The group? The Bee Gees! It was their last concert before they left for London to try their luck. Some town. Some luck”.

“I have herd everything now,” says Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook. “Several all-beef patties on the hoof entering the drive thru at Macca’s in none other than the Brisbane suburb of South Ripley!” Believe it, or not.

Granny reckons James White (C8) took it easy on her in pointing out that she’d mislabelled his Victorian place of residence, Beveridge, as Beverage. To make it up to him, he said, “I’ll just have a coffee.”

They still have a round to play – a trip to Accor Stadium next Thursday to face the Bulldogs – but there are growing concerns for just how the Broncos can bounce back in 2027. True when they last missed the finals they won the premiership the following year, but the nature of this campaign’s derailing has been particularly concerning. Sweeping changes will go through the squad – Reynolds, Payne Haas, Corey Jensen, Gehamat Shibasaki, Jesse Arthars and Grant Anderson all departing. Mitch Barnett, Dane Gagai, Jonah Pezet and Blore will arrive at Red Hill with an uphill battle to steady the ship. Adam Reynolds and Michael Maguire after Brisbane’s premiership victory last year. Getty Images



But there is no replacing the game’s best prop in Haas. Nor can the likes of Pezet and Tom Duffy be expected to fill Reynolds’ halfback void. The problems at Brisbane go beyond personnel. In the opening half of Thursday’s defeat, the first four tries they conceded were all directly from errors or needless penalties – Jordan Riki’s push on Jahrome Hughes as the halfback put up a kick seemingly a sign of the side’s frustrations. Heading into the clash, no outfit had conceded more penalties than the Broncos (128). The Melbourne clash was the 12th time in 2026 they had conceded 30 or more points. A team which boasts Walsh – sidelined with a syndesmosis injury – Mam, Staggs and Carrigan should possess enough talent to go deep into the year. An offseason of serious soul-searching is on the cards, not just for the players, but for how coach Michael Maguire unites this dressing room. What does the future hold for Melbourne?



Not since 2010 have the Storm not featured in finals football. On that occasion, it was due to the infamous salary cap scandal. This time around, it came on the back of their most inconsistent performances witnessed under Craig Bellamy’s tutelage – a seven-game losing streak at the start of the season one they were never quite able to recover from, despite winning eight of their past 14 games. News Bellamy had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative condition hardly would have aided their cause, nor did the fate of star edge forward Eli Katoa; who missed the entire campaign after undergoing surgery on a brain bleed suffered in the Pacific Championships last year. Melbourne were emphatic on Thursday night, spearheaded by their all-star spine. Getty Images But while they will lose Wishart, Meaney (Bears), Blore (Broncos) and injured winger Will Warbrick (Warriors) for 2027, their all-star spine of Grant, Munster, Hughes and Sua Fa’alogo – who all had some lethal touches against the Broncos – will enter next year as one of the best play-making combinations in the competition.



Munster’s decision in the second half to put in an early grubber for Fa’alogo to break any chance of a Brisbane comeback summed up just how potent this spine can be, with the quartet combing for six try assists. Tuimalatu-Brown’s length-of-the-field intercept try, before leaping above Karapani to score his hat-trick, was the icing on the cake. It has been far from the envisioned season for Melbourne, but they have the troops and coach to ensure this campaign is an aberration News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Dress code loophole revealed
World.content:
Jeff Apter of Keiraville reflects on the bare facts of dress codes (C8): “During my lively youth, a group of us were on a coastal holiday, and were advised a collared shirt was required to attend the local club. No problem, my friend figured, and that night he duly strolled through the door wearing nothing but a collared shirt and a broad smile. He didn’t last long inside, but he did turn a few heads.”

“In the early ’80s, a trip to Karumba revealed the local pub had two bars: The Animal Bar and The Suave Bar,” recalls Les Montgomery of Whian Whian. “On asking, we were told the Suave Bar insisted that footwear be worn, but that thongs would suffice. There were no other dress rules for either bar.”

Paul Hunt of Engadine has a bit of Chatswood Charles (C8) folklore: “I, too, used to frequent that popular place, which was famous for having one of the longest bars in Australia as well as booking some top entertainers. It was late on a Saturday night as the band took up their places on stage in front of a capacity audience. The excitement was palpable, the enthusiasm spectacular. There was no formal introduction, just a few notes that immediately conveyed who they were. The song? Spicks and Specs. The group? The Bee Gees! It was their last concert before they left for London to try their luck. Some town. Some luck”.

“I have herd everything now,” says Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook. “Several all-beef patties on the hoof entering the drive thru at Macca’s in none other than the Brisbane suburb of South Ripley!” Believe it, or not.

Granny reckons James White (C8) took it easy on her in pointing out that she’d mislabelled his Victorian place of residence, Beveridge, as Beverage. To make it up to him, he said, “I’ll just have a coffee.”

World.title: Two-thirds of New Zealanders willing to pay more tax for better healthcare
World.content:
A survey of 1600 people has found two-thirds of New Zealanders are willing to pay more tax for better healthcare - particularly when it comes to cancer.

The survey, funded by the Cancer Society and published as a nine-paper series in the New Zealand Medical Journal, also found consensus across voters for all major parties about the need for tougher regulation on tobacco and unhealthy foods, and more urgent action on skin cancer prevention, cancer screening and treatment.

A collaboration between University of Otago cancer researchers and the Cancer Society, called Te Rōpu Rangahau ō te Kāhui Matepukupuku, undertook the study.

Its lead director, Professor Louise Signal, a professor of public health at Otago University in Wellington, said the results showed a clear public mandate for evidence-based cancer policy - what was lacking was political action.

"We were surprised at the extent of the cross-party support from many of the policies that we suggested," she said. "Overwhelmingly, New Zealanders think they should be reinstated, including... significant majorities, in most cases, of the coalition partner voters."

The study found 1034 people, or 62 percent of respondents, supported the idea of paying more tax for increased healthcare funding. In contrast, 458, or 29 percent, were opposed, and the remainder did not know.

Signal said the survey was a representative sample of the New Zealand public, and the government often relied on surveys such as this for policy making. "So I think we can be confident that indeed New Zealanders are willing to pay more tax for better health care."

Professor Louise Signal. © University of Otago

The results also showed strong, cross-party support from voters for greater investment in cancer care, and it's particularly strong among older New Zealanders.

The Cancer Society's head of advocacy and public affairs, Rachael Neumann, said it created a clear mandate for the government to invest more in cancer diagnosis, treatment and care.

Public support for early cancer detection, treatment and care policies was higher than 90 percent, regardless of which party people said they intended to vote for.

"Together, an ageing population and entrenched inequities mean the demand for timely, equitable cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment will continue to intensify in the coming decades unless this action is taken."

Support for stronger regulations on unhealthy food, tobacco, alcohol and lobbying

The results showed wide-ranging support for reinstating tobacco reforms, sugary drinks taxes, protecting children from marketing for alcohol and junk food, stricter alcohol laws, and significantly more sun safety action.

On Tuesday, Labour announced if elected, it would reinstate its smokefree generation policy, repealed in 2024 by the current government. When it was first introduced under the previous Labour government, it would have meant that people born on or after 1 January, 2009 would never be able to purchase tobacco products again.

Health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall signalled this time, the cut-off date would change, but didn't say what to.

There was also strong support for stand-down periods for outgoing politicians before they could become lobbyists, and stronger regulations on lobbying in general - particularly in the areas of sugary foods and alcohol.

There were 1267 (79 percent) of respondents in favour of no industry involvement in healthy food environment policy, compared with 292 (17 percent) against.

World.title: Police continue hunt for those behind Wattle Downs suspected double homicide
World.content:
Police have been hunting through the night for those responsible for a suspected double homicide in Wattle Downs, South Auckland, on Thursday.

Emergency services responded to reports of a woman unresponsive at an address on Gambare Place about 1.45pm.

The woman was pronounced dead at the scene and, during a search of the property, police found a man who was also pronounced dead.

Detective Inspector Tofilau Faamanuia Va'aelua said the offender or offenders fled the scene prior to officers arriving.

On Thursday evening, armed police stood guard in front of the house, as neighbours looked on.

Dianna Kereopa-Turner had lived in the street her whole life. She told RNZ she had just returned home when "havoc started going on" outside.

"We thought it was our nail gun for our sleepout that we're building going off ... and then it was quite loud," Kereopa-Turner said.

"But no, it was shooting. All we heard was gun. Then my sister came out of her room and said 'somebody out there's shooting', so we gathered in whoever was loose around the house and stayed inside."

She said the victims had only just moved in to the street: "It's sad to know that whatever trouble was following them, obviously followed them right to the doorstep, and unfortunately it happened on this street where there's a lot of kids and a lot of elderly people."

Cordons in place around the house. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Many residents had been unable to return to their homes on Gambare Place and adjoining Volante Avenue while police cordons closed the roads on Thursday afternoon, with armed police stationed at the cordons.

Another Gambare Place resident, Bobbie, said she had been at the doctors and tried to return home around 2.45pm.

"The street was already closed off, so I thought, 'oh better shoot over to the school and pick up my niece', got over there and it was locked down as well."

Bobbie said they were allowed to go home just after 5pm.

She said, once home, she talked with neighbours and some were quite shocked.

While the cordon was in place, police were seen working behind a white tarpaulin on Volante Avenue. Police later confirmed staff had moved the victims to a safe location, away from the scene, to render first aid, while other staff continued working to clear the scene and make it safe.

Va'aelua said the incident appeared to be isolated, but police were not able to "rule anything out", and were now determining the exact cricumstances of the incident.

"This is an awful set of events and no doubt unsettling for everyone involved and the wider community."

World.title: 'Horrifying': NZ-based Nepali community pleads for urgent help
World.content:
A flash flood and landslide hit the Nepal-China border on Wednesday

Police in Nepal say 362 bodies have been found

Hundreds of tourists are among more than 1000 people missing

Five Kiwis are among the missing, MFAT says

It's believed a glacier collapse may have caused the disaster

Horrifying pictures of the Nepal flash flood are being described as "like watching a movie" by a New Zealand-based Nepali man.

Five New Zealanders are among more than 1000 people missing following Wednesday's catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-China border which killed at least 362 people.

RNZ understands four of the five New Zealanders missing are Suhasini Reddy, who lives in Australia, Auckland man Dejan Kuzmic, and Hamilton couple Mihir and Kinnari Patel.

The identity of the fifth person has not yet been confirmed.

Based in the Canterbury town of Lincoln, Dr Sulav Paudel said seeing the disaster unfold was unlike anything he had seen.

"It's horrifying. It's like things we see in dramatic movies," he said.

"Most of us haven't slept well."

Dr Paudel was the treasurer for the New Zealand chapter of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA).

The group had issued an urgent plea for donations as it tries to raise emergency relief funding for the Nepal government.

NRNA New Zealand was working with other NRNA groups within its international network, including a team on the ground in Nepal.

Its executive team met on Thursday to discuss how New Zealand-based Nepali could respond to the disaster.

A member of the security forces and his sniffer dog search for survivors. PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP

Dr Paudel said the group had reached out to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade to advocate for support from the New Zealand government for the disaster recovery.

He hoped the government would soon formally acknowledge the event, including what support it might be able to offer.

"In the meantime we're also looking after our members to see whether there are any families or people who have loved ones that need support," he said.

Given the event was still unfolding, Dr Paudel said it was too early to determine to what extent New Zealand-based Nepali may have been personally impacted.

"There are so many people that are out of reach that we don't know what has happened to them yet," he said.

"In terms of actual casualties, I don't think we've heard from anyone.

"We expect the number (of casualties) to go up."

There were about 1350 members of NRNA New Zealand.

World.title: Five New Zealanders among missing tourists after deadly Nepal flash flood
World.content:
The flash flood and landslide hit the Nepal-China border on Wednesday

Police in Nepal say 270 bodies have been found

Hundreds of tourists are among nearly 1500 missing people

Five Kiwis are among the missing, MFAT says

It's believed a glacier collapse may have caused the disaster

Five New Zealanders are among nearly 1500 people missing following Wednesday's catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-China border which killed at least 270 people.

RNZ understands four of the five New Zealanders missing are Suhasini Reddy, who lived in Australia, Auckland man Dejan Kuzmic and Hamilton couple Mihir and Kinnari Patel.

The identity of the fifth person has not yet been revealed.

Reddy's brother Rajeev Reddy told RNZ she and the group of hikers she was with were due to meet Chinese authorities to get permission to cross the border close to the time the raging flood hit.

Her appointment was at 11am local time, the tragedy unfolded shortly after 8.30am. He hoped she'd made it to higher ground.

Suhasini Reddy is one of the New Zealanders missing. SUPPLIED

Earlier on Thursday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) confirmed five New Zealanders were missing.

"Consular officials are providing support to the families of those individuals."

Consular staff were deploying to Nepal, where they would join the efforts of the High Commission in India and Honourary Consul in Nepal.

A spokesperson said the sheer scale of devastation was becoming increasingly clear and the loss of life in Nepal and China was likely to be horrific.

The aftermath. Supplied

Anyone concerned for loved ones should contact MFAT's Emergency Consular Line on +64 99 20 20 20.

Hundreds of foreign tourists are among those missing following the deadly flash flood.

Nations including India, Australia, the UK, Canada, Germany, Japan, Malaysia, Russia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Ukraine and the US also had citizens missing.

The flash flooding was believed to have been caused by the collapse of a glacier which sent water crashing through the valleys of the border.

Are you or is someone you know affected? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

CCTV widely shared online showed the moment a wall of water crashed through the Rasuwagadhi border point in the Himalayan mountain range.

People could be seen desperately running away from the scene before the water appeared.

According to state media, the area still faced the risk of further landslides, mudslides and flash floods, with three days of rain ahead.

The clean up in Nepal. Supplied

How New Zealand reacted

Dr Tom Robinson, who studied and modelled landslides at the school of earth and environment at the University of Canterbury, said the landslide and flooding were not isolated events.

He said he couldn't state climate change was the reason behind this specific avalanche, but there was a pattern in which the Himalayas were being destabilised by rising temperatures.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon described the images coming out of Nepal and China as "heartbreaking" and said New Zealand was in touch with Nepal authorities about New Zealanders who may be affected.

"My deep condolences to those affected and to impacted communities," he wrote in a post on X.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters echoed his sentiments, saying New Zealand is "deeply concerned".

Hamilton couple Mihir and Kinnari Patel are missing.

The son of Sir Edmund Hillary described the flash flood as "catastrophic" in an interview with The Panel.

Peter Hilary, who serves as chairperson of the Himalayan Trust, said the mountainous areas of Nepal had a history of glacial outburst floods (GLOFs).

"Because of the great altitude that it originated from, probably 4500 metres, and then descending very rapidly down a gorge, these things tend to be absolutely catastrophic and that's of course what we've seen," he said.

Hillary said a similar disaster wiped out a school his father helped develop back in the 1960s.

The Himalayan Trust was fundraising in a bid to support the Nepalese government's emergency fund.

A candlelight vigil would be held by the New Zealand Nepal Society for the victims in Aotea Square, Auckland, at 4pm on Saturday.

World.title: Bower, Parker and Carter into All Blacks starting XV for second test against Springboks
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has made several changes from the team that beat the Springboks at Ellis Park for Sunday morning's second test in Cape Town.

Prop George Bower, who helped steady the All Blacks scrum after coming off the bench in last weekend's 33-16 win in Johannesburg, replaces Ethan de Groot, who is out with concussion, in the starting front row.

Codie Taylor and Tyrel Lomax are retained at hooker and prop respectively.

Tupou Vaa'i moves from blindside to lock, replacing Josh Lord, who was also ruled out of the second test following a head clash with de Groot last week at Ellis Park.

Vaa'i will partner with Fabian Holland in the second row.

Tupou Vaa'i switches from the loose forwards to lock. Samuel Shivambu/BackpagePix

Chiefs loose forward Simon Parker gets the nod at blindside flanker, filling the spot left vacant by Vaa'i's move to lock. Parker beats out the likes of Wallace Sititi and Ethan Blackadder, who was man of the match in Wednesday's win over the Lions.

Ardie Savea captains the side from No.8 with Luke Jacobson at openside.

Hurricanes front rower Xavier Numia comes onto the bench to provide prop cover, while veteran Patrick Tuipulotu has been named in the reserves to cover lock.

In the backs, there is one change from last week's team, with Leroy Carter taking over on the left wing from Josh Moorby, who drops to the bench.

The backline remains the same bar the change on the wing, with Cam Roigard at halfback, Ruben Love at first-five, Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield.

Damian McKenzie, who will be playing his 34th consecutive test, is at fullback with Will Jordan, the All Blacks all-time leading try scorer, on the right wing.

Leroy Carter has replaced Josh Moorby on the left wing for the second test. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Jordan extended his record to 53 tries last weekend, joining English winger Rory Underwood in sixth place on the men's international test try-scoring list.

Japanese winger Daisuke Ohata holds the record with 69 tries.

Rennie said there's fierce competition for spots in the matchday 23 and he expects both teams to improve on their performances last weekend in Johannesburg.

"While we were happy with the win last week, I think both teams will be better this weekend," Rennie said.

"We've played four tests this year and are still growing as a group. I'm really excited about the competition for places and the performances of the squad across the matches here in South Africa, and we're really looking forward to this weekend."

Asafo Aumua is the reserve hooker, Fletcher Newell and Numia the back up props, with Peter Lakai the one loose forward on the bench, which also includes midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown and halfback Kyle Preston, who has played all five of the All Blacks games in South Africa so far.

Asafo Aumua will again provide impact from the bench. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks lead the four test series 1-0 and know a win in Cape Town this weekend would heap even more pressure on the hosts and go a long way to securing a series victory.

The All Blacks have played South Africa 111 times, for 64 wins, 43 losses and four draws.

The All Blacks will be playing only their second ever test match at DHL Stadium, with all ten previous Cape Town tests played at the old Newlands Stadium.

New Zealand won seven of those 11 previous tests against the the Springboks in Cape Town, with the last win nine years ago in 2017.

The Springboks won the most recent test, beating the All Blacks 31-27 in 2024.

This weekend's second test kicks off at 5:10am Sunday (NZT).

World.title: Nepal flash flood: What we know about the missing New Zealanders
World.content:
Five New Zealanders have been reported missing following the flash flood and landslide at the Nepal-China border that killed at least 270 people.

The identities of four of those missing Kiwis have been confirmed.

Here's what we know about those who are missing following the disaster.

Hamilton couple was celebrating 50th birthday in Nepal

The son of a Hamilton couple missing following the Nepal flash flood is holding onto hope his parents left the area in the hours before the landslide struck.

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, were also among the missing New Zealanders.

Their eldest son, Drishya Patel, told RNZ the couple were visiting Nepal to celebrate his mother's upcoming 50th birthday. The couple had been gone for about a week, he said.

"They're just on a trip to go visit some of the mountains in Nepal. It's like a pilgrimage of sorts."

Drishya Patel spoke to his father the day before the flash flood. He said the couple's trip was going "really good".

"They were having a good time."

He last got a message from his mother on WhatsApp about 5.30am local time from Timure.

"Leaving for Kerung," the message said.

The earthquake that triggered the floods occurred at 8.37am local time.

Drishya Patel said he was "shocked" when he first heard the news of the landslide. The family has heard nothing from the couple since.

He hoped that the couple left when they sent the message, about three hours beforehand.

"As long as like they actually did leave when my mum sent me that message, I'm hopeful. These guys tend to run things on time, these tour guides," he said.

"But again, haven't heard anything confirming."

He had spoken with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT), but he said "they don't know anything either".

Drishya Patel, who is a medical student, had an exam on Thursday. He said he was still coming to terms with everything.

"I don't think I've processed it… realisations slowly setting in as every hour passes, and I don't hear anything, and no one knows anything."

Suhasini Reddy is one of the New Zealanders missing following the Nepal flood. SUPPLIED

Mother of two missing

One of the New Zealand citizens missing is Suhasini Reddy, who has been living in Australia for the last four years.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev Reddy, told RNZ his sister, a mother-of-two, was believed to be in the Dhunche area heading towards the Nepal-China border on Wednesday morning local time.

Reddy was hiking with a group of friends from Australia with the Kailash Journeys Guides, her brother said. The floods occurred on day four of the 15-day trip.

Reddy said his sister was supposed to be meeting Chinese immigration about 11am local time. They had not heard anything from her since the flash flood.

"We really don't know. We've contacted the hotel, the person of contact says she's not there, and at the moment he can't provide any information regarding the checkouts and check-ins."

He last spoke to his sister the night before the floods, while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was all good, excited," he said.

"She had this trip planned for a while."

Before heading on the trip Suhasini Reddy visited her parents in India where she left her youngest son. Her other son is with family in Australia.

Rajeev Reddy said the family were desperate for information.

"We actually don't know what's happening ... we're just saying that she'll be okay," he said.

The family appealed for anyone with information about her whereabouts to contact them.

Hundreds of foreign tourists are among those missing after the deadly flash flood. Supplied

Another missing Kiwi was on pilgrimage

Another New Zealander, Dejan Kuzmic was travelling on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, when the disaster struck.

Nepal's Tourist Police confirmed Kuzmic's name to RNZ on Thursday morning.

He was part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks pilgrimage group, which was travelling towards Mount Kailash, revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva.

RNZ has also spoken to a family friend, who confirmed the family had been unable to contact Kuzmic since the floods.

"He was part of the Isha Foundation's walk group S3 and was at the border crossing, which was hit quite heavily within a reasonable time, which makes us believe he may have been involved," said Seyed Sepehr Hosseini, whose mother attends a meditation group with Kuzmic.

Hosseini contacted the Isha Foundation, which told him Kuzmic's emergency contacts had been notified.

He also contacted New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which said it had opened a consular case for Kuzmic.

Mount Kailash is revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva, while nearby Lake Mansarovar is also considered sacred.

India's official Kailash Mansarovar Yatra portal describes the pilgrimage as having deep religious and cultural significance.

World.title: Offender on the run, double homicide investigation launched after South Auckland incident
World.content:
A manhunt is underway after police confirmed two people found dead in South Auckland were victims in a suspected double homicide.

Police said they would search through the night for the person or people they believe are responsible.

Emergency services responded to reports of a woman unresponsive at an address on Gambare Place, Wattle Downs, at about 1.45pm.

The woman was pronounced dead at the scene, and during a search of the property, police found a man who was also pronounced dead.

The scene on Thursday evening. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Detective Inspector Tofilau Faamanuia Va'aelua said the offender or offenders fled the scene prior to officers arriving.

Gambare Place resident Dianna Kereopa-Turner said she had just returned home from a trip to the dairy with family when "havoc started going on" outside.

"We thought it was our nail gun for our sleepout that we're building going off ... and then it was quite loud," Kereopa-Turner told RNZ.

"But no, it was shooting. All we heard was gun. Then my sister came out of her room and said 'somebody out there's shooting', so we gathered in whoever was loose around the house and stayed inside."

She said it was quite sad because the people had only just moved into the house across the road.

"It's sad to know that whatever trouble was following them, obviously followed them right to the doorstep, and unfortunately it happened on this street where there's a lot of kids and a lot of elderly people.

"It's a shock to the system," Kereopa-Turner said.

Police at the scene of an incident on Gambare Place, Manurewa. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Va'aelua said police were working to locate those responsible and determine the exact circumstances of the incident.

"While this appears to be an isolated incident at this stage, we are unable to rule anything out.

"This is an awful set of events and no doubt unsettling for everyone involved and the wider community."

Armed police were stationed at cordons on Volante Avenue on Thursday afternoon. Residents, including school students, waited outside the cordon to return to homes on Volante Avenue and Gambare Place.

More than a dozen police cars lined Volante Avenue and nearby streets, and hearses were seen arriving at the scene.

Police appeared to be dealing with a body behind a white tarpaulin on Volante Avenue.

Police at the scene of an incident on Gambare Place, Manurewa. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Once the hearses and police cars left Volante Avenue, and the road opened around 5.15pm, a strong police presence remained on Gambare Street.

Armed police stood guard in front of the property where the alleged shooting took place, with a police truck parked across the road.

Residents were seen walking up and down Gambare Place and talking to one another over fences.

Two nearby schools, Te Haikura a Kiwa and Leabank Primary School, went into lockdown in the afternoon in response to the incident.

Leabank principal Caroline McLeod posted on social media after the lockdown had ended that everyone "did extremely well and responded to instructions".

World.title: Heavy snow closes highways, triggers severe avalanche warnings in South Island
World.content:
Fire and Emergency says Queenstown firefighters have responded to a number of reports of flooding and slips in the area on Thursday night.

A FENZ spokesperson said crews were using pumps to drain water away from a commercial building in Hansen Rd, Frankton, while another team was working to clear mud and water washing down the hill near a residential property on Arthur's Point Road.

They were receiving reports of cars aquaplaning on inundated roads and crews had attended an abandoned vehicle which had become submerged in floodwaters on Kingston Road, Frankton earlier in the evening.

Evacuations from homes or buildings had not been necessary, the spokesperson said. They described the current situation as "busy but not manic".

People in parts of Queenstown were also being asked to conserve water after a slip affected a water treatment plant.

Queenstown Lakes District Council said the Two Mile Water Treatment Plant was offline and water supply to some areas was relying on existing reservoir storage.

It said crews were working hard to restore normal service as soon as possible but conditions were challenging and repairs may take some time.

In the meantime homes and businesses in Fernhill and Sunshine Bay, the Queenstown CBD and Frankton Road should reduce their water use where possible.There is currently no need for a boil water notice.

A slip on the road between Blackball and Atarau. Grey District Council

Fire and Emergency urged people to avoid any unnecessary travel and take extreme care if they must drive in affected areas.

"Especially in the hours of darkness, it really heightens the possibility of a serious incident. The potential is much higher to hit floodwaters before you see them and [that] can have serious consequences.

"If you can not put yourself in a situation, don't," the spokesperson said.

Highways would be monitored overnight for any further flooding and slips, with more heavy rain expected to fall.

Orange heavy rain warnings cover Westland and headwaters of lakes and rivers in Otago and Canterbury, with a separate warning starting from midnight for the Grey and Buller ranges.

An area warning for surface flooding will remain in place overnight, covering the 278 kilometre stretch of State Highway 6 from Haast to Hokitika.

The Transport Agency said all highways except part of State Highway 94 to Milford Sound were open.

Any motorists travelling Thursday night were encouraged to check the forecasts and status of highways first.

Heavy snow at Arthur's Pass. Sean Moran

Wet weather triggers avalanche warnings

Parts of the South Island were hit with heavy rain and snow on Thursday, closing roads and triggering severe avalanche warnings.

More than 20 centimetres of snow fell in some parts of the South Island, closing state highways.

Large avalanches were expected to run to the valley floor in some areas as heavy snow prompted multiple alerts for very dangerous conditions.

People were urged to stay out of the backcountry until the stormy weather had passed and snowpack conditions settled.

The Avalanche Advisory Council had its second highest danger warning in place for Arthur's Pass, Aoraki Mount Cook, Ohau, Queenstown, Wanaka, Fiordland and Aspiring.

A considerable avalanche risk was also in place for Craigieburn Range, Mount Hutt, Two Thumbs and Nelson Lakes.

The council's advisory said Aoraki Mount Cook had already received plenty of snow and rain with more snow predicted.

More than 3.5 metres could have fallen on the Tasman Saddle over recent days, the advisory said.

The advisory said the risk at Arthur's Pass meant large avalanches were expected to reach the valley floor and people should keep out of runzones which included tramping terrain.

State Highway 73 which was closed earlier in the day but has now reopened. NZTA / Waka Kotahi

In Queenstown, the advisory said local ski fields had reported multiple natural and ski-triggered loose wet avalanches.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the return to blue skies could be deceptive and there would be a lot of instability in the snowpack.

"Currently across the whole southern alpine region, it's what we describe as quite treacherous conditions and people that are thinking about exploring the backcountry, be that hunters, trampers, skiers, snowboarders ... we highly don't recommend any travel in that backcountry at the moment," he said.

It was not just high alpine areas that were at risk.

The size and scale of the potential avalanches could run all the way down to the valley floor in some areas, crossing paths and tracks that were not in alpine terrain, he said.

A worker at Aoraki Mount Cook's Hermitage Hotel said he had heard avalanches rumbling on the mountains as snow battered the area.

Hotel activities manager Tim Thorstensen said Mount Cook Village had had a huge dumping of snow.

More than 20cm of snow fell in parts of State Highway 73. NZTA / Waka Kotahi

Heavy rain, rising rivers ahead on Friday

MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden said the storm was expected to weaken as it moved across the country and the worst of the snow had passed, but areas of heavy rain would persist into Friday.

More than 300mm of rain had been recorded around Franz Josef by 2pm on Thursday with more expected to fall.

Environment Canterbury said the rivers were expected to rise further on Thursday night and Friday morning and remain high through Friday.

Moderately high flows have been reported for the Rangitata, Rakaia, Waimakariri, Hurunui, and Waiau-uha rivers.

Ashley, Selwyn, Ashburton, Orari and Opihi rivers are all flowing slightly higher.

Out-of-river flooding was unlikely despite heavy rain and snow falling on headwaters of major alpine rivers.

World.title: Matildas follow Socceroo footsteps on path to World Cup
World.content:
The Matildas are looking to follow the Socceroos' blueprint when they play in next year's FIFA Women's World Cup, and two friendlies against Colombia will be a key stepping stone.

On Thursday the Matildas announced they will play the first of two games against the South American giants on November 28 at Canberra Stadium.

The date and venue of the second clash are yet to be determined.

The matches will be an invaluable warm-up ahead of next year's World Cup, which kicks off in Brazil on June 24, with the final on July 25.

And the Matildas, who finished fourth at the 2023 World Cup co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, are keen to set up the team for long-term success.

With current players including Sam Kerr, Steph Catley, Emily van Egmond and Mackenzie Arnold entering the latter stages of their careers, there are concerns about the Matildas missing such a wealth of talent and experience once they retire.
