Tech.title: Stop Touching Your Keyboard. Use This AI-Powered Microphone Instead
Tech.content:
How much do you hate typing? The advent of large language models has rapidly advanced voice-to-text technology. Whether it's Wispr Flow joining your meetings to summarize discussions or Google debuting smarter on-device dictation in its latest Pixel smartphone, these tools do far more than transcribe: They intelligently strip filler words, clean up unscripted thoughts on the fly, and seamlessly mediate multilingual conversations.

Now, a new startup is entering the fray. Unlike its software-focused peers, Relay is building a dedicated, portable microphone for high-fidelity voice-to-text anywhere. Based in London, Relay was founded by two former Nothing employees: Cookie Xu, who was Nothing's head of AI and services, and Raymond Zhu, a hardware product manager. While the company is debuting its software today, the hardware—what it calls the Relay Q—won't be available until early 2027.

Zhu says when he and Xu worked at Nothing, they used Wispr Flow's transcription software to “type” most of their messages at work. He says it greatly helped with thinking out ideas, but they kept running into an issue: talking loudly in an office.

“In the office, we never really could get the right volume for input,” Zhu tells WIRED. “If I whisper too quietly, the Mac wouldn't be able to pick it up; too loud and my coworker next to me can hear. Sometimes I would actually pull out my earbud and go like this,” he says over a video call, holding an earbud in front of his mouth to demonstrate. “It calls for dedicated hardware.”

Tech.title: The Best Google Pixel Phones of 2026: Comparison, Features, and Accessories
Tech.content:
You can opt for the cellular version if you want always-on connectivity even away from your phone, though you'll need to pay up for a separate watch data plan. Read our Best Smartwatches guide for other options.

Our Favorite Pixel Software Features

Pixels have many great software features, but some need to be toggled on. It can also be hard to remember that all these features exist, so here are most of the top ones.

Call Features

Some key features on Pixels aren't available on other Android phones, and some are available only on select Pixels—the Tensor chip started with the Pixel 6, and currently, the Tensor G6 is in the Pixel 11 range. Here's a breakdown:

Call Screen: When you get a call from an unknown number, Google Assistant will scan and flag it if it's suspected spam or a robocall. If it's simply a number you don't recognize, you can have Assistant take the call. You'll see a real-time transcription of what's happening, so you can end the call right away if it's a telemarketer or answer if it turns out to be a long-lost high school friend. If it's someone important, you can give Assistant responses to recite if you're unable to take the call—it now offers contextual replies, too. Remember to turn it on by opening up the dialer app and heading to Settings (three dots on the top right) > Spam and Call Screen.

Wait Times. Courtesy of Google

Wait Times and Direct My Call: When you call a business in the phone app, you'll see an estimated wait time until someone real picks up (it doesn't work with every business). Google's Direct My Call feature also transcribes the entire call and separates the menu options, so you can see them without having to listen intently. More recently, for some numbers, Direct My Call will cache responses so you'll immediately see menu options without waiting for the automated response to go through every number. You can turn this on by going to the phone app's Settings > Direct My Call.

Hold for Me. Courtesy of Google

Hold for Me: If you've been placed on hold with a business number, you can ask Google Assistant to take over. It will play a loud chime when the person on the other end is back. No need to listen to hold music! Toggle it on in the phone app's Settings > Hold for Me. This feature is available on most Pixels but only works in select countries.

Clear Calling: If you have a Pixel 7 or newer, you can turn on this feature to enhance the other caller's voice and reduce their background noise. Head to Settings > Sound & Vibration > Clear Calling to toggle it on. It also works on Google's Pixel Buds Pro.

Call Notes (Tensor G4 and newer; with 12-plus GB RAM): Enable this in the dialer app by going to Settings > Call Notes and making sure the toggle is on. This doesn't activate every time you're on a call. Rather, you have to tap the More button when you're on a call and tap Call Notes to start it. It more or less records the conversation (it notifies the other person that the call is being recorded), and at the end, it'll give you a summary of important points from the call in the call history log, such as price quotes, phone numbers, or addresses. Sometimes it gets information wrong, since transcription accuracy depends on call quality, but you can play back the entire recording to double-check.

Scam Detection: This feature detects conversation patterns while you are on the phone with a suspicious number and warns you when someone is using a classic scam tactic. It also works in Google's Messages app, where it vets chat notifications from “popular” apps and shows a “Likely scam” alert if it deems something suspicious. You can turn it on by going to the Phone app, tapping the three-dot menu icon at the top right, and selecting Settings > Scam Detection.

Reverse Phone Number Lookup: Don't recognize the phone number from an incoming call? In the call app, you can now quickly look up a number without manually running a search.

Take a Message. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Take a Message (Tensor G5): Google is revamping voicemails with Take a Message. It's similar to transcribed voicemails, though that feature doesn't always work and may depend on your carrier. Take a Message bypasses the standard voicemail (your normal voicemail will only kick in with missed calls when your phone is off or out of network). The caller will be told to leave a message, and this recording will be auto-transcribed and visible in the call history of the phone app. It'll even offer actionable steps, like adding a reminder or an event to your calendar.

Pixel VIPs: This new widget gives you one-tap access to your favorite contacts. But it's more than that. Tap on one of your contacts, and you'll see a beautifully designed page that offers quick access to call or message the contact on various platforms. It'll show the last messages between you two, share location, weather updates, and the time for their area, and you can add notes if you want to remember specific things. You can access this the same way you add a widget; it sits under the Contacts app. Notifications from these contacts are prioritized.

Transcription and Translation Features

Voice Translate over phone calls. Video: Joel Chokkattu

Translated Phone Calls in Your Voice (Tensor G5 and newer): You can translate a phone call in real time, but what makes Google's approach unique is that the company will make the translated voice sound like your own (or the person on the other end). That way, it still sounds like you're talking to someone you know, rather than a robotic voice. No audio is recorded, and data isn't stored (it works on-device). It's only available for a few languages, like English, German, Japanese, and Spanish.

Live Translate. Courtesy of Google

Live Translate: In select messaging apps, Pixel will automatically know when someone sends a message in a language other than your default. It'll translate it (if you wish), and you'll be able to respond in that same language. More than 50 languages are supported, though you'll need to download the languages you want to see translated by heading to Settings > System > Live Translate. If you toggle on Media, it can also now translate video and audio content, like YouTube videos or podcasts.

Live Caption: Pixels can automatically transcribe any video playing on the screen. You can quickly toggle this on by tapping one of the volume buttons, then tapping the square button below the volume slider (or go to Settings > Sound and Vibration > Live Caption). If the video is in a different language, you can even see it translated (only on Tensor-powered Pixels), though you'll need to download a supported language. It can even caption phone calls.

Assistant Voice Typing. Courtesy of Google

Assistant Voice Typing: Tap the mic button on Google's Gboard keyboard, and you'll be privy to the much-improved voice-typing experience enabled by the Tensor chip. It's really fast, pretty accurate, and knows how to automatically add punctuation. It understands when to send a message if you say “Send,” and commands like “Next” will move the cursor to the next paragraph. You can make sure this is enabled by heading to Settings > System > Language & Input > On-Screen Keyboard > Gboard > Voice typing > Assistant Voice Typing. The latest Rambler voice input system in the Pixel 11 series improves this further, automatically removing uhm and ahs, and allowing you to draft messages conversationally.

Dual Screen Interpreter Mode (Pixel folding phones only): When you trigger this mode in the Google Translate app on the Pixel 10 Pro Fold (or any Pixel Fold), the person you're speaking to can read your translated words on the exterior screen. They can also tap the screen to start speaking, and you'll see their translated words on the inner screen.

Google's Recorder app. Courtesy of Google

Google Recorder: If you record interviews, meetings, calls, or anything else, you'll love the Google Recorder app. It's exclusive to Pixels and offers real-time transcription, so you don't need to take notes. You can open these notes in a Google Doc to edit them later or tap on a word to jump to the point it was spoken in the recording. Google has added speaker labels, so the transcription will try to detect when different people are talking and indicate it. Recordings can be shared with anyone, even if they don't have a Pixel. Better yet, you can automatically back these up to your Google Account to access them anywhere (or find them here). You can also summarize (and download) these transcripts with Gemini. Google recently added the ability to add music tracks, too, in case you like using the app to record singing.

Voice Message Transcription: If you frequently get audio messages in the Messages texting app, then you'll be happy to know that these messages will automatically transcribe, so you won't have to listen to the audio message. The transcription can be hit or miss, but it's still handy. It only works in Google Messages and is available in select languages; it's available on the Pixel 4A and newer. Turn it on by opening the Messages app and tapping your profile icon. Then tap Messages Settings > Voice Message Transcription, and toggle it on.

Gemini AI Features

Gemini Assistant: Google's default assistant is now Gemini instead of Google Assistant. Gemini is more powerful and can handle almost all the same tasks and more. Gemini isn't exclusive to Pixels, but these handsets are some of the few to use Gemini Nano, Google's on-device large language model that doesn't need to access the cloud. Some Gemini Nano capabilities have expanded to other capable Android phones, but Pixels often have exclusive perks before the competition. One new addition is task automation, so with the Pixel 10 series, you can ask Gemini to call you an Uber or order a meal from DoorDash; no need to hop into any apps.

Multimodal capabilities in Gemini: When you open Gemini (pressing and holding the power button) while in another app, you can ask it to “Attach” whatever's on your screen. That can include asking Gemini to summarize a YouTube video or asking questions about a PDF. You can also upload your own photos and files to Gemini to ask questions about them. Just tap the plus icon next to the Gemini search bar.

Gemini Live with video. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Gemini Live (Gemini Advanced): This is a way to talk to Google's Gemini chatbot, except it's completely in real time, like a normal human conversation. You can interrupt Gemini; it understands context, so you can keep asking new questions about the same topic, and it sounds much more natural than voice assistants that came before. You can even turn on your camera and ask Gemini Live questions about what you're looking at in real time. Google also added visual overlays that let Gemini highlight specific items in your camera view, making it easier to identify what it's referring to.

Video: Joel Chokkattu

Magic Cue (Tensor G5 and newer): This feature works in the Messages app and in Gboard. Once you opt in, it will find relevant information from your Google apps that comes up in conversations. For example, if your mom texts you asking for your flight information, Magic Cue will have it ready as a little button above the text box, so you don't need to look anything up yourself. It'll even pull up relevant details, like your flight confirmation number, if you're calling United Airlines. You can dig into the settings for it by heading to Settings > Magic Cue.

Proactive Assistance: Building on Magic Cue, Proactive Assistance will float visual cards and contextual suggestions in chats and searches. It also integrates with OpenTable and Instacart, so folks with accounts can automate restaurant bookings or generate grocery lists in Google Keep. Go to Settings > Proactive Assistance and turn Use Proactive Assistance on.

Pixel Screenshots (Tensor G4 and newer; with 12-plus GB RAM): Got tons of screenshots saved on your phone? The Pixel Screenshots app puts them all in one place, and it uses on-device machine learning (Gemini Nano) to understand the context in them, from pictures to text. That means you can then just ask Gemini for information from a screenshot without having to hunt through hundreds of pictures. You can also add screenshots of tickets or boarding passes to Google Wallet from the app.

NotebookLM: Anyone can download this app right now, but NotebookLM is preinstalled on Pixel 10 devices. It's a note-taking app infused with Gemini, but the AI is trained only on your local documents, not the wider internet.

Courtesy of Google

Magic Compose in Messages: You can get a different draft of something you've typed up in Gboard in case you're unsure about your message's tone. It only works in select apps, like Google Messages. Start typing, and you'll see a pencil icon with a star next to it near the text box. Tap it, and you can now cycle through versions of your sentence in different tones, and you can even choose genres like Shakespeare in case you want to hark back to the past. This feature is available on Pixel 6 and newer, but on certain Pro phones, it works on-device.

Pixel Weather: Finally, there's a dedicated weather app on Pixel phones. It's not just a basic app, though—it uses Gemini's large language models to summarize outdoor conditions so you don't have to scan highs and lows. Google added a pollen tracker to see pollen index levels, handy for the spring season.

Saved info in Gemini: Gemini Advanced subscribers can ask the assistant to remember certain things. You can ask Gemini to remember that you're a vegan, for example, and any future recipes you ask for will be vegan.

Veo 3: Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 10 Pro (and Fold) users get a full year of Google's AI Pro subscription included in their purchase, which includes Veo 3. It's Google's generative video platform, allowing you to type in ideas and craft short videos. You can find this by opening Gemini and choosing Video below the text box.

AI Notification Summaries (Pixel 9, Pixel 10, and Pixel 11 series): If you opt in, you can receive AI-powered notification summaries from your chats. Head to Settings > Notifications > Notification summaries to enable it. It largely works with messaging apps, which can range from Slack to Gmail to Google Messages.

Camera Features

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Magic Capture (Pixel 11 series): This dedicated mode sits next to Photo and Video in the camera app and lets you hold the phone up to automatically capture several photos on your behalf. You even get a 1080p video clip (though you can boost it to 4K using Google's Video Boost technology). The idea is that you can enjoy events without having your face glued to the viewfinder, but still have photos of it.

Camera Looks (Pixel 11 series): Open the camera app settings to access Looks and choose a different visual style. This enables you to tune the camera, dialing up contrast or opting for warmer colors, and there are several different Looks to choose from.

Creator Suite (Pixel 11 series): This mode in the Video tab of the camera app enables handy tools, like an audio visualizer, so you know your wireless mic is picking up your voice, and a built-in teleprompter. It also lets you keep projects in their own folder and is tailor-made for content creators.

Instant Night Sight (Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL): You can snap low-light and nighttime photos far more quickly than before with Instant Night Sight. There's still a pause when you hit the shutter button, but Google says it is up to 4.5 times faster than regular Night Sight. This feature relies on the Tensor G6 and cameras in the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Camera Coach (Pixel 11 series, 10 series, and 10a): Tap the camera icon at the top of the camera app, and you'll trigger Camera Coach. It'll ask you to scan the scene and offer example photos if you're not sure how to take a good photo. Choose one of those examples, and Camera Coach will run you through instructions on taking a similar version of that photo. This can include asking you to switch to Portrait mode, to zoom in, or even shift your position and angle.

Pro Res Zoom Video: Joel Chokkattu

Pro Res Zoom (Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, 10 Pro and Pro XL): On the Pixel 11 Pro models, you can now zoom up to 120X (100X on the 10 Pro models), and Google's Pro Res Zoom will capture more than 200 frames, blend them all for sharpness and denoising, and will even generate some frames of what it thinks should be there. The result is a shockingly sharp photo considering the digital zoom level. How real it is, well, that's a different question.

Help Me Edit With Ask Photos: When you tap edit on a photo, you'll now see a text box that lets you ask the phone to make edits on your behalf. (You can still manually edit photos.) You can be super specific—ask it to remove the plastic bag in the background—or vague: “Make this look better,” or “Fix the lighting.” A newer capability even lets you replace a friend's sunglasses with their eyes, provided you have your friend labeled within the Face Groups in Google Photos, so that Google can use older photos of them as a reference.

Hands-Free Photos: If you have a Pixel 6 or newer, you can take a hands-free photo by showing your open palm to the camera. Once the camera detects your palm (it'll show a square icon over it), it'll trigger a timer.

Magic Editor Courtesy of Google

Magic Editor: This feature has morphed into the general Actions tab when you edit a photo, but some other capabilities are spread throughout the edit functions. You're given free rein to change up the photo in a variety of ways, like selecting subjects and moving them in the frame. You can also find it by tapping Edit on a photo, then tapping and holding anywhere on the image.

Magic Eraser. Courtesy of Google

Magic Eraser: In the Google Photos app, you can remove objects in the background of your photos (even those not captured on Pixels). Just tap the Edit button and head to Actions > Magic Eraser. It will automatically suggest things to remove, or you can highlight the object with your finger. You can also change the color of a distracting object instead of removing it entirely. It's available on all Pixel phones.

Astrophotography mode: Set your Pixel on a tripod (something like this will work), point it at the sky, open the camera, and go to Night Sight mode. Once the phone detects that it's completely still and on a tripod, you'll see Astrophotography mode kick in. Tap the shutter button, and within three to five minutes, you'll have a photo of the stars. Ideally, you should be in a dark area with little light pollution, but it'll work wherever you are. Don't touch the phone—just let it do its thing until the timer ends. You can also force this feature by opening the camera app, heading to the Night Sight tab, tapping on the moon or star symbol on the bottom right, and moving the slider to Astro.

Super-Res Zoom: If you're taking a picture of something far away, use two fingers to pinch and zoom in up to 30X, then snap the photo. Google uses software wizardry to upscale the quality of digitally zoomed-in photos, so you see a lot more detail. On the Pixel 7 series and newer, this process has improved further, as Google fuses images from the main camera and telephoto.

Zoom Enhance (Tensor G3 and newer): Much like on the old CSI shows, when someone says, “Enhance,” this feature generates pixels in distant objects to make them appear sharper. You can enable it by going to a photo and tapping Edit > Tools > Zoom Enhance. Zoom in on an area of the image, then let it do its magic.

Best Take Courtesy of Google

Best Take (Tensor G3 and newer): If you snap a series of photos of a group of people within a short time frame, you will get the option to switch their faces! This is weird, but truly helpful if folks are blinking, not smiling, or not looking right at the camera. Maybe another frame in another photo captured the face you want. You can use this feature by pressing Edit on a photo, then going to Tools > Best Take. In the Pixel 10 series and Pixel 10a, this has been upgraded to Auto Best Take, where the phone captures a series of photos automatically when it detects two or more people in the shot. That way, you don't need to make any changes after capture to get the perfect photo—it should already be in your camera library.

Auto Frame in Magic Editor (Tensor G4 and newer): In a photo, tap on the Edit icon, then tap on the ruler icon at the top left. Choose Auto Frame. This will generate a few different options of the same photo in different compositions. It might add a little extra imagery to the right or left of the subject to change the framing, or even give you a horizontal orientation if you shot vertically.

Add Me Photograph: Joel Chokkattu

Add Me (Tensor G4 and newer): If you and your partner are traveling and there's no one around to take a picture of you both in front of a landmark (or you don't want someone to run off with your phone), just use Add Me. One person takes the photo, then swaps places with the other, but you'll have to make it seem like you were standing next to each other. The resulting image is the two photos stitched together, and no one is the wiser. This is available in the camera app as the Add Me tab. Google updated the feature in the Pixel 10 to work better with big groups and pets.

Reimagine (Tensor G4 and newer): This terrifyingly powerful feature lets you completely change a photo with text. Open an image, press Edit, then tap and hold anywhere on the photo to see the overflow menu, and choose Reimagine. You'll be prompted to type some text in. There are guardrails, so you can't just expect anything to work, but you can alter the sky or time of day, add the moon, or even change a road into a lake. It's scarily easy.

Audio Magic Eraser demonstration

Audio Magic Eraser (Tensor G3 and newer): Have an annoying sound in the background of your video clip? Pixels can now erase unwanted audio! It works with only a few types of sounds, like crowds, sirens, and animals, but you can access it and try it by tapping Edit in a video and selecting Audio Magic Eraser. A recent update lets you turn specific sounds up or down and even separate the voices of different people.

Video Boost (Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro, and Pixel 8 Pro only): This feature is exclusive to the Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro, and Pixel 8 Pro series; it allows you to improve the quality of your videos. In the Video tab of the camera app, press the gear icon on the left in Video mode and toggle on Video Boost. (You can also just switch to the Night Sight tab in Video mode for it to automatically kick in.) Now take a video; you'll have to wait for Google to process the clip in the cloud. Once done—it could take an hour, or you may have to wait overnight, depending on the size of the file—the clip should be brighter, with better stabilization, less noise, and more vivid colors. It's particularly useful in low-light settings. You can still utilize the original clip if you want to share it immediately. The Pixel 10 Pro upscales this feature to 8K recording.

Photo Unblur Courtesy of Google

Photo Unblur (Tensor G2 and newer): You can unblur old (or new) photos in your library with the tap of a button. Results will vary, but it's impressive and might turn an unusable photo into something you'll want to share. It'll work with cats and dogs. To unblur a photo, press Edit > Actions > Unblur.

Portrait Light: You can change up the lighting in your portrait selfies after you take them by opening them in Google Photos, tapping Edit, and heading to Actions > Portrait Light. This adds an artificial light you can place anywhere in the photo to brighten up your face and erase that five-o'clock shadow. Use the slider at the bottom to tweak the strength of the light. It also works on older Portrait mode photos you may have captured. It works only on faces.

Health and Accessibility Features

Cough & Snore Detection (Tensor G2 and newer): On the Pixel 7 and newer, your Pixel can detect when you cough and snore while sleeping, as long as you place it near your bed before you nod off. This will work only if you use Google's Bedtime mode, which you can turn on by going to Settings > Digital Wellbeing & Parental Controls > Bedtime Mode.

Guided Frame

Guided Frame (Tensor G2 and newer): For blind or low-vision people, the camera app can now help take a selfie with audio cues (it works with the front and rear cameras). You'll need to enable TalkBack for this to work (Settings > Accessibility > TalkBack). Then open the camera app. It will automatically help you frame the shot.

Simple View: This mode makes the font size bigger, along with other elements on the screen, like widgets and quick-settings tiles. It also increases touch sensitivity, which should make the screen easier to see and use. You can enable it by heading to Settings > Accessibility > Simple View.

Safety and Security Features

Theft Protection: This feature launched in Android 15, but essentially, Google's algorithms can figure out if someone snatches your Pixel out of your hands. If they're trying to get away, the device automatically locks. Additionally, with another device, you can use Remote Lock to lock your stolen Pixel with your phone number and a security answer. To toggle these features on, go to Settings > Security & privacy > Device unlock > Theft protection.

Identity Check: If your Pixel detects you're in a new location, Identity Check will require fingerprint or face authentication before you can make changes to sensitive settings, offering extra peace of mind if you lose your phone or it's stolen. You can enable this in Settings > Security & privacy > Device unlock > Theft protection > Identity Check.

Courtesy of Google

Private Space: Pixel phones finally have a feature that lets you hide and lock select apps (Android 15 and up). You can use a separate Google account, set a lock, and install any app to hide away. To set it all up, head to Settings > Security & privacy > Private space.

Satellite eSOS (Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 series, excluding Pixel 9a): Like Apple's SOS feature on iPhones, you can now reach emergency contacts or emergency services even when you don't have cell service or Wi-Fi connectivity. It's available not only in the continental US, but also in Hawaii, Alaska, Canada, and even Europe.

Car Crash Detection: Hopefully, you never have to use this feature. As the name suggests, Pixel phones can tell when you've been in a serious crash with the help of mics and motion sensors. Turn it on in the Personal Safety app (or Settings > Safety & Emergency), and if a crash is detected, your phone will check to see whether you're OK. If there's no response, it can share your location with emergency responders and emergency contacts. It works in select countries.

Find Hub (Tensor G3 and newer): Select Pixels can be tracked via the company's Find Hub app even if the battery is dead or the phone is off, making it easier to find if you've left it behind or if someone stole it. (Your location data is encrypted and private from Google.) Open the Find Hub app, tap your device, then tap Settings > Find your offline devices to choose an option.

Built-in VPN (Pixel 7 and newer): With the Pixel 7 and newer, you have access to a VPN (virtual private network). It'll encrypt your traffic to give you peace of mind. You can access it for free for as long as the phones receive updates.

Miscellaneous Features

Quick Share and AirDrop (Pixel 11, 10, and 9 series): Google's Pixel 11 phones, Pixel 10 phones, the Pixel 10a, and Pixel 9 series (excluding the Pixel 9a) can “AirDrop” files and photos over to iPhones, Macs, or iPads. This new cross-compatibility is available through Android's Quick Share feature, but the iPhone owner must switch AirDrop mode to “Everyone for 10 Minutes” instead of “Contacts Only.”

DisplayPort Support (Tensor G3 and newer): You can finally connect your Pixel phone to an external monitor by using a data-supported USB-C cable.

Quick Phrases: When the alarm goes off, you can just say “Stop” or “Snooze” instead of fumbling for your phone. This applies when you get a phone call: Just say “Answer,” “Decline,” or “Silence.” To make sure this is toggled on, launch Assistant and say “Assistant settings.” Then scroll to Quick Phrases. It works in select other languages, too.

Power Saving mode in Google Maps (Pixel 10 series and later): If your phone is low on juice but you need it for navigation, Google Maps has a special power-saving mode that offers a simplified layout to conserve power. Google says it can extend your battery life up to four hours.

Courtesy of Google

Circle to Search: This is Google's way to run a Google Search on practically anything—whether you're reading a news story on the web, looking at a photo on Instagram, or watching a video on TikTok. Just press and hold the home button (the pill-shaped bar if you are using gesture navigation), and circle anything on the screen you want to search. An overlay menu will pop up with search results, and you can add text to the search query. You can even use it to identify music that's playing within your apps, like TikTok or Instagram, and ask follow-up questions. A recent update added a way to “Find the Look,” letting you select someone's whole outfit and have Gemini parse each item without you having to specify. With the Pixel 11 series, Google added the option to use Circle to Search in your camera app viewfinder without snapping a photo first.

Photomoji: You can create sticker reactions from any picture in Google Messages. Just press and hold on a message and tap the Create button. Choose a photo or take a new one, and it'll automatically crop out the subject. Now you can use that as a sticker reaction to any message!

Body Temperature Sensor (Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro, and Pixel 8 Pro only): The Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 8 Pro have a thermometer you can use to take the temperature of an object, but an update has enabled you to take a person's temperature. Just open the thermometer app, point the sensor at the forehead, and scan. You can save the results to the Fitbit app. Google received the FDA's De Novo classification for this feature, though you should know the results might not be very accurate.

Quick Tap: Head over to Settings > System > Gestures > Quick Tap to enable it. It lets you double-tap the upper back of your Pixel (Pixel 4A 5G or newer) to trigger a function. That includes flipping the camera for a selfie, turning on the flashlight, sliding down the notification bar, or, exclusive to Pixels, starting a Snap on Snapchat.

Pixel Journal app Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Pixel Journal (Pixel 8, 9, and 10 series): Google's new Journal app lets you jot down your thoughts, add images, and it'll offer up reflections on the words you write. It will also offer prompts based on the goals you create during setup, in case you're at a loss on what to write.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Daily Hub (Pixel 10): Similar to Samsung's Now Brief feature, this Daily Hub is nestled in Google Discover, but will also show up in the At a Glance widget a few times a day. It'll give you upcoming calendar events, reminders powered by Magic Cue, and even suggest new activities to try based on your Google Search history.

Now Playing: Ever hear a song at the coffee shop and wonder who it's by? Now Playing uses on-device machine learning to figure out what music is playing in the background, and it displays the artist and title on the lock screen (or in your notifications). It doesn't require an internet connection, so there's no data shared between you and Google. This isn't turned on by default, so head to Settings > Sound and Vibration > Now Playing and toggle it on. You can even turn on Now Playing History in case you forgot to write down an artist's name when you saw it earlier. Google added a button you can press in case Now Playing doesn't automatically identify a song, sorta like Shazam.

Adaptive Vibration (Tensor G2 and newer): You can toggle this on by heading to Settings > Sound & vibration > Vibration & haptics > Adaptive vibration. It auto-adjusts vibration strength based on the environment, so if it's quiet, the vibration may be less noticeable, and vice versa.

Device as a Webcam: You can use your Pixel phone as a webcam by connecting it to your laptop or desktop via a cable. This works on the Pixel 6 and newer.

Tech.title: The UK Power Grid Has a Phantom Data Center Problem
Tech.content:
As data center developers compete for a cut of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the artificial intelligence industry, the queue to join the UK’s power grid has become jammed with projects that will likely never get built. The snarl is exacerbating already years-long wait times for viable projects, and it's messing with attempts to forecast energy demand and plan grid expansions.

In July, the UK’s energy regulator, Ofgem, laid out a proposal meant to force phantom data centers out of the swollen queue. Under the plans, set to be finalized after an industry feedback process that ends in September, developers would be required to put down a steep, nonrefundable deposit that could balloon to hundreds of millions of dollars for the very largest data centers. Developers would also be required to line up customers in advance and prove they have the funding to complete their builds.

However, Ofgem faces a Goldilocks conundrum: The reforms must be burdensome enough to deter speculators but not so much that they drive legitimate data center projects to other shores, undermining the UK’s ambitions to meet the voracious demand for the compute required to run sophisticated AI models.

Data center developers face delays almost everywhere; similar grid congestion issues afflict the US and countries across Europe. But whereas the US is a highly desirable market, Ofgem’s reforms risk making the UK—already unattractive for the high cost of energy and dearth of land—one of the world’s most expensive places to build a data center, industry experts believe.

The frenzied data center buildout “is bringing a huge amount of capital investment into the UK,” says Alex Burgoyne, head of data centers at real estate consultancy Knight Frank. “We don’t want to shoot the golden goose.”

Ofgem says that it will take into account industry concerns before settling on a fee, but that differences between international energy markets make like-for-like comparison difficult. “We recognize data centers are a key part of the UK's AI ambitions and future economic growth. Enabling viable data centers to connect more quickly is an enabler of this,” Nathan Macwhinnie, deputy director of strategic planning and connections at Ofgem, tells WIRED in a statement.

Tech.title: Plaud One Is a Reinvention of Headphones for the AI Note-Taking Age
Tech.content:
Last year, I made a bold declaration: There’s no need to invent a new AI wearable, because the ultimate wearable technology is one you already own. I was referring to headphones — something most of us have used for decades.

Plaud — one of the world’s biggest AI note-taking companies — seems to agree, as it’s now built its industry-leading agentic AI into a pair of headphones. The company announced its latest device ahead of IFA 2026 in Berlin next week, where I’ll be able to see the headphones in person for the first time.

At first glance, they don’t look any different to any other earbuds. They have a sleek and discreet design, and they come in an off-white color. I’m keen to find out how comfortable they’ll be and how good the audio quality, is in addition to the device’s AI capabilities.

Plaud One look like any other earbuds.

Plaud is known for its slim, wallet-like device, which attaches inconspicuously to the back of your phone, and for its wearable pins. Both of these devices function as hardware gateways to the company’s true secret sauce — its agentic AI and software platform. The same is true of the Plaud One headphones, which have the same software built in.

The headphones will capture and upload ongoing conversations around you, as well as phone calls, using the built-in eSIM with 4G LTE. We’d always recommend informing people that you’re using a recording device, and it’s important to note that recording phone calls without permission from all participants can be illegal in some states.

Plaud’s software will then provide automatic transcriptions of your meetings, and can turn these into summaries, follow-ups or reports. The company’s agent allows for native integration with other tools you likely rely on, including Google, Gmail, Slack and Notion.

“AI agents become truly useful when they understand the context in which human intent is formed,” said Nathan Xu, CEO and Co-founder of Plaud.

“That context lives in conversation.”

The added bonus of Plaud One is that it allows for a two-way dialog between you and Plaud’s AI. You can speak directly to the agent, asking it questions or giving it instructions in a way that hasn’t been possible with Plaud’s previous devices. To activate the AI, you either need to say “Hey Plaud” while wearing the earbuds, or hold down the agent button on the case.

The Plaud One Explorer edition is available for preorder now for £229 ($311) and will come with £150 ($204) of Plaud credits. Plaud expects devices to start shipping later in the fall.

Tech.title: Fitbit and Pokemon Made a Fitness Tracker That Might Actually Help Me Catch My Zs
Tech.content:
When Pokemon Sleep was first announced in 2019, I wondered if the company behind one of the most iconic animations was dreaming too big. Getting people out of their houses and onto streets and parks with Pokemon Go was already a huge success. But did people care as much about their sleep hours as they did about their steps?

After several delays, Pokemon Sleep finally launched in 2023 to high interest, becoming the most downloaded sleep game app in the world, according to the Japanese news outlet Famitsu.

On Thursday, the Pokemon Company is partnering with Google and Fitbit to help people take their sleep even more seriously – while still having fun – with the new $129 special-edition Fitbit Air.

It’s a pairing that makes a lot of sense. The minimal design of the Fitbit Air is tailored for extended wear, including for sleep tracking, and Pokemon Sleep gamifies the resting experience so you hopefully rest for longer each night.

Here’s everything that’s included in the box. Kerry Wan/CNET

The stylistic touches will resonate with fans

I’ve been wearing the new special-edition Fitbit Air for half a day now, and it comes with a deep blue woven wristband and a cutesy Pikachu etching above the adhesive. On the wrist, it feels a lot like the original tracker, which launched earlier this year.

That’s a good thing, as CNET lead reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana found the Fitbit Air slim, lightweight, and comfortable to wear during testing. Like the standard model, you can also pop out the pebble, which encapsulates the optical heart rate monitor, gyroscope, and other health-tracking sensors, and swap out the band.

The Fitbit Air with the Sleepy Blue wristband. Kerry Wan/CNET

Unfortunately for Pokemon fans who already have a Fitbit Air, Google tells me that the new band won’t be sold separately

Beyond the special-edition fitness tracker, I spotted some tasteful Easter eggs that decorate the box and packaging. I noticed various sleepy Pokemon, including Psyduck and Slowpoke, on the flipside of the cover, and a Mew that’s hidden on the wristband holder.

Everyone can play (and sleep)

The special edition Fitbit Air can sync with both the Google Health app and the Pokemon Sleep app, so you can track metrics like your daily movement, heart rate and cardio load during the daytime. Then you can more accurately log the duration and quality of your sleep overnight.

Google says the Pokemon Sleep app will sync with the special edition Fitbit Air, as well as all other Google and Fitbit wearables, including the Pixel Watch. That means you now have more wearable options to help build up your Drowsy Power, the in-game mechanic that determines how many wild Pokemon appear in your campsite, and how rare their sleeping styles are.

Previously, you either had to set your phone beside your pillow or wear a now-discontinued Pokemon Go Plus band to properly track and record your sleep.

The latest special edition Fitbit Air is geared toward Pokemon fans. Kerry Wan/CNET

Availability and release date

The Fitbit Air Special Edition Pokemon Sleep, in its sleepy blue color, is now available for preorder online or at the Google Store and Target for $129.

That’s $30 more than the retail price of the standard Fitbit Air, but it does come with the thematic wristband, a unique code that gets you Pikachu Incense in Pokemon Sleep, and a three-month trial of Google Health Premium.

Orders will start shipping on Sept. 15, just a day before the release of Pokemon’s 30th Celebration TCG set, in light of the company’s anniversary.

Tech.title: This $10 Tool Finally Fixed My Latte Art
Tech.content:
Whether dialing in espresso or refining a pour-over recipe, I’ve long felt comfortable with technical coffee-making. Latte art, though? Not so much. Too often, I’d ruin my painstakingly extracted shot with overly steamed milk, pouring an unsatisfying blob of dairy into my cup. After many renditions, I convinced myself I lacked the artful touch for tulips and hearts. Still, I coveted cafe-quality textured milk, so I sought a reliable fix.

Turns out, simply an attachable instant-read thermometer is what made the difference. An analog or digital thermometer (mine’s the former) eliminates a whole lot of guesswork. While the milk swirls and hisses, I can check the temperature, pulling away the steam wand at the ideal time. No longer do I venture into stiff, overheated foam or flat, watery dairy; my milk coffee tastes just right.

A thermometer guides the milk steaming process

Several tools can be used to aerate milk: simple handheld models, dedicated heated milk frothers and steam wands integrated into espresso machines. A thermometer could benefit all three setups; I use it with my espresso machine. The steam wand rapidly creates vapor, producing velvety, satisfying milk.



The downside? A powerful boiler system steams fast. My model heats the vapor nearly instantly, which is then integrated into the milk via four holes in the wand. In 30 seconds, the dairy goes from cold to aerated. A few moments longer, and the emulsion breaks into runny milk and stiff foam. Not pretty and not delicious, either.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Baristas often suggest halting the steaming process when a milk pitcher turns too hot to the touch. Truth be told, I’ve found such subjective guidance misleading. To my fingers, the pitcher turns excessively warm early in the steaming process. I used to hold on too long to compensate, which led me to scald the milk. A thermometer provides a welcome technical metric instead of this sensory step.

Best Espresso Machines We Tested See at CNET

I simply clip the tool onto the side of my milk pitcher, then watch the degrees steadily climb. Now there’s a visual rhythm to the steaming process. I can focus on rolling the milk to create abundant microfoam. Then once the temperature is exactly 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius), I know I’ve adequately frothed the milk. The single tool serves as pragmatic guidance, directing the steaming process.

Don’t neglect proper frothing technique

Whether or not you use a thermometer, good technique is required for dense foam.

Chris Monroe/CNET

Using a steam wand requires the proper approach — a thermometer won’t address every mishap. To attain a foam with small, suspended bubbles, it’s essential to submerge the frothing tip at the ideal depth. The goal is to create a vortex of spinning milk, a sign of uniform aeration. Place the wand too deep into the liquid, and not enough air is introduced, yielding a runny result. Too high up, and the bubbles get too large, occasionally even sputtering out of the pitcher.

I introduce the steam wand angled and just barely submerged to kickstart this rolling motion. Once the milk has adequately expanded — yielding a layer of foam atop — I’ll submerge the wand deeper into the dairy, ensuring aeration throughout the pitcher.

The process is easy to mess up. There’s trial and error regarding steam wand placement. Even when the resulting milk reaches 149 F (65 C), latte-art-quality foam isn’t guaranteed. The thermometer is there to supplement, though. I’ve learned to switch from surface aeration to the milk body at 104 F (40 C). Milk frothing requires focus on several processes in parallel — a thermometer helps keep track of everything at once.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Art is subjective. Well-aerated milk is not

Even with a pitcher full of perfectly foamed milk, there’s still more to producing latte art. Tracking milk temperature didn’t miraculously take me from blobs to elegant, layered hearts. My latte aesthetics still err on the simple side, with continued trial and error regarding design. The height, speed and even angle of how milk is poured all affect what appears on top of the espresso.

Post-thermometer, though, I can pour shapes with confidence. The white foam is well-contained on the top layer of the coffee — no liquid consistency that spills across the cup. With properly textured dairy in hand, I can focus on making designs.

Good frothing isn’t only about visuals, either. Foaming milk to the proper temperature brings out dairy’s intrinsic sugars, which meld with the bold notes in espresso. Texturally, there’s a silky mouthfeel to sip on, even when the latte art looks bad. Properly frothed milk heightens the espresso, rather than diluting it.

Adjust the temperature per milk type

A thermometer makes experimenting with nondairy milk easier. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

I prefer whole milk for my coffee — its fatty composition creates a thick, stable microfoam. Other forms of dairy offer their own advantages. If you’re after a dryer foam — say for a traditional cappuccino or an espresso macchiato — consider skim milk. The leaner consistency turns meringue-like when frothed, perfect for dolloping atop a cup. Skim milk scalds quickly. A thermometer proves even more handy with this one; I’d pull the pitcher away at 140 F (60 C) when steaming skim milk.

The same adjustment applies to the best milk alternatives, too. Although many plant-based milks struggle to produce microfoam, barista-grade oat milk can be used for latte art. Like skim milk, I’ve noticed this dairy replacement froths swiftly. Steam too long, and you get quite a dry foam (useful for cappuccinos). Not enough heat, and this less stable emulsion falls apart. When a thermometer is in the pitcher, there’s less estimating involved. With my machine, I pull away oat milk at an even lower temperature than skim milk — around 131 F (55 C).



A thermometer makes experimenting with the many types of milk easier. Steaming tempo varies widely depending on both the liquid and the frother. There are unique nuances to each setup. With an attached thermometer, though, it’s easier to replicate good results. When there’s an ideal resultant consistency, it’s handy to write down the temperature, gaining more coffee-making confidence in the process.

Tech.title: Stop Turning Off Your AC When You Go on Vacation. An HVAC Expert Explains Why
Tech.content:
When it’s time to leave for vacation, you know the drill: Turn off all the lights, double-check every door is locked and have a neighbor on standby in case you have any packages delivered while you’re away. But what about your air conditioner? Should you turn it off, or is there a magic energy-saving temperature you should set it to?

We turned to an HVAC expert for answers. Here’s everything you need to know ahead of your next trip.

Should you turn your air conditioner off when you’re on vacation?

Although turning off your air conditioner while you’re away may seem like a way to save money, it could do more harm than good in the long run.

“If your home overheats, you risk damage to your electronics, losing houseplants and unsafe conditions for pets,” Erin Katz, the operations manager at Allen Service, which provides HVAC, plumbing and electrical services in Colorado, told CNET.

She also pointed out that once you return home from your vacation, your air conditioner will have to work extra hard to get back to a comfortable temperature, which can put extra stress on the system or air conditioning unit.

What is the ideal air conditioner temperature when on vacation?

While you shouldn’t turn off your air conditioner completely, you can slightly adjust its temperature so that it isn’t running consistently while you’re away.

“I recommend setting it a few degrees warmer than you would when you’re at home,” Katz said. “For example, 75 degrees Fahrenheit instead of 70 degrees Fahrenheit.”

This type of adjustment will mean less energy is used, but won’t allow your home to become excruciatingly hot while you’re away.

“The goal is to pick a slightly warmer but stable temperature that your system can maintain without too much trouble while you’re away,” Katz said. “It uses far less energy to make micro adjustments than it does to turn the system on and off, or ask it to make a big change, such as going from 85 degrees Fahrenheit to 70 degrees Fahrenheit when you get home.”

The smart thermostat swap

The Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium is our favorite smart thermostat thanks to its air quality monitoring, ability to learn your schedule and more. Ecobee/CNET

If you’d rather have full control over your thermostat, even while you’re away, a smart thermostat is the best option.

“They are great for optimizing your energy usage,” Katz explained.

Smart thermostats have connected phone apps, so you can adjust your home’s temperature from anywhere. They also have scheduling features to automate temperature changes, helping keep your home at an ideal temperature and ensuring it never gets too hot or cold, even when you’re away.

Tech.title: Trump’s FCC Just Scrapped Its Most Ambitious Broadband Goal
Tech.content:
It’s just one word, but it changes everything. In its latest broadband deployment report, the FCC quietly backpedaled on its mission to expand high-speed internet to every American and eliminated an ambitious gig-speed goal entirely.

“High-speed broadband is often essential to full participation in modern society,” the opening sentence of the Aug. 14 report reads.

That sounds pretty uncontroversial at first glance, but it stands in stark contrast to the previous report issued under President Joe Biden’s FCC, which called access to affordable, reliable broadband “essential to full participation in modern life.” The United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres went even further, calling the issue “a matter of life and death” in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic.

“That word ‘often’ — the fifth word in the whole report — just sets the entire tone that suddenly broadband is not as important as it was five years ago,” Christopher Ali, a professor of telecommunications at Penn State University, told CNET.

These FCC reports are mandated by the 1996 Telecommunications Act to evaluate whether advanced telecommunications capabilities are available to “all Americans in a reasonable and timely fashion.” Today, that’s commonly referred to as the digital divide, or the gulf between people with a modern internet connection and those without. President Donald Trump’s FCC, led by Chairman Brendan Carr, stopped just short of declaring the mission accomplished.

“The digital divide is rapidly closing. And a range of data sets show that speeds are up, prices are down, and competition is intensifying,” Carr said in a statement.

The report says that 96.9% of Americans now have access to speeds of 100Mbps download and 20Mbps upload, which the Commission adopted as its standard for broadband in 2024. But those numbers should be taken with a grain of salt, as they’re self-reported by internet service providers.

“I still think there are ISPs reporting exactly 100/20Mbps speed capability to the FCC while delivering something slower,” Doug Dawson, a longtime expert in broadband and author of the industry blog Pots and Pans, wrote in a post on the report.

Carr voted against the 100/20Mbps standard when it passed two years ago, and he took particular exception with the FCC’s long-term goal of increasing the standard to 1,000/500Mbps, calling it a “Trojan Horse to exclude fixed wireless” that would inevitably lead to “wasteful overbuilding” in his dissenting statement.

That gig-speed goal is now scrapped. In its annual report on the state of broadband deployment, the Commission argued that the long-term goal of 1,000Mbps download and 500Mbps upload speed was unfairly biased against slower technologies like fixed wireless and satellite.

“At present, it is impossible to predict long-term technological developments and the evolution of consumer preferences,” the report says. “The private sector, driven by competition, does not need the Commission to centrally plan technological development.”

Key takeaways:

The FCC has abandoned its long-term target of bringing gigabit internet to every American, citing a need for “technological neutrality.”

By reframing broadband as “often essential” rather than “essential,” the FCC is effectively lowering the standard for universal access.

Critics argue the shift favors satellite providers like Starlink over future-proof fiber, potentially leaving rural communities with slower, inferior connections.

Critics also argue the new report minimizes affordability as a policy priority, side-stepping the primary reason many Americans remain disconnected.

Why the FCC is lowering the broadband bar

The report paints a rosy picture of the state of broadband in the US, but the reality is more complicated.

“They’re saying that 99.7% of the country has access to broadband if you include satellites. Of course, if you look at who they’re citing for that percentage, it’s Starlink,” says Ali.

Starlink says speeds on its fastest plan reach 320/40Mbps, but in practice, they’re much slower. Data from the speed test site Ookla found that the median Starlink customer 127/21Mbps in the first quarter of 2026. That squeaked by the FCC’s current definition of broadband, but it’s nowhere close to the previous stretch goal of 1,000/500Mbps.

The FCC report states that the gig-speed goal “could appear to violate our obligation to conduct our analysis in a technologically neutral manner.” Fiber is the only connection type that can meet that lofty goal today, although many cable companies are getting closer every day through network upgrades.

We are not being ambitious anymore. We have just given up. Christopher Ali, a professor of telecommunications at Penn State University

Anna Gomez, the only Democrat on the commission, said that reasoning ran counter to the FCC’s mission of bringing high-speed connectivity to Americans.

“Lowering standards to ensure certain technologies can meet a benchmark is the opposite of technological neutrality,” Gomez wrote. “Technological neutrality requires that we evaluate all technologies against the same standard and support the ones that perform best.”

She also cited an analysis last year from Penn State University’s X-Lab found that Starlink can support only 6.66 households per square mile before speeds drop below the 100/20Mbps mark. So far, Starlink has pulled off the incredible double feat of increasing its speeds as it adds millions of customers. But it’s done that in part by imposing massive surcharges in areas where it’s at capacity. At my Seattle address, there’s currently a $250 demand fee to get Starlink.

The gig-speed goal wasn’t tied to any specific outcomes, so it won’t change the internet options for Americans overnight. But by abolishing it, rural Americans could get left out of any future funding because they’ll technically already be covered by satellite.

“It really sets a bad precedent for any sort of future-looking deployment,” says Ali. “A lot of communities are going to get stuck with Starlink or Amazon Leo, but then they’re going to find the neighboring communities who got fiber are going to be surpassing them in terms of business opportunities and tax revenues.”

Were gigabit speeds a reasonable goal for the FCC?

In abolishing the gig-speed goal, the FCC report argues that it’s impossible to know whether consumers even want internet plans that fast.

There’s an argument to be made that gig speeds are overkill for most people, and I’ve made it plenty myself. You need only about 25Mbps to stream Netflix in 4K; what could possibly require 40 times that bandwidth?

But that’s starting to change. Data from the analytics company OpenVault found that 22% of fiber subscribers get speeds over 1,000Mbps, and 95% over 200Mbps. Traffic has grown every year since it started publishing data in 2019, and the upstream side in particular “accelerated at its fastest pace ever” in the second quarter this year – a trend OpenVault attributes to accelerated AI use.

If the speed is there, people will use it, says Mark Trudeau, Open Vault’s CEO. As cable ISPs have upgraded their networks over the years, usage has grown hand in hand.

“Every time they did that, you would see an explosion in usage, which just tells you that it’s the speed holding people back,” Trudeau told me.

A task using AI generates 450% more traffic than a human doing the same thing, according to Cisco. An inordinate amount of that traffic happens on the upstream side: 10% of AI flows carry more data upstream than downstream, compared with 0.5% for typical web traffic. AI applications also require latency below 30 milliseconds; Ookla’s data currently has Starlink at 39.

“We keep talking about needing to be competitive with China. And let me tell you that this 2026 report is not competitive with China,” Ali says. “We are not being ambitious anymore. We have just given up.”

No mention of affordability

It’s a truism in broadband circles that the reason most people don’t have an internet subscription is because they can’t afford it, not because they don’t have access.

A 2021 Pew Research Center survey found that one in five people who lacked home internet cited affordability as the main reason — the highest of any answer and three times the percentage who said service isn’t available. Another analysis of state broadband plans in 2021 found that all 50 states, plus Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico, identified affordability as the primary barrier to closing the digital divide.

Affordability is mentioned in some form 177 times in the 2024 FCC report; it’s used just 27 times in the 2026 iteration, primarily in references to the 2024 report and in Gomez’s statement.

“The FCC is abdicating responsibility,” Angela Siefer, executive director of the National Digital Inclusion Alliance, told me. “If we don’t talk about affordability, then we don’t have to address it.”

The FCC’s report argues that broadband prices are going down even as the overall cost of living increases. Broadband access advocates disagree. “The record makes clear that broadband providers themselves are concerned with and proactively addressing consumer costs,” the 2026 report says, citing the CTIA, a wireless trade group headed by Ajait Pai, the FCC chair during Trump’s first term.

They don't seem to understand that it's more than just about what the companies want, but it's also what is best for the residents of our country. Angela Siefer, executive director of the National Digital Inclusion Alliance

We’ve found that large ISPs like AT&T, Spectrum and Xfinity all currently offer discounted plans for low-income customers, but there’s no federal mandate that requires them to. States can pass their own legislation to support low-income internet access, but New York is the only one with a law on the books right now. (AT&T pulled its internet plans from New York entirely last year when the state passed the law, then reversed course last month.) The FCC is essentially saying that ISPs are addressing the affordability issue capably on their own.

But the FCC’s claim that broadband prices are actually going down isn’t backed up by the data. An analysis from the Benton Institute found that the average price of home internet grew by 4.8% in inflation-adjusted terms from 2024 to 2025. A 2025 CNET survey also found that 63% of Americans saw their internet prices increase in the previous year.

“The FCC is saying, ‘No, that’s not in our purview. Affordability doesn’t matter,’” Ali says.

The bottom line

An internet connection is often referred to as a “social determinant.” It significantly improves health outcomes for those who have it, increases employment rates in areas with good access and even boosts our psychological well-being. It wasn’t a stretch when the UN called it a matter of life or death in 2020, and it’s still true post-pandemic. While the new report cites legitimately encouraging signs of a narrowing digital divide, it also risks creating a permanent class of internet have-nots.

“It is consistent with this FCC,” Siefer says. “They don’t seem to understand that it’s more than just about what the companies want, but it’s also what is best for the residents of our country.”

Tech.title: Samsung’s Galaxy S26 FE Has Flagship Features, but It’s Harder to Call It a Bargain
Tech.content:
Samsung’s Galaxy S26 FE may be the company’s lower-cost flagship, but the phone’s getting nearly all of the same software features we first saw on the company’s more expensive phones. And it better be, as it’s also getting a $50 price bump over last year’s S25 FE, with this year’s phone starting at $700 for 128GB of storage and $800 for 256GB.

Announced Thursday, the S26 FE’s biggest hardware change is its 12-megapixel selfie camera. That’s the same megapixel count as last year’s selfie camera, but its new wider field of view allows you to photograph more of your surroundings.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE has a front-facing camera with a wider field of view than last year’s FE. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

But I’m most excited about all of the camera software features the phone is getting from Samsung’s more expensive devices, like the $900 Galaxy S26 and the $1,200 Galaxy Z Flip 8.

Super Steady Video with Horizontal Lock helps keep your video shooting stable even when your hands are shaking or you’re moving around while recording. My FanCam automatically frames specific subjects within a video. Samsung’s Audio Eraser removes background noise from videos you take on the FE and also supports Netflix and YouTube.

The My FanCam feature, first seen on Samsung’s folding phones, creates autoframing videos centered on a specific subject. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

All of these features are part of Android 17 and Samsung’s One UI 9 — and the S26 FE’s lower cost makes them more accessible than any of the other phones in the company’s lineup. Plus, the phone works with Samsung’s new Smart Switch app, making it easier to move your apps, data and texts over from an iPhone by connecting directly with iOS 26’s Transfer to Android feature.

I still need time to test the S26 FE after my brief hands-on time, but I do think it has a decent opportunity to stand out thanks to its software features and lower price — even if it’s certainly not cheap at $700 for 128GB. Compared with the $100 price increases to the base Galaxy S26, Google’s Pixel 11 and Motorola’s Razr, all prompted by rising memory costs, the S26 FE’s $50 price increase isn’t as harsh.

Upgrading to it from a Galaxy S23 FE or earlier will provide the most noticeable jump, thanks to its larger 6.7-inch display, Samsung’s year-old but still punchy Exynos 2500 processor and the aforementioned camera features. I do wish that display was brighter — the phone’s peak brightness of 1,900 nits should suit most environments, but other comparably priced phones like the Pixel 10A are hitting 3,000 nits.

Samsung’s 30x digital zoom on the Galaxy S26 FE has been improved over last year’s phone. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

I’m also concerned with the phone’s starting storage: 128GB could fill up fast if you’re using it for video. You’ll be better off with 256GB if you plan to use this phone long term. And despite all of these features and Samsung’s promise of seven years of software and security updates, the S26 FE is noticeably more expensive than similar phones like the $499 Google Pixel 10A and Apple’s $599 iPhone 17E.

There’s also a lot of hardware that didn’t change much over last year’s S25 FE. The S26 FE’s camera system includes a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 12-megapixel ultrawide camera and an 8-megapixel telephoto camera with a 3x optical zoom. Those specs didn’t change from the S25 FE, but Samsung improved the clarity on its 30x digital zoom and says that details should look sharper for images shot at 1x and 2x zoom.

The phone also has a 4,900-mAh battery with 45-watt wired charging and 15-watt wireless charging speeds. That’s also unchanged from last year, but in our 30-minute wired charging test, the S25 FE’s battery recharged from 0% to 69%. That’s very good, and hopefully the S26 FE pulls in a comparable result. Samsung will also sell cases for the S26 FE that add support for magnetic accessories like chargers and wallets.

The S26 FE will come in three colors: Pistachio (green), Blueberry (blue) and Graphite (dark gray). It goes on sale Sept. 3.

Tech.title: Apple Maps Has Ads Now. They Might Not Be Terrible, but You Can’t Turn Them Off
Tech.content:
Apple, as expected, has introduced s into its Maps navigation app, though you might not notice them at first.

The company confirmed in March it would bring ads to Maps and other services, including Mail, Wallet and Siri, as part of an Apple Business platform it launched in April. The ads are expected to roll out for Maps in the US and Canada before appearing in other regions.

The only way to tell that you’re seeing a paid  in Maps, at least for now, is a very small “ad” marker. Suggested locations appear alongside ones that aren’t marked as ads.

In CNET’s testing, ads in Maps only appeared next to some search results, and unlike what you’d see in Google Maps, there are so far no sponsored pins. Not every search result showed ads, even in highly populated areas like New York City and San Francisco. So at least on the initial rollout, users might not notice a major design change.

But many say this isn’t a good look for the tech giant. One headline on the popular site 9to5 Mac called the Maps ads “as bad as expected.” The other concern? Apple hasn’t introduced an opt-out toggle for ads, so you can’t even turn them off.

Apple customers on a subreddit devoted to the company were not happy about the ad rollout, with some arguing that paid iCloud account holders should not have to see ads. Others complained about advertising being introduced into the App Store, News and other applications. “This ad overload on everything is getting unbearable,” wrote MarkE2020.

Digital Noise on X predicted that this isn’t the end of Apple’s advertising push. “Music is next,” they wrote.

Apple ads and privacy

As part of the ad rollout, Apple posted about how it’s handling privacy: “Our advertising platform is designed to protect users’ information and give them control over how we use it for advertising.”

The post states that Apple Ads doesn’t buy or share personal information with other companies, doesn’t track users across apps and websites owned by other companies, and doesn’t serve ads to users registered as under 13 years old. Apple Pay transactions, Health app data and Home app data aren’t used to deliver ads.

A representative for Apple pointed CNET to its post about Maps ad privacy, but didn’t comment on whether information from other apps might be used or if it uses anonymized or aggregated user data for its ad business.

In a bid for transparency, Apple says that clicking the “ad” icon shows the information used to serve the ad.

Google vs. Apple navigation tools

At the time of its announcement, there was speculation about how closely Apple’s ad approach would resemble what is seen in Google Maps. Tim Berney, founder and CEO of Oklahoma City-based VI Marketing and Branding, told CNET that Apple is playing a different game and its Maps ads wouldn’t be identical to Google, which seems to be the case.

“Apple will likely take a more subtle, integrated approach,” Berney said. “Where Google Maps or Waze can feel more ad-driven, Apple will make it feel like a recommendation within the experience,” he said.

Some commentators online have speculated whether advertising in Apple Maps is purely a revenue play. But because the move is positioned as part of Apple’s small-business toolset, Berney said ads could be a way for Apple to lure business owners into its own ecosystem of apps and device management platforms. And that would, not coincidentally, put it in direct competition with Google.

Tech.title: Flock Has New Rules for Police Surveillance, but We Found Plenty of Loopholes
Tech.content:
Flock Safety has updated its police regulations, but gaps remain. SOPA Images/Contributor/Getty

As police officers continue to be arrested for misusing Flock surveillance — more than 70 now across the US and counting — Flock has announced new guidelines for how cops can use its ALPR and person detection cameras. However, I also spotted exceptions for nearly every change, making me wonder if this update really has teeth.

Flock Safety cameras can track license plates, car features and, on the right models, humans. They can also listen for disturbances such as gunshots. These camera networks have drawn scrutiny over their potential to enable casual surveillance of communities, as well as documented abuses, including police using the systems to monitor former partners or inventing pretexts for searches that result in information being shared with agencies such as ICE, as I detail in my full guide here. That’s led to protests, Flock contract cancellations and in some cases, cities blocking cameras by wrapping them in trash bags because Flock won’t take them down.

This is Flock’s largest response to these issues that I’ve seen to date, with a series of changes governing how police can use its surveillance systems. Most of these changes won’t be required until the end of the year, and some won’t affect existing contracts. Flock has also created exceptions to the new rules, leaving police and sheriff’s departments responsible for enforcing them while giving them mechanisms to continue using the cameras as they see fit.

According to a statement from the American Civil Liberties Union, Flock operates more than 120,000 automatic license plate readers in at least 6,000 cities.

“Flock has attempted this before, and the security measure failed because police were easily able to circumvent the system’s requirement that they input the purpose of their search,” the ACLU says. It encourages Flock to use an independent evaluator to oversee its regulations.

Representatives from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Workarounds abound for Flock’s new regulations

Flock is putting more responsibility on law enforcement, which is problematic. Justin Sullivan/Staff/Getty

Every new Flock rule announced seems to come with a caveat. One of the biggest changes is a reduction in the length of time Flock retains camera data — and, consequently, how long that data can be used for searches — from 30 days to seven. But Flock also says that “Existing customers will keep their current, democratically approved retention periods,” meaning most users won’t see the change for some time.

There’s also a new evidence mode that ignores the new retention period, allowing police to hold data indefinitely while pursuing active investigations of their choice.

Flock is also adding a feature called “offense filtering,” which can limit the specific Flock camera information that outside agencies have access to. This doesn’t change much because police departments can set their own limits when sharing data. As previously reported, police departments have already violated state laws by sharing information with ICE, the FBI and other agencies.

Another change makes Flock’s new audit assistance feature mandatory by 2027. Audit assistance flags suspicious camera use, such as repeatedly searching for the same license plate. It’s unclear how the system could differentiate between tracking a stolen car for a period of time and stalking someone. When it flags suspicious behavior, the audit assistance tool locks the user out of the system and requires an administrator review.

Another change requires users to enter a case code for every law enforcement search, in addition to the existing option to provide a reason for the search. There is an exception for emergency searches, which can still be conducted without that information but are flagged for administrator review.

So who will conduct these reviews? I asked Flock, but have not yet received a response. Based on the company’s documentation, the administrator appears to be the person designated under the agency’s contract with Flock — potentially a sheriff or police chief, including officials in positions where Flock cameras have previously been misused. That raises questions about whether the new safeguards provide meaningful independent oversight or simply place accountability back with the same agencies responsible for using the systems.

Changes like these place greater responsibility on departments to police their own use of the technology, while potentially limiting Flock Safety’s responsibility for how its surveillance systems are used. At the same time, Flock has built in several exceptions that allow departments to bypass the new requirements, with the conditions for those exceptions appearing to depend largely on individual agency policies rather than clear, uniform standards.

These rules apply only to law enforcement. Cities, neighborhoods and businesses that contract with Flock don’t need to follow the new regulations. Recent research has also found error rates ranging from 30% to 70% in Flock camera systems, raising broader questions about the reliability of this increasingly widespread surveillance technology.
